Okay, so after finally pouring 100 hours into this game in such a small time, I've decided to actually write a review on this game now. This review is rather lengthly. Sorry for being boring.
First off, the description for this game is outdated. It is not updated weekly, and has been 'abandoned' by the developers. There has not been an update since early 2013. Uber Entertainment said multiple times on their forums that if they have a small chance to revive the game, they will. For now, they shall focus on bigger projects. Let's hope they keep that promise. Now to the review.
After acquiring over 100 hours, I can say this game is
to get into. The game has been 'dead' or rather, has a low playerbase, and has done for about 2 years now. There are the occasional new players, but they don't stick around after what they find.
So, before you decide whether or not to play this game, or dive in blind and think 'Yeah! This'll be great and fun!' I'm going to post all the negatives so you don't have to experience them getting thrown at your face first hand.
As I have previously stated, the playerbase for this game is rather at a low. Due to this factor, you'll find most players you run into will be fully geared to the teeth (completely cosmetics..
Now, I'm not saying every experienced player in this game is a huge butt, but most of them are.
You'll find people will find ways to get angry in almost any situation. Whether their team is winning or losing. They'll find ways to insult you, no matter how. Be it your interests, name, how you type/play. You name it.
I'll probably go as far to say the community on this game is worse than Dota 2 or League of Legends.
Okay, so. Endorsements! I'll give you a quick run down on what they are.
In SMNC, you start off at level 0. Every 4 levels, you unlock a new Endorsement slot, getting up to 25 slots in total. You can go above the level 100 mark, but this will not unlock any endorsement slots.
Now, Endorsements themselves are small buffs with a positive advantage, and a negative disadvantage. These can be bought with coins, and are permenant, so you can buy and keep as many as you like. Mixing and matching different Endorsements at level 100 can help in giving you a huge advantage against players.
Now, here's the thing.
As I have previously explained, playerbase is rather low. So you'll be finding if you're a new player straight off the bat, you'll be running into all these powerful and experienced pros...
This feature alone is probably one of the single handed reasons along with the community that I
Now, this is what I feel to be one of the game's biggest flaws.
As explained above, most of the community is experienced players. Now, if you get new players joining, or less experienced ones, this won't change anything. Matchmaking is COMPLETELY random. It won't pair you up against players based on their level/skill/endorsement sets, it'll just drag and drop you into a list and not care.
As you may have guessed just by reading this...
This game is
hard to get into. To the point of masochism. It's easy to get stressed out over the various negatives at this game.
Now, you may be wondering... Why did I go through with it? Why did I continue to play, despite the horrible negatives?
I can't deny it. This game is special. Something is so fun and quirky about it.
Simply put, this game has an amazing atmosphere. A futuristic combat sport set in an arena, crowd going wild, announcers with funny voice lines, fitting situations well. What's not to love?
The Crowd is dynamic. Say if you were to make a kill, make something happen, or an event happens in the map, the crowd will respond. Being either cheers of joy, or jeers of disappoint.
The Announcers are fun to listen to. They sometimes share interesting stories, talk about what is happening in the match, and will respond to any kills/killstreaks/annihilator use. It all feels so real, and well done. The voice acting is great in this game. That is undeniable.
Though it may feel strange or possibly even unnatural at first, SMNC has a really great feel once you get the hang of it. A MOBA with Third Person Shooter hybrid elements? At the time, it was pretty new. Fresh, too. I'm not sure if there have been any since.
Each pro has three abilities, all bound to SHIFT, Q and E by default. It's simple, really. Each pro is easy to understand, and there are many to choose from.. Although there are no longer 'free pro rotations'. I've had fun playing a lot of them though!
All in all, I feel like this is one of those games where you have to 'play it yourself to understand' it.
I honestly don't think I really need much of a conclusion here, as most of it is explained above. I can give a bit of advice though.
And that concludes my Super Monday Night Combat Review! If you've read this far, I'm amazed. Thank you for reading, as I appreciate it. Sorry if I might've bored you though. Have fun playing!

This game has 20 levels, and I beat 10 at this point, so this is a "first impressions" sort of deal. I figure, it's got to be better than what the other guys wrote who spent 30 minutes in the game, right?
First off, this game has language settings for english, spanish, brazilian portugese and
- the latter is workable and fits the theme of the game well. Also, it's not lying when it boasts low minimum specs. To test it out, I dusted off my 8-year-old machine, and it works without a hitch; it's only a 141 MB download, so it is really quick to set up.
I mentioned you get 20 levels (plus random encounters) of small-arena turn-based strategic combat. At first you only get your brawlers (and a 5x5 playing field), but level 6 opens up archers, and wizards and healers come into the game at level 9 (you're up to 10x10 by level 10). The difficulty's pretty forgiving, and so far I've had no opportunity to set the difficulty level (I guess I could just select weaker units, or try to beat the game from start to finish without replaying levels), but for people who are newer to this genre the size of the battles and the difficulty will be just right.
As a "seasoned pro" in this genre, what attracts me is the silliness in the characters I'm playing; the battle system is decent, and the interface is slightly clunky, but workable once you have figured out that the fighter portraits have a) the damage display integrated as dark shadows, and b) tell you about everyone's special moves once you click on the portrait. So, yes, casual, I wasn't agonizing over strategy and don't expect I will be: I get to select up to 5 units, have a slightly wacky battle (for example, one enemy brawler *is* armed with a fish) (and you do get to select one of the enemy team for your side after each battle) that last a few minutes, and that's that.
For a bargain game, that's all I need. Recommended.
------
Notes:
The HP of your team can be qickly assessed by looking at the unit portraits in the bottom corners (click on them to see details and special moves) - a good solution since the status effect are already above the units' heads.
You can do two actions per unit per turn, but some of them have cooldowns (standard attack has 1 turn, so you get 1 attack per turn). Having to budget one action point for changing the direction a unit is facing is a tactical challenge -- you can move sideways and avoid it, and you can use the fact that the enemy has to turn as well to creep up on him from two sides. This is good!
AI was 10-15 seconds per turn at most on my slow machine, and it is slowed down mostly so you can see what is happening on the battlefield.
Combat maps are mostly square grids with some obstacles.
The visuals aren't much to look at, but I like the character designs. Story is neglible, but I wasn't buying this game for that - get Scott  Lynch's novels if you want to read excellent pirate fiction!

I played the Run for Rum for half an hour so, so far. I liked it.
The presentation of the game is good. I liked how the characters looked looked and moved.
As you can see you move units on a grid similar to a chess board. Sort of like in chess each piece moves a certain way. After each level you can add a fallen enemy to your team roster for use in future battles. Each character in your team can level up by gaining experience from each battle.
I played games like X-Com a lot. I like carefully making my moves and that sort of thing. This is that sort of strategy game. It is turn based. You can only have a limited capacity in your pool of characters so you basically have to take care of which class of characters you keep and commit to leveling up. Which I think is a cool mechanic. I also like the fact that you could tailor your team to a variety of different styles. You could have a team full of tanky melee dudes or ranged units or a mix and so on.
So yes I really liked the game so far. But from what I could tell I got around two thirds to half way through the world (to the extent that I could see that it existed) in the short time that I played. Hopefully the games not that short. Still it's a pretty good price.

I cannot recommend this game.  I will preface this review by stating that I could not get more than 30 minutes into it.  But what I did see in my time with this game is horrible enough to make me want to willingly walk away from this $5 purchase so as to not also waste more time than I already have.
Gameplay -  Clunky and unresponsive, you have to fight the UI.  There is no confirmation on your target if the enemies are bunched together, and the game provides no above head HP bar to your enemies for quick assessment of unit vitality.  Also the game play and movement are a chore, you get two actions per turn, one being a move and one an action, or two movements if you do not feel like taking an action.  the problem comes with the fact that turning your character is not included in movement and you must spend a second movement (thus ending your chance to attack) just to turn your character towards your enemy.   This is frustrating because it makes positioning and strategy not intuitive at all.
Game speed - REDICULOUSLY SLOW.  This further compounds your problems of the UI and Movement because every action takes a long time and AI decisions take a long time. (10-15 seconds per unit).
Combat Maps - Bland and very claustrophobic. I guess the claustrophobic aspect is a good thing considering how moving your character is such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Story - Seems to be written by a child who enjoys Adventure Time since they try to reference it at least twice in the first 10 minutes.   I couldnt stomach this game for more than 30min.  At $5 a little more effort should be put in.
Visuals - The art itself is ok, but there is little movement in the sprites, it makes the whole game feel wooden and unalive.
Conclusion -  I cannot see anyone truly liking this game unless they are hard up for a Turn-based RPG and have no other choice.  I cannot recommend this game.

Like many people, started playing this back in the early Xbox 360 days, and I find it still holds up as being an extremely enjoyable arcade game, and if you at all enjoy these types of games, I really can't recommend this enough.  Geometry Wars feels like an homage or love letter to classic games like Defender, Space Invaders, and Asteroid.
The gameplay is extremely fun and finds the right balance of casual gameplay and simultaneously being very challenging while even approaching unforgiving/punishing in how hard it can be.  It's hard to explain the experience of how playing this game can be relaxing and leasurely and, in the same session, become intense and anxiety-provoking, causing a release of adreniline in the player.  It's also difficult to explain how rewarding it is to feel yourself naturally responding to the challenges the game throws at you and finding yourself handling situations and reacting differently, getting through a point in the game that used to have you stuck.  The game itself is very well made and has a great feel to it, and the graphics are beautiful.
My only two minor quibbles with the Steam release are lack of an online Leaderboard (probably has something to do with Activision getting shutdown and that they just used Xbox Live's leaderboard functionality before) and that the Steam release doesn't have any of the unlockable achievements the Xbox 360 version had (how hard would it have been to include those?).
I payed $1.99 for this on Steam and would have actually paid more.  Again, I can't recommend it enough for a modern take on classic Arcade gameplay.

I throroughly enjoyed this game, even though it isn't complete as of writing this review. This game takes horror and video games and merges them together in a very creative and fun way. I love the horror genre, and this game takes that love to a new level. I've never played a game that has made the simple act of turning around one of the most frightening things you can do. Every corner your turn, every sound you hear, everything in this game isn't what it seems and it constantly throws new twists and turns that keep you on the edge of your seat.
What makes this game so engrossing for me is the premise - you are a man, a painter, who is going insane. Through the games progress you find out reasons as to why he may be going insane, but it's the insanity that really sticks out to me. The games level design perfectly depicts the absolute nightmare that this man is facing. His insanity is literally manifesting itself before his eyes. That's what makes this game so good in my opinion. It's how well the developers have depicted this feeling of losing your mind. Nothing is as it seems when exploring a room in this haunted house of madness.
For fans of horror and thriller I absolutely have to recommend this game. In my opinion this is a masterpiece, a game that MUST be played.

I guess I'm not the only one to have forgotten about this game. ACE really hasn't changed much since last year. The menus changed (for worse), there are some new characters and storyline stuff, and the tutorial is even less helpful, but the core game is unchanged. Network problems are undetectable, mostly because you will be placed in all bot matches within 60 seconds, and there is no one playing anymore. There's a bunch of skins and tournament stuff, but the game is pretty lifeless now.
Yes, the game is free, give it a shot if you are interested. Maybe you'll be one of the people that jumps in and gets hooked. I really don't expect most people to be like that. I found more players months ago, and I think server region splits really hurt. Even if you can find players, I don't feel the gameplay is satisfying enough. The arena feels huge and everything feels sluggish for a 5 minute match. Abilities will only be used a few times in a match, and it just doesn't feel fun. Those abilities are also still hard to land or identify, with particle overload making the game hard to understand as a viewer.
The developers work on growing a community, but I don't feel Early Access is being used to make the game more appealing. The old list of stretch goals has disappeared, and little issues remain. Updates have mostly been fixes and Ranked stuff, it seems like gameplay is not going to change. The tutorial uses a lot more words to teach less (it doesn't even teach passing now), and the menus are still unintuitive. Currency and progression systems are not explained clearly, and I still feel the power progression system is a mistake for a competitive game. There are only 2 supported resolution options listed, and graphics options are barren. Oh but they give away game currency and items, so usability issues disappear because free stuff. The Trello board is empty, the forums are full of "we appreciate the feedback, updates are coming", and the match lobby still doesn't have team-only chat.
The game won't be marketed until it is finished, and I expect there will be another overhaul to the menu and graphics, but the core issues won't change. It's not an engaging game for most players. With goalies, the game is a sluggish 2v2 centered around blocking everything. The VERY early alpha feeling still shows up, with even the tutorial throwing up error codes. It was interesting to see the process of development, but I can't see myself putting even dozens of hours into this game, or recommending it to friends.
Almost a year ago I felt the game wasn't ready, and hoped it would be stronger in 6 months. Dozens of small tournaments later, the game is still rightfully Early Access.

A testament to the ideal that graphics mean absolutely nothing in terms of a game's quality!
(Short Answer)
It's a solid game with brilliant mechanics and wonderful gameplay that completely overshadow its terrible graphics!
(Long Answer)
I'm a strong believer that, while amazing graphics can really help captivate players, they should ALWAYS be an afterthought to a game's mechanics. Mount & Blade: Warband only helps to reinforce my beliefs in such thinking. Graphically I'm sure that a 10 year old could come up with a more visually compelling game, however you'd be hard-pressed to find another game that matches this one in the solidity of its mechanics.
The fighting is complete chaos incarnate as anywhere from a handful to hundreds of soldiers on each side of the battlefield scurry about like chickens with their heads cut off. Yet somehow amidst all of the carnage, there is a beauty and complexity. The melee is simple enough to control, and the ranged weapons offer a fair way of taking out enemies with skilled/lucky shots.
Of course Mount & Blade isn't just about the fighting! There are equal amounts of strategy required for every bit of bloodshed. This aspect is simple enough when you travel alone or in a small contingent, but throw in a few dozens (or even hundreds) of soldiers at your beck and call and things begin to get more complicated. By the time your character leads a small army and a few larger settlements, every single move you make in the world can have serious repercussions. The age old question of, "Should I befriend him and marry his daughter, or murder him and pillage his kingdom?" comes into play more often than you'd think.
On a similar note, the AI show quite a bit of competency. The lower ranking soldiers might as well be armored gorillas, but train a few of them to higher ranks and you now have extremely capable officers in your army. The same can be said for your enemies as well as your subordinates, as enemy commanders are often quite challenging to defeat without the proper preparations. For NPCs, they make the interactions in the game truly political.
It wouldn't be entirely fair if I didn't talk about the graphics for at least a little bit, since there are plenty of you out there that graphics matter the most. The graphics honestly look like something out of the 90's, beloning on the N64 or PS1. Character customization is turned into something of a joke, trying to make the derpiest looking creature possible rather than something that could at least pass for human without a second glance. Despite the simplistic (if not atrocious) appearance of most characters and landscapes, the movement (especially the combat) is suprisingly fluent. You won't really have to worry about messing up in a vital shot of your bow/swing of your sword in combat.

HuniePop is pretty unabashedly a player simulator, you go through, you win over all these women, and...in a slightly strange note, you get to keep whatever panties they were wearing your first time with them, the girls are quite stereotypical for the most part, and if you expect to 100%, there will be much lying involved, and the yuri mode feels a little...well, underdeveloped, so why am I still suggesting it? Because despite being a cast of stereotypes, the girls are handled in a way that makes them endearing, and if you can look past the unrealisticness of it, the cgs are well drawn, the match-3 game play has a pretty fun difficulty curve, and the voice acting is pretty decent.
Now to complaints, when I mention that unrealisticness, I mean it, for example, Beli is 5ft11, she complains about only just having gotten her weight to 132 pounds, now, realistically at that height, her weight would have become a medical concern for being too /thin/. For the most part the cast is somewhat reasonable in their stats, if generally on the thin side of acceptable, and while I'll give the dev much credit for even including the yuri mode, by playing a woman, you also agree to have less cgs, as there are male-specific varients to each girls 4th cg, but no female specific to match it
Oh, and whatever you do, when you've got a girl in your room, try to avoid the left side of the date grid, the game has some odd detection issues on the edges and while usually they won't get in the way, you don't really have time to waste there in bedroom mode
Pros:
Cute girls to have your way with
Protagonist gender option
Actually fun puzzling
Great cgs, with a reasonable amount for each girl considering the goal of winning all of them
Unlockable dress up, with enough of a range for each girl to near-guarentee you can find the perfect look for them, or, if you like surprises, go ahead and set it to random once you've unlocked some things
Cons:
Has inaccuracies about the female body even beyond that which is typical of the genre
Mouse detection can get a little screwy towards the left and right edges of the screen
Could use a couple female protagonist specific cgs to match the male specific
All in all, if the dev announced a "HuniePop 2" I wouldn't hesitate to preorder, as for a first game, this is a damn good effort, and for the price it's definatly worth it, but...there is room for improvement and I'm strongly hoping the valentines update will tackle at least a few things

So...The Evil Within, a good old fashioned survival horror, right? Well...
First, let's start with price. It's £34.99 without a sale. I picked mine up for about £5 which was a good deal in my eyes. The fact this is £34.99 on the PC and the console versions are half that cheesed me off a little, but I can live with it.
Next let's talk about how it runs. With everything on full the game ran...awfully. I have a middle-of-the-range PC, nothing marvellous, but certainly not lacklustre, and only when I decreased the resolution and the graphic quality would the game even run smoothly, and even then every now and then I would get lag spikes and frame drops, especially in the rainy areas. If you have a low-end PC, proceed with caution.
Now let's get onto gameplay, which I did enjoy. The upgrade system is great, and I like how you can upgrade the stock of weapons. The lockers and keys are also fantastic. Some of the keys are very, VERY hard to find, and they are rewarding to find, as you can gain a respectable amount of upgrade material, ammunition or bolts for the crossbow. The shooting zombies aspect of the game is also a positive, the zombies are challenging in hordes, especially in the harder difficulties. The guns are satisfying to fire and the gore is enough to feel like you wounded one but not enough to turn it into a Jack the Ripper show. All in all, the gameplay is good for a survival horror genre.
Now, the bad things. The story is the first most obvious gripe. It's very disjoined and has nothing explaining why you blink from setting to setting by the villians will. The ending is a little crazy too, a little too crazy for my taste, and the main character has absolutely no morality nor compassion for his companions (literally his friend starts zombifying and he acts like it never happened). I feel the story could be a bit more meaty, but the gameplay is good enough to forgive it of it's horrendous plot.
And my final gripe is ammo. In my opinion, there is too much of it for the game to feel challenging. Pistol bullets are everywhere, and considering you can kill a zombie in one hit with it (shoot him in the leg and burn him with a match) they feel far too common to make you consider your ammo usage too much. Shotgun shells are also relatively common, and the shotgun feels like it should have far less ammo than it does. The only ammunition I felt was genuinely hard to get your hands on is Magnum ammunition, as the most you will ever find is what comes in the gun when you find it in the first place. I've seen lots of reviews saying the ammo is very scarce, but I found as long as you consider the game mechanics and how to take out enemies using them, there is more than enough to get through the game rather easily.
Overall, the game is a good solid game. The story could be alot better, and I feel the ammo could be a little more scarce, but it is a solid game. I would not reccomend getting it at full price, as £34.99 is too much for a game that is a year old. If you can pick it up on sale though, you will enjoy this thoroughly.

Has all standard features of F2P games: random bugs, mysterious glitches, a cash item shop. However, it seems like at least 90% of the game is indeed free, with the paid benefits essentially being more space, or buying special or better ships (not needed to participate in everything unless you feel the need to over power everything). The game is very accessible whether you're a power player or just want to casually blast space ships or funky aliens.
The story is pretty well written, if you're romulan or starfleet (got awkward with people not acting like you expect at the end). If you're klingon then it might feel awkward because it will seem like your character is acting like it's in starfleet at times, and not acting like a member of the klingon empire. I suspect the reason is they simply copied stuff from federation quests for klingons, but made no change to dialogue.
Character progression happens very quickly, and you will attain maximum level before finishing the storyline (plan carefully!), and any growth after that is much slower and based on a separate reputation system.
Space combat seemed pretty solid, depending on what you expect (pretty good if you expect original series star trek)
Ground combat will take some experimenting to decide how you want to control things
This is definitely worth playing through the story at least once, which could be about 100 hours, but after that it's basically how much you like space ships and star trek.

This games has incredible potential as an esport once dedicated servers are put in place and I highly suspect this to become one of the main esport games of the future with the right support. It's like a chopped-down NHL game with comic-book cyber-fi competitors.  And it's awesome.
The game's simply a blast.  Rather, it's fun in its own simplicity.  You control one of three team mates (decently effective bots or players take the other slots), and a disc-puck-thing is dropped between you and the opposing team (where it is placed, precisely, is determined by last goal scored).  The teams rush for it, and use their unique players' abilities to snatch, slow, and stop the puck-handler.  Goals can be made by either dunking/running for a touchdown (run the puck into the net), or by shooting it in.  The grab-release mechanic allows for quick execution of shots, and easy interceptions.
This is still a very young game, so as long as the core components aren't messed with and there is some major (and I mean major, as far as the magically-laggy home screen is concerned) MAJOR performance issues addressed.  Personally I feel this game should run just fine for everyone, but for some reason it hates my (more than adequate) graphics card, and pretty much any time I'm not actually in a game (where there are zero server side or client side latency issues), the graphics seem to progressively drop the framerate.  It almost feels like their fog effects don't ever fully dissipate and just stack invisible particles, or something.
tl;dr Try it!  It's free, and it's fun!

As someone who is particular about how they like their FPS games, any criticism I may have regarding this game is firmly ignored by my sheer adoration for the warhammer universe.
I spent weeks meticulously painting an army of dark elves and "cold ones", inspired by the persistent hate of my favourite literary warhammer anti-hero, Malus Darkblade. All of the admiration and joy (and satisfaction) I felt when reading about this universe and bringing the characters to life in small figurines which I promptly marched off to battle on a table-top terrain came back to me upon the installation and playing of this game for the very first time.
I did not care that the loot system was entirely up to chance, or that progress would be slow, or that the social aspect left much to be desired. No, I was immersed entirely in the surroundings, the scenery, and the banter between the characters. In this aspect, the game is excellent. The characters were not just mediums for us, the players, but actual characters in their own right. This was conveyed so well that I was convinced I was playing in one of my books.
The flavoure text in the loading screens was the cherry on top.  Seeing Khazalid terms written, and hearing them being used had me squeeking with delight.
No complaints, Farshark. Well done and thank you very much for bringing the imaginary friends of what used to be a very lonely girl to life in this game.

The Fall is a short Deus Ex game (maybe, 8 hrs for full exploration), indeed, it is just the first part of a game that terminates with a disappointing 'to be continued,' ending that will likely never be completed. It is also a mobile port and suffers various glitches and reductions due to that. In particular, some doors cannot be hacked because you can't zoom out far enough to see the full node set regardless of screen resolution, there is clipping through walls into empty space, and perhaps most importantly, you can't jump. They let you vault over some short obstacles but that's about it.
Despite these failing, though, the game plays like a Deus Ex game, and is an enjoyable short jaunt back into that IP. You have the standard assortment of upgradable implants taken directly from Human Revolution, allowing you to infiltrate through stealth and hacking, as well as do silent and deadly takedowns. You can also upgrade the number of energy cells you have, your strength, and so on. Plus there's a large assortment of weaponry, from pistols and assault rifles to EMP grenades and mines, and you can upgrade these as well.
One of the oddities of this game is that you can buy weaponry on the fly. Short an EMP grenade? Just buy one for 200 credits through the inventory interface. Short ammo? Same thing. You can even buy Praxis kits and new guns no matter where you are. Indeed, if you have enough credits, you can buy anything you want at any time. It's a bit of a cheat, but aside from EMP grenades, I found plenty of ammo and picked up the basic guns as I played. Praxis kits can be found too if you search around, so mostly, this buying through the inventory is a pretty minor reduction of the normal Deus Ex gaming experience. The other oddity is that enemy bodies disappear in about 15 seconds after a takedown, so there is no need to clean up after yourself. Guards will still react if they see a fallen comrade before it dissolves but no guards will ever be awoken from a silent takedown here. Again, another reduction from the usual Deus Ex experience, but one that doesn't really change things a whole lot.
Overall, as long as you're willing to accept that this is a diminished Deus Ex experience, it still plays like a Deus Ex game, and can give you a day's enjoyment at a very cheap price.
Lastly, the story is a bit thin but enough, the graphics are acceptable, and I didn't encounter any crashes, lockups or game-breaking problems. This is with a modest rig running Win7 with an Intel i7 @3.47 GHz, 16 GB RAM, and an Nvidia 970.

At first I just played multiplayer against other people. It was fun to go one on one with another player and see who was the best at fighting with a sword - there is quite a big skill gap between the best and the worst. A bow and arrow was also fun to use.
I then started a singleplayer campaign which I found was even better. I started out with a character levelling up his skills to be an all-rounder but I wasn't very successful, and my army stayed small because I kept losing battles.
After having learnt more about the game I made a new character, levelled up certain skills for myself so that I could rely on my companions to offer party skills - a better use of skill points. Different companions like and dislike each other, so I had to find a group of companions which all liked each other if I didn't want them to leave my army. I earnt money by trading which involved learning different locations where I could buy cheap items, and where I could sell them at a big profit. When I came across a tournament in a city I would bet all on myself and earnt some money through winning those. Meanwhile I've been collecting new recruits from different towns and levelling them up, making my army stronger.
As well as this, there are a lot of full game overhaul mods which I've just started trying out. These change the whole map, the factions/characters/warrior types and the weapons, armor and other purchasable items.
There are a lot of things you can do in this game - these are just some of them. Edited for badge

Its ok. The game stopped being scary after about the 2nd chapter once you figure out the nuances of the combat system. I quickly found out that if greeted with a room full of baddies, i dont need to run, i can shoot a flash arrow and stealth kill most of them, then burn the bodies to kill the rest in an aoe. The game is balanced around the amount of bullets it gives you, so it becomes extremely easy to horde when the two things you have a ridiculous supply of (trap parts and matches) provide you with endless strings of one hit kills.  Since combat was so easy it really left no sense of fear. The things i became scared of most in this game were the traps.  One wrong move with those things and youre dead.  I felt that i moved slower because of the traps, and they artificially padded the games length, since they were the only reason i had to take caution when playing. The game also overstayed its welcome in my opinion. It took about 17 hours to tell a very interesting story, but poorly. You will NOT understand the story if you only watch the cutscenes. You absolutely need to read the documents that you find. I consider this a con, because in the older survival horror games this is modeled after, there was a main story, the one you were playing, and then documents were a ton of back and side stories. If you didnt want to, you didnt have to read a thing and the story would still make sense. If you did, it just made it that much more engrossing. Making it a necessity, once again, just slows things down for me.  If this game was condensed to about 8 hours and the story wasnt so random it'd be a classic. Instead, its just a fun little horror themed shooter. I say buy it on sale. I saw a review say that this is what RE4 fans wanted RE5 to be, and thats exactly what it is.

I appreciate what this game sets out to accomplish, the setting and scope of Heroes and Generals is one I would like to see more of in video games. I also appreciate that the developers made this title free. However, I find that the execution of the game is flawed at best, and downright abysmal at worst.
Tier 1, the kidde pool of matchmaking, was increadibly fun for me. Prior to reaching rank five on any one of your characters, you are restricted to only skirmish maps, and can only meet other rank >5 characters on the battle field. These infantry engagements were quite plesant, if repetetive, and made me really excited for the following content. The highlight of this period was when I had purchased a jeep and an smg on my main character, and would roll up on cap points like a stormtrooper.
Tier 2 was exactly the opposite of what I expected, it is a festering cesspit of rage and one sided matchups, as you slowly work your way up to the gear that you want, and even slower to the money necessary to purchase it. I have hated almost every single tier 2 battle that I have participated in, and now that one of my characters is past rank 5, all of my characters get tier 2 matchmaking. In this tier you will find yourself up against tanks that you can not hurt as infantry, unless you have explicitly purchased equipment to do so. Aircraft which will bomb and shoot you into oblivion without repercussion because AA emplacements are laughable. And, enemy infantry which will have better equipment than you, and will come out on top in every fair engagement that you find yourself in. This is not helped by the lack of any form of communication apart from text chat, which is not adequate for the type of teamwork necessary to deal with opponents, and whisling.
This game's presentation is lazy, the menus and out of game UI are such an eyesore that I am suprised that this hasn't been something brought up before, and the matchmaker is either awful or the number of registered players is nowhere near the number of active players. Yet Heroes and Generals unapologetically asks for your money after each match, showing you what you could get if you spend a little money to buy a vetran membership all the while tauting you with a pittance of free premium currency every day. Just to try and get you to put a little money into the game to actually be able to use the gold that you have gotten.
This game doesn't look to me like an Early Access title, it looks like a pre-alpha build, but the developers have the gall to ask you with their hands out for your hard earned money none the less. Don't give them the satisfaction of an additional registered user until something is fixed, no matter how fun it is to combat roll off of a bike and panzer faust an unsuspecting sniper.

My favourite survival horror game ever. Sure the story has some weird moments, but it overall holds together really well.

It's also incredibly violent, and Tango Gameworks have gone to a lot of trouble to provide a AAA experience. They really captured the essence of horror and anyone who thinks otherwise clearly hasn't seen enough oldschool scary movies.
It's also quite a long game. Took me 15 hours to beat the main story and there's New Game+ and a couple other interesting modes to complete. There's definitely a lot of replay value to unlock all of the hidden secrets/collectibles.
I'd definitely recommend getting The Evil Within if you're a fan of horror in general. It's a challenging game, but very easy to become immersed in. Most importantly, it's fun and quite creepy. Definitely worth playing, plus the DLCs are  absolutely amazing.

This game is hard.
And when I say hard, I don't mean Metro 2033 (non-Redux) hard, no, no.  I mean You Can't Run Properly, Hide Properly, Shoot Properly, or Fight Properly kind of hard.
Now, I'm a fan of survival horror: Resident Evil 1, 2, 3 and Silent Hill 2 being among my favorite games of all time.  Those were fun.
The Evil Within isn't fun.  It's tedious.  Tedious and unscary -- as if in the mind of the people who made it, that was somehow going to make it frightening.  It isn't frightening.  At all.  It is gross, yes.  The graphics convey a good atmosphere... but that all becomes meaningless as the game controls and gameplay will destroy any sense of foreboding the game could offer.
Now, I don't regret buying the game as I got it on sale and I was curious enough to see what it was about.  I'm glad I did, too.  But I can't recommend it to anyone except maybe to die hard horror fans who want to have a look at it and see.  But then again, those folks ought to be playing Outlast (good game!) if they haven't already instead of this.

There are 15 chapters, so there is no way you can play this in one sitting. Plus upgrade keep you coming back for more, even after you beat the first playthrough. In addition, you unlock a more challenging difficulty after you beat the game for the first time, so the replayability is high, and that is key for any singleplayer expeirence. This game does superb in atmosphere, and it spaces out it's jump scares enough so that you are not on the edge 24/7, but you still don't feel safe. This is a casual survival game. The game has a good core: the genetic mechanics are well-developed, but the gameplay built around it is lacking content both in breadth and depth. You can only play the 'nicheling', the cutesy creature you see in the game's screenshots; you can make your nicheling be more aquatic, more of a hunter or more of a prey that gathers fruit and nuts, but you will never be at the top of the food chain or sustain your entire colony without berries, fish or nuts. Food doesn't spoil, it is infinite, and stored everywhere at the same time. You don't have hitpoints, you have lifespan, and strikes reduce it. The mechanics are still too simple.
If you are very curious about the setting, do try the game, but if you don't get very much into it within the first 2 hours, refund it; you saw everything you needed to see in those two hours.

TL:DR: at the end as well as EDITs about my experience playing this. Starts off as a recommended game and moves towards the opposite.
I would say this game is a diamond in the rough but its not exactly a diamond. Its really rough around the edges and its clunky. But its enjoyable and captures some of the STALKER/Metro vibe that I personally have been looking for. I played this game back before it was added to steam I have made a total of 4 characters in my time and each time I ended up abandoning them because I had no idea what to do until recently when I found a clan. FIND A CLAN it will make your life easier and you will enjoy the game with the help.
Lets start with the veggies first:
Okay english translations - its more or less accurate to what you actually have to do but the dialog is laughable sometimes.
Large RU population - I play on the NA server and I would say about half of the population doesnt speak english.
Clunky combat and movement - you can move past it once you get used to it but it can be annoying at first.
Poorly optomized - Im running a hex core i7 and a 660 ti and on medium settings I get 70 fps with drops to 30 fps and when memory leaks happen which they happen a lot I get forced to sit around 20-30 frams. But a simple relaunch fixes it.
Not Graphically impressive - not much to say here.
Not Newbie Friendly - The game can be hard to understand and doesnt do a good job of pointing you in the right direction. Dont epext it to theme park you like WoW. A lot of players, myself included, didnt have an idea what to do when they hit the first big zone.
On to the desert:
Interesting PvP system - There is a flagging system in the game so its managable to not have to worry about other players. But there are areas that flag you/force you into pvp which you need to watch out for. There is a wealth system that means if you collect enough value on your person whether its in ammo, mutant parts, artifacts, or junk you eventually are forced to flag. Thankfully when you die you can get back up or spawn back to a safe zone. Going to the same zone has a change to drop some of your loot. But never your guns/armor.
Vibe - It has that STALKER/Metro vibe where the world is dangerous and even in high end armor the world is a dangerous place. No dying is not linked to your gear or level but the gear can come in handy. It mostly comes from experience. Much like it is supposed to in the STALKER series.
Why would I suggest this game to anyone? Because its a small download and its free. And due to the atmostphere I would suggest any Metro or STALKER player out there at least give it a try.
TL;DR: Its clunky, tough, russian, and sometimes downright frustrating. But its fun, free, small to download, and it scratches that STALKER itch. If you give a try hit up the steam forums to see if you can find a clan to join. It helps a lot.
EDIT 7/22/2015 : also, you are basically screwed if you ever need support. So far half the responses for my support tickets in the english support area have been in russian. One ticket has been in for almost a week now and the other for a day or two. They give a response very quickly but actually solving the problem they seem to be inadept at. So god help you if you need support

Very few games have left me with as many conflicted feeling as The Evil Within. It swings from being a genuinely scary game to feeling like a decent-if-forgettable RE4/5 clone and back again. There are hurdles to jump over in understanding how the gameplay works before you can get into it and then the game never leverages the strengths of that system. There's a creepy element of psychological torment that pervades the game and story, but when it pokes it's head through the story is, quite frankly, kinda stupid.
The gameplay takes the Resident Evil 4 route, but where Leon Kennedy was a badass and thoroughly capable of handling any situation Sebastian Castellanos is a wuss who's not particularly great with a weapon and whose physical attacks are hit an enemy like a weak gust of wind. You'll quickly find that open combat is a terrible option as enemies are tough and even headshots that blast away large portions of their skull only seem to moderately annoy them. It's easy to burn half your ammo on one enemy. While it's not particularly scary the early sections are like a playground where you slowly stalk enemies and carefully choose your point of attack.
Then you find out the game has an upgrade system. Suddenly you're given a lot of options for improving you physical prowess and the usefullness of your weapons (of which you'll get a small arsenal of) The game begins to force you into open combat more often and it become obvious that ammo conservation isn't important because the game is regulating how much ammo is dropped by enemies and from crates. I just blasted my way through the stealth sections at the end because they're just set in boring corridors that are a pain to navigate carefully though and there's not particular penalty for going rambo through it.
What really saves the game is the middle third of the game which slows down the pace and uses the game's atmoshpere to good effect. You'll traverse torture chambers, crypts, a deserted mansion, and caverns and that pacing, sound design, and enemies just feel right. I constantly felt on the edge of my seat waiting for something horrible to happen.
Then you hit the city and the game loses momentum through to the end. It lacks both the atmosphere of the middle third and the well designed stealth sections of the first third. You're too well equipped and upgraded for the action sequences to feel like a desperate fight for your life or the stealth sections to feel imposing. The big bosses are silly rather than imposing. It's not bad, but it's not the type of horror game that The Evil Within should have been.
If you're a fan of horror games it's worth it to pick up on a sale because when it works The Evil Within works really well and when it fails it's never bad, it's just disappointing. Despite everything I still liked The Evil Within even if I wanted it to be so much more than it was.
Some further thoughts if you're still reading.
- The game is very linear and features little exploration. The idea was to constantly warp you around and keep your bearings off, but I don't think it worked that well although I respect the theory behind it. Interestingly one of the best and creepiest sections is set in a mansion that you have to explore.
- Has a Dark Souls thing going on graphically where most of the architecture of the buildings looks great, but any thing natural looks like doo-doo. There's a part where you walk through a field of sunflowers and the texture on the ground looks like it was ripped from an N64 game.
- Jennifer Carpenter (who played Debra on Dexter) gives one of the most bored and unenthusiastic voice acting performances you'll ever hear in a game. Fortunately she only gets a handful of lines.
- I really like what they did with the RE style save room by making you question the safety that it provides you.
- Textures are constantly loading slowly. Scenes cut to aother angle of things that don't have textures loaded. At one point a gate drops revealing a boss monster whose textures pop onto him a second later.
- (SPOILER ALERT) If you want to be overly analytical about things you could certainly draw parallels between Ruvik's story and the nature of game development when surrounded by corporate culture. How he both has control of his creation taken away from him while simultaneously being trapped by it. As a game developer Shinjo Mikami is both typecast as "The Horror Guy" as well as having a lack of ownership over Resident Evil and being forced to watch it taken in directions he may never have intended. Ultimately, as this is Mikami's last game in the Director's seat (allegedly) Ruvik is ultimately looking for escape (and to try and scare the out of Sebastian/The Player along the way.
But that may just be me looking too deeply into things , 11/10 .

My Review:
At first the plot seems simple, and perhaps knowingly reminiscent of the opening of Resident Evil. Three cops answer a distress call at a lunatic asylum in the middle of a city, and find it’s been torn apart by dark forces. Separated from his colleagues, down-at-heel detective, Sebastian Castellanos, finds himself in a desperate battle to survive. We won’t tell you more for fear of spoiling The Evil Within’s many curveballs, but it soon becomes clear that not all is what it seems.
The action spans two distinct worlds, areas blur or warp suddenly from one to another, and the scenarios seem to reflect shifts in psychological state as much as any conventional chain of cause and effect.
Along the way we get a tour of horror idioms, ranging from slasher movies and the torture porn of Saw to the creepy hospital corridors and rusting barbed wire of Silent Hill. Nor is Mikami averse to rifling through his own back catalogue. The over-the-shoulder viewpoint and general controls ape Resident Evil 5 – basically Resident Evil 4 but with movement while you're shooting.
verdict:
The Evil Within is almost the game that Resident Evil fans have been waiting for, but almost still isn’t close enough. For all its great moments – moments where it’s genuinely terrifying and utterly compelling – there are too many sections where it’s unbearably frustrating, repetitive or held back by technical issues and poor, dated games design. It might win a cult following with hardcore fans of survival horror, but it’s just too sporadic in its brilliance to be anything more than another near-miss.
Pros:
Classic survival horror gameplay
Can be very scary and unsettling
Fractured narrative keeps you on edge
Cons:
Hideously frustrating
Poor performances and patchy visuals
Assorted technical issues

Having initially played it way back for a couple of hours and not having given it a fair shake, I revisited this game and must say that it is really quite enjoyable.
Star Trek is about two things: space battles and away missions on planets. The default keybinds are a bit awkward but, obviously, these can be changed to your liking.
The visuals are very good. As with all games, a better computer will be able to deliver better graphics. Even on the lowest setting, the visuals are better than WoW. The game delivers exactly what it promises - a Star Trek MMO. You fly around, blow up Klingons, and shoot nasty aliens on planets. As stated, it is F2P so you can download it, try it, and if you don't like it all that much, you don't have to buy a sub for it. So you really can't go wrong.

I'm usually not a fan of Early Access titles, but Layers of Fear is one of the major exceptions. Don't go in expecting a survival horror game like Alien Isolation, Outlast, The Evil Within or even Soma. Because you'll be disappointed. What you do get is a walking simulator akin to Dear Esther with the odd puzzle element and jump scares thrown in. If you've played (or seen footage of people playing) P.T. you'll have a good idea of what to expect. The story reminds me of the gothic horror novels by Edgar Allen Poe and the game does a good job of invoking a feeling of uneasiness. You're made very aware that something terrible has happened to the main character and that this event (or series of events) has made him quite mad. And you get to experience his hallucinations first hand. The back story is slowly revealed through sketches, letters, notes and objects that you find. The game is also incredibly detailed with very realistic textures and a lot of time is spent making the house look and feel like a real house that is being lived in. One of the things that has made a positive impression is the fact that the disturbing events that take place aren't being recycled but the developers have managed to keep coming up with new ways to confuse and scare the player.
Be very aware that the game is not complete. Much of the plot is not revealed in order to leave the current owners of the game with new information to find once the complete version arrives. The five chapters that are available right now took me about 3,5 hrs to finish so the complete game should be 4 to 5 hrs long.

Saw this advertised on the main store page, and I must admit the description didn’t really sell it to me, but the overwhelmingly positive reviews on Steam did.
Layers of Fears, still in early access, but soon to be retail, sees you in the shoes of an, as yet unknown, artist, who is clearly in a dark place and trying to get out.
The game charts his journey, possibly through his own mind, of the traumas and horrors that plague him, and make him face his demons.
In terms of the quality of the game, it really is up there with the very best psychological horror games out there. Its atmosphere is brooding, foreboding, intense, and superb at eating away at you – you can actually ‘feel’ the horror around you, as opposed to just seeing it.
It does have a jumpscare or two for the fans of ‘boo’ moments, and they’re reasonably effective, but these aren’t its strength – this game excels in a slow, disturbing and deeply unsettling journey through a broken man’s mind where nothing makes sense.
It is a psychological horror which recaptures the kind of fear we had at the original Slender games, but which adds so much more without being anything like those kind of games.
It was just nice to play a horror game I didn’t feel I’d seen all before, and which managed to work on every level.
Can’t wait to see the final game when it’s released.
Update: This game, months on, still hasn't had the 'judderwatch' problem fixed. The game's quality is undeniable, but the inability have a smooth experience is a total game-breaker for those who experience it.

I thoroughly enjoy this as a game, and in my opinion I got my money's worth for it. It's enjoyable, and I put entirely too much time into it and realised far too often that it was suddenly 2am when I had to be awake for something in five hours.
I have to stress that this is a casual game. There's no real hard-core survival mechanics built into it, it's not "if you don't do everything EXACTLY CORRECT your chances to live are slim". You can build up food very quickly if you gene right for it, and I often had populations of creatures on an island in the 30-60 range. Once you have the set-up for an island and the genes unlocked, surviving is rather simple (barring some of the harder islands). If you're looking for something with a lot of challenge consistently through the game, this is probably not for you.
That said, the learning curve can be high if you decide to start on a medium or higher island - without the genes you normally need to survive those islands, you can very, very easily end up going extinct.
The real draw is the genetics manipulation. I liken this game to a builder in that aspect - I'm not trying to survive (that's an initial goal that becomes less important the more you're succeeding), I'm trying to create a creature that looks a certain way or is prepared for a certain kind of island. Or I'm just breeding in random genes to see what the resulting creature ends up looking like! It's all about what you want to do.
Which is my next point: there isn't really a 'goal' in Niche. The story mode gives you an option to try and strive for, as you start as Adam who's been taken from his home and you can try and get your creatures to get back there over the generations. But the game doesn't end there, and you don't even have to do it if you don't want to. Niche is a game that lets you decide what you want to do. It's open-ended, and that's usually the reason so many of the major Let's Players of this game are storytellers - they're creating more depth to a game that's allowing for inspiration to be taken and run with into whatever you want it to. You can make it easier or harder on yourself with your own rules - think Pokemon Nuzlock challenges. You can do similar challenges here.
There are some issues that still need resolving, I won't pretend that there isn't. The tutorial isn't that great, it's extremely basic and doesn't go into the genetics, which are the core of the game. There are bugs here and there, but to the dev team's credit, they're doing their best to try and fix them as they show up. Achievements in particular are bugged as of my posting this. The challenge of the game does diminish as you get better genes, and it turns from survival into whatever you want to do, which isn't bad but having something that remains tricky to deal with throughout the game would be nice. The music is also very repetitive the longer you spend on an island. I don't dislike it, but when I can spend 3-5 hours session on one island, it's incredibly boring after the first half hour.
All in all, it's a very enjoyable game in my opinion, and I whole-heartedly recommend it.

You find yourself crouching behind a tree, trying to see what's on the other side without being seen yourself.
You finally muster the courage to emerge from your hiding place to take a shot at the mutant standing 5 yards away. Suddenly you find yourself squinting at the screen. What's that thing on the ground off to the left?  Is that what you think it is?
YES. IT'S AN ARTIFACT. Change of plans. The value of that Artifact dwarfs the value of some mere mutant's pelt.
You holster your weapon and equip your Magnetic Grip Device.  You toss a rock in the general direction of the Artifact to check for deadly anomalies. You'd been fooled before and this time you know the drill. No unusual sounds or lights emerging from the ground where the rock was thrown. All clear.
By this time the mutant has wandered away to haunt some other sector of wasteland, uninterested in your rock-throwing antics. You're free to go collect your bounty in peace.
You sprint towards your newly found treasure, not because speed is necessary at the moment, but simply because you've understandably acquired a sort of paranoia that only surviving in a post-apocalyptic world can produce. You know running isn't the safest move right now, but you get the feeling that if you don't hurry and grab your Artifact, you'll somehow lose your chance.
BIG mistake.
You find yourself in a strange orange cloud of dust. Your legs don't seem to work correctly anymore. You double over in pain, your lungs full of what feels like cement... living cement.
It is then that you remember: You never equipped your Air Filtration Mask. You knew that going to Vesuvius meant an inevitable run-in with air-born toxins, but the only PPE mask you had at the time was so dumb looking! No one would talk to a nooby looking player wearing that thing! Alas, your pride has finally allied with the reaper. The first effects of Sporosis have set in, and it's second deadly stage is closing in fast.
With the Artifact only a few feet away, you know that there's a good chance you can at least pick up your prize before surrendering completely to Sporosis, or anything that happens to take advantage of your weakened state. You know that upon dying, it will be up to The Fates to decide weather or not you will be allowed to keep your valued Artifact. The Fates can be cruel, but it's worth the gamble.
Stumbling and wheezing in agony, you soldier on towards your goal. Nothing else matters now; not the quest to find Vlad's son, not that new assault rifle you've been saving Ruples to buy, not the mysterious disappearance of those helicopters. This is all that matters: You must, nay, you WILL acquire your intended target.
You're close now. So close you can make out the beautiful patterns and strange designs forged on the Artifact's multifaceted surface. Forged by what, you do not know. By some force of nature, some unearthly power, some will of pure evil, or will of pure good? Does it matter?
Out of the corner of your eye you see leaves and other forest debris pick themselves up as if of their own volition. They twirl and spin, faster and faster. Soon you find yourself no longer looking upon a graceful ballet of nature, but instead you find yourself gazing at a terrifying Vortex anomaly. It moves in unnatural patterns as if pacing, hunting it's prey. To your dismay it has decided to move in your direction.
A few more steps and you will have the coveted Artifact in your hands.
The pain hits you again. Not now. Why now? Your chest heaving, your lungs struggling to take in the next breath, you double over again. Movement is now nearly impossible for you, and moving faster than a Vortex anomaly is out of the question. The swirling mass of radioactivity intercepts your movement towards the Artifact with ease, and you feel yourself being pulled towards it's center. You are thrust skyward and for a moment you get the feeling that it's safer up here than on the ground. Your false sense of security is short-lived, however.
After being carried several yards away from your flight's genesis, you are hurled to the ground with what feels like an unfair amount of gravity assisting your trajectory. You hear as much as feel the crunch of bones being devastated by the force of your landing.
You are only allowed a few milliseconds of time lying on the ground before feeling an intense heat coming from underneath you. You've been thrown into a fire anomaly. The air around you seems to explode and you find yourself engulfed in hellish flame. Barely holding on to sanity, acting purely on animal instinct you roll to one side to escape the inferno.
Everything is pure white. A rush of cold air brushes your skin. You feel like you're flying again. Not like the last time, but faster. You feel as if your body is hurtling through time and space. You know this feeling; you've felt it many times before: A teleportation anomaly.
The rush is gone. The warmth of Vesuvius's volcanic region is back. The pure white is gone. The blood red sky of this time and this space is back, and with it the pain. Though discombobulated and mangled by the events of the last few moments, you manage lift your head from the ground and get your bearings. That's when you see it. The most beautiful thing you've ever seen. THE ARTIFACT! The teleportation anomaly brought you right back to being practically on top of the Artifact. With your last ounce of energy, ignoring the pain, you rise to your feet. It's time to claim your well deserved reward.
[*CRACK*]
You hear the unmistakable sound of an silenced sniper rifle. You don't have much time to interpret it's meaning though, because to recall such things requires a fully intact brain and a fully intact skull to protect said brain.

My Review:
At first the plot seems simple, and perhaps knowingly reminiscent of the opening of Resident Evil. Three cops answer a distress call at a lunatic asylum in the middle of a city, and find it’s been torn apart by dark forces. Separated from his colleagues, down-at-heel detective, Sebastian Castellanos, finds himself in a desperate battle to survive. We won’t tell you more for fear of spoiling The Evil Within’s many curveballs, but it soon becomes clear that not all is what it seems.
The action spans two distinct worlds, areas blur or warp suddenly from one to another, and the scenarios seem to reflect shifts in psychological state as much as any conventional chain of cause and effect.
Along the way we get a tour of horror idioms, ranging from slasher movies and the torture porn of Saw to the creepy hospital corridors and rusting barbed wire of Silent Hill. Nor is Mikami averse to rifling through his own back catalogue. The over-the-shoulder viewpoint and general controls ape Resident Evil 5 – basically Resident Evil 4 but with movement while you're shooting.
verdict:
The Evil Within is almost the game that Resident Evil fans have been waiting for, but almost still isn’t close enough. For all its great moments – moments where it’s genuinely terrifying and utterly compelling – there are too many sections where it’s unbearably frustrating, repetitive or held back by technical issues and poor, dated games design. It might win a cult following with hardcore fans of survival horror, but it’s just too sporadic in its brilliance to be anything more than another near-miss.
Pros:
Classic survival horror gameplay
Can be very scary and unsettling
Fractured narrative keeps you on edge
Cons:
Hideously frustrating
Poor performances and patchy visuals
Assorted technical issues

I generally don't play horror games, or at least action-horror games like this, such as Resident Evil. Having said that, I am really enjoying this. It's a solid product, and I feel like it has elements of Outlast, The Last of Us and Resident Evil. It isn't quite pure horror survival akin to games like Outlast or Amnesia, as you can fight back to a limited extent (you're no Rambo though, don't go in guns blazing all the time)
With fifteen chapters and extra DLC, it'll keep you going for a while. The horror elements stem from atmosphere/tension, rather than outright jumpscares (there are a few scattered around though) and it certainly made me feel on edge at times. It has to be pointed out that the main character is hilariously dumb, both emotionally and by an intelligence standpoint. The story I find is decent, I like both the antagonist Ruvik and Sebasatian, despite his...robotic tendencies. Combat is tight, the puzzles are enjoyable and the bosses, whilst a bit frustrating (Amalgam Alpha can go ♥♥♥♥ itself) they're always fun to kill.
Overall I think it's a great game, not quite sure why it gets so much hate, but I enjoyed it nonetheless. If you enjoy Resident Evil you'd enjoy this. Just bear in mind it isn't pure survival horror as there are guns, and you can fight back.

I'm writing this review after playing through this game and both The Assignment and The Consequence DLC, but this writing focuses on the actualy main game. So my god, where to start.
So the game starts off as a mess. You're paying as Sebastian Castellanos, a police detective who is trapped in a living nightmare with his crew, two detectives, Josheph Oda and Juli Kidman. He wants to get out, that's the story for the most part. Or well it's not, but it's not very developed in the main game. You get the idea that there is something very shady about all of this (which is pretty obvious when you face mutants and see gore everywhere but whatever), but ultimately your only goal is trying to save who you can and surive.
Therefore, the story is all over the place. Holes, no real explanation, but it works. It's mysterious and tense, with the 15 hours game time that's pretty impressive. I don't really want to spoil anything, but if you like datamining, reading documents, trying to figure out what's going on then this game is surely going to appeal to you. The DLCs answers some big questions, just saying.
The gameplay oh boy. That's the biggest problem with this game. Not that it's bad, it's just suffering from the fact that it wants to be everything. Even though I think it does everything kind of well, except melee combat the mixture of everything takes it's toll. I guess it wants to be more of a shooter, but then there are stealth parts, running away (which is optional, but advisable for first playthrough) too so really, I have no idea. The shooting is good, sneaking around is fine, running away as a wimp is alright. But you mostly feel like that the game has no idea what to do with itself.
And that's issue, this game tries to appeal to both Silent Hill fans and Resident Evil fans by getting the ♥♥♥♥ed up disturbing nature of Silent Hill and the gameplay from Resident Evil with some other elements, but it fails riding both horses, but then it kinda pushes itself back between the two and still succeeds.
I have no idea how it works, I should hate this game, but I still love it. Waiting for the sequels, and if you have serious doubts about the story, play the first two DLC. I hope they solve the identity crisis and make it so that it has a unique gameplay. Otherwise, this game is great, if you love old Silent Hill and Resident Evil just buy it.

Imagine Resident Evil 4. Remove most of the ammo and make the controls wildely erratic and you've basically got Evil Within. This game is so similar to RE4 at points. It almost likely they altered Leon a little bit and threw in some new set pieces and decided they were done. The only difference is, the hitbox mechanics of this game are so incredibly bad. Bullets will curve around enemies in an effort to remain true to the targeting reticle. Enemies themselves seem to die based on arbitrary damage amounts. And lets not forget the match mechanic. Enemies can be burned with a match. But only if theyre on the ground. And then they go up like gasoline. But if for some reason the enemy is standing, they are made of water. And the match only works if the game decides it wants to work. There are many times you will merrily be attempting to deploy a match on fallen enemis only for your character so stand their mindlessly waiting for an enemy to strike. This on top of the fact that the player character lumbers about the game like he learned to walk yesterday. The only real difficulty in the game comes from the fact that the character is so ungraceful that you end up putting him in harms way just out of sheer frustration. At a certain point, any sort of survival-horror feeling in the game is taken out when its simply not that difficult. Rather than limping along with a meager portion of health left, the game in many ways just lets you replay the scene. Wait for your character to die, redo the scene so you can get it right. The game ends up feeling more like extra gory problem solving rather than a horror game.

Leidub trükivigu, mida ma ei viitsinud parandada!
The Evil Within on õudusmäng, mis on sildistatud kui horror, survival horror ja psychological horror mäng. Enda poolt lisaksin adventure ja mystery. Jaapanis tuntakse mängu Psycho Breaki nime all. Tegemist on ainult üksikmängija mänguga, mis maksab Steamis 60 eurot. Mängu arendajaks on Tango Gameworks, mis loodi 2010dal aastal vana Resident Evili seeria loojate poolt ning 2014 oktoobril tuli nende esimene mäng, milleks ongi The Evil Within. Mängu avaldajaks tuntud Bethesda Softworks. Mainin ära, et Steamis olev tagasiside on mostly postitive, täpsemalt öeldes 77% postitiivne. Kas see ka tõele vastab, seda saate kohe käesolevas ülevaates teada.
Mängus kehastad Sebasstiani, kes on kogenud dektetiiv. Teda aitavad kolleegid Kidman ja Joseph. Lugu algab sellega, et hakkate koos oma uurima massimõrva vaimuhaiglas. Kohale jõudes avastatakse, et kõik haigla töötajad koos politseijõududega on mõrvatud. Mõni hetk hiljem on Sebastian teadvuseta ja ärkab segases Krimson Citys, kus toimuvad maavärinad, maastikunihked ning liiguvad ringi erinevad kurjad olendid. Ta kohtab seal arsti Marcelot, kes otsib enda patsienti Lesliet. Kui Sebastian leiab doktoriga Leslie, siis nad kohtuvad ka Ruvikuga, kellel tundub olevat kontroll reaalsuse üle. Ta suudab teleportida ning muuta maastiku ja keskkonda. Ta lahutab dektetiivitrio ning püüab Sebastiani lõksu. Mis aga edasi juhtub, jätan ma teie endi avastada.
Kui kritiseerida mängu graafikat, siis tegelaste näoilmed ja emotsioonid oleks võinud olla paremad, või tähendab, neid peaaegu polnudk! Loodan, et ei ole suur spoiler, kui ütlen, et mängu edasi jõudmisel satute linnatänavatele.  Just siis tekkis mõte, et kas arendajad väsisid ära või mis juhtus. Linnas olid osad tekstuurid väga madalad ja koledad. Hoolimata sellest oli kõik teised kohad väga ilusad. Alguses tundub graafika kuidagi tuhm ja tume, kuid peale mõnda mängutundi harjute sellega kiiresti. Kuna tegemist on horrormänguga, siis on enesestmõistetav, et oli vaja luua õudsat atmosfääri, mis neil ka väga hästi välja tuli. Hoolimata nendest nõrkustest võib graafikaga rahule jääda ja öelda ,et see on suurepärane.
Nagu eelnevalt mainitud, on loojad tegelenud ka Resident Evili seeriaga, millest võib järeldada, et mänge võrreldes leiab sarnasusi. Olen veel lugenud üelvaateid, kus inimesed ütlevad, et tegemist on Residet Evili ja Sient Hilli seguga. Endale meenutas mäng veidike The Last of Us-i. Just selle scavange ja oskuspuu uuendamise pärast. Veel võib võrdlusesse tuua Hitman:Absolutioni, kus peab palju silent kille tegema. Ka The Evil Within-is on silent killid väga tähtsa, kuna nende jaoks ei kulu lastemoona. Keskkonnast leiab elude jaoks süstlaid ja meditsiinipakke. Muud kugutavad esemed on dokumendid, võtmed, kaarditükid, kadunud inimeste postrid, ajalehed ja roheline geel. Roheline geel annab võimaluse Sebastiaeni oskuste uuendamiseks, mida saab teha ainult spetsiaalses kohas – hullumajas. See on spetsiaalne koht uuendusteks, mängu salvestamiseks ja kappide avamiseks. Terve ümbruskond on täis ärapeidetud püüniseid, mille kahjutuks tegemine annab rauadetaile, millest omakorda saab valmistada vibupüssile nooli. Kui kogud kokku ka kõik kaarditükkid, saad suure üllatuse osaliseks. Muidugi leiab maast, kastidest ja muudest kohtadest relvi ja kuule.
Kui õudne see mäng siis reaalselt on? Ütleme nii, et tegemist ei ole mänguga, mille eesmärk on tühiseid jumpscaresi tekitada, vaid eesmärk on rohkem lugu edasi anda, kuid sellegi poolest suudab see üllatada mitmeid korda. Pinget jagub pidevalt, kas siis bossidega võitlemisel või niisama ringi rännates. Ka ühe loading screeni nõuanne on see, et vahel on jooksmine parim lahendus. Pean tunnistama, et ise olen olnud liiga uudishimulik, et mõnda kohta lihtsalt läbi joosta. Tapsin absoluutselt kõik vastased ja otsisin kõikvõimalikest kohtadest endale nodi.
Minul kulus mängu läbitegemiseks 15 tundi. Terve selle ajajooksul nägin kokku kuni 3 buggi, mis on üsnagi üllatav, kuna steamis liigub palju negatiivset tagasisidet just buggide ja graafika glichide kohta. On jutte ka sellest, et mäng on kinni 30 fpsi peal, aga see ei vasta tõele. Saate rahus nautida just nii hea fpsiga, kui hästi teie arvuti seda mängu jooksutab. Ise kasutasin Nvidia GTX770 videokaarti maksimum sätetel ja mäng jooksis umbes 45-70 kaadrit sekundis. Tundub, et mängu on parandatud ja vastavad uuendused on välja lastud. Koos keskklassi videokaardi ja kõige uuemate draiveritega ei tohiks probleeme tulla.
Kui alustate mängu esimest korda, siis on saadavalt ainult kaks raskus taset: Casual ehk kerge ja Survival ehk keskmine või otsetõlkes normaalne. Peale mängu läbimängimist avanevad uued mängu moodid ja tasemed. Avaneb Nightmare Difficulty ehk raske ja AKUMU mode, mis tähendab seda, et oled surnud ühe löögiga. Ise mängisin terve mängu Survival tasemel. Mäng ütleb ka seda, et taset saab muuta, aga ainult madalamaks. Ehk kui paned Survivali pealt Causalile, siis pead terve edaspidise mängu kerge tasemega läbima. Ka ise kaalusin seda varianti mängu alguses, kuid õnneks ma taset ei madaldanud ja pingutasin lõpuni. Arvan, et raskustasemete süsteem on hästi läbimõeldud ja kutsub kindlasti uuesti mängima. Mängus on ka vahebossid ning lõppboss. Tapmise meetodid on enamjaolt erinevad.
Mida öelda kokkuvõtteks? The Evil Within maksab Steamis 60 eurot, mis on üsnagi krõbe hind, kui arvestada sellega, et tegemist on üksikmängija mänguga. Ise soetasin selle soodusmüügi ajal 9 euroga. Arvan, et mäng ei vääri 60 eurot, kuna sisu pole piisavalt. Sellegipoolest on tegemist ühe hea ja kvaliteetse mänguga. Arvan, et mängu on natuke isegi alahinnatud kuulsate kriitikute poolt. Kui te olete horror mängude fän, siis just see on must paly teie jaoks. Mina paneksin 8/10-st.
