I cannot recommend this game enough to all lovers of Star Trek, outer space, spaceship simulators, MMOs, RPGs, and futuristic battles! It's even pretty good for people who like single players--for the most part, people will ignore you in group places like Earth Spacedock, unless you talk in instance chat or interact with them in some way, and the rest of the time you can go off into your own mission instances.
The game is free to play with optional purchases, and is actually fun even without them. Dedicated players can earn some of the paid items by grinding the Energy Credits and buying stuff from other players on the exchange, so there's a lot of flexibility.
It's a lot of fun to play with friends, with whom you can form a fleet and gain other benefits, like fleet credits to purchase things from your fleet store--But the biggest benefit of playing with friends is buddying up to run enjoyable missions together and have a blast, or maybe have an impromtu party in Club 47 in Earth Spacedock. (no kidding!)
Other fun things are pets that follow you around, and breeding tribbles (yes!) by keeping a tribble in your inventory and adding a food item. If you add one tribble and one food, you can control which tribble eats which food and what they breed. There are charts showing what tribbles breed what offspring for what foods, for the dedicated breeders--but if you just want to casually breed them, just throw one in your inventory or bank with a load of food and watch them breed--like tribbles! lol Petting tribbles gives you (and your bridge officers) buffs that last for about an hour, long enough to run a mission. The buffs can be extra damage output, damage resistance, or health regen--or even a combination of the above! (Klingons can't get these buffs, sadly, since they and tribbles have a mutual dislike).
For the fashion-minded, there are many uniforms (from all the TV series and movies!) and off duty uniforms that you can get/buy and mix and match! And after you've got the perfect outfit, visit the arms dealer or weapons master to get upgrades and armor--or jaunt over to Vulcan, Andoria, and/or Risa for some fun exploring and a vacation! You can investigate logic on Vulcan, engage in Andorian hand-to-hand combat and see their parks, or play on the beach at Risa! While you're doing all that, if you're not using the new in-game voice chat to talk to all your awesome buddies, you can tune in to one of the star trek radio stations to hear some great music and humorous trek related "commercials"!
Lovers of crafting will find a cool crafting system based from Memory Alpha. Captains scan systems to find "anomalies" of different types from which crafting is done, and when they find some, they get to play a mini-game of matching a wave frequency in a limited time to gain more of whatever they've found.
For those who look for the rare and limited, there's some rare items, ships, officers, and equipment gained from particpating in various events, doing some harder missions, or higher level crafting, or lock boxes from the store.
You start out as an ensign at Starfleet Academy on Earth (if you play Federation--if you play Klingon you start on Q'ronos and you can now play Romulan too) and gradually make your way up the ranks, getting better and better ships, gear, and bridge officers. There are two modes to the game--a spaceship simulator type space mode, and an RPG/FPS type ground mode. Everyone plays both at different times in missions, just like the TV series' and movies.
Definitely give this game a try--it's got a lot to it and you might like it for its game qualities even if you don't really like Star Trek--buf if you DO, you won't want to miss this. :)

6.5/10, but would recomend!
You start off with 1 critter named Adam who is kidnapped from his pack by a bird of prey. He escapes by lashing out at the beast during a storm and lands on an island. Though you are not alone for long, you find a female named Eve and become mates. The game gives you two goals: Find adam's original pack and/or start your own pack and grow.
---
The art is wonderfully done and the basic control mechanics are simple. However, the game's tutorial is lackluster beyond that. The game really throws you to the wolves with some mechanics that you learn by trial and error. Each creature is given several traits and genes and it shows you can mate to pass them on, yet it doesn't fully break it down. Some creatures are able to swim, but when I moved them into a water tile I soon learned that some of the tiles are considered to be 'under water' and they would still take damage.
It really feels like an adventure for your cats as the generations pass and you learn the ins and outs. Once you figure out a way to manage your food source and deal with  the random events, the game snowballs in your favor.  It also started to lose that 'adventure' gleam and feels more 'sandboxy' as I found the last bit of content and came up with ideas of how to play the game to give longer replayability.
The menus are organized and intuative, but I have a yearning for more. When you get more than 10+ cats I'm wishing there was an in game tables to view and organize all my felines: I find myself needing to pause and take inventory of my cat's current genes and abilities about every 12 or so turns as their life spans are around 20 days. A table page would definently give me some ease of life as my current pride is 30 cats and I'm spending so much time organizing now.
A day counter is a MUST. After I unlocked the days survived achievements I no longer have any idea what day I am on in future runs. I hope to see one added in the future.
Though the game is far from perfect, I have enjoyed my experience. Definently a Niche game that many will love. The game is quite the gem that has loads of potential and I hope to see it continue to evolve into a bigger and better game.

A genetics simulator wth cute cat-dogs and derp snouts? Count me IN. 11/10.
tl;dr Game is good, genetics are great, amen.
Good
- I am addicted. I keep turning it off to do something else and within 30 minutes I get the urge to just try, try again.
- It is difficult to grasp at first, but I think of the Dwarf Fortress model every time my entire tribe dies horribly: LOSING is FUN
- The graphics are adorable, even on Low settings.
- The variety of "play styles" based on the interaction between genetics and the local environment make me desperate to try EVERYTHING.
- The genetic mechanics, in general, are obtuse and complicated, just like real life! (I graduated with a degree in Biology, so the complexity and detail and the sheer amount of research and time that went into crafting the genetic mechanics are ENTIRELY appreciated and I love every bit of it. This is what pushed the game from "huh, cool nature sim" to "MUST BUY NOW.")
Meh
- Sandbox is great, but I love a good optional story mode. The Adam story is mostly a brief tutorial, which would be fine if there was a more substantial tool tip system or Help menu that didn't open up to a webpage.
- There is a mysterious absence of hotkeys, other than the map modes.
Bad
- You know how there's a column of all your household Sims on the left of the Sims screen? This game doesn't have that. Finding a lost/forgotten animal requires actual searching (damn you, tall grass!) or cycling through with tab. It is infuriatingly slow and a Sims-like display (menu?) of all your living tribe members would be awesome. There's plenty of room on the screen!
- I mentioned the Adam story mode previous as a Meh, but I really, really want more objectives outside of Steam achievements. I'm at a loss for ideas though so I can't blame the developers...

Late Medieval Left 4 Dead with rats and dice.
The good
-Hack and Slash.
Melee feels right. You can left-click your way through normal mode, but anything above will require you to put some effort into the timing and position of your attacks and guards.
-With fire and steel.
Ranged weapons are cool, but not the focus for most of the characters. The homing ability of some of the magic is ubsurd.
-Gotta get that loot.
Special loot items take up precious inventory space normally reserved for healing tools or reduce the health of your whole team. Yeah it's great to get them, but will you be able to make it? It is a unique mechanic.
-Trinkets, odds and ends, that sort of thing.
You can customize your characters with little knick-knacks that give passive boosts, buffs to your team, or reduced damage. Also, each of the playable characters has cosmetic hats to find. That's good, right?
-The woeful world of Warhammer.
Environments, items, and characters all have great detail given to their models and dialogue. This game feels more invested in its' own world than you may think for a Left 4 Dead type grind would care for.
The Meh
-Elves.
I think the elf character is the only one who has a passive advantage over the other characters. She also has homing arrows and some of the best melee weapons. The only thing she can't really do is clear a horde, but that's what all the other characters are supposed to do for her. I'm not saying she need to be nerfed, but rather have the other characters buffed in one way or another.
-The grind
Yeah, you need to grind levels for better loot. Daily quests help to break it up by giving out additional rewards. This is best played with friends, but jumping into a level with new people giving eachother tips is fun too.
-Rat Orges
The amount of health these things have seems to cross the line between challange and annoyence.
The Bad
-Bugs
Sometimes you may fail to connect to a lobby, or your game crashes between menus or little things like that. Nothing too bad.
-Difficulty settings
At its' hardest, this game is less about playing and more about exploiting the A.I.

There are about 2 dozen maps, plus a few more with the DLC.
Several difficulty levels and a bouty board for specific guaranteed loot.
Replayability is where this game really falls short.
This game plays a lot like Gauntlet, only in first person; the character classes are locked, using only class specific weapons, and the customization of characters is severely limited (unique hats and charms).
Game play ranges from strategic to run 'n gun, but gets tired very quickly unless you're playing with good friends.
Inclusion of a single player campaign would have been nice, or a randomly generated dungeon crawl (think Hellgate London).
Otherwise the game is beautiful and true to lore.
2.75 out of 5 Stars...till (or if) more features are added.

I absolutely love this game, althouth I've only played it for 125 hours so far. It's a realtively simple concept but with plenty of variety, so I contantly want to replay, get better gear, try different weapon combos and take on harder levels of difficulty. What I like most is its classic multi-player coop. You need to watch each other's backs, rescue each other from time to time and work together to be successful. You dont need to use voice chat if you dont want, but once people start backing each other up, success follows. Then there's the fantastic warhammer fantasy role-play world, grotty and dark, brought to life with carefully constructed levels. Lots of multi storey buildings which look like they might fall over, nasty sewers, wizards towers and even some wilderness levels. While you could get through all levels on easy setting quite quickly, there's lots of things to discover and massive replayability. For its price, it has to be one of the best value games out there!

Alright, so this is my first review ever, but I wanted to jump in since the game is getting a lot of hate and I aim to justify the existence of this entry and to tell you how not everything is as bad as many people say. If you are unsure about this game let me tell you this: this game will only please a select few hardcore fans, so if you are one, this could be a gamble. If you are not a big a fan, save your money and time, and play the big titles instead. Prepare for a wall of text.
Before anything else, I need you to know that the book "Deus Ex: Icarus Effect" written by James Swallow (main writer for the modern DX games) is canon and takes places before the events of this game and not only introduces all of the characters mentioned in The Fall, but also talks about many events that impact the game and Human Revolution as well. For you to maximize the enjoyment of the game, read the book (if you have the patience) or the summary
. Doing so will give you a deeper sense of the narrative and perhaps a different perspective when you play this game, seeing as the novel basically sets up this game. The game takes place after the events of the book, and follows the story of Ben Saxon and the Tyrants, the group of mercenaries that attack Sarif Industries on DX Human Revolution.
Let me start with the bad things about the game: Deus Ex: The Fall is simply a PC port for a mobile game that came out in 2013, so do not get you hopes up about nice features, big areas and details like in DXHR or DXMD. That being said, the port is simply a copy paste from the mobile versions with graphic upscaling and Anti Aliasing and added keyboard support, everything else is the same and it feels really limited. The game is very short, bodies disappear, enemy AI is bound to a specific area and they do not go past said area, the controls feel clunky and many other limitations exist (and it makes sense for a mobile game), there is no inventory management and there are no physical shops in the game. You can simply pause the game, go into the different parts of the menus and purchase anything at any moment using in-game currency, and you can carry everything that is available to use by the player without consequence. It is practical, but not challenging to use this system. You also only have one save slot and this is terrible for a PC port, this should be unaccpetable, but here we are. Finally, the story starts off slowly and it's not very interesting at the beginning. Some characters are oversimplified and feel bland, but the story is still somewhat interesting for those who aren't hardcore fans. The game is supposedly episodic, but only part 1 has been released so far and you will be left in a cliffhanger. No talk about part 2 is making people angry and uneasy about this game's future, and rightfully so.
Now, the good things! The story, characters and lore all tie in with the main series and this is a rich addition to the world of Deus Ex as far as narrative is concerned, so from the get-go many characters already seen in other games are more likeable. The locations in Panama are very interesting, and is a nice refresher from the locations from Human Revolution. The music is mostly borrowed from Human Revolution, so it is very nice. All characters that have appeared in other games are still using the same voice actors and most main characters have solid performances, but are limited by the engine. If you enjoyed the weapons from Human Revolution, most are in the game and new variations are presented in the game, with different stats and skins, the Belltower Shotgun is my favorite, being fully automatic with a press of the trigger. A new augmentation, the stealth dash, is fun and serves as a balancing measure since the Typhoon is still experimental. There is a good replay value with the New Game +, and the economy of the game presents a challenge for those seeking to get all items or augmentations.
Bottom line: The game deserves a better treatment. If the story was to be all finsihed up, and was given the AAA treatment, with big city hubs and more sidequests, nicer, updated graphics and better AI, I am sure it would become a fan favorite. There is potential, and it is a shame to see it wasted in a mobile version ported to PC. But the game is good in it's core, only limited by the parameters of a mobile game. If you are interested in the Deus Ex universe, this is a nice side story with more to be told. Give it a shot.

I'll start this review with the following statement: Give your money to the creators of 'Layers of Fear', they deserve it.
'Layers of Fear' is more of an interactive horror story than properly a game. It offers no challenges or puzzles to solve, let alone enemies to defeat or scape from; you basically roam in this labyrinth of madness inspired by an old Victorian style house, always ending in the same places. Is that a good thing? YES! It's absolutely brilliant!
It feels like walking and visually exploring a Lovecraft story; the imagery present in 'Layers of Fear' is surreal, frightening and utterly bizarre. The unfold of the story, which happens mostly through notes is a piece of brilliant storytelling narrative. The caracters have no name nor face, and yet they are strangely familiar. There is more character development in the detais of 'Layers of Fear' than in most games out there. It's a short game, so taking your time to explore every piece of art and small detail is highly recommended and rewarding. The art design in this game is sheer perfection; there are some truly jawdropping moments here, more than any realistic landscapes from Far Cry.
The jumpscares are plenty, but they are used in the good way: after the scare happens, the tension still continues due to the music, the imagery or the noises, which creates a lasting sense of dread. I can't think of a game with a more appropriate name other than 'Layers of Fear'. Madness and the loss of contact with reality are great horror subjects that should be more commonly explored in games and horror movies.
Layers of Fear is not finished yet, so I hope to see even more craziness in the final version. I would love to seek for other collectibles like the rat drawings. The narrative structure is amazing and quite different from other games I have played, however, it is far more engaging than the overly repetitive hide-and-seek kinda of horror that seems to reign in Horror games nowadays. Not that contemporary horror games are bad, quite the contrary, I just like the idea of diversity in my games.
Grade: 9.5/10 (Outstanding)

I originally purchased this game for my four year old son, who is amazed with genetics and animals . He was very mad when his species died out, he smashed his  laptop and bawled his eyes out. Lucky for him we got him a much better one haha! I wanted to try the game and Ive never had this much fun in my whole life. My son and I have our own little world with 18 niches! We love to play this game when he comes home from preschool and devote all our free time together playing it. Ive only recently purchased this game but already we are both in love!

It's fun and actually not that hard once you get the hang of the system. Breed like rabid, get a few viable breeding families with different immunity genes, and populate the map. While doing so you do your best to eliminate weak genes via selective breeding.
The game's biggest flaw in my opinion is a lack of any automation. The best part of the game is when you migrate to an island and struggle to find your niche and adapt to the environment with a small tribe. However, once you grow, most of your time will be spent tab-clicking the same food resources for hours on end. It's quite a slog, and unfortunately where most of your gameplay time will be spent, while all you really want to do is focus on the genetics aspect of the game.
Other than that, it's a fun critter game with a lot of variety in environments and traits. A little pricey for what it offers though. Wait for a sale.

*This Review is Written as of December 30th 2015
The current state of the game for not being finished is very promising. Currently play time clocks in at about 2 hours or at least that is how long it took me to complete the available chapters. The graphics are great even with below average laptop the graphics still looked nice and performance was not sacrificed drastically. I did notice that gameplay would stop or freeze as the result of trying to enter a new room I'm not currently sure if that is my pc running slow or a result of the game needing time to load the new rooms. Gameplay revolves around you walking around the mansion through rooms that change as you progress in the game and at times it plays like Silent Hill PT demo if you are familiar with that (If not you are moving through the same area again and again as the environment changes and new things pop up). There are a few puzzles in the game and they serve as a nice change of pace of from the constant tension. The game does rely on Jump Scares it does a good jump of disguising them and holding their use so the scares do not become repetitive and no longer scare you. In the game their is no possible way to die as far as I learned from my playthrough not sure if this is a gameplay decision or just a placeholder for showing the basic designs of the game before full launch.
Overall I give this game a 9/10 it is very atmospheric and one of the best horror games I've played in a while probably since Outlast and also touches on a great story and the challenges of mental disease, alcoholism and loss.

The game mechanics are complex but easy to understand if you take one minute or two to assimilate them.
It gives you an idea of how complex genetics are.
The designers also build their game in a way that it opens doors for expansions (not just tiny dlcs that adds stuff, but big expansions).
It is not an easy game, especially if you do not take that one or two minute to understand how things works.
The tutorial is rather small, I would include an entire part to the genetics and how it works in the game. For example, the tutorial does not tell you how to get rid of trraits you do not want in your breed nor does it tell you how to develop new traits. Since this is a genetics game, why is the tutorial deprived of any genetic-related instructions? It's sad.
The story mode should be by steps, each time you change island, you should get another story part, giving you hints where your family is. That way, you can either follow your own path or seek your old family.
On more superficial, and unimportant for me, aspects of the game...
- The graphics are nice and cute.
- Music is pleasant, but I would add more tracks in its first big expansion
- Sounds are also entertaining.
I strongly recommand this game to everyone. It is well worth its price, and if it is on sale jump on it. It is relaxing yet not too easy. Just take two minutes to learn how the genetics work and keep an eye on those genes so that you do not get sickly descendants.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a perfect example of a good game that is completely spoiled by a single bad system.
The Loot System in this game while part of the appeal, is also the title's largest downfall. You want better loot to do the higher difficulty to get better loot. The problem with this is that each mission has the same RNG possibility of different loot types. You can do the very first mission on the hardest difficulty and get the same loot as if you had done the final mission on the hardest difficulty. This gives very little incentive to go after ANY loot once you have completed the entire story. In addition, if you want to chase more loot, there is NO reason to not do whatever mission you find to be the easiest to complete.
The very system that is designed to promote progression in missions in difficulty is the same system that completely hinders that goal.
It is a VERY FUN game and I would recommend it if you can justify that purchase. But for someone like me that would like to continuously play it and truly embrace the advancement of gear and difficulty, there is nothing here.

After playing the free weekend, I thought this game seemed like it might be worth $15.  It isn't. Perhaps $5.
The hit distance is absolutely ridiculous--a rat can dagger-melee you from what seems like 25 feet away.  You can do the same, but for people who have played L4D (or really any game involving first or third person combat), this takes a while to get used to, isn't realistic, and looks stupid.  It also affects your play, because you think that that rat coming up on you isn't quite upon you yet...and then all of a sudden you're taking damage.
There are a ton of little annoyances in this game beyond that:
1) You can't walk up certain stairs; you can get to the final stair near the top, but have to jump to reach the new height of about one foot.  This wouldn't be too bad if you didn't have to BACK UP first, and then jump.
2) The Skaven themselves don't have much in the way of variety (aside from the specials).
3)  Nearly every chest I opened had nothing in it, whereas potions and bombs are simply lying around.
4)  Playing as a dwarf, my massive warhammer should be able to sweep through multiple enemies; it can, but it takes seriously two full seconds to wind up, rendering it useless for swarms, since you get hit repeatedly while the swing is winding up.
5) You can climb ladders, but getting down from them without taking fall damage means you need to jump off the top and then turn around in midair to grab the ladder.  If you try to simply walk toward the ladder and let it "catch" a la Half Life 2, it'll catch (making you think that you can then go down the ladder safely), but then it will throw you off for damage instead.
6)  The level design is also very convoluted--me and my coop partner got lost many times.  I haven't gotten this lost since Warframe, and Warframe at least has a minimap...this game does not.
7) The friendly AI makes L4D's look like the most competent squadmates ever (and that's saying something--they're more useful than Bill).   They seriously went after a ratling gunner, swung at him and hacked him up, stopped, and came back without killing him.
8) You can't Alt-Tab out without the game windowing (even though the game will tell you, upon going back in, that the game is not windowed).  This feels like nitpicking, but there are 10-year-old games that don't have this issue.
9) The action sounds are pretty weak.  There no visceral thrill of a strong thrum of my crossbow, and the chop of my axe sounds like I might as well be slapping the rat with bologna.
Seriously, this game feels incredibly unfinished.  Like an Early Access that was released well before it should have been.  The biggest issue, the hit distance, shouldn't have made it out of pre pre pre alpha.
The game is somewhat fun when things get chaotic, but L4D did it MUCH better.  By comparison, this comes across as sloppy.

Still, this is a positive change and it's good to see this game is still being worked on.
It's also worth noting that the friendly AI is really pretty bad so play with friends or randoms for a better experience.

MMOs are tricky things, and what they do more than anything else is excel in one area and totally crash and burn in another.
Star Trek Online is, in this regard, a quintessential MMO.
When you are piloting your ship, its an engaging, albeit repetitive experience that is well executed, beautifully rendered and full of promise.
When you walk around on your own two feet, you have to wonder why the developers even bothered.
Recent reworking of many portions of this game have improved the overall experience, but the planet-bound experience is pretty miserable.
The graphics for the 3rd person experience are shockingly bad, the movement is relatively humorous, but not necessarily in a good way, the animation is weak and the combat while better than you might imagine, the AI of your "crew mates" is disappointing.
In contrast, the space-faring portion of the game is, if you pardon the pun, stellar. Certainly flying in circles during drawn out battles can be boring, but there is enough going on, with the strategic choices, the balancing of shields, positioning in 3 dimensional space to best use your speed, or lack there of, weapons and special tactics can make even the more tedious battles at least moderately interesting.
The space map is less pretty than it should be, but it's certainly not terrible and transwarp travel can get you around quickly at least in one direction.
there is some charm to having access to some of the known "landmarks" such as DS9 as well.
Other aspects of the game are generally typical affair - items are colour coded, a la everquest and world of warcraft, and as a free-to-play, most the desirables are available, for a price.
For free, the game is worth it for the space alone. For a full fledged, MMO experience which will capture your imagination and keep you coming back for more? Go elsewhere. Even for free, there are better choices.

is a stealth action game. Although they can be played as a first-person shooter if you prefer a more aggressive approach, the Deus Ex games do encourage the player to take a stealthy approach. This means you study the pattern of patrolling guards, try to single out one of them and sneak up behind him, and then press a button on your keyboard or controller to take him down. While doing this, you want to avoid being caught in the act by other guards, security cameras or patrolling robots.
You earn experience points (XP) for your actions and when you've earned enough XP, you get one point to spend on 'augmentations' (skills). Roughly, there are combat-oriented skills, exploration skills that allow you to get to places you wouldn't otherwise be able to reach, and hacking skills.
To hack a computer or an electronic lock you need to complete a minigame. The minigame is based on pure luck, but you can invest in skills that raise your chance to succeed. You will also find items that can make hacking a bit easier.
There's a main questline that will take you through the story and through every area of the game world. There are also 5 optional side quests that yield some additional XP, coin or useful items.
In the world of Deus Ex, technology has evolved to a point where humans can be 'augmented' with technology like much stronger limbs or sophisticated eye prosthetics. Unfortunately, augmented people are dependent on a drug called Neuropozyne to prevent rejection of the implants, which would result in death.
You're Benjamin 'Ben' Saxon, an augmented former Belltower agent who's recruited by a team of independent mercenaries called the Tyrants, led by Jaron Namir. Ben soon finds out what people who played
already know: they're not the nicest bunch of people. While on the run from both Belltower and the Tyrants, Ben and his girlfriend Anna find themselves in Panama when they start experiencing physical problems due to a lack of Neuropozyne. So Ben sets out to look for a solution to that problem, while trying to stay out of the clutches of the people who are after them at the same time.
Panama consists of three small zones that each have a few buildings you can enter and where you'll find quest givers, quest targets and loot. It's not a huge place at all. If you rush through the game doing the main questline only, you'll probably be finished in 3 or 4 hours. If you do all the side quests, it takes about 5 to 6 hours to play through the game.
was originally a game for mobile devices, developed in Unity. While I must say that graphically it's the best Unity-based game I have played so far, this is a big step down from
. The developers of
clearly added quite a few fringes to the basics that the Unity engine provides, but Unity graphics always look a bit crude and austere.
Menu controls are clumsy: sometimes you need to click several times on a button before it registers. In-game, items dropped by opponents tend to sink into the floor. You can still pick them up if you know more or less where they are, but you can't see them. This is annoying and it looks and feels plain sloppy. Also, when an object you want to pick up is close to another object you can interact with, you will interact with the other object. In that case, you need to move around to try and focus the camera in a way that only the item you want to pick up is highlighted, which can be a pain.
The music is okay. It sounds mostly copypasted from
but toned down a bit. It's certainly not memorable, although it isn't intrusive or annoying either. The same goes for the sound effects. They're probably copypasted as well, but they sound dull compared to

Rating: 6.5/10
I want to like this game
badly, but unfortunately it leaves a lot to be desired. I simply can't recommend this game as it is. I would love to see the developers continue to work on this game, or produce a vastly more complex version.
The core theme of the game is fantastic, and I believe that the developers are truly onto something, but as it currently is It feels much more like a demonstration on genetics, or educational game for young kids rather than a complete game. If you are buying it for these purposes then its definitely suitable. As someone looking for a complete game with objective, progression, complexity, "win condition", challenge, sense of accomplishment, or possibly even limitless creativity the game is not fulfilling. Despite these flaws I maintain a positive outlook on the game, because I can imagine that in the right hands this game could be incredible. With that said I am not going to pull any punches, and I want to address the things this game lacks, which would otherwise make it a 10/10 title in my opinion.
: One of my biggest complaints is that every single turn I need to perform the exact same collection actions to harvest nuts and berries. This task is tremendously mundane when you have fully a colonized island. Hundreds of turns of harvesting berries and nuts over and over is super boring. Automatically performing collection duties eliminates this unreasonably tedious chore, and allows the player to focus on the genetics aspect of the game.
: There is very little demand for specialization.
-Going beyond +2 collecting is more of a mechanical luxury because you get to click less.
-Basically no advantage to going beyond +1 cracking, because it's sufficient to break acorns.
-Fishing is a terrible and poorly balanced mechanic, which probably results in net food loss anyways.
-The only DEMAND for specialization is in temperature resistance, which I'll say in some ways is decently balanced.
-Although there is a lot of opportunity to specialize in combat strength, it's much easier to just poison something or avoid it entirely.
: The mutation menu should be removed from the game. All genetics should be worked toward as a product of random mutations and cross breeding with foreign nichelings. The mutation menu is a lame mechanic that encourages stockpiling of food on noob islands, while still getting any genetics you want. It eliminates the need for travel, exploration, and adaptation to unfavorable environments. Similarly the idea of being able to bring as much food as you want to the next island is ridiculous. Food reserve should have a hard cap upon traveling based on difficulty or something.
: There is no actual advancement of genes. Evolution of genetics often occurs as a product of internal competition of a species. The fastest, strongest, and smartest animals are the ones that continue to reproduce. There should be traits that are OBJECTIVELY superior to others. For example, consider a claw hierarchy of Super Sharp Claws > Sharp Claws > Claws > Dull Claws. This gives players incentive to continue to push forward, and to temporarily find value in a terrible attribute like Dull Claws since it takes a large number of generations to get a lucky mutation toward regular Claws. To elaborate I think the 'ancient' genetics should have to be worked toward, and should be monumentally more rewarding.
: Barring aesthetics the amount of genetic diversity is fairly trivial in my opinion. I would love to see this game implemented with 10+ viable traits per gene, with tiers of functionality, as explained in the last point. Instead most traits are relatively binary in the sense that the trait is either good or crippling. For example, there are only 3 eye traits in the game, and in no circumstance would I suggest making your nichelings blind or short sighted, thus regular eyesight is the only reasonable choice, and since it's unlocked at the start of the game it is quite easy to eradicate these undesirable genes.
: There should be certain challenges that require you to make very 'niche' nichelings. For example maybe a mega predator, that will reward your nichelings if defeated, but cannot be damaged by any nichelings that lack maximum physical strength. Similarly challenges like a part of the map that is so cold that a nicheling will immediately die if they lack capped cold resistance, but huge rewards for accomplishing this tremendous feat.
: At the end of the day it's nice to complete a game. This game seems to drag on forever with no true purpose. A purpose doesn't have to be grandiose, but even something like unlocking improved aesthetics or additional customization for completing many objectives would be great.
TL;DR : This game is a good choice if you want a short demo of genetics, or a game for an infant child to play. The lack of many quintessential mechanisms of evolution, combined with the highly tedious chore of turn based collection take a huge chunk out of the enjoyment of what this game could be. $17 price point is high, I would suggest buying in the $9-$13 range.

I like this game. I don't mind if a game is less exciting, and more of a slow-paste, relaxing game. I can really enjoy those types of games. However, this game simply lacks depth. The story mode, which I was really excited about, is more like a basic-tutorial sandbox mode. So that was a little disappointing. Nice animation, but it doesn't add anything to the gameplay or story.
The travel element is a nice way to make things more interesting, but it's unbalanced. After a few hours of playing I just ask myself "What's the point?". And if you travel to an island unprepared (because how can you know at your first try what kind of dangers you are going to face?) your tribe can be extinct really quickly and the hours you have put into your game are gone. There is no "load game" option and there is really not enough time to adapt your tribe to the new “dangers” of the island.
Don't get me wrong, I like this game. But there is still a lot of work to do and right now I don't think it deserves a "recommended" review, because I would recommend to wait and see if the developers are going to make the game more interesting and make a real story mode.
If a relaxing sandbox game with no real challenges and not much depth is all you are looking for, then I would say go for it. And if you don't mind putting hours into playing and then loose it all in a couple of minutes.

Alright, you like horror games?  You like games that tell a deeper story through discovering little pieces in the game?  You like jump scares?  You like games that make you question whether or not your next step is worth the rise in heart rate?
WELL THIS IS THE GAME!
Even in early access this game will make your skin crawl.  The atmosphere gets you on edge from the start.  It starts off slow and guides you into a game you believe to be nothing more than just creep scene after creep scene, but things go crazy once you start to realize just what's going on in the story.
The developers' ability to place you into the mind of your character as you take terrified step after step to find out the truth, is beautifully executed.  You take 2 steps forward and realize that you need to check behind you.  Up is down, right is left, and Hell has been unleashed.
The game is linear and pushes you in the direction it wants you to go.  The level design has an uncanny ability to draw your attention to just where it needs to be while it prepares to test your heart's strength just two rooms down.  You get hit with one scare, and you're put on edge for the same type of scare next time, but the developers liked to mix it up, rarely utilizing the same tactic multiple times.
This game keeps you on the edge of your seat, and you adrenaline pumping.
Overall great horror game.

I would normally never write a review but I think people getting into this game need to understand that the downsides to this game.  I am very conflicted on this review as it has good merits but I am going to give it a thumbs down for a few reasons I will cover now. I will include some of the things I enjoyed as well for those that want both sides of the coin.
- Prices on items are obscenely high and gives uneven advantages to people who pay (essentially Pay 2 Win)
- The current match making system is extremely flawed after you hit level 5 - I hit level 5 and was immediately thrown into repeated games with people that were almost max rank with Machine Guns, Tanks, Paratroopers, etc. while I was only using a small rifle
- You can be team killed or team kill by a bicycle bumping you
- You can run over a rock with a bicycle and commit suicide
- Players can suicide while driving a vehicle with you in it, causing you to commit suicide and have a long death timer (read below for inconsistency)
- Players can run into the grenades you throw and in return, give you warning points as well as lost experience/money
- Vehicles with mounted weapons kill you extremely fast and most of the time from extremely far distances
- Length from base to objective points will require a vehicle to be of use as a player (bicycle, truck, jeep, etc.)
- Grenades almost always one shot people even when a decent distance away
- Disliked the water physics and how it would screw any vehicle that entered water, even if the vehicle was above the waterline
- Lower graphics than most standard FPS
- Extremely disliked the repair cost, again trying to force you into paying money
This is all I can think of currently. Now for the positive aspects.
- Enjoyable as a casual FPS game
- I found nostalgia in this game, making me miss the old Medal of Honor
- Good fluid motion and gameplay
- I loved the effort put into players exiting vehicles, you basically roll out of the car and come up shooting
- Loved the indicator on the grenade to show where it would go
- Loved the iron sights and swaying, as well as how the stamina effected the stability
- I loved the creative addition of the bicycle, it made me laugh to tears when somebody team killed me accidentally while ringing the bike
- Loved the maps and the creativity put behind it
- I liked the physics behind vehicles
Due to the demanding aspect of the game that really tries to force you into paying, the poor match making system and (cannot fault the game for this) the lack of players for higher ranked games forcing me into constant red ping, I am going to give this a thumbs down.  If it wasn't for these three aspects, I would love this game and tolerate the other minor aspects.
Sorry.

Heroes & Generals is a combined first-person PVP shooter and strategy video game in a World War II setting. It is being published and developed by independent studio Reto-Moto, which was founded by some of the original founders of IO Interactive and the Hitman series. The developers call it a "mass participation game" in contrast to a traditional massively multiplayer online games, where the actions in the FPS-part of the game reflects into the strategy-part.
Pros:
Does have ok graphics, sound, and gameplay.  Does have bicycles you can ride.  You can drive/steal enemy vehicles without any skills or level requirements.  Does have environmental cover.  Does have plentyfull grenades.  Headshots are easy kills.  Fast paced combat in large maps.   Environmental Sound is your friend.  Does give 4 gold for the first battle of the day.  Does have healing and supply stations, anti-aircraft guns, rocket grenades on maps.
You start out as plain infantry men, have to level your skills up to specialize in recon, paratroop, fighter pilot, tank driver and later earn General. But your specialization choice is permanent. Requires Real shooting skills, has ballistic drop and velocity and recoil rise, sight movement.   Eventually, You can fly planes and drive tanks into combat.
Cons:
According to other's reviews, this game is Very Pay to Win. Try it till level 3 then quit. After reaching Level 3, the matches are Brutal with all the advanced P2W players in matches.  Unbalanced matchmaking. Cheaters are rampant. Easy to get spawn killed. Does not have many maps.  No punishment for match quiters.
You have to pay for repairs and reloading ammo for your modded weapons, while matches don't pay enough for that, plus having enough to pay for new weapons.  The grind for new weapons is Brutal, unless you pay real money.  Infantry Anti-Tank weapons are too expensive and tanks are common on the battlefield. Snipers and Tanks now rules most matches.  Does not have much of a tutorial. You can shoot LMGs from the hip.
Warning: I don't recomend you spend real money on this game.  It is still in Beta, maybe later it might improve.

First off, don't let the screenshots fool you, this game supports 16:9 (1080p). Here's a quick 15 minute overview/review video I made:
Majesty 2 is one of my favorite go-to games, and has been since 2010 or so when I first picked it up on DVD (non-Steam version). There's something about the RPG elements, where your heroes level up, buy new gear, and get new abilities, that really appeals to me. As almost anyone even remotely familiar with the Majesty series can tell you, this is not a game where you select a group of units and give them orders, like a standard RTS. Instead, you set flags on things to tell them to attack, defend, explore, or stay away. How much reward you put on those flags roughly determines how many units will join in the effort.
I won't go into too much detail about the actual mechanics here. That stuff is easy to find out. Instead, I'll discuss why I love this game, and why I think you should pick it up.
First off, pretty much every expansion besides the base game, is insanely difficult. There are balance issues or I'm just a really terrible player, probably both. I don't know how it would be humanly possible to complete some of the missions on the later expansions without either a ridiculous amount of patience and luck, or maybe a little cheating. There's just one cheat I recommend: You can edit an .ini file in the game directory to change the effects (and costs) of some of your spells. The "Extortion" spell normally collects a % of the taxes you have coming, and by default it has a 0 cost, since you lose a little of your tax income by using it. You can actually set the cost at a negative value, and it will give you a bit of bonus gold. I only use this after trying and failing at a map 2-3 times. I know, I'm a terrible person, but it's my game and I'll play it how I want to!
It's important to keep in mind that cheating is not always necessary. Often times (at least in the base game), there's a trick to beating a map. Usually it involves a certain combination of units, like building a certain type of unit first, other times it involves avoiding or exploring a specific area as soon as possible. Sometimes there's a "bonus" objective that, if you know where it is, you can get to it early and earn a huge chunk of gold from it.
With a bit of breathing room, this game becomes a soothing sandbox to play in. That's why I love it so much. I can just zone out for a few minutes (or hours), placing buildings, forming parties at the inn, placing towers, and just stomping around. There are spawners placed around the map, like bear dens or hell gates, that will continuously send creatures out to attack you. Sometimes, just for fun, I like to leave them in place and let my heroes level up for a while before destroying them.
After a game you can select one of your heroes to save for later. Then when you place a "Hall of Lords", you can hire that hero and he/she will continue to level up. You can rename them too. Awesome.
Each map takes around 45 minutes or so to complete, depending on how well you set up your economy and building placement. There are also special maps you can play, outside the main campaign, but you don't get to take your saved heroes into those.
It is a shame the developers have basically abandoned this game. There's the long-standing "DLC missing" issue that has plagued the game for a few years now, and the fix for it requires some mucking around in the file system, running sketchy batch files and the like. Bah. That and the insane difficulty (which, after 50+ hours sunk into this game, I do believe might require cheating at times) are the main reasons people have for giving this game a thumbs down. For me, and my tastes, I don't mind too much.
Back in late 2011, a cat I'd had for 14 years (since moving out from home) was getting in bad health. He would snooze on my lap for hours while I played Majesty 2. I was job hunting at the time, but being unemployed gave me more time to spend with my little friend during his last weeks. I will always remember that time with a mix of sadness and warmth. Because that cat, he was such a good friend, and there I was spending time with him playing Majesty 2. I guess this game kind of holds a sentimental place in my heart, and maybe that's why I can so easily overlook its flaws. Now I'm crying again.
Whatever the reason, I love this game. If someone asked me "What's the lowest rated game that you just love anyhow?" it would probably have to be this one.

'Layers of Fear' takes place in a Victorian style house, and you get to play as an insane artist. As you start exploring the everchanging house, you start to notice the hidden messages in every chest and drawer. The protagonist (and you) experiences heavy hallucinations, his fears and false beliefs shape into something physical -- like a smudged painting right behind your back or corpses trying to choke you to death.
You'll never know what will meet your eye the next time you turn the doorknob, and that keeps you hooked till the end of  of released content. I am very eager to continue playing as soon as the update hits. Tiny details and the game overall leave a strong impression that leaves you eager for more. As a game lover and a biology lover this game has two places in my heart. One place is that it's a generally fun casual game, the other place is that I kind of went in expecting an evolution simulator and was a bit disapointed. So here's my review from both ends:
+Fun to play
+I like planning a perfect strain of these guys to go hide out and interbreed start a master race of rabbit things
+Pretty to look at
+Nice music
+I grow attached to these guys and then they die on me but I can't hold a funeral or eat their rotting corpse.
-Could use a lot more variety with genes and islands.
-There's a tutorial but doesn't really go into the nitty-gritty of breeding and evolving, which is is aggravating because that's the reason I picked up this game
-Islands don't make any sense because you can just keep hopping until you find a new one you like, there's no real pressure to stay on an island that you don't like
-Maybe I need to get further into the game, but there doesn't seem to be too many predators and when there are combat is basically chase someone and click to attack
+Heard that the Dev wanted to study biology or game design. Happy they kind of got to do both.
+Holy ♥♥♥♥. Breeding 10000x better than Spore's dig-up-genes-and-use-them-whenever-you-want system
+Overall pretty good model of how basic genetics works (half genes from mom, half from dad, one is expressed, etc.)
Nothing like epigenetics, or codominant traits, but I wouldn't expect that from a AAA team
-Biggest complaint about the game is the fact that food is communal. Eliminates like half the selective pressures on the creatures. I'd really love to see personal food stocks implimented for each animal, that way you actually can weed out the weak quickly.
-Not really a negativve but I'd love to see more gene variety. I know the game just came out, but it'd be cool to see a clear divergence between different tribes or subspecies. Hell speciation would be awesome to see.
Overall fun game, I think it could use some more polishing, but if you're like me and love biology, genetics, and/or evolution or just want a fun game to play I'd say this is well worth the price.

Don't go into this game with the expectation that you're going to be scared. This game is not something that will keep you scared after you finish playing it. The game will throw a lot of blood and gore at you with scary looking things, but that's the extent of the scare.
What this game is, and what you should go into with the expectation, is an action game with horror elements. There are horror-style monsters, but the game is thoroughly an action game with resource management.
The movements can be a little clunky, and deaths will be frequent on higher difficulties. Buried in the mess, there is a very interesting and thought out story to the game. I am on my second playthrough now, and am enjoying it.
I believe this game got a lot of negative reviews because of the way it was talked up and advertised. It was said to "revolutionize" and "reinvent" the survival horror genre. That is not the case. Moving past that, this game is a very enjoyable and challenging experience with a cool story and begs for a sequel to answer the loose ends.

This game......
Let's start by saying I love Star Trek, particularly The Next Generation, and also that I don't play many other MMORPGs. Maybe the galaxy isn't as vast as other in-game worlds, but it's still huge and loyal to the Trekkie's interpretation of the Star Trek universe. So, maybe my review isn't impartial enough or something, but I don't really care, and I may be boring you with my boringishness, so let's get on with the review.
You begin STO with a waaaaaay too long tutorial. We can figure it out on our own, Perfect World! This is one of my only gripes with the game, the hour-long tutorial holding your hand throughout every single button on the HUD. Fortunately you can skip it after you do it once, and get to the game. You can play as 3 factions, Federation, Klingon, or Romulan. Each one has extensive territory, and you can explore the entire galaxy no matter which faction you choose. I have not played as the Romulans yet, but I am going to begin tomorrow, since I don't have the time tonight. You can play as pretty much every sentient species in the galaxy, and then customize them to your heart's content. The Federation characters start on Earth, the Klingons on Qo'nos, and the Romulans on New Romulus. You traverse the galaxy through your extremely customizable ship, being able to upgrade everything from your phasers to your warp core. There are also many different ship models you can use on your journey from Lieutenant to Vice Admiral/Lieutenant General. There's lots of armor and weapons for your ground character too, as the game HUD can switch to third-person shooter mode in an instant. While you can't explore entire worlds, the parts you do are very detailed, the graphics very good for an F2P game. Unfortunately, you can't go very far without noticing the pressure to pay money to get ahead. Almost every awesome ship either requires either months of grinding or $5-$10. You can join fleets made up of other players, which greatly enhances the social aspect. And since we're talking about other players, the group playing is pretty solid, although there is more group PvE than PvP. But what really makes the game shine is the sheer variety of the galaxy. You could spend days exploring it-and I have, trust me-and still be surprised by a planet in the outer reaches of deep space. And the atmosphere of the missions are great too. At the beginning of each mission, the heading is in shown in a Next-Generation-esque font in the opening cutscene, after you are personally briefed by your faction's high-ranking official. You then proceed through normally a minor space battle first, then there is a ground section, and then comes the plot twist. While the structure is rather predictable, the plot is not, and though I know there will always be a twist, I can never figure it out until it hits me. This is then followed by a major space battle, then rewards.
All in all, while the store is frustrating, and the grinding may get a bit tedious, Star Trek Online is a great game for anyone, especially a Trekkie, and it's free! You should be playing it right now!

- Micromanaging sucks, and Majesty is ostensibly free of it. You get to sit back, mind the economy, and watch your heros level up and become stupidly powerful.

The bad:
- This game is incredibly unforgiving -- and you can't change difficulty! The combination of lack of control and punishing AI makes this an infuriating experience.
Sure, it's engaging. Addictive, even. But it's not fun to spend an hour per campaign mission fighting game mechanics rather than a fair enemy.

[TL;DR] My recommendation... avoid if you are looking for a game that rewards the time you invest.
Let me start by saying that there are attributes I like about the game. The Warhammer setting has always been one of my favorites and Vermintide lives up to that. The story line, classes, characters, and atmosphere all bring the Warhammer universe to life. Even the game play, as minimal as it is, is fun and often engaging.
Sadly for me this is where the main good points of the game end and the failure begins for me. Ultimately it fails in making a rewarding experience for the time I invest in it. Character progression is woefully lacking. What can you look  forward to getting? A whopping two extra trinket slots by level 30. Other than a gating means for minor enhancement up to level 30 the only thing it does is give you a single item each level of paltry quality. Even when you succeed at a mission all you get is one random quality item plus a minimum amount of experience. Sure there are "quests" to give you a shot at one more thing.
Ultimately Vermintide seems like a niche game with a very limited player base to appeal to. In fact the base seems to increaingly be comprised of people that use Cheat Engine. I can't blame them either as they are trying to make the game actually worth playing. If I truly wanted to continue to play I probably would join them as the current reward system stinks.
I hope that it continues to meet the minimum financial performance goals that Fatshark is seeking because there is a place for this type of game. Personally though I wish they would look to games like Warframe. I look at Digital Extremes as a company that understands broader appeal without impinging on the quality of the game or game-play.

I love Niche! It's a great game to just immerse yourself in and create your own stories for the creatures you shape over time. There's not much hand holding in Niche, it's a lot of trial and error and there's a very good chance you'll kill off a tribe (or two or three!) before you start getting the hang of everything. Because of that, succeeding at conquering new islands, breeding in those difficult recessive genes, etc. all feel really rewarding!

This game becomes very addictive very quickly, but it is difficult to understand in the beginning. There's little to no tutorial, save for the mechanics of moving around, getting food, and traveling. It was only after watching a few YouTube videos that I discovered that I could actually choose which genes I wanted to mutate. Even then, I've played through several games, all of which end with species extinction because of pure unluckiness (for example, breeding an endless line of females, so that my male to female ratio was extremely skewed, or bearyenas chomping at my creatures).
Three small things - in the tutorial, particularly when you're talking about status effects or the family tree, it would be helpful having some line pointing to WHAT you're talking about. I finally figured out where the family tree button was after three games.
Two,  I'd prefer some small tips towards breeding genes/alleles (but that is something I probably could just google).  Two, THE GRASS. Does it have to be so high?! Having it so high makes everything so much harder to see, and scrolling up to change the camera does not help much.
Still though, Niche is an awesome game to play. Frustrating, yes, but that's what makes it so addictive. You just want to keep going back in so that you can play it right.

Niche is one of those unique games that don't succeed very often due to being very different from what you usually see on the market. It looks and feels very much like a board game at times, with as much strategy involved as you feel like having. It can be a casual breeding game or an intense battle for survival (if you decide to play on one of the more difficult islands), all depending on how deeply/seriously you want to get into it.
The game is basically about keeping your family of creatures alive and well by helping them get food, protect themselves from predators and survive the various natural hazards of their environment, mostly by breeding for different features and genes that allow you to shape your creatures any way you like. The gameworld consists of "islands" that have different bioms (savannah, jungle, mountain, grassland, etc.). Your animals can travel to different islands if you wish, but keep in mind that each one has its own challenges based on its bioms.
The game offers two types of play. You can play the Story mode which starts you off with a creature named Adam and includes a simple tutorial that helps you get started (good for beginners). After the tutorial you are free to play as you like. The other option is the Sandbox mode which allows you to set your own difficulty from the get-go by letting you choose any island you want to start on (good for advance players).
You start off with two creatures and with them create a tribe which you will expand with further breeding. Periodically you will encounter stray creatures which you can invite into your clan, thus expanding the gene pool.
Movement is turn based. Each creature has three moves per game day (when adults) and two or one move when they are babies. You can use their free moves to forage for food, breed, explore (by moving from tile to tile), and do some other actions/interactions. When you have used up all the moves of all the animals you can end the day to progress to the next one/trigger aging, giving birth to cubs etc.
You can collect different types of food like berries, digging up roots, cracking nuts, or hunting for rabbits, moles, fish, etc., or even collect meat from enemies that you defeat. Each creature will consume food at the end of the day. If you lack the food, they will starve and slowly die with each passing turn.
The core of the game is breeding for specific genes. There are many genes available, and hidden ones that you unlock by inviting animals with given genes into your tribes, or by performing actions (for example, trying to dig up roots will eventually unlock/strengthen your digging paw gene). Combine animals with traits you like to produce animals with desired characteristics while avoiding defects, doubled up immunity etc. By having different physical characteristics, some creatures will be better for hunting, defending, fishing, digging, foraging, etc. For more difficult bioms you might need certain creature features to help you survive. There is also the ability to mutate genes into your creatures if you wish and much more. The possibilities are endless and each time you breed, you will get a slightly different creature.
The game is well done, works very well (though it's not very graphic intensive), doesn't have that many bugs/glitches, so kudos to the dev team. There are also planned expansions for the game if they get enough funding through sales here on Steam.
All in all, the game is a fantastic choice for anyone interested in genetics, biology, strategy, survival, etc. There is so much more I could talk about here, but Steam has its limits. It's great to play with kids and other family members as it does a very good job of teaching the basics of genetics. I couldn't recommended it enough.

So, like, I haven't played very far into Niche, but I feel like I have a pretty good handle on how the mechanics work in terms of how they're going to be read by the average gamer.
Basically, I think there's two ways you can look at the game.  You can look at it as a game that you play to achieve a specific goal, and you can look at it as a sandbox simulation of genetics.  As such, I've split my review into two parts, based on which perspective you're going for.
There's also a five-second TL;DR at the bottom if you REALLY want it, but I advise looking over the details before deciding on a purchase.
--------------------------
If you ask me to pick what this game's
genre is, it's definitely survival.  There is no goal in this game save surviving as long as possible, which is accomplished by wandering the wilds looking for food and fighting or avoiding hostile creatures.  Death not only comes easily, it is inevitable, since every creature has its own designated time-based lifespan which is visible on their HUD.  You have to be okay with dying.
However, in addition to survival, there's a fairly strong presence of the strategy genre here as well, and it's the main genre informing the game mechanics that make this game different from other survival games.  First, it's turn-based--time won't pass until you tell it to, so no quick reactions are required, you can take your time planning.  To compensate, though, resources deplete much more quickly than most survival games in terms of how long it takes your characters to actually reach resources.  So you don't have to plan quickly, but you do have to plan WELL.
The other new mechanic introduced by the strategy aspect is that you're controlling an entire tribe of creatures rather than just a single creature.  The more creatures you have, the more you can accomplish in any given day.  This allows you to multitask.  The idea is that you can have a few creatures focused on gathering resources to outpace/match the rate that those resources are being depleted by the tribe as a whole, and if you can accomplish that, then you're free to send a spare creature or two to go exploring or doing something else entirely.  This is why resources deplete as quickly as they do, and it's why the game can get away with allowing creatures to die of old age--your goal isn't the survival of any individual creature, it's to keep a family going for as many generations as you can.
I feel like the game's also a bit like a roguelike in the sense that there is no way you can prepare for every situation the first time you play the game.  Other reviews have mentioned that the tutorial doesn't really explain very much, but I feel like that's intentional--part of the fun in roguelikes is dying in new and unexpected ways, so you know to plan for that your next time through, which allows you to last long enough to see a new enemy and die in ANOTHER new way you didn't expect.  Gradually, you organically develop your own personal strategies to account for all the different possible ways you can die.  You do it on your own, not because the game explained how to do it.
--------------------------
If you are totally okay with your creatures dying, then technically this game doesn't have any specific goals at all, at which point the "genetics" aspect becomes the central focus of the game.  Congratulations, you now have an edutainment title on your hands!
Except it's not really an edutainment title, because it's not meant to be 1-for-1 accurate to how genetics work in real life.  It's more meant to provide a big-picture simulation of how genetics influences survival, reproduction, and consequently evolution and/or death in real-world environments.  The genetics in this game are more about phenotypes than genotypes--and if you understood that statement without needing to look up the words, you probably understand genetics well enough that the way they work in the game will make sense to you.
If you DON'T know what genotypes are, then too bad, because the other reason this game isn't really an edutainment title is because it doesn't actually EXPLAIN any of this stuff to you.  If you're planning on interfacing with the genetics in this game in any meaningful way, you will need to come into this game with your own knowledge of certain concepts related to genetics, including (but perhaps not limited to):
1. How inheritance works
2. How mutations work
3. The difference between dominant and recessive genes
4. Why males have only one of a certain gene and females have two
If you don't know/care about any of these concepts, that's okay, you can probably still play this game as well as anyone else.  The reason for this is because, like in real life, you don't really have a whole lot of
over what the genetic makeup of your tribe is.  You can lean in certain directions, but ultimately you're limited to what's available.  The most effective way to introduce new genes to the pool is to look for creatures to mate with outside of your own tribe, and sometimes you have to take what you can get.  Otherwise, you're limited to sporadic (semi-controlled) mutations and inbreeding--which is a totally viable option if you don't mind halving your creatures' lifespans through autoimmune deficiencies.
All this is why I think the game doesn't totally work as a sandbox, though, because the game is too
to be a sandbox.  In something like the Sims, you have total control over what your character looks like, what their house looks like, who their parents, are, etc.  There is currently no game mode in Niche that lets you do that, and as far as I know, they're not planning to introduce one.  So there's no REAL way to play around and experiment to see the direct correlation between genetics and body makeup.  Instead, you're limited to the other half of the Sims, which poking around to get food, getting bored, and then goading your characters into dying in a variety of creative and horrible ways.
--------------------------
TL;DR: You may like this game if you are:
1. A gamer interested in survival and/or strategy games, and want to see a game that blends the two genres together.
2. A science-oriented person who already knows basically how genetics work, but wants to see how it practically functions and influences survival in nature.
Ideally, both of the above will apply to you to some extent.  If neither of these things appeals to you, you should probably give the game a pass.

Bethesda plying it's hand to horror, with Shinji Mikami at the helm, it looked like everything I had ever hoped for in a horror game. Expectations were high. Then it was released and I read the negative reviews with chagrin. My heart sank. And so I waited. I tried the demo and was... underwhelmed. Finally it went on sale for 8.49US and that seemed a reasonable risk. If nothing else, the atmosphere alone was worth the sale price.
This is one of those games that is difficult to recommend, but the aspects that I didn't like aren't quite enough to not recommend it. The atmosphere and graphics are genius, superbly well done. The gameplay however, is lackluster and often irritating. Instead of jump-scares, there are jump-murders. You may suddenly, without any warning or provocation, be killed. The game wants to teach you how not to get killed, by killing you repeatedly. While this is not new in games, and is even much lauded in some games, it is irritating here. The learning curve is made deliberately steep, and it is not an easy game to complete.
Complicating this aspect is the player movement mechanics, coupled with picky hit-boxes and quirky targetting for item interactions. Stealth is almost never a viable option, and renders the dev's assertions, that you can own your play-style, disingenuous. The game soon devolves into a run-n-gun, mash this button 400 times, cut-scene formula. My least favorite aspect is that the game takes over the camera far too often, making it feel as if you really have little control. It is almost a laughably absurd level of player control hijacking. I understand if the director has a vision and he just really wants you to experience it the way he intended, but it feels bullyish and invasive. This theory is backed by the fact that there are no settings to change the post-processing affects in the game. You see it the way it was intended, or not at all. These issues have been addressed in other reviews, but still, not enough to not recommend it.
Another aspect that has been addressed is the feeling of disconnected, disjointed levels. And the fact that this may be due to each level being an homage to other games, as if the game itself is a collection of Easter Egg levels. Many masterpieces of horror are given a nod here. While I do love the levels, it still leaves one feeling as if it's a puzzle with beautiful pieces that just don't fit together. While it may be an homage to past masters, it ends up feeling, more than anything, like Shinji Mikami's homage... to himself.
All in all, I have to recommend The Evil Within for hard-core horror fans, even if only for the atmosphere. That is were this game truly excells. And while I enjoyed immersing...basking...even bathing... in the environments for the very first time, the sum of all the little nit-picks prevent any desire to experience them a second time.
