So, like, I haven't played very far into Niche, but I feel like I have a pretty good handle on how the mechanics work in terms of how they're going to be read by the average gamer.
Basically, I think there's two ways you can look at the game.  You can look at it as a game that you play to achieve a specific goal, and you can look at it as a sandbox simulation of genetics.  As such, I've split my review into two parts, based on which perspective you're going for.
There's also a five-second TL;DR at the bottom if you REALLY want it, but I advise looking over the details before deciding on a purchase.
--------------------------
If you ask me to pick what this game's
genre is, it's definitely survival.  There is no goal in this game save surviving as long as possible, which is accomplished by wandering the wilds looking for food and fighting or avoiding hostile creatures.  Death not only comes easily, it is inevitable, since every creature has its own designated time-based lifespan which is visible on their HUD.  You have to be okay with dying.
However, in addition to survival, there's a fairly strong presence of the strategy genre here as well, and it's the main genre informing the game mechanics that make this game different from other survival games.  First, it's turn-based--time won't pass until you tell it to, so no quick reactions are required, you can take your time planning.  To compensate, though, resources deplete much more quickly than most survival games in terms of how long it takes your characters to actually reach resources.  So you don't have to plan quickly, but you do have to plan WELL.
The other new mechanic introduced by the strategy aspect is that you're controlling an entire tribe of creatures rather than just a single creature.  The more creatures you have, the more you can accomplish in any given day.  This allows you to multitask.  The idea is that you can have a few creatures focused on gathering resources to outpace/match the rate that those resources are being depleted by the tribe as a whole, and if you can accomplish that, then you're free to send a spare creature or two to go exploring or doing something else entirely.  This is why resources deplete as quickly as they do, and it's why the game can get away with allowing creatures to die of old age--your goal isn't the survival of any individual creature, it's to keep a family going for as many generations as you can.
I feel like the game's also a bit like a roguelike in the sense that there is no way you can prepare for every situation the first time you play the game.  Other reviews have mentioned that the tutorial doesn't really explain very much, but I feel like that's intentional--part of the fun in roguelikes is dying in new and unexpected ways, so you know to plan for that your next time through, which allows you to last long enough to see a new enemy and die in ANOTHER new way you didn't expect.  Gradually, you organically develop your own personal strategies to account for all the different possible ways you can die.  You do it on your own, not because the game explained how to do it.
--------------------------
If you are totally okay with your creatures dying, then technically this game doesn't have any specific goals at all, at which point the "genetics" aspect becomes the central focus of the game.  Congratulations, you now have an edutainment title on your hands!
Except it's not really an edutainment title, because it's not meant to be 1-for-1 accurate to how genetics work in real life.  It's more meant to provide a big-picture simulation of how genetics influences survival, reproduction, and consequently evolution and/or death in real-world environments.  The genetics in this game are more about phenotypes than genotypes--and if you understood that statement without needing to look up the words, you probably understand genetics well enough that the way they work in the game will make sense to you.
If you DON'T know what genotypes are, then too bad, because the other reason this game isn't really an edutainment title is because it doesn't actually EXPLAIN any of this stuff to you.  If you're planning on interfacing with the genetics in this game in any meaningful way, you will need to come into this game with your own knowledge of certain concepts related to genetics, including (but perhaps not limited to):
1. How inheritance works
2. How mutations work
3. The difference between dominant and recessive genes
4. Why males have only one of a certain gene and females have two
If you don't know/care about any of these concepts, that's okay, you can probably still play this game as well as anyone else.  The reason for this is because, like in real life, you don't really have a whole lot of
over what the genetic makeup of your tribe is.  You can lean in certain directions, but ultimately you're limited to what's available.  The most effective way to introduce new genes to the pool is to look for creatures to mate with outside of your own tribe, and sometimes you have to take what you can get.  Otherwise, you're limited to sporadic (semi-controlled) mutations and inbreeding--which is a totally viable option if you don't mind halving your creatures' lifespans through autoimmune deficiencies.
All this is why I think the game doesn't totally work as a sandbox, though, because the game is too
to be a sandbox.  In something like the Sims, you have total control over what your character looks like, what their house looks like, who their parents, are, etc.  There is currently no game mode in Niche that lets you do that, and as far as I know, they're not planning to introduce one.  So there's no REAL way to play around and experiment to see the direct correlation between genetics and body makeup.  Instead, you're limited to the other half of the Sims, which poking around to get food, getting bored, and then goading your characters into dying in a variety of creative and horrible ways.
--------------------------
TL;DR: You may like this game if you are:
1. A gamer interested in survival and/or strategy games, and want to see a game that blends the two genres together.
2. A science-oriented person who already knows basically how genetics work, but wants to see how it practically functions and influences survival in nature.
Ideally, both of the above will apply to you to some extent.  If neither of these things appeals to you, you should probably give the game a pass.

This game impressed the hell out of me. Though I'll admit, looking at the screenshots I was a little put off since it looks a bit cartoony. So pleased I decided to pull the trigger and buy it! There's actually a real challenge to trying to balance survival and continuation of your species with "good" genes.
The concept is rather simple on the surface: Reproduce and attempt to get the best genetic combinations possible through breeding without producing sickly offspring (deformed, inadaquate immune systems, etc) all while trying to find enough food to keep the herd going. There is definitely a taste of Spore involved, but unlike Spore where you do all the creating, Niche is almost like playing a cute virtual game of Gregor Mendel where instead of peas you're breeding (possibly) deadly creatures. Taking a page from Don't Starve, you do keep some of your genetic bloodline if your herd dies and you have to start over which allows you to have a bit of a headstart on subsequent playthroughs. Additionally, Each playthrough islands are precedurally generated so things stay interesting. Don't expect your first herd to survive forever.
Most importantly, watch out for derpy rogue guys perpetuating sexually aggressive culture (Steam censors the R word). It's a thing. It'll mess up your bloodlines and possibly your game if you let the offspring survive... For such a cute game on the surface, there's some REALLY messed up choices to be made.
Overall, this game has A LOT of replayability!

UPDATE: Seeing as Vermintide 2 has been announced and seemningly all DLC for this game has been released I have decided that I might as well take the time to update this little review. Gird your loins children, I've more to say!
If it's a quick summary of a review you're looking for scroll down to the bottom of this post.
I hate to say something along the lines of "Like Skyrim with Guns," but what you have with Vermintide is basically Left 4 Dead with a Warhammer skin. That is, of course, barring the fact that the weapons here are lore-friendly to the Warhammer universe. Rather than fully automatic rifles, snipers, etc. you got some neat magics and some satisfying guns.
Now this game being akin to the L4D franchise does not mean it is completely unoriginal, though it is pretty easy to make comparisons betwixt this game and the former. The two gamemodes you'll participate in are Missions and Survival. You might find survival a bit boring sadly, considering there are only two maps for it, one being DLC. Unlike L4D there is no Versus mode where players can actually control the Skaven and fight the heroes, which I think would be a rather dope addition. Let's not forget many of the special enemies you come across in Vermintide are like the ones from L4D.
Gutter Runners = Hunters
Rat Ogres = Tanks
Pack Masters = Somewhat like Jockeys
Globadiers = Spitters
The other two specials in this game, Stormvermin and Ratling Gunners, are luckily unlike the ones seen in L4D. The first of these two is a simple, heavily armoured oppenent who can be seen both amongst common Skaven, and in packs of 6 to 8 of it's own. The Ratling Gunner is a rat with a gatling gun (obviously). They fire their gun with reckless abandon without much regard for their fellow vermin, allowing a particularly cheeky player to use them to mow down hordes.
The fact this game is similar to L4D shouldn't deter you from buying it, it's not exactly a cheap carbon copy after all. However every rose has it's thorns, and this title is no exception. There are some exceedingly atrocious bugs in the game, the most glaring one causing players to disconnect after speeding up the game incredibly and freezing all enemies in place. On top of this you have your general balancing issues, like with the mages staffs. Furthermore you might find their to be a dearth of players, though I personally have not had this problem. You are certainly better off playing with friends, as playing with random strangers can sometimes prove difficult due to lack of communication and their potential to be pitiful morons. The AI isn't much better, mind you, sometimes lagging behind or playing pattycake with you, rather than reviving your sorry♥♥♥♥♥ Mind you, the AI will use whatever equipment the host has equipped on them in their own save game, which is pretty nice depending on the gear they have.
The devs may have taken some time to begin releasing DLC for this game, but the wait has proved well worth it. Each set of DLC missions have their own unique feel to them and feel fresh rather than being half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥cash-ins. These DLC give access to some pretty nice, new weapons for most of the gang (no love for Fuegonasus D: here). Sad to see that Fatshark did not expand much upon the Survival gametype, but game's missions make up for this in my opinion. Fatshark has also included some free content updates, such as contracts and the hardcore update.
Whether or not you should buy this game comes down to whether or not you have friends to play with. If so, go ahead with this purchase, you're not like to regret it. If you don't exactly have any friends or slavethings to play with then you may want to buy this game when it's on sale. This game will more than likely see a decrease in price with the release of Vermintide 2, but prepare for the community to move on.

Scrap Mechanic is one of those games you can't deny does what it's meant to do very well. Here are some PRO'S, CON's and CRITICISMS of the game Scrap Mechanic:
Pro's
-Very small download size (currently <1GB)
-Beautiful worlds and generally on-par-or-better visuals
-Innovative building mechanics that make combining simple machines into complex working constructions a breeze
-Online multiplayer
Con's
Before I start Cons I would like to mention the game is in early release and is continually being added to and improved
-World sharing and blueprint saving nonexistant
-Online multiplayer is limited to friends, no active public servers
-Multi funtion outputs are nonexistant (IE button 1 rotates left and button 2 rotates right)
-No form of "wireless" input available (you must be the driver/passenger to control the construction)
THAT BEING SAID:
For what I paid for Scrap Mechanic, and what it has delivered, I offer up this rating:
***********  8/10   *************
Endless possiblities with this engine and I'm looking forward to review this game after it has gone through some further development.

More than just a reskinned L4Dead clone. It blows it away. A very immersive first person combat experience. The hits/shots/magic feels very satisfying. The animations and overall graphics are very good. Its hard to find fault with its combat so far.
I guess the 3 main glaring flaws are firstly the lack of a real story. Despite the store page telling us you will "Experience an Immersive Story" Lets be honest. I would not count a single line pre mission and an extremely barebones explanation about what the hell you are doing even remotely anything like an immersive story. Secondly the lack of a tutorial or explanation for potions and some of the ingame concepts/aims. Lastly the loot system which is absolutely terrible and almost single handedly caused me to doubt my recommendation.
I will expand a bit on the loot system as its a big bone of contention with the community - The loot system is basically rng, each time you complete a mission depending on the collectibles picked up during the mission a number of dice are rolled and an item is allocated. The quality of the item is dependant on rng, difficulty level, and collectibles picked up.  This leads to a very grindy and punishing experience and lets down the core of the game itself which is a great combat system. They seem to be aware of this and have introduced a few systems to try to change it, a crafting system of sorts breaking down old or unwanted items to make new ones, a trinket which can ensure you get drops relating to the class you are playing if you equip it and recently a dlc featuring a quest type system which can reward gear for completing specific achievements and objectives. This is all going in the right direction and is welcomed.
Overall one of the better warhammer ip games for a good while. Great with a group of friends.
I can't comment on the state of random grouping as I do not bother. But I can imagine it proves difficult to manage some of the missions with only typed chat to communicate. It shines with voip and a few friends.
Recommended as a combat experience not in the slightest for its "immersive story"

My definition of a horror game should be that of immersion and story driven motivation to finish the game, and Layers of Fear accomplishes just that. I don’t care for those types of horror games that make you run from something, kill an enemy, or even give you the ability to fail. In this game, the only obstacle standing in your way is your curiosity. Driven by a need to find the next artifact, you are continuously guided from room to room, hallway to hallway, basement to attic, all with their different ambiance, feeling, and design. Your search of clues allows you to piece together a very intriguing, unique, and dark story that only aids in your continuation to finish. Along with a great soundtrack and visual appearance, Layers of Fear makes you feel as though you are undergoing the same psychological strain as the main character and genuinely freaks you out without having to make you feel challenged. I cannot wait for the next chapters to be released!

The Evil Within is an okayish game with lot of potential but unfortunately it has its weaknesses.
Pro:
+ The plot of this game is quite good. It felt like something new and innovative.
+ The gameplay feels like Resident Evil 4. You can upgrade your abilities and weapons the way you like.
+ There are 4 different difficulties.
+ Once you played through the game you can start a New Game+ with all your upgraded weapons.
+ The voice acting is okay. Sometimes the main character lacks emotion in his voice.
+ You visit a lot of different areas during the game and though it looks chaotic at first it makes sense in the end, trust me.
+ The achievements of the game are not too easy and not too hard to get.
+ One of the chapters gave me a really uneasy feeling. You feel like you are constantly haunted and you know someone is watching you. THIS is how horror games should be like. Further there is boss that is constantly hunting you down and that boss gave me the shivers!
Con:
- Though the story is innovative the producers fail to tell it in a proper way. They added some other plots around the main story and that felt totally misplaced and some characters made no real sense to me until i looked up there motives in the internet. Further you need goddamn DLCs to understand it completely -.-
- In my opinion there are way too many trial and error parts. You try something, you die, you start anew.
- There are too many enemies that kill you with one hit.
- There are too many traps. They are everywhere!
- Once you've completed 66% of the game the enemies learn how to use guns. This is so annoying and this happens in way too many zombie games. From that point forth the game turns into a wanna-be action game but it just doesnt work. The game failed at the last 33%.
- Sometimes it feels like the producers added some gameplay parts just for the sake of having them. For example you sit on a stationary machine gun for 20 seconds or you drive a car for 10 seconds. That was absolutely unnecessary...
- Do not upgrade Melee strength, this perk is totally useless. I don't know why they added this in the first place.
Steam offers this game for 60 bucks. The DLCs combined have a price of 25 bucks. Is the game worth that price? Absolutely NOT. I bought it on a sale for 8€ and that was totally okay. But 60... hahaha...hell no. All in all I'd still recommend it during a sale.

Y'know, I think this is the best "adult" video game I've ever played. That's not saying much. Most "adult" video games are either picture books with text boxes and boobs, or sloppily-thrown-together Breakout clones that reveal terrible artwork of boobs. This game though actually has a legitimately good puzzle game at its center with some fresh ideas that keep it interesting, actually good art, and pretty good voice-acting.
It also manages to treat its girls as respectfully as a game of this style possibly can. Instead of chasing after virgin barely-legal never-been-kissed high-school girls, your dates are WOMEN. Worldly, experienced, aggressive women who are more than capable of deciding what they do and who they want to do it with, and who are the aggressors when it comes time for the erotica to start. They're not exceptionally deep, there's simply not enough story in the game for them to feel well-rounded, but for as little development as they get, they're pretty solid.
To top this off, you actually have the option of playing as a woman yourself, which comes complete with a lot of spoken dialogue changes. Unfortunately it doesn't give you a selection of men to flirt with (it is still a low-budget indie game after all), but it smoothly transitions its cast into lesbians. You could argue that this is to serve men's lesbian-lusts, and it's a fair point, but I'm sure it'll still be welcome for any women who choose to play it.
I see a lot of poeple comparing the puzzles to "Bejeweled", but it feels more akin to "Puzzle Quest" to me. Simply throwing together any matches you see willy-nilly will not get you very far in the game, foresight and strategic thinking, planning several steps ahead, are pretty much requirements once you get past about the halfway point. There's also a dating-sim in here, but it's so stripped-down that it barely feels like a dating sim. Even the items you can buy are marked as to whether a girl likes it or not, rendering the process of getting to know them pointless. Maybe this is for the best, though, as even with the streamlined Dating-sim process, it starts to get tiresome fairly quickly, with the puzzles definately taking center stage.
Overall I love this game, both for what it does right and for what it tried to do right and didn't quite achieve. I want to see more legitimate video game erotica, that combines GOOD gameplay with tasteful eroticism. The "tasteful" part is open to personal opinion, of course, but for me it basically means portraying the relationship as being on equal grounds, which it is here, with the sole exception of one hidden character who is crammed with so many Japanese tropes that she's practically a parody.
Let's hope you can kick this genre into high gear, Developers, because you did a pretty good job of it here.

The horror comes from knowing that -- when you get one-shotted because you got stuck on an obstacle you couldn't see due to the camera position or because you were facing 2 degrees off-centre from the switch you needed to pull -- the inconsistent autosave will probably mean having to replay a whole section of killing minions, smashing crates, and watching an unskippable 10-second cutscene of a door opening before you can even get back to the boss who will instantly kill you again if you get too close.  Honestly, the only feeling of dread in this game is wondering how long it's been since the last save as you watch your character's umpteenth gruesome death animation.
I don't mind challenging games.  I like the sparse ammo in this kind of survival horror genre that forces you to place your shots carefully, or look for alternatives.  (I also thought the visuals and general mood -- at least the first time through each section -- were outstanding.)  But the challenge here comes primarily from the picky, sluggish controls and the restrictive camera.  Even just picking an item up off the floor requires precision aim, made worse by the fact that when your character breaks open a container he lunges past it, so that you have to turn around to find any item that may have been inside.
And, speaking of item crates, this game commits the classic game sin of penalising you for trying to role play the character you are given.  Often the game or NPCs tell you to move to a goal urgently, but if you do so instead of examining every dark corner and breaking open every container, you'll miss out on myriad much-needed upgrade items, because almost every single time you go through a big door, it slams behind you and you're forever cut off from that part of the game, with the autosave annoyingly deciding that *now* -- and not just before a boss fight -- is the best time for it to take action.
If you like playing sections of a game over and over (and over) because the game actively fought your commands, this may be the game for you.  Otherwise, steer clear.

This is kind of a sad negative review. I have been following the game for a while and was waiting on it exiting EA to get the full experience. After the long wait, I was pretty disappointed. The tutorial was abyssmal, you learn nothing but the absolute basics, it doesn't teach you what any icons mean or do, it doesn't teach you how to manipulate the genes besides "Mate these two".
You have an entire dna helix representing the presumably predisposed genes the animal has but with no background on what they mean or how to manipulate them, short of seeing that you are likely to have offspring with bad or slightly less bad eyesight/hearing/smell/strength/etc and if its +0, +1, or +2 to an attribute.
Ultimately the gene choices mean nothing, they make VERY little impact on the actual game. It is incredibly slow paced and boring. You can decide to fight, forrage etc. but, they are all literally the same. Wanna be warriors? Try to manipulate genes to give you attack power, click on an enemy and that's it. Forrage? Exact same thing, find a nut/berry bush/clam/etc. click on the icon and that's it.
Take the term strategy VERY lightly, as there is very little. You just blindly wander through a map looking for other npcs to mate or kill and that's about it. There is no strategy to speak of, find someone that you will get killed by, run away. Find something you can kill but, can't offer to join your tribe, kill it. The game lacks depth.
One of the very interesting ideas the game put forth was senses, you can choose to perceive your surroundings using sight, hearing, and smell. They allow you too "see" different things. Sight will let you see things like acorns on the ground, smell and hearing let you see other animals in the bushes, and so on. The downside however, the is virtually no reason to use sight, tall grass renders it pretty useless and it's way easier to just use sound or hearing as not only does it let you "see" through things like grass, it by default gives you a larger range to "see". Which is unfortunate as the game is actually quite nice to look at when you can see the vibrant colors and details, all of which you miss in the superior hearing/smelling modes.
There are not a lot of genetic mutations to unlock, and a vast majority of them are strictly cosmetic and add nothing to the game.
This could have been a much better and deeper game and might very well be with updates but, as it stands now fully released with very little depth, an atrocious tutorial for a game with very unobvious mechanics, and generally boring gameplay I cannot recommend buying this game.
Take the vast amount of positive reviews with a grain of salt, as the majority of them are staunch Niche supporters and have been playing well into EA and are pretty biased. It won't break the bank to buy, or try by any means but, there are much better games to shell your money out for.

I got Niche a year or two ago, and it's been one of my favorite games since. It's a great turn-based strategy game and, although it may not be everyone's cup of tea, I recommend buying it.
Pros:
1: You can replay it as much as you want without getting bored with the game. Every time you start a new game, it's different. You can give your creatures personalities and a story, unlock achievements (some of them are really hard, for those of you looking for a challenge!!), get the weirdest genes possible, or you can see how long you can survive in a world that is constantly changing.
2: It has an amazing, supportive, and extremely helpful community. Not only that, but the developers are incredibly helpful and invested in what their community has to say: It really is a wonderful thing to see developers working with their community to improve the game.
3: There are tons of genes you can unlock for your creatures! From prehistoric genes to underwater breathing abilities, there's a type of animal for every person waiting to be created. (you can even make hybrids!)
4: There are countless islands of varying difficulties and sizes to explore, and hidden creatures in them waiting to be invited into your pack. Once you start a game in one of the islands, you can still move to another island with travel ports. (but be warned!! if you make creatures suited for the snow and go to a savanna, chances are you won't last very long. thankfully, the ports have different colors and designs so you can tell which one you're about to go to.)
5: There's a sandbox mode and a storymode, both of which have tons to explore. In sandbox mode, you can choose which island you want to start off on and you have randomized creatures. In storymode, you start with Adam, who is lost and looking to come back to his old home. Storymode is recommended for new players because it's also the tutorial. I would go into greater detail, but then it'd spoil the story for you, and I'm not going to do that. ;)
Cons:
1: There are very short lifespans. While the short lifespans (only around 20 in game turns) provide more of a challenge and can be exciting, it also makes it harder to get attached to certain creatures before they die. You can still get attached (and then it's heartbreaking when they die!!) but you don't miss the creature as much when you lose them as you might if you had more time with them.
2: At the beginning of each game, you have two starter creatures: One male and one female. (used to be called Adam and Eve but now have randomly generated names.) When you start a game, you have to cross your fingers because you have no idea how your starters will be. They could have extremely bad genetics, or incredibly good ones. It's all about luck, and I only consider it a con because it can create an unexpected challenge.
All in all, I think it's a great game and recommend it to anyone who likes strategy, genetics, and cute animals.

This is exactly how an online STALKER game should be. It needs work, but it nails the atmosphere and style which is unique to that universe.
Your character is of no significance at all.  No world saving or god-slaying heroes here, just you and your crappy AK against hordes of mutants, deadly environmental anomalies, and fellow scavengers.  I'll run through what's good, what's bad, and what could be improved.
The Good:
-Atmosphere:  Mostly cloudy days running through abandoned towns, old factories and railway stations, with not much more than the sounds of nature to accompany you is in line with how STALKER is supposed to be.
-PvP + PvE:  There aren't strict divisions between PvP and PvE;  rather, you can opt to turn on PvP at any time using an icon in the upper left, which will change the color of your name and render you vulnerable to other players' weapons.  PvP is automatically turned on, however, if the total worth of your inventory/gear exceeds a certain threshold, which I think is a great way to put you in the mindset of a scavenger among other scavengers - you don't want to have your most valuable stuff with you for too long and around too many people, lest they try to take it from you.  Killing other players within sight of town guards/NPC's will net you a negative reputation temporarily, meaning players who get too trigger happy find themselves losing out on certain conveniences for a time.  There's also a PvP arena with different modes similar to the multiplayer in the actual STALKER games, with rewards even for when you lose.
-Quests:  There are an ungodly number of quests, and while they can be difficult, I've yet to run into more than one or two which explicitly required a team of people.  Rewards are usually shown before the quest is completed, meaning you can make more effective decisions about how to use your time, and you rarely get surprised with a bad reward for a hard quest.  Some involve a LOT of traveling, though, which can wear on you a bit.
-Maps:  They're gigantic.  Lots of places to explore, with randomly-generated, respawning loot, as well as valuable artifacts if you choose to investigate anomalies.  It is not hard to make a lot of money outside of questing, if you learn where to look.
-The Community:  It's weird to say this is good when the dominant quality of the community is indifference.  People don't seem to communicate much, and when they do it's usually very short and to the point, but it's so fitting with how STALKER works that I see it as a plus for the game.  You'll get used to aiming first and asking questions second, as you never know who might decide to pull the trigger and rob you.  And  yes, you can get robbed.  That said, helping people goes a long way, and you build trust more by actually doing something rather than talking to someone.
The Bad
-Sounds:  Sound quality is fairly basic, and some of it doesn't work consistently.  Music plays in some locations but is apparently so specific to a location that it just cuts out when you move.  Monsters make noise, but you can only really hear them when they're on you, meaning you could have a small horde of them chasing you and not actually know it until you've been gored and left for dead.  It's highly annoying sometimes when you're exploring only to be killed without so much as the sound of a footstep for warning.
-Aggro distance:  Sometimes a monster sees you and comes after you in a way which totally makes sense.  Sometimes they show up almost out of nowhere and kill you in one hit.  Sometimes they kill you, leave, and when you respawn show up from some crazy distance away to gnaw on you again.  Combine that with the lack of audio indicating their presence, and you'll feel like you're getting cheap-shotted a LOT.  "Verliokas" are especially terrible about this - they make no noise, travel very quickly, and will aggro from insane distances in places where you can't see anything.
-Graphics:  The graphics are dated and have some issues here and there.  Textures flicker, sometimes whole sections of the map won't load (you have to quit and restart to remedy that, I've found).  The aesthetic is spot on, it's more that it just looks old and the performance doesn't quite match what you'd expect from what you're seeing.  It performs smoothly for the most part, but some locations lag like crazy for reasons I can't grasp.
-Stats and Mechanics:  It's not that things here are broken, more that there's little explanation as to how different things work, and the requirements for raising skills are crazy even when you specialize in something.  You spend experience points to get specialization points, which are then used to unlock skills, but the "exchange rate" for these can get insane quickly.  The upshot is that you receive EXP for practically everything you do (you can gain quite a lot by opening a rare loot box or by eating a large meal early on), but it doesn't feel like it means much when you can't use it for anything for a looooong time.
-Pay-to-Win:  While the paid items usually have a time limit, their being available at all means PvP in some areas is ridiculous without paid gear.  PvE doesn't suffer much from this, as even with some of the best gear you can still get completely wrecked if you're not paying attention, but if you're big on the arena, you'll be investing some real money to stand a fighting chance.  I will say though, in comparison to a lot of other pay-to-play schemes, you do get a lot for what you buy.  Things like experience and stat buffs are very cheap (a 2-hour EXP rate buff is 6 cents, for example), and almost all of the paid gear has a limited time of use.  Permanent benefits come more in how you can accumulate different items and sell them off for lots of in-game money, which while not exactly the best, could be (and is, in many p2p schemes) worse.
Overall:  It's worth it if you're a big fan of STALKER.  If you're not, you'll find this to be a difficult game that's really tough on you from the get-go, without much in the way of a payoff until a long ways into it.  You do NOT need to pay anything to get far - if you are adventurous and remember to mark valuable spots on your map, you can easily make money to get good gear without ever dropping a cent.  Outside of the arena, PvP is done in a way which I think suits the type of game extremely well, where your personal wealth affects others' perception of you as well as having PvP mode as a punishment for shooting people in major areas.  It fits, and that's what I think is most important - Szone FEELS like STALKER, and STALKER was all about feeling like you were in a weird place.
Feedback:  Sounds for creatures would be tremendously helpful and add to the realism a lot.  While animals and mutants do make noise, they need to be heard from a greater distance, if only because it's ridiculous that a bunch of them can gang up on you without you hearing anything.  Very, VERY annoying.  Ambient audio and music needs work too, as they're not  very consistent in, well, being present.  A better explanation of mechanics, via a more comprehensive guide than the forums would be great too, as there's a lot of numbers but not a lot of info as to what they really mean (one assumes higher = better, but one also wants to know by how much different amounts affect things).

So, now I'll be that guy who writes a serious review of a porn game. Because make no mistake -- that's what this is. The cutesy art style in the sample screenshots may deceive you, but as the game progresses, it becomes quite explicit. If you're not comfortable with that, stay away --  and probably don't buy this for your kids. It is, however, as wholesome as a porn game can get; there is no violence and no coercion, no "bad ends" or gruesome situations. It's just purely consentual, happy encounters and positive outcomes.
In gameplay terms, it's simple and repetitive, but fairly fun. It's basically a match-three game with a rudimentary dating sim tacked on to the front, but with none of the (rather arbitrary and frustrating) mechanics dating sims often suffer under. There are no lose conditions in this game; you can fail at individual puzzle boards and botch sim interactions, but there's no way to lose the game entirely, nor is there any way to screw up your relationship with any of the girls such that you can't just try again tomorrow. Each of the girls (there are several) has her own likes and dislikes, and must be appropriately courted with gifts and flattered with question responses in order to unlock her outfits and hairstyles. Meanwhile, you can also ask them out on dates, which brings you to a match-three board. Completing the board increases that girl's affection for you, and brings you that much closer to the explicit scenes.
The actual sex scenes are, strangely enough, also match-three puzzles, but these are of the "speed matching" variety, and are easily the most annoying thing in the game. The pleasure meter drains
rapidly that strategy becomes next to impossible; mainly, you have to grab and drag whatever you can as fast as you can, or you'll lose all the progress you've made. Still and all, it doesn't appear to be possible to fail at these -- in extremis, your meter will drain all the way back to zero and you have to start over again.
The game has, as the screenshots above demonstrate, a definite anime art style. It's fairly well executed, though entirely static -- there is no animation anywhere in the game. By default, the game is also censored, though the developer has made available a patch that removes the censors; be aware that the uncensored images are
explicit, so don't use the patch if you aren't comfortable with that.
The "abrasive western writing style" certainly is quite abrasive. The dialogue consists of annoying internet memes, distrssingly on-the-nose faux-cool talk, and swearing. Lots of swearing. Call me old-fashioned -- or, not to put too fine a point to it, just plain
-- but I don't appreciate the girls in this game all cursing like sailors all the time. It's not just one or two "edgy" characters, either; all of the girls are rather foul-mouthed. It's rather a shame; if a bit more work had been done on writing decent text rather than just internet in-jokes and foul language, it would have done wonders to improve the experience. There is, after all, quite a lot of dialogue.
There is voice acting. It is exactly as bad as you expect. Fortunately, there is a quite simple way to disable it, and you even have the option of replacing it with "bloops" so the dialogue boxes aren't purely silent.
Overall, this game is worth your ten dollars if you like match three games and porn. If either of those things is not to your taste, then give it a miss.

Developed by the makers of Magika, Arrowhead, The Showdown Affect is a side-scrolling, action movie inspired online multiplayer brawler. I saw the trailer for this game before it was released and thought it looked really fun and seeing it scored only a 67 on metacritic puzzled me a bit. The Showdown Effect is not a bad game, but it's metacritic rating is deserved.
On the up side, The Showdown Effect does deliver the action they advertise in the video so if you watched the trailer and thought it looked fun chances are you will enjoy it somewhat at the very least. The gameplay is only average though and I feel like the developers spend more time and energy on the game's theme.
There are microtransactions in this game but they appear to be exclusively cosmetic and game changing unlocks cannot be purchased with currency in anyway. I am still a little bit offended that microtransactions were introduced to this retail game.
What's lacking in this game is any longevity. My impression is that after you got your chuckles from the theme and played a few rounds you've seen all the game has to offer. There are additional characters to unlock but they are largely all the same with the exception of a single special ability.
In my two hours of gameplay I did experience a few non-crashing bugs - weapons not reloading when they should and my screen blanking out a few times.
The Showdown Effect is an exclusely multiplayer game so unless you can find people to play online then this game is effectively useless. There is no bot matches or local multiplayer to speak of. I was able to find matches for about 2 hours but they were pretty slim and my session with this game was ended due to the lack of populated servers.
Even though it's a pretty reasonable game, I can't recommend getting this because as gameplay goes it only average and there's no guarantee this game won't soon be a client with no server to connect to.

Ok, here goes: This is a game made for mobile and sloppily tossed onto pc in an attempt to please a screaming crowd of deus ex fans wanting to be able to play the game on computers, and it's quite evident in its content (or lack thereof).
The game looks.. OK for the most part. The character models suffered the most, while the environment is close to deus ex: HR which this game obviously borrowed most of its assets from. Even the soundtrack is the exact same as in HR, which collides a little bit with the whole idea of bringing a unique sound depending on the setting or city the players find themselves in.
There are still a lot of augmentations to choose from, but the casie-mod has been dumbed down to simply activating it to win a conversation. Merchants have been completely removed, making you unable to sell the stuff you pick up, and instead replaced with a menu from which weapons, items and ammo can be directly bought.
Inventory space is also gone, allowing you to carry several metric tons of crap without having to drop anyting.
During my playthroughs I also encountered some frustrating bugs.
The most common is the horribly unresponsive "E" key for picking up small items or choosing a dialogue option.
If you see a little energy-bar or credit-chip anywhere on the map, you need to make sure there are no NPC's nearby, since the game assumes you're activating them instead of the item you want. You will find yourself spamming the E-key when trying to pick something up.
There is also the chance of enemies you've taken down falling into walls, making it impossible to get the stuff they drop.
In a few locations you can even takedown an enemy from a floor below if your position is right.
Like countless reviewers have said before me, this game is amazing on mobile, but severly lacking on pc.
The animations are stiff, making it difficult to connect with the characters because of the primitive movements, and character models are repeated as much, if not even more, as in the original deus ex from 17 years ago.
The game teases you with more locations in its opening scene, like Australia and New York, but all you get is a quick tutorial level, a miniscule plane flashback-mission and Panama city which serves as the main hub for the first (and only) act of the game.
That being said, the voice acting is quite alright, and has the original actors return to their roles of characters such as Namir and Barrett.
The different variations of weapons is also a plus, having 3 models (or reskins) of pistols and crossbows
If you head into this game thinking it's gonna be like DX:HR in all aspects, you'll find yourself dissappointed.
DO NOT purchase for the full 10-dollar price tag. At this point with the lacking content, it's a robbery.

The Evil Within is a highly cinematic third person action/horror game. It does a great job at making you feel as though you've already played it. Just give me a moment. It feels like every game you have ever played. It's Resident Evil, it's Eternal Darkness, it's Bioshock, it's Dead Space, it's F.E.A.R. and Saw simultaneously. This is not an inherently BAD thing or ideology for game development studios to adopt. It just lacks, for want of a better term, valor.
The Evil Within is fun, it's nerve racking it's... familiar; and it has all the bells and whistles of a modern “triple A” title. I enjoyed my time, I honestly like the game but there is something missing which leads me into this next bit.
I understand that the video game industry is new and budding, at least comparatively to other forms of media; and I hate this mentality of big budget games having to be these cookie cutter pristine must follow each bullet point to the T sort of endeavors. I realize however that precisely because these big budget titles are so costly and take so much time that it is near impossible for proper business practice to try something completely off the wall.
Which is why we see the rise of the indie developer; between free engines, a programmer, writer and an artist can (CAN is important) build worlds, write stories that stick with you. Things that make you think afterward. Things that make you wonder about things in a way you didn't before. Most triple A games today are fun, they work, they give you a nice good happy fun time. But for me; these experiences are fleeting. As with going out to the theater, you've spent a lot more time and money than it took to watch at home and yet what you end up taking away from the experience of seeing the film is more likely; who you saw at the theater, how the traffic was and why was that person laughing so loud.
What I mean to say is nothing new is emerging for triple A games. They have become this amorphous cloud of I already know what this is but I'm going to do it anyways and pretend its new sentiment.
Anyways back on point.
The Evil Within is a very enjoyable game. You collect green gel, which I lovingly referred to as brain juice the entire game, which can be spent at a very ominous chair reminiscent of the early days of studying mental health.
The game is broken into chapters. I've reached just over 1000 hours, I think it's time I do a well thought through review... wow, 1000. Probably stanard for an MMO title.
Anyways, I will divide this review into 4 different sections: do not expect this to be a short read.
1) Summery
2) Gameplay, the good and the bad.
3) Social - MMO aspects, the good and the bad.
4) Summery of review.
Summery of the game:
Star Trek Online is a F2P (Free to Play) MMO which uses the Star Trek I.P. to it's full advanage.
Over the years special guests have reprised their roles through voice-acting, these include, the most recent apperences:
1) Tim Russ - Tuvok (ST: Voyager).
2) Michael Dorn - Wolf (ST: The Next Generation).
3) Denise Crosby - Tasha Yar, Commander Sela (ST: The Next Generation).
The first FULL expansion was "Lecgacy of Romulus" (free download). This indroduced a new UI, the famous Trek L.C.A.R.S, not only that, but it's been designed specifically to match the current 3 faction's style; Federation, Klingon, Romulan.
The latest Season, Season 8/8.5 has introduced quick-equip and starship swaping. These are one of the great features the game offers for convenience. Also, a new enemy; Voyager's - The Voth.
Things to expect for the future of STO after this review:
1) More voice-acting.
2) Another expansion.
3) New content.
4) Re-vamped missions.
5) More special events.
Gameplay:
The Good:
1) Space combat is probably the most enjoyable asspect of combat.
2) Different styles of gameplay: Tactical, Eng, and Science. Each with "different roles".
3) Long line up of solo or teamed "story-arc" missions.
The Bad:
1) Ground combat can be a bit repetitive sometimes.
2) Some dilithium currency requirements for speical projects can be tedious with a standard refine rate of 8000 per day, if you hit that amount of course anyways.
However. Once you gain enough dilithium e.g. over 30k unrefined dilithium, refining 8000 per day doesn't become so bad of a task to complete.
3) Zen. Technically everything is "free" however, if you wish to have more space in your storage then you'll need some Zen points. These cost real money however, Zen can be exchanged for in-game dilithium.
Tip: Once reached level 50, buy a 1 month gold subcribition; you'll unlock all possible extra spaces for bank, inventory and get 500 free Zen, an extra character slot, plus an account bank of 20 slots to trade certain items and "Enery Credits" between your characters. You can also save Zen and buy extra slots for your bank or incenrory on top of that too.
4) PVP (player versus player), PVP needs to be revamped. At the time of this review I've heard that a PVP revamp is in the works, but currently most of your main gameplay will be PVE (player versus enemy/A.I.). Meanwhile, dedicated chat channels and the odd chance of a PVP match are available.
Social - MMO aspects:
The Good:
1) If you want to be social, you can be social. If you'd prefer not to, then you don't have to.
2) At least 95% of the playerbase are more than welcome to new players. Kind and helpful. You might get the odd one out but they are usually "butt-hurt" about a certain thing.
3) You can join a Fleet (MMO - Guild) to contribute to joint player projects of that fleet to gain access to higher-leveled gear and ships.
4) Social Zones can be a great way to talk to other players about recent news, in either a dedicated chat channel or zone-wide.
Many iconic social zones are from Star Trek lore; these include:
1) Vulcan.
2) Earth Space Dock.
3) Deep Space Nine.
4) Qo'noS.
5) Bajor.
6) Deep Space Station K-7.
5) "Adventure Zones" such as New Romulus, Nukara Prime, Deferi, The Dyson Sphere, are zones with repeatable joint-player missions where you'll help out other players, as well as yourself achieve objectives to gain rewards. These can be a great way to team up with friends and play together.
6) Role-play. Well yeah, you can do that. It's completely up to you who you wish to be or become. There can be some breaking immersion moments but other than that, it's pretty good.
The Bad:
1) Some iconic social zones, especially the now dated ones, can become very empty. This is due to new content "pushing" players to move forward into new areas and zones. From my knowing at the time of this review, a re-vamp of Earth Space Dock (which isn't very empty at all) is on the drawing board, one can assume other zones are too.
Summery of review;
Star Trek Online continues the story from Romulus destruction. This is the "prime" universe Trek. The game rewards you for your time, but if you wish to get the goodies quick and fast then be prepeared to pay a little bit of cash. I would recomend a one month gold account and then cancel after it's finished. The special guest appearences are very cool and are very welcomed which everytime makes the game feel even more and more like a trek universe.
Shame currently there's no William Shatner, Patrick Stewart, Kate Mulgrew or Scott Bakula voice-overs. Thankfully though, there's the legendary Leonard Nimoy!
Zen is probably the most hardest 'grind' to gain if you're completely F2P, like myself, I've occasionally paid a small amount to obtain extra bank slots etc and have became very helpful. I do this as thanks after a new season or piece of new content I've enjoyed.
I hope this review has been helpful. If I sound slightly biased towards the game, then that is due to the enjoyment it has brought and the entertainment it brings. If I could give it a rating, I'd say:
8.5/10.

There's plenty of things going for Layers of Fear. Stunning graphics (you explore a beautiful old mansion, put together in what must be loving detail), gorgeous musical soundtrack, and a story that is intriguing, if not somewhat predictable at this early stage of the game. Unfortunately, the mechanics it uses to scare you just aren't that great. Instead of building slowly on what could have been the creeping dread of the environment, you get lengthy sequences of exploration before something jumps in your face, appears behind you, makes a loud noise or flies off a shelf. While there are interesting sequences of the environment changing and warping to reflect the main character's state of mind, these don't seem to follow much of a theme outside some paint-related effects (to reflect the PC is a painter) and perhaps some of the warping meant to represent a state of drunkenness (to reflect the PC is a drunk) and so become a bit dull after a while. At its core, the game is a trek through a jump scare house. As a result of it being the Alpha, there is currently no ending (you just get a "Thanks for Playing" and note to wait for more), so there's some hope that perhaps the developers will expand further on the experience. If that's the case and there is more thought given to the scare mechanics and atmopshere, I'll happily try again and do another review. There's certainly something beautiful here, but that alone just isn't enough.

If you've played Majesty, then this game and its mechanics won't be foriegn to you. If you haven't, then the game may feel strange and difficult to understand. The premise is that you, the "King" do not directly control the Heroes in the game. Each camp that you build (Rangers, Warriors, Thieves, Wizards, Clerics along with Dwarves and Elves in certain scenerios) allows you to recruit 3 of that class. Upgrading the camp gives you certain bonus abilities to the class, and some directly to you. Since you don't control the Heroes directly, you have to use Rewards (in Gold) to influence where the Heroes explore, avoid, or with bounties, kill something. That's the basic gist of what made Majesty so fun, and what should make this sequel fun as well.
HOWEVER...
This game is ridiculously hard. Not impossibly hard, but there are times when you have to slow down, take a break, and seek a different solution to some enemies. As you build up your settlement with camps, the peasants will build houses, and with that comes the sewers, which place vermin (rats, ratmen, and such) directly into your town. Guard towers help, by allowing a Guardsman to patrol and hopefully attack said vermin, but you'll need to place the towers in overlapping COI (Circles of Influence) to have a really good patrol of guards. The guard towers increase in price as you build them, so it does get costly early on. Once a Hero dies, you then spawn a graveyard in town, which spawns undead, so that's yet another threat to try and maintain control of, as it can rapidly escalate and detroy your camps and castle if you aren't careful.
The biggest problem with this game is the (as yet, unsolved on steam) broken Internet detection for the DLCs. Majesty had a really simple story, but Majesty 2 seems to have went for a more episodic mission line, and left connections to previous missions out. It seems that there isn't any connection to the DLCs as such, so you'll be playing the game for the gameplay, not the story. It doesn't really subtract from the game, though, since there isn't really any "lore" for the game anyway.
As of this review, I haven't played any of the expansions yet. The main game is entertaining and fun, and appeals to my love of solving puzzles, each mission having multiple ways of doing so. I highly recommend this game, but with the expansion issue in mind, I'd wait for a steam sale or discounts to purchase it, until steam fixes the DLC issue.

The mission designs for this game are mind bogglingly aweful. After the initial maps (which are enjoyable), you are placed into scenarios where you will have multiple enemy spawn points within view of your keep and they WILL spawn monsters before you get your first building completed. You will attempt to get buildings erected but your pesants will get killed (slowing or stopping construction), or the buildings will be attacked (slowing down or destroying your construction and wasting your gold), your tax collectors will get killed as they make their rounds (delaying or halting your income), and your heroes will constantly get mobbed (forcing them to hide in the guild hall for healing and be ineffective, or they'll die), dead heroes cause a graveyard to spawn nearby (which also spawns more monsters), etc...
Administrative style games (where you do not have direct control of your units) requre a build up phase to allow a player to prepare for threats. Especially because a player is unable to directly send the heroes to address threats at a moments notice. Using the flags and bounty system to incentivize your heroes takes money from your coffers and only works if you make the bounty large enough to grab their attention. Setting bounties, of course, hinders your ability to build essential infrastructure.
The issues that this game has is not a matter of lack of player skill. There is very poor balancing in the game's economy and combat systems. There are some well concieved scenarios in the first third of the game where you are under constant pressure and the challenge is intense and enjoyable. However, in other scenarios where the waves of enemies constantly intensify, your base's capabilities will palteau and eventually crumble, but the enemy will not plateau. When this is combined with a scenario that causes you to constantly struggle to build and keep two or three buildings standing, you end up with a frustrating and disappointing experience.
Unfortunately, it takes more than two hours to find this out, so a refund is off the table. My time with Magesty 2 makes me wonder if the devs actually had the game playtested it to understand exactly what kind of play experience they were actually creating. The genere is one of my favorites, the gameplay can be at times enjoyable, but there is too much in this game that is not enjoyable.
I recommend not buying this one.

I'm going to be blunt.  This game was made to be a mobile game, unfortunately the mobile version sucked due to crashing all the time so the PC port is great.  The graphics aren't amazing, but they aren't awful by a longshot.  The best thing I can suggest is plug yourself a 360 controller, or PS3 as the case may be, in and play it like a console game.  With an actual controller it's a good game, the controls are simple due to it being a mobile game originally... but once you get used to it, it's a pretty decent addition to the Deus Ex franchise.

For starters, go in knowing that it's a port of a mobile game and you'll be much better off. I'm not sure how more touched up it is (if at all) compared to that version but still keep that in mind.
Anyway, this game feels very much like diet Human Revolution; it's not as big, pretty, or challenging, but it still retains the spirit of that game in a compact package. The graphics are decent and capture the HR style well. There's quite a bit of dialogue, a good number of augmentations, and the controls for a 360 controller are well-done. (I haven't played with M+KB so I'm not sure how that is)
My only real gripe with the game is that it's fairly short and feels like it ends somewhat abruptly. Again, since it's a mobile game, I'm not too surprised on the length, but the execution could've been better or more climactic.
With all that said, I recommend this game for fans of the series who are looking for a fun spin-off title with a different protagonist. To everyone else, I would say play this after playing the other games so you can (hopefully) become a Deus Ex fan and look at this with a different viewpoint.

Now, I backed this game on Kickstarter in early 2016, and have been playing some form of it since then, from a rough early access test version made available before it hit Steam all the way up to it's official release today (Sept. 21, 2017).
Over the course of that I watched the game and community as a whole grow. The developers have created an amazingly inclusive community. They've demonstrated in multiple ways their willingness to cater to their players and their sincerity in accomplishing their promises to the best of their abilities.
In regards to the gameplay itself: personally, I adore it. The general breakdown of the game is that you start with two randomly generated adorable little Nichelings on a small island with very few dangers and plenty of food.
You breed your founders to grow your group, and sometimes find random wanderers to join you. Meanwhile you're deciding which members to breed together, what kind of nose is the best (or the cutest) what kind of feet you want, what kind of tail, what color, what pattern.
Do you want them to crack nuts? Do you want them to catch fish? Or do you want it to be so beefy they can smash rocks?
Then you eventually move on to another island to try and adapt and survive there, constantly evolving to new enviorments.
The freedom you have in creating a genetically unique and intricate tribe is so much fun.
(Currently my group of little dudes are rainbow colored with skunk tails and snake fangs)
All that being said, the game is quite slow-paced and intricate, with a considerable learning curve on the UI.
There's a good tutorial storymode available though, and it's pretty efficient for how much information you're given, and how much control you have over your group's genetics.
Overall, I highly recommend this game ^.^

This game obviously has a lot of promise, so please take this as a very tentative "thumbs down". The game just feels too.. small, or bare-boned at the moment to be a full release at 17$.
When you start a new game, you have either the option of playing "story" or "sandbox" mode. I highly recommend playing story mode if you are new to the game, because it's actually more of a tutorial than a story mode (almost should be labeled "tutorial" instead of "story), which leaves sandbox mode as the main focus of the game. The tutorial does seem fairly lacking in explaining many of the game functions as well, which I believe should be addressed at some point. An example of this is how to pass on dominant/recessive genes, or how to use mutations, I have not seen anywhere in-game where this is explained.
The sandbox mode allows you to choose from among a fairly large amount of maps, which is great. However, it does not give you an option to pre-set any of your starting creature attributes, which are instead decided through sheer RNG (randomly). This feels like a HUGE feature to be left out. You can just restart over and over until you get a specific starting attribute that you were hoping for (I.E. horns, digging claw, etc.). It would also be great if there were at least 1-2 more body types to choose between, maybe something bipedal, or the option to begin in the sea and evolve legs eventually. Something to hope for in the future, I suppose.
Another feature that I feel should have been included is a difficulty setting for younger, or less experienced players. Something requiring less food per turn, less predators or longer creature life. Any custom settings at all would have been nice, in fact. I realize that the map you choose does this to some degree, but it's not enough at the moment.
The sight/smell/hearing toggle is a great concept, but I find that there is very little practical use for sight in general due to the tall grass that is prevalent on every map. This leaves me playing the game in black and white, which detracts from it to a degree. I wish that the "senses" could have been implemented in a way that caused items or creatures detected by scent or hearing to just appear in a color that signified what sense it was detected with. For example, items detected by scent could show with a yellow silhouette, hearing could be blue. Something to that effect, rather than a full toggle.
Those are my only complaints about the game currently. I do not plan to refund it, as I can see Niche becoming a truly great game with several updates. The developers have been responsive and friendly in the forums and when replying to reviews, and that gives me a lot of hope for the future of this game.

I'm not an RTS player by any means, but Niche made a convert out of me. Not only is the game design sickeningly adorable (have you seen those twee faces??), but the fact that it's based on actual biological principles makes it a great game for players of any age. You have to figure out how to manage resources versus individual animals' aptitudes and protect them against bearenyas, rogue males, sickness, giant birds, and any number of obstacles I haven't encountered yet. Be forewarned, even though these are tiny digital creatures you do get a bit attached to them, so make sure you have someone or -thing nearby to snuggle in case of feels-mergencies (where you get the feels so bad you've gotta hug something), but to see generations thrive as they travel from island to island is so very worth it!
Much of the game can be figured out via trial and error, but there's a very helpful wiki on Fandom to get you by in tough spots. Much like Kerbal Space Program, it's definitely not the kind of game you'll be able to master in an afternoon, but once you get the feel for it, the possibilities are endless (and honestly, I'm glad it's so complex, because it's eminently replayable). If you're on the fence, definitely check out some Let's Play videos online, but if you like games that are both cute and savage, this is a winner. Looking forward to whatever Stray Fawn Studio does next!

As expected of Shinji Mikami, the guy knows how to make survival horror,
The game starts with Sebastian Castellanos(the character you will play throughout the game), Joseph Oda, and Juli Kidman in a vehicle en route to an unusual police call. Things go from strange to gruesome as an unknown visage with mysterious powers murders officers, hospital wards and nurses with an unknown force, butchering them with grostesque amounts of blood and gore. The visage eventually makes its way to you from across the building after being aware its been spotted on the surveillance camera, and renders you unconscious.
You awake tied up-side down, and the first thing to greet your ears are the sounds of a man being hacked alive, hearing the man's screams being choked out by the blood rushing to his throat from being disemboweled, your first instinct is to get loose, and get the keys to the exit of the room,
.
The game is pretty amazing. My only complaint is the clunky controls that make the game harder than it actually is(and it's actually pretty difficult to boot). For starters, the "true third-person" aspect the game forces on you is a huge fault. In most recent Third-Person shooters, the shooting scheme functions like a FPS; as long as your reticle is on the creature the shots will hit. In this game, if the monsters are too close, and the reticle is on the monster, the shot will whiff. Throughout the game, this will cause shots that look like they are lined up to just completely miss the target.
The other complaint I have is the complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥that is the camera and lack of shoulder swap for aiming. The camera is UNCONTROLLABLE. It's based entirely on movement and how your character is positioned. So for instance;
You are creeping along a wall, going from the east to the west(holding A), and you approach the corner, HOWEVER, your character is facing the EAST while walking like this. The camera will NOT move towards the West, and you will get NO vision around the corner unless you unlatch from the wall by going south slightly(press S), and use an arc'ing motion(D then S then A) to completely rotate your character to face the WEST. It's a completely huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥control scheme with this camera.
+ Story is great. It's original, and just outright creepy as♥♥♥♥♥♥from the start.
+ Wide variety of sounds to indicate types of hostiles or whether they're nearby, get good headphones!
+ The game is undoubtably terrifying at all times when playing on the harder difficulty.
+ Ammo is scarce. Many additional resources are available to you(bullets, explosives, heals, single-use weapons that can kill weaker mobs) only if you find and eliminate threats with minimal resources and without alerting the rest.
+ Promotes many styles of play, but nigh-impossible without some stealth. Sneak-killing enemies will save you a ton of ammo, and that's because there isn't a ton of ammo in the game to begin with. I think the most ammo i've ever had was about 25 bullets(15~ probably were in my pistol + back-up pistol ammo alone) across all my guns excluding my cross-bow bolts, which at times become extremely scarce.
+ Plenty of jump scares due to high ambient noise, you really need to listen hard and focus to find the hostiles, but sometimes they'll just catch you with your pants down. Clench those buttcheeks.
+ Enemies are a threat at all times, melee is awful for killing, it's like the middle-man between a L4D knock-back, and a very light stagger knock-back.
- True Third-Person aspect of the game causes shots to miss at point-blank and makes shots from medium range to just completely miss its target.
- Really awful movement options makes disarming traps and peeking around corners almost impossible.
- Lack of shoulder swap makes it really hard to get a decent grasp on the camera control, especially under high pressure.
- Jump-scares eventually get really repetitive because it starts to stale the horror experience.
7.8/10 - I bought this for 80% off, and it's way worth it. I'm about 12 hours in and probably 85% through the story.
If they had a better camera scheme, shoulder options, and better movement, this game could've very easily become an 8.5.

This is a beautiful walking simulator, but a terrible game.
Sure, the same walls and sofas and bookshelves and carpets are used in every room, but the rooms look nice and photorealistic.  The lighting is up there with the best Unity games.  Sound effects and music are also well done, as are the few visual effects.
Prettiness aside, there is literally nothing to do in this game but wander around and read boring notes.  And there really isn't even that much wandering, as it is a set path and doors lock on you until you hunt around the screen looking for the next note that will unlock a door and let you move to another random location.
There aren't even really any puzzles.  There is a padlock you need to find the number for, but they are floating right in sight.  The only thing difficult about finding them is that they are in a completely illogical place.  Who would look for numbers there?  Not clever at all, just lazy.  There might be a puzzle involving a record player, but I have no idea.  I just flipped switches until it played fast and then slow and then the door magically opened and let me out.  The worst kind of puzzle is the one you can "solve" without even knowing it is a puzzle.
I'm no stranger to the "walking simulator" genre.  Some people put Outlast and Soma in that category.  That is fair, but Soma had real puzzle and exploring, and Outlast had a hide-and-seek aspect--real danger and enemies.  Layes of Fear has no threat.  There is nothing to be scared of or hide from.  I know there are a lot of casual gamers who don't mind just walking around looking at things.  If you liked Dear Esther, Kholat or The Park, you might love this game.  If you didn't like them but liked Outlast or Soma, you might still want to give this game a try.  It is quite nice to look at, but really nothing more than a tech demo.

As an avid lover of the Star Trek franchise (Trekkie), this game is great! It gets all of the Star Trek references right (I would know, I've seen every episode of every series and all the movies), and it even adds new stories, though I'm not sure whether they're considered canon or not. However, it is not without its problems. On my old computer (9 years), it has a quite low framerate- usually about 12, though that is probably to be expected, but be warned that it doesn not run the best on older machines, as my brother's 4-year old machine gets about 30 FPS. It also does not have a first-person ground mode, which, in my opinion, would make it even greater. That said, the ground and space combat is great, though it may happen a bit too often. There are sometimes diplomatic or stealth options to avoid this, which makes it seem much more like the series. If you enjoy Star Trek at all, I highly reccomend this game. Don't worry if you haven't seen all the series as I have; most of the history of the aliens or major events is covered in dialogue. An optional subscription model is in place, but the ships and equipment gained without this subscription is more than adequate, and Zen (Cryptic's own form of currency) can be bought to get the paid equipment through a microtransaction. Again, I highly reccomend getting this game if you are at all interested, which you probably are, considering you're looking at this game in the first place.

Vermintide is a fairly fun game, living in a L4D2 type of gameplay while presenting a more unique, objective-leaned setting in terms of gameplay. The shooting and melee mechanics are fun, and all this is enchanced by the fact you can earn different variations of loot. What i feel the game falls short on itself is the loot system itself, since you are only rewarded for each successful quest, and even then you may not roll that greatly.
If you have friends, i would say this game is a worthwhile pickup, but i wouldn't recommend it alone.

If you like Left 4 Dead style co-op, and you like to smash hoards up close and personal rather than shooting from a distance then this game is definitely something you should try!
Most of the negative feedback on Vermintide revolves around the randomness of the loot. I feel however that the game is fun enough thanks to the core combat and co-op mechanics, just like left 4 dead is. The loot system just tacks on an extra layer of feeling like you are rewarded for playing each map, especially since the chances of getting better loot increase when you play higher difficulties and/or picking up tomes/grimoires in the maps that essentially make it more risky for you to wipe, but increase the chance of great rewards if you succeed. So instead of playing  a hard difficulty and just feeling 'satisfied', like it would be in Left 4 Dead, here you also get a new weapon that might be fun to use on the next map, or failing that you can salvage it for materials to upgrade your other weapons. Furthermore I feel that even though the characters and weapons that they use may be fairly similar, the playstyles are just varying enough to make it interesting to swap a character or weapon for another map - once again this way of diversifying the characters is still a lot more diverse than just having the same weapons that can be picked up on each map.
Anyway concluding, for me Vermintide is a lot of fun because I play it like I did Left 4 Dead - to get a great co-op experience in which you essentially fight against a RNG that sometimes beats you down hard. But as an extra sauce over this experience you are rewarded for playing each map (especially at higher difficulties) by getting new weapons.

It plays pretty much exactly like Left 4 Dead, except with a class system and loot, leveling and crafting. If you're looking for something new to fill that 'frantically swinging at oncomming hordes' niche that's been left while we wait to be left for dead once more, this is your game. Worth the full price, definitely pick it up if it goes on sale. Play with friends though the bots are morons.

I recommend this game with a but.
I love the concept and most of the execution.  The visuals are pleasing given the time of release.  The themes are enjoyable.  The interface is intuitive.  I also like the humor tucked into this game.  It's mostly dark humor to be sure, and goes somewhere along the lines of "Who just died?  Oh so-and-so (generally a Rogue or a Ranger, sometimes a Wizard or Warrior), why am I not surprised?  What is that, like, the fourth time I've resurrected you this week?  When are you going to learn not to run into that pack of Elementals?" or when you see a Cleric cast Divine Hammer on an enemy for the first time and watch them get flung basically across your town (even more humorous for me they landed right in the midst of a group of warriors who were more than happy to take the XP and gold for the kill).  Dirtiest trick in the game I've found so far is build two Cleric Guilds off the start and heal your enemies to death through the amount of sustain you can bring to a fight.
As for the "but", the largest issue I have is this game has no sense of scale.  Pretty much every mission is survive the attrition of the early game, and once you've survived till mid game the levels are basically unloseable.  If the game was better balanced to have some form of mild scaling it would make the early game more enjoyable/less punishing while still giving something of a challenge late game.  RNG is another problem with this game.  Some levels you get a Werewolf or some such spawn super early and it one shots its way through your base.  Most levels rarely last till the late game either.  Either some boss you need to fight randomly runs into your town, or one of your explorers procs said boss, or the level is designed with a timed trigger.  This means you rarely get to just sit back and enjoy the immensity of potential this game has to offer in the late game once you've levelled everything, have properly organized your parties, and are ready to fight everything on the map.  Instead most levels end prematurely in a frantic cluster shart as you try and keep your mob of heroes alive while they battle the Big Bad.  Most times it's anticlimactic cause you had more things you wanted to do before the final show down and instead your plans fizzle to "Well I guess it's just time to win then".
So far my favorite levels are Lich King and the Vampire Lords because their starts are not too ridiculous (for Lich King just randomly generating undead portals that are easy for early heroes to deal with and offers them nice XP and for Vampire Lords just a constant stream of Serpents and Undead for heroes to easily level off of), they offer you the ability to do everything you want to (in the case of Vampire Lords even building four temples), it allows you to decide when to fight the last battle because the Big Bads stay in areas that are easy to keep foolish explorers from procing the end fight, AND that last battle is still somewhat punishing even to late game heroes (More so in Lich King, in Vampire Lords my parties were so strong and the Big Bad got so chain cc'ed that it was a foregone conclusion from the start).
Despite these issues I picked the game up for $2 on a weekend sale because I originally bought this game back when CDs were a thing and remember enjoying it immensely, and I still do.  There's nothing more satisfying than watching the heroes you've raised from newbs work as an army of parties to steam roll some hapless Big Bad.
