The first thing I should let you know is that I only recommend that you buy this in a sale. It certainly isn't worth the full price.
Now that that has been said, I will review the game. Many people complain about the low-res textures and low polygon count visible in the graphics, as well as the lack of any sort of jumping mechanic and the awful evaporating corpses. The reason that these problems are present is because this game was designed to run on much less powerful systems, so complaining about this is redundant. As you can see, I clocked in at around 5 hours for a first time playthrough, and I did all of the side missions as well as the main story. The game is very small, but somehow conveys a sense of scale, for example the view you get of Panama from the hotel window is stunning. There are only about 4 side missions to go with the main quest, and all of them involve going to exactly the same place and retrieving different items, which is only slightly more fun than it sounds. In Human Revolution, there were at least 15 separate takedown sequences, but in The Fall there are only about 6 and they are all poorly rendered.
The game is full of annoying bugs, some of which are worse than others. For example, when I was infiltrating a gang hideout in Panama, I literally fell through the floor of the map and continued to fall until I reloaded the save file. Yes. THE save file. This game only has one save slot, which can be potentially game-breaking if you save in the wrong place. Basically what this means is that every time you save, you have to overwrite the previous save.
This is definitely the worst game in the series, but it's still a fun way to spend a few hours.

1. What is Deus Ex The Fall?
Deus Ex The Fall is a mobile port after the successful game Deus Ex Human Revolution (and DLC).
2. Why all the negative reviews?
I think people expected a full quality deus ex game, which is definitely not the case. It has a lot of flaws, but there are some things to like about The Fall. You should definitely ask yourself to try it out, it is NOT BAD IN EVERY CATEGORY!
3. Do I have to play human revolution before?
I highly recommend to play human revolution before and you absolutely have to read the official book "Icarus Effect - James Swallow" to fully understand the storyline and characters, because there is no explanation at the beginning of the game
4. Do I still play as Adam Jensen?
No, you will play as Ben Saxon, who gets hired by the Tyrants. The game continues where the book ends.
5. What does the game right?
It continues the story of the book in a good way. I liked the new setting around Panama city with the spanish speaking characters and there is still a lot to explore in the city, even if it is smaller. The music is great again and from the same composer. You will be able to play stealth or to do it the rambo way. You can again arm and augment yourself to upgrade your character and improve in a similar way as in human revolution. You will also have different side missions, It took me about 10 hours to complete the game.
6. What does the game wrong?
It is a mobile port which means that the graphics are worse than human revolution. The movement ingame is not as good as in human revolution (a bit clunky and you cannot jump). The voice acting is not as good as in human revolution. To upgrade yourself you have to open the shop und buy it, which breaks the immersion. When you shoot, you have this weird zoom effect, which simulates the recoil (If you play stealth as I did you will not recognize this). The game ends with a cliffhanger and no one knows if it will be continued some day.

Two things sour this title: Too much insta-death and too much cutscene.
Quite a few times, you just die instantly, and then rinse-repeat the same section, the same cutscene, which you can't skip, all so you can finally proceed again.  It's maddening sometimes.
This game had a lot of promise, a renowned lead developer who created the Resident Evil series, amazing graphics, very good sound and ambient sound to set the mood, and a crazy plot that takes you through a twisted world.  The mechanics at first teach you to be stealthy, to use the environment with cover, to be patient, and to use distractions like broken bottles to get behind the enemies to make stealthy kills.  That's great stuff, all of it.. then things turn bad.
The mechanics of the above are not strictly enforced, enemies can suddenly 'know' where you are no matter if you were stealthy or not.  The 'normal' mode is all about resource restriction, which really translates into, low health mode with very limited ammo.  Which brings on the player deaths to higher frequencies, then the rinse-repeat, watch a cutscene, rinse-repeat.. dead.. rinse-repeat.. you get the idea.
You die so often it's hard to really care about the main character.. it's hard to even be fearful of the bosses or enemies.  When the game starts, you have that fear.. as you play through it, you lose it.. especially after dying so much that you literally begin to just choke down yet another death so you can see the story you've invested yourself in.
If you like rinse-repeat / cutscene gaming.. you'll enjoy this.. otherwise, spare yourself the misery and spend your time and money elsewhere.

This seems very likely given that several of the DLC are free and were released shortly after the game went live in an attempt to save a game that players perceived as boring and shallow. Unfortunately, like almost always happens with gamers; that ship already sailed, the reviews were written, and virtually no amount of stuff was going pull disillusioned players back in. I hope other developers learn from this mistake and give players a full featured game for their money instead of trying to sucker players in with a DLC bait shell of a game.
+ The graphics are good.
+ Well done Warhammer Fantasy atmosphere.
- Shallow gameplay. Very grind heavy.
- Problematic UI. There is no map overview or minimap so you spend a lot of time running in circles. The UI simply provides little or no feedback on nearly anything going on in the game.
- Extremely limited character differentiation. There are no character stats to improve. Only one armor slot (the head?) and a couple trinket slots you unlock later. You cant even tell if the dwarf with axe and shield is any tougher that the wizard running around with a stick. Its not even clear that when you "level up" it actually does anything.
- Limited weapon types. There are a few base weapon types but nothing that differentiates them. The limited weapons (stats) have virtually no ingame way to differentiate them. Weapons have different damage values but there are no damage indicators ingame. Did I just clobber that rat or scratch him? No way to know. Floating damage numbers above enemies would help. Weapons have special procs but there is no indication when an item procs ingame. Weapons have some kind of swing arc but nothing ingame tells you where that arc is. So basically the weapons come down to you swing it or shoot until the thing in front of you is dead and thats it.
- Limited enemy types. Only 6 or 7 maybe and really 5 are just variations of the same basic Skaven (Ratman).
- Limited map selection. Several of the maps are way too large (i.e. take too long to run) meaning players rarely do them.
- Poor map design. The maps look good themselves but are very confusing with little or no indication of where you are suppose to go. All the maps are way too dark and any interesting details the level designers might have added are lost in the shadows.
-- Horrible, horrible, horrible RNG loot system. Everyone loves grinding for the sake of grinding.

About technical issues, graphics and design are better than Left 4 Dead 2 (it is not a surprise, because Valve's game was launched in 2009), but Vermintide is not a Crysis, Titanfall or Battlefield. On Windows 8.1 x64, you must run stingray_win_32_dev.exe (click on "Alternate exe" on the launch screen). If you are in doubt, pick the original one: the sprinter zombies game is too much better.

This game is a shining example of how free-to-play all too often = pay-to-win. Eternally in "Early Access", this game is yet another sad reason why Steam's "Early Access" program is an overall failure.
Big money weapons are completely OP (e.g. M1/M2 Carbine, Thompson, etc). If you don't pay, good luck spending a few weeks with a catheter and hot pockets and without seeing the sun to earn them without spending cash.
Balancing classes and levels for both teams in skirmish games is a joke. Sometimes it will give more/better tanks to one side or give one side tons of paratroopers. It also doesn't balance player levels properly so newbies often get seal clubbed. It makes for imbalanced and frustrating gameplay if you are a newbie.
Also, the game is riddled with cheating. There are several cheating programs that you can easily find on the Internet which reveal the locations of all enemy players and puts boxes around them, making camoflage/cover almost useless and allowing you to always get the drop on an enemy. I've seen people with 20 or even 30 to 1 K/D in a game. As it is so easy to die in this game, I can imagine that those players were using these programs.
Overall, this game really isn't worth investing any serious time into unless you like pay-to-win games and have the cash to pay so you can win. If you're looking for a free-to-play game that doesn't bone you for not spending tons of cash, look elsewhere. This game is not for you.

This game is amazing.  When I was a little girl, I was fascinated with genetics and heredity.  I used to make up games where you could see the genes of imaginary creatures, then breed them and see how those genes were passed on to their children.  I fervently wished that someone would make that game for real.  20 years later, I got my wish. :)
Niche is full of adorable creatures whose genes have a real impact on not only their appearance, but the ways they can interact with the world around them.  Your job is to take control of a tribe, helping them to explore and ensuring their survival as they move from island to island.  Each island has different challenges for the Nichelings to overcome, and the abilities they get from their genotypes will determine how well they can gather food and deal with predators in each environment.
There are many, many different ways to survive, so you're not locked into keeping a specific set of genes.  Nichelings use real genetics (including mutations!) and you can use this to guide the direction of your tribe.  Will you breed a tribe of mighty hunters?  Efficient gatherers?  Or maybe you just want your Nichelings to have adorable tiger stripes?  It's up to you!  You can even ignore the mutation system entirely and see what nature gives you.  An individual Nicheling's lifespan is relatively short, so making sure there are children who can carry on the tribe's legacy is an important part of the game.  My favorite part is just watching how the tribe evolves over time and seeing all the changes and mutations that my choices have introduced.
If you have even a passing interest in genetics, cute creatures, and survival games, I highly recommend Niche.

I have been eyeing this game for nearly a whole year now, watching a let's play on youtube. Finances didn't allow me to buy the game despite me being in absolute awe for it - but as luck would have it, I recently won this in a giveaway. Needles to say, I was super excited to try it out myself!
With the current update of 0.9, a lot of changes have happened, but in all honesty I don't think describing what used to be, and what will be for the official release, does not benefit anyone. Let me just tell you that Niche has come a long way and constantly improved, making it a lovely enjoyable game! I am therefore sure that the final version is going to be just as adorable as the previous builds :)
Niche is all about surviving. Starting out with Adam and Eve, your task is to breed the most adapted animals to ensure survival. There is a great variety of genes varying from fur color and pattern (influencing camouflage) to which limbs they possess (digging paw? Nimble fingers? Runner's leg? Claws? That's just a few of the options!). Big ears or small ears; Cracker jaw or Poison fangs; a dozen different immunity genes; ram horns or antlers - Niche gives you a great amount of genes to play around with! Or do the genes play with you? That is the feeling you sometimes get when you're desperately trying to breed a creature with poison fangs and 5 children later you still don't have them, or breeding a couple that have blind eyes in their recessives with normal eyes in the mutation menu and yet all 3 children end up blind.
Breeding isn't as easy as it sounds at first because some genes really just don't want to play along! The mutation menu can help greatly with this. Each creature has two slots in which the player can place certain genes to make them more likely. However, be prepared that this isn't always going to work ;)
Moreover there are multiple biomes and difficulties that your creatures can adapt to. Want to live a peaceful life on a lush green island, or do you prefer the hardships of the snowy mountains? Do you wish to live an easy life, or are you seeking the thrill of multiple bearyenas at once? No matter which one is for you, the Sandbox mode has you covered.
Breeding the "perfect" creatures can be quite a challenge, but it definitely is a fun one! And the feeling of joy when you finally manage to get that double-clawed, poison fangs and ramhorns creature that you've been trying for for the past 10 turns is more than rewarding.
Niche is a great game, and I am excited to see what's next :)

Before you even consider buying the PC version of this game, be aware that the requirements specs are completely false.
First, the game has a horrible memory leak to it.   Unless you're ok with it crashing to desktop every 30 min, you need at least 8GB of system RAM (even then, don't expect to play it more than 1:30 at a time).   The 4GB minimum spec that's listed on the box and on Steam gets thrown out the window as soon as you contact BethSoft's tech support.
Second, the video card?  It says 1GB is the minimum.  However, that is apparently the minimum spec for the first little bit of the game.   The first part of the intro is a rail sequence, where you're expected to hold down a key get things to move forward.   It may as well have been a cutscene, because that illusion of control is all the control you've got until just after you get inside.   After that, if your video card has less than 2GB, just mouse looking around will be a stop motion slide show.  BethSoft tech support will tell you outright that 2GB is the real minimum video requirement but you have to contact tech support to find that out.
On the plus side, now that I've upped everything to the minimum spec (not the one posted before you buy this piece of crap), I can now very smoothly look around .   That's about all I can do though, because the game no longer registers the keyboard at all.   Awaiting response from Bethsoft, and I fully expect them to tell me about some other deviation from the advertised minimum specs.
The game is apparently quite good on PS4 and XBox One though.  Don't waste your money on the PC version at regular price.  The bugs and the inaccurate official system reqs for this game make it only worthwhile if your system has double the memory and double the video card memory that's listed..   The game's a year old now, and Bethesda has not fixed all the bugs and WILL NOT patch it further.

On it's own merits, it's a unique game as far as strategy games go. It's not like most strategy games where you build a base and recruit a bunch of units, although it's similar. Instead you build guilds and hire heroes, who have their own unique AI patterns they follow and can't be directly controlled, only influenced by the player. Essentially this means the game is more of a simulation with the player playing the part of a quest giver for a typical RPG, with some town building aspects thrown in. You direct heroes with reward bounties for defending, attacking, or exploring whatever you put the bounty on. This costs you gold, which then goes into the heroes pockets, which they then use to buy equipment for further adventuring.
This is a bit of a mixed bag. You rely on the AI to choose what to do, so your heroes might pick fights they can't win, run from fights they can win, ignore bounty targets with bounties that are too low, or put off buying better equipment to buy potions instead.
It's arguable whether or not this game is better than the original, but it does have a lot of a quality of life improvements over the original. Heroes are always available to be brought back from the dead and the Hall of Lords can be used to recruit already leveled up heroes from past missions. Additionally there is a party system that allows you to have heroes group together. However hero AI is a bit simplified. Heroes don't wander off on their own as much as in the first game, and rarely have unique AI quirks such as the Ranger from the first game exploring on his own. This can make the game feel a bit less alive compared to the first game. The temple system  has been reworked as well. Now both temples and trading posts are built in specific spots on the map. This simplifies things, but also somewhat limits strategy in comparison to the first game.
This version also comes with a lot of extra DLC missions. Including a neat and hilarious DLC campaign that has you using monster heroes instead of the typical human ones. Perhaps the funniest part of that DLC is the vampire tax collectors, who will actually attempt to defend themselves when attacked.

This game is one of the best World War Two Simulator Games i've played in a long time, the story follows Sergeant Matt Baker as he and his elite squad of Paratroopers are dropped behind enemy lines to take out targets of value that would prevent the American Invasion of Normandy from succeeding. While Baker is initially distraught of the idea of leading men so soon in his military career, he soon learns that he must focus and lead both himself and his men to victory and glory. Throughout the campaign, Baker's squad is picked off one by one by the germans, changing Baker's initial objective of completing the mission, he now must keep his men alive, complete the mission, and get back home alive himself against the odds with only a handful of men. The gameplay to the game is pretty spectacular, the way to defeating the overwhelming odds of germans ranges from the four "Fs" of military tactics in that time, finding, fixing, flanking, and finishing the enemy. As the game progresses, Baker and his squad start to go from fighting untrained grunts to the elite "Fallschrimjager" division of the German Paratroopers aswell as encountering situations where your tactics must adjust to the new circumstances and choosing whether or not sacrificing a member of your squad is worth it to complete the mission.

The Fall is the simplified byproduct piece of Deus Ex Human Revolution - not complex, not clever, not accurate with details. And not so required to see as a part of full picture, even if you're a big fan of reincarnated franchise.
The game is using mostly the same mechanic as the big one - only dumbed down, without ability to jump, with crude controls and levels designed for mobile platform - which is, obviously, means smaller size and far-from-the-edge graphics. Some are comparing it with N64, but that is an exaggeration. Still, nothing too fancy.
The narrative, which I liked for some point, felt more pure cyberpunk, than in Human Revolution case. Sadly, that feeling was not lasted for long, as the "professional" merc Ben Saxon started to act even more unnatural than Adam Jensen in his quest, with all those morality checks and sudden bursts of unpredicted generosity, which is so inproper in the merc's praxis...
Why thumbs up, then? As of little product, which is now sells in bundle either with Deus Ex titles, or with all Eidos anthology - even with all simplicity and the feeling of unfinished product the Fall is providing - still the gameplay is not completely broken. It feels like separate level of Deus Ex HR, which was cutted off as improper, and then sold as separate game - yes, that's true. But, it is still a piece of the great game. Just one of the worst pieces.
My mark is 5.8/10. I recommend to start it only for achievement hunters - as this one is so simple for full complete - or for people who played in Human Revolution for too long, but still not enough for satisfaction. Maybe "The Fall" will work as a sobering pill - if Mankind Divided was not chilled you out yet.

I thought I wouldn't like "Niche - a genetics survival game" at first. But here we are, a year later, still playing.
So in this game, you are sent to survive in different islands as an animal tribe, avoiding extinction as you try to keep your animals alive as days pass by. You mutate your creatures, collect food/hunt/fish, run from dangers, build nests, travel to new islands and even create hybrids; every turn, you have decisions to make.
+ Every playthrough is unique
+ Your decisions matter
+ You are given a lot of freedom
+ You quickly lose track of time when playing
+ You can decide the difficulty by playing (easy to toggle between different difficulties; islands)
+ You can always make it more challenging to yourself
+ The game will get more content and updates after the release
+ The dev team is very responsive and listens to the game's community
+ You aren't forced to learn anything or expected to know genetics
+ Every save file is an adventure
- The game can get repetitive if you are not very invested
- It can feel very difficult to understand and learn
~ It is very boardgame-like
~ It is not very deep
~ It is not super customizable (you can't develop your nests to better ones or such)
~ You can't build or transform your surroundings (it's about animals and genetics rather than that)
~ It can feel very slow paced when playing, rushing usually gets you killed
~ At harder difficulties, it demands planning and strategies, which can overwhelm some players
~ It appeals to certain kind of players; animal-lovers, biology/genetics geeks, "organizers", storytellers, strategy enthusiasts... many females, I can tell you that, the animals are surely considered cute

A lot of negative reviews out there recently and as I read them, I noticed that most of them bought the game thinking it's something that is not.
So here's what you can expect from this game:
-It's a game that values teamplay. No Ramboing here, if you go alone, you will die alone.
-Amazingly fun melee combat. No one can deny that slaying rats in Varmintide feels great and satisfying. This is the main reason you keep playing this game and this is where Left4Dead and Vermintide fundamentally differ. If you think massacring hordes of vermin isn't the main thing to do, don't buy the game.
-The missions are challenging and can get very intense. Each mission has a particular order of things that you need to do in order to complete them in the most optimal way (and the highest possible extra loot), but while most of them are long, there are also quick missions you can do for fast loot. Of course there are also the RNG Elite spawns to keep you on your toes and punish the Rambo players :)
-Loot system, it's grindy but nowhere near as grindy as it used to be. You get random items depending on the difficulty of the mission you completed, so when you first start playing it may seem impossible to get an item you want, but with the crafting system it's not as bad as you might think. There are items that are easy to get and others that can take hundred of hours to get, depends on your luck.
-The characters. Their voice acting and dialogue are just excellent. Each has his own quirks and special relation with each other. There are times that you will hear them say the most ordinary of things in the most theatrical and over the top manner and you will catch yourself with a big smile on your face, especially the Witch Hunter says some very hilarious stuff about the other characters.
-The presentation of the Warhammer world. From the grim graphics, to the beautifuly crafted weapons, to the gruesome vermin rats, everything looks and sounds like you are in the Warhammer world. The game looks great, this IS Warhammer!
Lastly, like in every co-op game, don't expect to enjoy the game playing with strangers, as much as playing with friends. This game was made to be played by 4 buddies, despite the game providing you with good mechanincs to quickly alert other players about dangerous or important stuff, this is the internet and people seem to blame the game for the faults of the latter.

Ammo is very rare, so in most cases you have to do mele combat which reduces the effectiveness of most of the ranged classes. Players constantly rush for new ammo and health packs which are often placed around the corners of the limited map. The game design destroys teamplay in my opinion as your party is wandering around the map looking for loot. Also the restricted map sections make it impossible to help someone left behind. As in Left 4 Dead fallen team members can be "set free" later on.
If you don't have 3 friends available you'll have a hard time finding servers. The playerbase shrinked from 4,331.3 Average (October 2015) to 545.5 (October 2016) Average ( Source:

All in all it's not a bad game. But not as good as the games it tries to mimic in terms of balance and contents.

An open ended game, with a variety of settings (though I have stuck to the original).  Basically, you start as an individual new to the challenge of life in the world.  You quickly get the chance to develop a small band of followers, an option to serve an existing king, a claimant to the throne or stay freelance.  As time goes buy you can raid villages or capture castles and cities.  Each gives the oppertunity for riches, but can really needle the rightful owner.  Over time, the basic aim is to build a Nation and unify the continent under one (your) banner.  The map is basic but pleasant, the interface easy to learn and use and the battles are excellent.  No matter if you prefer to deliver a crossbow bolt from afar or an axe blow from up close, you will find the weapon of choice for you here.  The chance to develop your own kingdom is good fun, and can certainly leave you rushing from one fight to another to keep the wolves at bay.  Additional options to include empire troop reports etc make it even easier to keep track of who and what you have around the map.  This game was great several years ago, and the new gameplay has made it even better.

This game is one of the best World War Two Simulator Games i've played in a long time, the story follows Sergeant Matt Baker as he and his elite squad of Paratroopers are dropped behind enemy lines to take out targets of value that would prevent the American Invasion of Normandy from succeeding. While Baker is initially distraught of the idea of leading men so soon in his military career, he soon learns that he must focus and lead both himself and his men to victory and glory. Throughout the campaign, Baker's squad is picked off one by one by the germans, changing Baker's initial objective of completing the mission, he now must keep his men alive, complete the mission, and get back home alive himself against the odds with only a handful of men. The gameplay to the game is pretty spectacular, the way to defeating the overwhelming odds of germans ranges from the four "Fs" of military tactics in that time, finding, fixing, flanking, and finishing the enemy. As the game progresses, Baker and his squad start to go from fighting untrained grunts to the elite "Fallschrimjager" division of the German Paratroopers aswell as encountering situations where your tactics must adjust to the new circumstances and choosing whether or not sacrificing a member of your squad is worth it to complete the mission.

I thought I wouldn't like "Niche - a genetics survival game" at first. But here we are, a year later, still playing.
So in this game, you are sent to survive in different islands as an animal tribe, avoiding extinction as you try to keep your animals alive as days pass by. You mutate your creatures, collect food/hunt/fish, run from dangers, build nests, travel to new islands and even create hybrids; every turn, you have decisions to make.
+ Every playthrough is unique
+ Your decisions matter
+ You are given a lot of freedom
+ You quickly lose track of time when playing
+ You can decide the difficulty by playing (easy to toggle between different difficulties; islands)
+ You can always make it more challenging to yourself
+ The game will get more content and updates after the release
+ The dev team is very responsive and listens to the game's community
+ You aren't forced to learn anything or expected to know genetics
+ Every save file is an adventure
- The game can get repetitive if you are not very invested
- It can feel very difficult to understand and learn
~ It is very boardgame-like
~ It is not very deep
~ It is not super customizable (you can't develop your nests to better ones or such)
~ You can't build or transform your surroundings (it's about animals and genetics rather than that)
~ It can feel very slow paced when playing, rushing usually gets you killed
~ At harder difficulties, it demands planning and strategies, which can overwhelm some players
~ It appeals to certain kind of players; animal-lovers, biology/genetics geeks, "organizers", storytellers, strategy enthusiasts... many females, I can tell you that, the animals are surely considered cute
Should you buy it? If you like the idea and believe you'd enjoy it, yes, I was never disappointed with Niche. Check out some gameplay videos of it if you aren't sure. Should you buy it as a present for someone? Maybe, you really need to know if they would enjoy it.
Never played "these kinds of games" before? Then I'd say this is a good way to dive in, the community is filled with different aged players who ended up enjoying this game, and play it with their own styles.
Community - It's good there, people share ideas, challenges and suggestions. I don't spend a lot of time in the discussions.
The game will be released next week, and I write this review to support the game and its developers, who really deserve it! Five stars out of five from me, I truly enjoy this game.
Now I'm off to play some Niche, to finally conquer the island I struggled to live in (it was the most epic struggle though!).

"Yes"
I've seen that simple word in many reviews of different games, and I thought it was kind of funny, but now I understand the meaning behind "yes."
Niche is a "yes" game. One simple word could describe a game in many ways, and yes is one of them. When I first started playing this game, I'll admit it, it was a bit difficult to get used to, but I wasn't a hardcore gamer back in those days so I wasn't really a pro in playing games (Not that I am, I just never played a lot of games on a laptop or computer). I've seen reviews where people say that it gets boring, and that it's not entertaining. When I first started, it was different for me. There were so many things I could do, and I wanted to try them all. My tribe ended up almost starving to death and I gave up on them. Yup. They starved. Yay. It was my first tribe, so it was to be expected. However, I learned a lot from playing on that tribe. One of them being that crippled paws are cute and sad and all, but this game is about "survival," so it doesn't really help. You can choose what you want your creatures to be in this game, and it doesn't always have to be about surviving, sometimes you just want to test things out and kill off a tribe, I've done that before.
Your creatures can fish, hunt, or just eat from a tree and berry bush. All the patterns create such interesting and beautiful creatures, and you can make up your own story with their genes and what they do in the Tribe. I always have something to do in this game, and I'm always scared that my tribes will die because I get so attached. A simple creature that has, let's see, crippled paws, derp snout, doubled up immunity, would make me fall in love with them. I do love how all the beautiful and "perfect" creatures look, but.. There's just something about those creatures that don't have those "beautiful" and "perfect" genes that make them so... beautiful.
Rogue children are mostly disliked and fed to the birds. which is kind of how some humans don't like how their child looks and they leave them alone or give them to someone else or an orphanage. It's sad, and I pity them. I have a soft spot for them, and I never just let them die. I always try to find them a mate, and a purpose in the tribe.
Overall, this seemingly simple game has so much potential, and I absolutely love it. From the "ugly" creatures to the "perfect" creatures, everything in this game has a story. I can't wait for the future of this game, and I hope the community keeps growing. I also hope my friend gets it soon, because I'm already addicted, and I want to have an in real life buddy play it with me.
A feature I would really love to be added or maybe a website someone can do is where we can make a creature to see how the genes (that you have maybe unlocked) and patterns look like so you can know what you wnat the creatures to be in your tribe. It would also help with making stories (if you like to write stories, this would be very helpful) Maybe like a button somewhere or something like that? It's just an idea.
I really do love this game, and I hope it keeps growing. This game really has really kind and awesome developers, and I am very thankful for them for creating this game.

Niche is a nice little survival game where you have to breed the creatures for their recessive or active genetics to make a strong tribe that can survive through collecting berries, hunting rabbits, moles and fish and defending themselves from predators while exploring each island you end up on after travelling on the ports. I genuinly enjoy the game, the design of the creatures and how they have develpoed it so far. However, like every game there are pros and cons:
Pros
- The game is nice and relaxing and depending on the person you can play it for hours.
- It has the choice to play a easy, medium, and hard modes so players can challenge themselves.
- The art style is cute.
- It is nice to breed new babies, while you can control their genetics you never know what they are going to look like so it's exciting to find out.
- It is challenging and it really pushes you sometimes, especially when facing a drought.
cons/ contructive critisism
- In the new update when all of your turns are used up the sun or next day button no longer flashes, this means when you have larger tribes of 20-30 creatures, you may waste turns by going on to the next day without noticing.
- I feel there aren't very many goals in the game, while I can play it for hours and feel entertained, I do feel there is a lack of purpose in the game. Even in story mode this is an issue, it is basically the same as sandbox mode except you get an achievement for finding adams family. The only thing that makes you feel like you accomplished something is when new genes are unlocked and even with that when you click to see which gene is unlocked it is no longer highlighted like it used to be. With that said, without having goals players are able to do what they want but there should be an option for those who want more of a drive to play the game.
- While the art is nice the animation of the game is rather simple, though that is understandable due to the type of game it is though mnore animation would be cool or different stances for the creatures maybe.
- SOME OF THE BOSSES ARE INSANELY HARD. Okay, so i mistakenly went into the jungle way too early when migrating to a new island and it was all good and fine until the poison ape thing came and wiped out my tribe and if you have under 5 attack you can't do anything about it!! I know that breeding to be scentless, or distasteful or be really strong are part of avoiding these things but even on the MEDIUM islands it is difficult to fight the larger bosses/ predators.
- Nichelings with two of the same immunity genes are sick for their whole life now, while it does say they are more prone to getting sick, it isn't as realistic to have them sick throughout their whole life, there should be a plant that serves as a medecine, not to heal them but to stop them from being sick, even if it is temporary. In addition to this, I feel that the creatures around this sick animal should be less likely to get sick from them because they hhave immunity genes to prevent that, I feel it should only apply if a creature has the same immunity gene as the one who has double. Although this problem can be easily avoided by isolating the creature. While many may deem it useless when it is sick, it is still beneficial to use them because you can breed it without fear of one of the immunity genes being the same and use it to collect food far away.
In conclusion, I love this game  and while I have made a lot of critisisms, it is just me rambling about some things and commenting on how some parts of the game were changed that were helpful and beneficial. I do reccommend it as it is a pleasant and easy going game: I will warn you tho, MIND THE BIRDS FIRST TIMERS, the first time i went onto an island with a bird i got such a fright.... :(

Star Trek Online I started playing this game a few years ago when it went Free to Play (F2P).  If your a trekkie or a scifi lover I recommend this game.  The different story lines are well put together.  And unlike most F2P games it isn't a pay to win game.  The reasons for that is you can achieve everything the guy that just dropped some of that hard earned cash on a ship or items through just grinding and playing the game.  Play as Klingon, Romulan or the Federation character.  This Star Trek Universe takes place after the Star Trek Nemesis movie. (cause JJ Abrams universe is an alternative one) Leveling your character is fairly easy think I capped out in about two weeks if not sooner.  There is both ground and space missions.  And once you have done all the story’s because you will there is the end content like Special Task Force fighting the Borg and few others.   One cool aspect of this game is the foundry where players like you create there own missions in the foundry and upload them so you can play there missions.  Some of the people creating missions for you are fantastic at it and creating missions and its is pretty fun to give it a go.  Also if your a lonely gamer and don't play nice with others this isn’t the game for you because a lot of content is only accessible if your in a fleet ( guild).  Now there are good fleets and bad fleets.  You will jump from fleet to fleet till you find one you like.  Now on to the four types of currency the pay Zen, Dilithium which you achieve by doing missions, or different events. Energy Credits you get just by playing the game and buying and selling items, and Fleet credits.  Each has its own role in this universe the Zen enough said you buy zen to purchase different items in the zen store.  Now the dilithium which is the most important because you can sell dilithium on the market to turn into zen there is a daily cap on how much dilithium you can earn each day because Perfect World wants you to spend money.  Now the fleet credits are earned by joining a fleet (guild) and helping contribute to fleet projects.   I do however recommend you subscribe for one month if you are getting into the game because of the added perks you receive like ship slots, character slots, inventory, bank, and also the 500 zen they give you for subscribing. Then unsubscribe and you still still have those added benefits.  I still subscribe to this FREE TO PLAY game because you also earn other perks.  But as you progress in the game you will see if its for you or not.  But STO is probably one of the best F2P MMORPG's on the market.

I've been playing STO for a couple weeks now and I must say I was pleasantly surprised.
The space combat and ground combat systems seem interesting and fun.  They fit the bill for the "easy to pick up, hard to master" motto, as ship combat does involve a bit of strategy as far as weapon use - flanking maneuvers - etc.  There is also enough diversity in ground npc's to keep fight's there interesting with mobs using flanking maneuvers on your team along with cc's to keep you adjusting during combat.
The FTP system isn't bad at all - I'm up to level 36 thus far and I haven't run into any instance of NEEDING to spend money at all.  The ships and equipment you have access to are generally the same with the pay component being slightly better skins/cosmetics usually from what I can tell.  Normal fair for the rest, like more inventory space, bank space, etc.
I have already recommended the game to my friends and would do so again -  at the very least it's worth a try to see if it's your "cup of tea".  It's defintely a nice break from the typical fantasy sword/shield and spell slinging.

And, of course, the second unique feature is that this game uses a puzzle game (similar to Bejewelled) in order to determine whether you win the affection of the ladies. Honestly, at first I thought this game was a complete joke just by seeing the puzzle mechanic. Regardless, I soon found myself not wanting to stop and I do believe this is because of the addictive features that the puzzle mechanic brings to HuniePop. In addition, the soundtrack is nice and relaxing which makes completing the puzzles less of a stressful chore and more of a welcoming game that you actually want to spend your time playing. Now I'm not going to lie, I enjoyed this game way more than I should have and I have no idea why. In fact, I enjoyed it so much that I played 5 consecutive hours of it in one sitting which is really hard to believe for a game that is so repetitive. Other than that I would say that this game doesn't really have a good ending story wise causing it to lack replayability (unless you are a speed runner), but for the price I really couldn't call that a complaint.
To wrap things up, this game is genuinely nothing less than simple addictive fun which makes it something you would want to whip out when you have nothing better to do. Although, if you're like me then you may find yoursef unable to stop playing purely because you've been 'hooked'.
I'd rate this game a 7/10 for it's unique twist on the generic dating sim and for it's reasonable pricing on Steam

A first impression of this game will tell you it seems clunky, poorly thought out, and slightly oddly made.  Unfortunately, that first impression is correct.  The game takes an excellent concept piece, one still fully playable as 'Build and Shoot' online, and makes it meaningless by attempting to radically increase the pace.  Instead of a functional if slightly featureless WWI game with building blocks (leading to exciting dynamics emphasising patience, careful basebuilding, and long-distance accuracy along with the occasional high-stress trench assault), the new developers attempted to create a game with the speed of Team Fortress 2 with building blocks.  Inevitably, this makes it too fast for the blocks to be any use (the addition of a jetpack and variety of explosives don't help) and too clunky for patience to be important.
That, combined with my multiple connection issues and latency problems on a pc with adequate hardware and excellent internet leads me to think you should avoid it.

Okay, let me get this to you straight: Battle Builder is an overstatement. In the games that I have played, it's ideal, but not necesssary to build during a game. However, most gamers rely on this for traps, obstacles, and blocking easy entrances to their base, and I applaud them for that. As for building your own arena, most people go on the public maps, so it's not likely anyone besides other friends will see your map.
I stopped playing this a while ago, but while I did I loved it. Think of it as Minecraft combined with a version of TF2 that only has 4 classes...maybe...
I found it very addicting, but however, it's a really simple game, and you might not be addicted for long. That was my case. The game is pretty simple:
This is a map. There is one team's spawnpoint, and the other team's spawnpoint. You can use your weapons and tools to alter the map in any way you can (so long as a marksman doesn't shoot you in the face while doing so). Shoot the other team 'till they die and steal their flag.
That's basically it.
You have 4 classes, Commander (who has a missile launcher and a minigun), Marksman (who has a sniper rifle), Engineer (who uses an assault rifle and can place turrets), and Miner (who basically is the guy you rely on to dig secret tunnels to the other base). There's also the "classic" and the "gangster" classes, but they never appear on public servers, and therefore you will never use them. And I've never found a way to get any new weapons besides the few you start out with, which is a major disappointment. But it was a while since I last played it, so maybe they added some way; I don't know. But it's still very limited in what you can do.
People who like simple action games will like this, however "COD 4 LYFE" people might not have a thrilling experience.

It's apparent this is a near spiritual successor to the Resident Evil 4 formula and Shinji Mikami is very fond of his habits. Thankfully the game doesn't falter when it comes to atmosphere and the confusing/detached characters add to the mystery of "what is going on in this place?"
I'll keep it short and sweet. The gameplay is enjoyable, the locations and options to explore every nook and cranny is very satisfying. Enemies do not revive if you blow up their heads, but they do return if you unload ammo into them and do not burn the body, ala "Crimson Head" from Mikami's beloved Resident Evil REmake for the Gamecube (and now all other platforms!). The upgrade system works well and combat is awkward, especially aiming, which in my opinion only adds to the horror element.
It might seem strange for me to say, but in your first playthrough you should try and play on Hard (if you are looking for a good experience). I managed well on Normal, but felt mid-way that if I had increased the difficulty I would have less ammo to blast away and would be more concerned about how I approached each enemy encounter.
Yes, the gameplay does point towards Resident Evil 4 a lot, and it's to be noted that the characters are quite dull and do not respond to their surroundings accordingly, with Sebastian (main character) seemingly unaffected by the warps in his surroundings and the enemies too. He never panics, he never freaks out and screams, he simply keeps his lips sealed and walks on through. Like Leon, just... with no personality.
Nevertheless, Evil Within is an enjoyable game and the Season Pass was worth the money I put into it. It's no REmake, RE4 or Silent Hill but it does a fantastic job and keeping you interested throughout.
A solid 8/10. Not perfect, and not bad. Just right.

I recommend all three components of this game: The base game, the Kidman chapters (Assignment + Consequence) and the Executioner. But, I recommend them to varying degrees and for different reasons.
The Evil Within's base game is the story, and it's the only story you need to experience. It's amazing, and I recommend it 100% because its story is interesting, it's very scary and it's presented beautifully (extremely complex texture set, really cool special effects, and a great sense for body horror).
By the end, you'll certainly know generally what happened. If you're clever, you'll have theories about why it happened. If you're reallly clever, you'll figure out the signficance of all of the game's elements--the upgrade system, the weapons, the scene changes, different effects that are never explicitly explained, and what happened during the ending.
The pieces of the puzzle are all there, but they're really difficult to organize, mentally. The chief challenge is one that strains memory rather than critical thinking. The story drip feeds you its details out of order and with lots of space in between drips. Remembering that something happened earlier will help you understand what's happening, now. But, it will likely be hard to remember what happened earlier.
This works in the game's favor, though. By the end, there's no way Sebastian would understand what's going on. Why should you?
Mechanically, the game is pretty varied. Often you're hiding, often you're stealthing, often you're shooting, sometimes you're fleeing and sometimes you're super goddam shooting. You never feel powerful (well, ok, you feel powerful twice). Your guns are tools with very limited uses and very slow firing rates. You need to aim for heads, but heads are really hard to hit. Monsters move in seemingly unpredictable fashion, giving their heads really wide fields of movement. This makes lining up a headshot a really stressful affair. If you're confronting a group, you have the extra stress of landing a headshot on the closest enemy while the others are moving in on you. To make matters more stressful, heads are sometimes only partially destroyed by the first gunshot, meaning the mutilated enemy is still coming at you until you can put a second shot in the smaller half-a-head.
Bosses are more complex than they first appear. There's typically an easy way to beat them and a more challenging way to beat them more efficiently. The easy way is emptying all of your clips into it. The fight will take awhile, and you'll leave the fight without any ammo, but you'll get it done and you'll be rewarded with lots of upgrade material. The challenging way involves exploiting the boss's behavior and the environment to reduce the length of the fight dramatically. The challenging way is never obvious, but it's always pretty clear if you're paying attention. This method ends the fight quickly, but conserves ammo and sometimes forfeits the upgrade material you would have earned if you had bulleted it to death.
If the base game is the story, then the Assignment and The Consequence are the exposition dumps. You don't need to care about them. Rather than adding anything to the story, they simply explain more explicitly what Sebastian went through in the base game. They are equally as beautifully grim as the base game, but they're much less weird. What Kidman experiences is a little more predictable and straightforward than what Sebastian experienced (and the reason for that is grounded in the narrative). An additional bit of interest is that Kidman rarely gets the chance to fight. She can sometimes stealth kill, but usually she's hiding and stealthing. This makes monsters that would normally become bullet bags for Sebastian a bit more threatening for Kidman.
There's also an absolutely awesome unbeatable instakill enemy that stalks Kidman throughout her story. It's really, really cool.
The Executioner is something you should play for the gigs and not much else. It's a first-person, mostly melee arena combat game. It's really short and really cheap, so why not? But, it doesn't add anything meaningful to the story. You fight a bunch of lesser enemies, then go to the boss room and fight something familiar from the base game. But, this time you're the Keeper. Most of what you do involves bludgeoning with your meat hammer until you get a set of prompts. When the prompts appear, you can execute an enemy, or you can pick them up and throw them. The throw has a pleasantly surprising bit of tactical depth to it. Some enemies react to being thrown in unique ways, while others react to being hit in unique ways.
All three parts of this game are worth playing. If you want a good horror game/story, 100% play the base game. If you want to see the game from a modern avoid-the-enemy perspective and want the expo dumps, play the Kidman chapters. If you want to be the Keeper for 2-4 hours, play The Executioner.

Technically, this is a prequel to the story in DX:HR (based on a novel) and although it was released afterwards as a game it was still fun to play. ****

This is a delicious Deus Ex morsel. It has all the stealth, exploration, choices, and combat from Human Revolution but in a tiny package. There's only one main location with a handful of quests, but what is here is absolutely quintessential Deus Ex.
The huge caveat is that the game only includes Part 1, which ends on a huge cliffhanger. Part 2 was supposed to be made, but at this point it will never happen. Hence, the abrupt ending is very sad, but I enjoyed using my imagination as to what would have happened next.
On the tech side, I had zero issues. The game looks very nice despite the mobile origins, and the controls are great with rebindable keys and hotkeys.
Overall, this is a must-play for any serious Deus Ex fan. It's a nice 5-hour experience, with 3 to 4 more hours if you want to do multiple playthroughs on New Game Plus to unlock all Achievements.

If there had been a follow up to the Fall, it would have been a more easy recommendation.
As it stands, the game is for those who are curious or are fans of Deus Ex as it stands already.
The story is incomplete, which is disappointing, but what is there is serviceable. Obviously the graphics aren't super great but if you enjoyed the gameplay of Human Revolution and wouldn't mind playing another couple of hours of something new with a slightly downgraded feel, this is available.

Not what you were probably expecting. There are plenty of go-pro laps of the ring, but this is more documentary, just the right length at about an hour.
Definitely 1990s video feel to this. 540p max resolution but very watchable, made long before the era of go-pros but an interesting movie about the ring. watched it four times right through already.
After a slightly bewildering intro it gets into its semi-documentary style of the time, to educate, entertain and inform, and not in any particular order.
It's produced by Duke films, and includes background history and the obligatory archive cameo clip of Duke himself racing at the Nurburgring, so typically its a video by bikers made for bikers. With some polish, this game could be something pretty great. As it stands in its current state, it's a fun little 2-hour romp that will give you a few shocks and scares, but I'm not quite sure it's worthy of the $14 asking price. If you liked PT, this is right up your alley.
The thumbs down isn't for lack of quality, necessarily; it's to draw attention to some issues that, hopefully, will be fixed for the final release to make this game stand out amongst its peers, and for the price.
GAMEPLAY: WASD first person controls. You will navigate the artist's house in a pretty linear fashion. You will point and click to pick up the odd door key and a few items to add to your painting. There are two or three "find-the-number-combination" puzzles, and otherwise you will traverse the house in a fairly linear fashion, using your mouse to open doors and drawers. Minus the hiding from monsters, it plays a lot like SOMA.
VISUALS: The game has some optimization issues, as I had to bump it down to "low" graphical settings to keep from stuttering (and I have a pretty powerful machine). Otherwise, the environment is detailed enough to keep you immersed. The highlights here are the thematically appropriate paintings by artists like Goya and Fuseli that decorate the house. There are an abundance of recognizable works of famous art here that really sell the experience. The assets created for the game work pretty nicely too, giving the house a realistic flair. Another highlight is the "melting" effect, for lack of a better term used in at least one memorable portion of the game. This game uses lots of visual tricks to keep you on your toes, and are generally pretty effective.
AUDIO: Not a lot of music here. Most of what you'll hear are in-game sound effects - thumps, bangs, clattering, and some screams, as well as character monologues. It all works pretty well, but it's not hugely noteworthy, and some sound effects (such as the screams) become repetitive to the point of almost taking you out of the immersion.
HORROR: The game provides a few decent scares, especially early on. This game isn't so much reliant on jump scares (though there are many), opting instead for making dramatic environmental changes to create a feeling of doubt and and instability for the player. Unfortunately, they start to lose their effectiveness after a while, as a lot of the same techniques are repeated many times, while the game also doesn't give the player much (if any) reprieve from their occurence (read the final section for some more specific examples). There are serious problems with the pacing here, and this is an issue that many works of horror suffer from. I hope that the final release addresses this, as it takes the game from being scary to a railroaded trudge of expected jump scares and predictable turns for the last half of the game.
STORY: In typical horror fashion, the narrative is told through audio flashbacks (typically monologues by the protagonist) and scattered notes discovered throughout the environment. Layers tells the story of a disgraced artist seeking to redeem himself by creating a masterpiece. It's intriguing as it needs to be, but this early access version doesn't give the story a conclusion. I'm eager to see how the story turns out in the final version, though what we're shown so far isn't groundbreaking. As with so many horror games, it seems as though the story is a means to move the gameplay along - which isn't a bad thing.
SUGGESTIONS FOR THE FINAL VERSION (mild spoilers):
The pacing is the biggest issue here. The first five minutes or so has the player do a quick once-over of the house, then it plunges you straight into a series of primarily visual chicanery that persists for the rest of the game without respite. The player needs time to get comfortable with the surroundings before the rug is pulled out from under them. Let us explore this beautiful old house. Let us see glimpses of the family while they were happy, and while the artist was at the top of his game. Perhaps there could be a room where he displays some of his favourite works and awards he's won for other pieces. Then, slowly, give us hints that something isn't right. It's a tried - but true - horror formula. Lulling the player into a false sense of security, and from there, providing a series of catch-and-release to keep us on our toes. In this current version, the artist is subjected to all types of distortions of reality early on, continuing for the rest of the game, to the point where it ceases to be shocking. I got used to walking into a room, finding every door locked, then going back through the door I entered only to be somewhere new, so the tactic quickly became ineffective (which is a big problem, as it's used in every other room).
Another problem is the very liberal use of dolls. So far as I can tell, there's not much that's thematically significant about them, so they come off as just being a cliché. The bit in the  child's bedroom was especially jarring, but not in a good way - being stuck on a carousel with disembodied doll heads floating about was not scary nor threatening due to the lack of fail states in the game. It was lame, and left me wanting the section to end so I could continue onward.
Overall, Layers of Fear is a good experience for lovers of horror, and its faults can be largely excused due to its developmental state. I look forward to seeing the final version, and hope it reaches its full potential, as there is some real talent in the creative team.

It's been a while since I felt that rising chill as the hairs on the back of my neck stood on end.  A while since every floor boards creak made my heart leap into my throat and stop, waiting for the unknown to bring itself forth.  But it doesn't.  Not yet.
Layers of Fear is currently an extremely highly polished, almost complete early access offering.  It has overtones of P.T. and in some regards the twisting of the visuals surpasses it.  A wonderful example of the Unity engine used to the best of its ability.  The presentation is beautiful - darkness in very few places the rooms brim with light and colour but this can often make them even more terrifying as you feel like there is nowhere to hide.  The sound direction and scant voice acting adds to a feeling of isolation and every sound feels like it has meaning or is a warning.
As you explore the stunning victorian-era house, unravelling your characters sordid, bitter past through notes, art, newspapers and the detritus of his life you start to understand more of what is happening and it tests your empathy as a player and makes the game more frightening  - you may not be able to stop this, you may only make it better, or worse and the only way to know is to continue on.
Currently, the completed game is due for release in the first quarter of 2016, though additional content, such as the extra Halloween story, updates and patches are made available regularly and the developers are easy to reach via the forums.
I run a quite high spec rig and had no issues with running this on full high settings at a stable framerate, although some users seem to have issues.  It does seem to depend on system setups.  Personally, really loved playing this would be happy to consider it an 8/10 as it stands.  Completed, I expect that to potentially rise, but we'll see.

This is the second game in my life where I cheated on the first playthrough. Only because I payed some freaking money for it I wanted to see the end of it, no matter what. And - admittedly - the gory and brutal gameplay can indeed keep the fun above the bare minimum needed for an action horror title to keep me going. Unfortunately, that's about it when it comes to the positive aspects of the game. The negative outweigh the positive by far.
Take the story, for example. To be honest, I didn't even understand what the game was trying to tell me. There simply is no real story, it's a strange mix of involuntary brain surgery and drug induced nightmare fantasy hotchpotch ... thingy. And it is the inconceivably thin layer of background for the strange creatures (and your two companions) and their even stranger actions that is supposed to keep you motivated for about 14 hours - I call an epic fail, Mr. Mikami.
Secondly, the game mechanic for character and weapon development is total crap - you collect puddles or jars of green gel to buy weapon and character upgrades. Because that's the way the world beyond our consciousness works, we turn snot to ammo pouches...?! WTF?! What is wrong with dead enemies dropping some good old coins, for heavens sake?
Next annoying "feature" are the doors (yes, I am serious, the doors). Especially the ones in the "safe harbor dream world" (a small floor in some kind of hospital with a nurse mumbling strange stuff where you trade in your snot for upgrades). You return to this world in between levels and can move around between several rooms, each having a door you need to open. Each time you enter this safe heaven and walk into one of these rooms, you have to watch the slow door opening animations again. There is a Resident-Evil-4-style quick door opening mechanic, but you can only use it on doors you have already openend once. It sounds like a stupid thing to mention but it just gets on my nerves, big time. It sucks so much that I need to include it in this review - think about that!
Almost as a side note comes the fact that about half of the cutscenes are not skippable. Which really sucks when you reach a tough area and have to watch it over and over again.
On the technical side there are also more downs than ups. The game runs on the Id Tech 5 engine, inheriting the supertexture lazy loading effect where you turn quickly and see the objects get texturized with a little delay. It's very unfortunate that this engine seem to be uncontrollable since it offers great flexibility in level design and texture detail. And this is one of the pros of The Evil Within: you won't find any repetitive texture patterns, every level and every room comes with a very distinctive design.
The one big fun savior of the game is the fighting, which I think is really good. It is fluent and brutal and exciting. The weapon and hit sounds are pretty good and the guns have a nice splattering effect on most of the enemies (always aim for the head). The enemies are mostly humanoid zombies with some kind of a extreme piercing fetish where they have huge nails stuck in their heads. The bosses are even more disfigured: you fight a king size dog having his throat turned into a shark yap as well as a grown-up version of F.E.A.R.'s Alma, crawling on all fours with an extra pair of large arms. Overall, the monster design is pretty creative and it is kind of funny to see how the different types of creatures react to your weapons.
So, why and how did I cheat? I used god mode just to get on with the crappy story and to skip some of the areas that were simply annoying, just because I wanted to see where the trash plot was going and what the rest of the levels have to offer. The fights are fun, turning the monster's intestines inside out is just cool - even cool enough to lure me into a second round in New Game Plus mode, where you get to keep all weapons and character attributes. I simply farmed that stupid green gel, upgraded everything to the maximum and played on easy difficulty, just to run around in my character's head as the superior bad♥♥♥♥♥cop he probably thinks he is.
Not a Game of the Year game , but still wonderful nevertheless. Weird Story though , insane monster design, worth getting ,,, 4/5 stars

My first couple of playthroughs on survival difficulty were very enjoyable. It's gory and creepy with Shinji Mikami's classic RE4 style combat and a nice helping of stealth mechanics. The boss fights are varied and fun and you're constantly being introduced to new enemies. Also in typical Shinji Mikami fashion, the story devolves into nonsense by the end, although I ended up liking some of the characters more than I expected to.
Visually the game is beautiful. I've never played a game where the darkness felt so imposing and dense, without ever being frustrating, but rather tense as you hear the gurgles and growls of enemies emanating from unlit corners and hallways. Speaking of growls, the sound design is also excellent.
The game falls apart to me once you play it on AKUMU difficulty. If you look up guides to beat AKUMU they all revolve around breaking the AI and using various exploits. The games mechanics aren't balanced for this difficulty and so you have to beat AKUMU by essentially cheating.
I didn't care for the DLC either. "The Assignment" and "The Consequence" revolve around the slightly awkward stealth mechanic, but without the ability to resort to combat when you're inevitably discovered. "The Executioner" is basicly a first person melee combat game which is nowhere as fun to play as the main games combat.
I was determined to get all achievements and if you're an achievement hunter prepare to get frustrated. Beyond the issues with AKUMU mentioned above there's an achievement for speedrunning the game. I don't mind speedruns, but this should have been delegated to an online leaderboard, rather than encouraging players to speedrun what is mean to be a slow paced atmospheric horror experience. There's also an achievement for ignoring an entire aspect of the games mechanics: the upgrade system.
is an item Sebastian is rewarded with for exploring and defeating enemies, that he can use to upgrade his skills and weapons. Why make an achievement encouraging players to disregard an entire game mechanic?
with all that said I still recommend the game. It's gory RE4 style fun with a couple of good jumpscares, but if you go for all achievements the game will severely outstay it's welcome.

I'm sure the game has die hard fans, but after 25+ hours I just had enough of it. Ageing graphics and poor audio aside the gameplay is designed around F2P model and really poorly. The game feels really grind heavy. You either sink a lot of time to unlock weapons and vehicles or spend real money to skip some levelling to unlock levels so you can again buy guns and vehicles. It took me 20+ hours to gather enough money to unlock BAR which admitidly is one of the more expensive weapons. Still I realised the game is more frustrating than fun and I simply don't want to spend another 20 hours to unlock another gun and upgrades for it.
It's poorly balanced too, the weapons, vehicles and upgrades behind the pay wall give you a clear advantage. For example a not upgraded semi-automatic rifle needs 3 shots to kill, while upgraded 2. An upgraded bolt rifle kills in one shot while the default one in two. Then there are the vehicles. Tanks easily snipe infantry from long distance and experience tank crews will position themselves next to well known spawn points resulting in easy kills. To get any kind of anti-tank defence you again need to grind your level and buy AT weapons.
The art style or simply dated graphics result in game environments which just beg you to camp in shadows between grey textures making it hard to spot. The maps are poorly designed too, with a lot of flat, empty spaces making it easy target for tanks and well equipped veterans so expect to be killed a lot. From all the maps I found only few acceptable, mainly those which come with a town, making it harder for snipers and tankers to farm kills.
The character movement is slow and clunky. The same can be said about weapon handling. The gunplay feels satisfying, but it doesn't rescue the rest.
I like WW2 setting and I really hope we will some some more decent FPS soon, H&G is simply not one of them. For now I will stick with Red Orchestra2 / Rising Storm combo.

to start with the positives, the game itself is stable enough to enjoy good playable framerates on a low-mid range rig, and on the higher settings has a very gritty, muddy artstyle which suits the genre perfectly and is particularly immersive.  furthermore to get a kill is very rewarding and the gameplay seems to collaborate the best arcadey style of cqb and very realistic long range firefights.  also the map design is well enough designed to balance attack/defence as not to be in a commanding position with one or the other.  i found the main menu to be confusing in the sense that it was difficult to first work out what does what and where you access certain customisations but on the whole it didnt detract too much from getting into the game at the start.
on the more negative side though there are two key problems... 1- this is the most pay to win game i have ever come across, you want a tank? well you can either play for 200 hours... or buy it! or how about a plane? play for 300 hours to save enough or... pay £50 to unlock it now!  i cant comprehend the sanity of the man who thought it would be a good strategy to make you pay for every last gadget and gismo there is.  this problem is then amplified by the fact that it takes hours and hours and hours to grind out enough currency to buy anthing so you have a massive gap between players with extremely over powered guns and vehicles against you with a default stock rifle which you dont stand a chance at getting a kill with past 25 metres.
and the second problem is the fact that it takes hours to access the best feature that the game has to offer... in order to join the mmo aspect of this game (which in itself looks very good, where you have a birds eye view of europe and three factions fight lots of mini battles to exapnd there empire) you have to be a level 5, which takes a damn long time to reach (unless you pay for it!!!)

This is the second game in my life where I cheated on the first playthrough. Only because I payed some freaking money for it I wanted to see the end of it, no matter what. And - admittedly - the gory and brutal gameplay can indeed keep the fun above the bare minimum needed for an action horror title to keep me going. Unfortunately, that's about it when it comes to the positive aspects of the game. The negative outweigh the positive by far.
Take the story, for example. To be honest, I didn't even understand what the game was trying to tell me. There simply is no real story, it's a strange mix of involuntary brain surgery and drug induced nightmare fantasy hotchpotch ... thingy. And it is the inconceivably thin layer of background for the strange creatures (and your two companions) and their even stranger actions that is supposed to keep you motivated for about 14 hours - I call an epic fail, Mr. Mikami.
Secondly, the game mechanic for character and weapon development is total crap - you collect puddles or jars of green gel to buy weapon and character upgrades. Because that's the way the world beyond our consciousness works, we turn snot to ammo pouches...?! WTF?! What is wrong with dead enemies dropping some good old coins, for heavens sake?
Next annoying "feature" are the doors (yes, I am serious, the doors). Especially the ones in the "safe harbor dream world" (a small floor in some kind of hospital with a nurse mumbling strange stuff where you trade in your snot for upgrades). You return to this world in between levels and can move around between several rooms, each having a door you need to open. Each time you enter this safe heaven and walk into one of these rooms, you have to watch the slow door opening animations again. There is a Resident-Evil-4-style quick door opening mechanic, but you can only use it on doors you have already openend once. It sounds like a stupid thing to mention but it just gets on my nerves, big time. It sucks so much that I need to include it in this review - think about that!
Almost as a side note comes the fact that about half of the cutscenes are not skippable. Which really sucks when you reach a tough area and have to watch it over and over again.
On the technical side there are also more downs than ups. The game runs on the Id Tech 5 engine, inheriting the supertexture lazy loading effect where you turn quickly and see the objects get texturized with a little delay. It's very unfortunate that this engine seem to be uncontrollable since it offers great flexibility in level design and texture detail. And this is one of the pros of The Evil Within: you won't find any repetitive texture patterns, every level and every room comes with a very distinctive design.
The one big fun savior of the game is the fighting, which I think is really good. It is fluent and brutal and exciting. The weapon and hit sounds are pretty good and the guns have a nice splattering effect on most of the enemies (always aim for the head). The enemies are mostly humanoid zombies with some kind of a extreme piercing fetish where they have huge nails stuck in their heads. The bosses are even more disfigured: you fight a king size dog having his throat turned into a shark yap as well as a grown-up version of F.E.A.R.'s Alma, crawling on all fours with an extra pair of large arms. Overall, the monster design is pretty creative and it is kind of funny to see how the different types of creatures react to your weapons.
So, why and how did I cheat? I used god mode just to get on with the crappy story and to skip some of the areas that were simply annoying, just because I wanted to see where the trash plot was going and what the rest of the levels have to offer. The fights are fun, turning the monster's intestines inside out is just cool - even cool enough to lure me into a second round in New Game Plus mode, where you get to keep all weapons and character attributes. I simply farmed that stupid green gel, upgraded everything to the maximum and played on easy difficulty, just to run around in my character's head as the superior bad♥♥♥♥♥cop he probably thinks he is.
Not a Game of the Year game , but still wonderful nevertheless. Weird Story though , insane monster design, worth getting ,,, 4/5 stars

My first couple of playthroughs on survival difficulty were very enjoyable. It's gory and creepy with Shinji Mikami's classic RE4 style combat and a nice helping of stealth mechanics. The boss fights are varied and fun and you're constantly being introduced to new enemies. Also in typical Shinji Mikami fashion, the story devolves into nonsense by the end, although I ended up liking some of the characters more than I expected to.
Visually the game is beautiful. I've never played a game where the darkness felt so imposing and dense, without ever being frustrating, but rather tense as you hear the gurgles and growls of enemies emanating from unlit corners and hallways. Speaking of growls, the sound design is also excellent.
The game falls apart to me once you play it on AKUMU difficulty. If you look up guides to beat AKUMU they all revolve around breaking the AI and using various exploits. The games mechanics aren't balanced for this difficulty and so you have to beat AKUMU by essentially cheating.
I didn't care for the DLC either. "The Assignment" and "The Consequence" revolve around the slightly awkward stealth mechanic, but without the ability to resort to combat when you're inevitably discovered. "The Executioner" is basicly a first person melee combat game which is nowhere as fun to play as the main games combat.
I was determined to get all achievements and if you're an achievement hunter prepare to get frustrated. Beyond the issues with AKUMU mentioned above there's an achievement for speedrunning the game. I don't mind speedruns, but this should have been delegated to an online leaderboard, rather than encouraging players to speedrun what is mean to be a slow paced atmospheric horror experience. There's also an achievement for ignoring an entire aspect of the games mechanics: the upgrade system.
is an item Sebastian is rewarded with for exploring and defeating enemies, that he can use to upgrade his skills and weapons. Why make an achievement encouraging players to disregard an entire game mechanic?
with all that said I still recommend the game. It's gory RE4 style fun with a couple of good jumpscares, but if you go for all achievements the game will severely outstay it's welcome.
