Welp. It certainly brings new meaning to the term “single player” I suppose.
I should begin by saying that I’m not terribly experienced with dating simulators. Outside of
which I absolutely loathed, the last dating sim I played was some flash-based game on Newgrounds called
back in 2002 - a guilty (…) pleasure back in my younger days. Due to the sour taste that
left in my mouth, I lost interest in the abundance of dating sims now plaguing Steam. It took a special video to pique my interest:
And so I played it. I played it for 10.5 hours, apparently. Somehow, I even got my non-gaming girlfriend hellaciously addicted to it.
begins with a dream sequence, in which you meet a very perky and attractive female. After some pathetic attempts at flirting, you wake up in your bedroom and find a “love fairy” in your room, who spends the rest of the game helping you pick up girls that are so stereotyped that it puts Mean Girls to shame. Such stereotypes include ♥♥♥♥♥y teacher, ♥♥♥♥♥y milf, ♥♥♥♥♥y high schooler, weird spiritualist, geeky girl, mega ♥♥♥♥♥ and a young single mum, among others. Your goal is to sleep with each and every one of them.
The developers described the game perfectly. For those too lazy to read the top right of their screen right now, the basic gist of it is that it’s half dating sim, half match-three puzzle game with an
lot of “plot”.
The dating sim portion of the game involves you talking to each of the girls, asking them questions and every so often, answering their questions, which may include them quizzing you on questions that they’ve asked you. Talking to girls and answering their questions correctly earns you points, which can be used to purchase upgrades to your stats (charisma, sexuality, etc), which will make the other main portion of the game (the puzzle portion) easier. You can also earn these points by buying gifts for your target waifu.
After you’re done talking, you can choose to take a girl on a date. The dating portion of the game plays as a very simple match-three puzzle game. Each gem on the screen has a different purpose, and your goal is to match three or more of these gems to earn enough “affection” to successfully complete the date. Just like the real world, certain girls seem to favour some attributes more so than others – matching three “sexuality” gems may work wonders for the cougar lady, but won’t quite do against the shy little geeky one. Other gems don’t contribute directly to the affection count, but assist you in earning more affection. The passion (pink hearts) gem, for example, provides passion which will increase the amount of affection that other gems provide, whilst the sentiment gems (light blue) allow you to use certain gifts in the middle of the puzzle which provide extra bonuses. Each puzzle has a limited number of moves that you’re allowed to make. Running out of moves before reaching the target “affection” level (which increases with subsequent dates) will result in you failing the date. Successfully completing the date will reward you with a decent sum of money and more importantly, greater admiration from your future waifu. Once you successfully date a girl 3 times, the game allows you take a girl out
, which results in… Yeah.
Unfortunately, the game never really gets deeper than that. Yes, you can buy food, drinks and gifts for the girls, but there’s no challenge to this as each girl’s favourite foods and gifts are not only listed in their profile but also indicated with a star or heart next to the item in the store. The getting-to-know-you portion of the game never really offers anything challenging or original compared to any other dating sim ever. On the other hand, the simple-yet-addictive puzzle portions of the game do provide some value in breaking up the monotony of scrolling through lines of cringeworthy-but-hilarious dialogue.
I imagine anyone reading this review will understand that there’s a huge different between a “story” and a “plot”.
Honestly, I was actually surprised at just how graphic some of the depictions of the girls were. I’m not even sure if I’m allowed to talk about it here. If Steam reviews censor swearing, then they’re probably not going to be happy with me talking about pictures of naked anime girls bent over and dripping♥♥♥♥♥♥♥from their nether regions. In a weird sense, I think I’m legitimately too old for this stuff now. I’m sure an 18-year-old virgin might feel differently though.
Then there’s the other major thing that differentiates this title from
– The absolutely hilarious voiceovers. Seriously, the dialogue in this game is golden and the voiceovers are spot on. I really wouldn’t want it any other way.
Honestly, I enjoyed this game because of just how incredibly hilarious and inappropriate it was. The puzzle sections of the game were a fairly welcome addition to the genre and helped to keep the game more engaging and challenging than its contemporaries. A word of warning though – you will be judged by your Steam friends for playing this game. Whether you choose to proceed despite that is up to you.

Showdown mode.
Our rivals were dropping like flies; falling with a new lining of bullets in their chest, a missing head thanks to a katana, or exploding in a shower of guts, blood, and bone from a well placed rocket.
Then it was only us. 1 v 1. The map began to change, chunks of the background exploding in fiery torrents of Michael Bay's wettest dreams. A fast tempo rock tune kicked in to signal that this was about to get serious.
I chased after my final opponent, wary of the fact that he had a rocket launcher and liked to show it off. Wall bouncing away from his first rocket, I tried to cut him off at the opposite end as I landed beneath the platform he was defending. To my surprise, he jumped down behind me and began to chase me-- resulting in a quick turn around as I dashed at him with my katana. I was out of bullets, and had to make do with my sword.
I struck him once, the strike throwing him far out of reach for a follow-up strike. He knelt down, the red laser pointer on the rocket launcher wildly flailing up and down. Much like a hissing snake, it was a warning to back off.
I couldn't, not if I wanted to win the showdown. I rolled forward, hoping the quick gap closer would make him re-think firing a rocket; if it hit me at this range, we'd both die.
He fired.
The rocket was arched slightly up towards the ceiling. I jumped away to avoid splash damage and he took the opportunity to flee, jumping and wall-bouncing to a higher floor.
I followed after, finding him on one knee yet again. Ready to fire. I had no idea how many rockets he had, but it was time to end this. In the next ten seconds, I was either going to be a bloody mist, or he was going home in several pieces.
I ran at him one final time, watching carefully as he lined up his shot... and then performed a running slide just as he fired. His shot, which was aimed at my head, completely missed. I rose back to my feet, sprinting through the smoke trail of the rocket.
One swing was all it took. His head parted ways with his body, and the spectators of the match went wild.
LAST MAN STANDING.
I turned to look at the fallen, now spectators, cheering wildly for the underdog that overcame the rocket-wielding madman whose death grip on the scoreboard ensured he was first place the entire match.
A smile spread on my face, and I uttered four simple words as the screen faded to black..
"Get on my level."

I've never heard of Majesty 2 until the recent steam sale.  I'm a fan of real time and turn based strategy games and I must say that I've thoroughly enjoyed playing this game.  Just finished the original and kingmaker campaigns, it sure was fun.
Don't think multiplayer works for this game but singleplayer is great.  In 64 hours of gameplay it has crashed on me only once.  So can't say it has many bugs.  The game is nicely polished and has good graphics for its age.  Haven't played Majesty 1, the graphics there are a bit of a turn off unfortunately, although many people think the gameplay of the older version is better.
The campagn missions can be very difficult but they are beatable.  The increasing difficulty pushes you to explore the game more and read up on some strategies if you get really stuck.  When you are finally able to beat that difficult mission,  like the Rat King or The Avatar, then it feels really satisfying :)  With the Rat King mission I built a mage guild and then a wizard tower and kept activating it to protect my warriors until they levelled up.
Economy is very important in this game, try to position your marketplace next to a trade post and then build a tower next to the market so the tax collector doesn't have very far to walk.   Group your economic buildings like the blacksmith and the potions bazaar next to that tower as well.
There are a variety of strategies available with each mission.  You can create 'tanking' groups of 3 clerics + 1 dwarf.  Although groups don't seem to retreat as well as individual heroes.  Rangers are a good early to mid game option.  Some players build the Hall of Lords straight away.  Some of the cheap lords like levelled up Rogues and Rangers can be very useful in the early game and mid game, and that's usually the most crucial time.  A levelled up lord is not always the best option, it may be better to have lower level templars with good weapons so they are cheaper to buy.  And so on a so forth.
Sure the first game may have more options but Magesty 2 also offers alot of good gameplay so I think this game is sometimes rated unfairly, because it is a great game.  And if its on sale then its definitely worth it :)

Some changes from Majesty 1, of which a lot of my childhood was spent playing.
Improved AI: You can use this to cheese any map, as your peasants actually repair things in Majesty 2, hero AI is a lot better, with heroes making better choices. With new flags like guarding, you never have to worry about a skeleton ruining your entire economy because it got lucky and killed the caravan carrying much needed gold.
Stronger guards: Palace and guard tower guards can now stand toe to toe with moderately strong enemies. Tax collectors seem much happier in this game. Arrows come with the guard tower, no need to spend gold researching them.
Stronger classes in general: Mages and Rangers no longer die in 1-2 hits from rats anymore, clerics not only do actual damage, but they are even harder to kill than before. Mages do not have the extreme overkill capacity as they did in Majesty 1 if they survived to level 10, but they make up for it with better defenses / ai / and utility (freezing enemies). Elves have been buffed to the point of being useful unless you have to go with dwarves to fight early dragon onslaughts.
Skeletons now reliably killable by level 1 Warriors: Skeletons are no longer magic resist / dodge gods and for the player, dwarves have taken their place for fighting strong magic monsters like dragons.
Parties: You can now assign 4 heroes to a party. This allows you to tactically place your clerics where they need to be, and generally makes your heroes almost invulnerable.
Enemy spawn rates increased: If you do not plan accordingly, you can have your low level heroes die to hordes of rats and skeletons while your better heroes are off doing the objective. Guard towers fix this problem easily, but I like to keep them to a minimum so that my heroes can level up and acquire gold for upgrades.
More upgrades: Your casters now gain magic attack when they upgrade their weapons, and every class has a plethora of upgrades to purchase.
I've read many reviews saying this game is too difficult. Without spoiling too much, learn the strengths and weaknesses of the heroes and learn how to set up and properly defend your economy, if your tax collectors die, you get no gold. Do not overlook palace upgrades. Remember your build orders so you can try something different if you fail.

I'm not going to pretend DX:TF is a great game. It has very cheap production values, at times cringeworthy voice acting that rivals the original Deus Ex and pretty bad models. But taken into consideration this is essentially a mobile game, it's actually pretty impressive.
Gameplay-wise I would say it plays a lot like DXHR though you can access the weapon store anywhere which makes the gameplay a bit more interesting as you don't need to visit hubs to buy new weapons. There are also more variations available. There's still a ton of options available for each mission.
Worst issue might be the controls, specifically the way the game emulates touchscreen control. You have to be very precise with your clicks for them to register, cause if you move your mouse even slightly while clicking it counts as if you swipe the screen. But once you get used to this, it's not that big of a deal.
The main reason I recommend this game is the story and just the chance to play as a protagonist who isn't a superhuman man-machine, you're just a regular augmented soldier who still needs Neuropazyne for your augmentations and it adds a more relatable human aspect to him. I also love exploring the backstory behind the Tyrant group and some of the things leading up to Human Revolution.
All in all, DX:TF is not by far the worst Deus Ex game and if you get used to the controls and lower your expectations a bit, I find it very enjoyable. Shame it seems they canned the sequels.
STORY: 8/10
Very well written and there's tons of stuff to read and explore for fans of the lore.
GRAPHICS: 7/10

Let's be honest here.  It's essentially the same game as Sniper Elite V2, especially as far as mechanics go. The sniper rifles look and feel the same, the shoot them same, the still fill you with excitement as you hit a headshot from 900 yards.  Nazi Zombie Army 2 is essentially a re-skin of V2.  You'll find yourself in some of the very same maps and locations, recognizing much of the same scenery as you did the first time around.  However, there's one important difference:  Every single one of these maps has been decimated by war and they're filled with shambling zombies!
There's a couple of details about this game that makes me love it, just a hair more that V2.  Almost all of that love steams from atmosphere.  Nazi Zombie Army 2 is fantastic in that atmosphere department and I'm not even talking about the zombies.  I'm a horror fan.  A big horror fan at that.  I co-host three fairly popular horror podcasts, so I'd like to consider myself well versed. (Check the links in my profile if you're a podcast fan!)  The devs took a lot of time and research to make the horror tropes in NZA2's looks and sounds really pop to make this a really stellar horror experience.  From the very start of the game, we're struck with an orange color pallet that screams Halloween.  The music is an homage to bands like Goblin that have crafted many common themes in the genre to make the game even sound familiar if you're a fan of horror movies.  It's just a really great package as far as horror nerdery goes!
Then, we get to the zombies.  Even they’re creepy!  They’re also a good homage to horror nerdery, pulling more from the Romero Zombie well vs. the Zak Snyder fast zombie well.   The shamble, wobble and lurch, which makes getting those sweet sweet headshots all the harder.  But those headshots will happen.  You’ll get those amazing slow motion long distance shot ending in an x-ray that shows the bullet pass through the skeleton of your zombie of choice.  This time around though, you can feel all giddy and excited without feeling bad for it.  You’re shooting the undead, not other humans!
The only note to be wary of with Nazi Zombie Army 2 is that it is clearly designed towards a co-op experience.  Most missions end in a “survive the waves” shoot-a-thon that while flying solo, can be a bit tiresome and difficult.  You can play solo however!  Just make sure you’re going to have to work for it a bit harder.

LEGO with guns.
You might take one look at Ace of Spades and think "Minecraft Clone!" before moving on to the next game.  If you do, you'll be missing out on a fun title that takes pieces of multiple genres and snaps them together like children's building blocks.
At it's core, Ace of Spades is a competent shooter with most of the staples you'd expect today:  classes, weapon selection (albeit limited) and large, open maps.  What differentiates it is the fact that everything on the map can be destroyed.  I mean it - everything.  I'm not talking pre-designed collapse in a building from a tank shell or artillery strike, but rather block-by-block devastation.  Add to this the fact that all classes are able to place blocks (or pre-fab structures) down on the map at will, and you'll see the landscape of a round change completely in only ten or so minutes.  Forts are built and destroyed.  Snipers erect networks of towers that fall to crafty engineers.  Vast, sky-bridging platforms extend from one base to another, only to be eliminated by a stray rocket that plunges six men to their doom.  Opposition too stiff on the front lines?  Mine out a tunnel into their base like a medieval sapper and hit those pesky snipers from behind.
Ace of Spades offers several game types, although only two of them are consistently played on populated servers.  Team Deathmatch needs no explanation.  The second is Zombie mode.  In this, the start of the round sees one or two random players become the zombie.  They must hunt down the other players using blips on their minimap and claw them to death, thus creating a new zombie.  Non-zombified players will erect vast defenses in the vain hope of staying alive for a few extra minutes.  Overall, quite a lot of fun.  I wish more of the modes were played because some of them are really good, but it's still a lot of fun and worth the $15.
Server load is low at this point, and was even when I first got the game in 2013.  You might find 2-3 full or semi-full servers in your region depending on time of day, but it's usually enough.
To sum up,
Pros:
-  First Person Shooter goodness on maps that can be completely destroyed by the players.  Watch as landscapes rise and fall all through human effort.  Dig secret passages into enemy bases, destroy their carefully-built structures and be a general nuisance.
-  A mild building element allows players to construct temporary defenses to aid in their skirmishes, leading to interesting scenarios as players deal with what are essentially castle sieges.
-  Fun, fast-paced action combined with sneaky digging and relaxed building.  The game rewards you for doing basically anything that you'd like to do.  It is, after all, a LEGO set with guns.
-  Pretty much bug-free.  I've had one or two lock-ups in nearly 40 hours of play.
-  Casual-friendly.  Great for short-period time-killing or for longer stretches.
Cons:
- Snipers.  Every single round sees 75% of the players taking the role of sniper.  More variety would be nice, especially given the fact that other classes can manipulate the map in far more interesting ways.
-  Autobalance issues.  Good luck joining a round with a friend and getting on the same team.  Autobalance kicks in even during the opening moments when players are loading between maps, and it isn't possible to change teams (in spite of a change teams button) unless you quit and re-join.  On the other hand, if half a team drops during a match the game won't autobalance to adjust for that, so you can sometimes see 10 v 5 scenarios.
-  Liberal kick-votes.  It seems in most rounds that half a dozen players or more will be the target of an unexplained, undefended kick vote.  Usually for "Hacking," even though I have yet to see a hacker in many dozens of rounds.  In spite of the map being easily destructible (and rebuildable, like a LEGO set), many players will take offense if someone so much as damages a block they've placed down with a stray bullet.  Erroneous "Griefing" kickvotes pop up all the time - usually because a sniper gets mad when someone blows up their tower.  Never mind that they can just build a new one in half a second.  If you get irrationally angry when people damage something you've made, even if you can rebuild it quickly and with minimal effort, you might not like this game very much.
Overall, Ace of Spades is well worth $15.  If you consider the price of a movie in theatres and the amount of enjoyment you could get out of this game, the price is a steal.  If you wait for a sale you'll be even better off.
DISCLAIMER:  The video on Steam shows players flying around with brown jetpacks, painting things and building complex structures.  I think that was the developer's attempt to show an artistic representation of their own map-building process.  If you buy this game thinking you can join unlimited-time servers and tool around like in Minecraft, you'll be disappointed.  Rounds are about 15 minutes apiece and anything you build can and *will* be destroyed.
Additionally, many of the reviews for this game are quite negative.  Ignore the old-timers comparing it with the free version from ages past and just take it for what it is - a shooter with maps you can blow up at will.  I have to wonder if some of these people even know what fun is that they consider Ace of Spades a bad game.  After a quarter century of gaming and playing the same experiences in new boxes dozens of times, I am genuinely delighted to have a game that is so different from the rest.

This Game looks AMAZING. The lightning at times is so breathtaking I stopped more than once to make myself short gameplay videos. The mostly perfect textures, the great level design, the architecture, the attention to detail. If not for the the fps drops this would be a perfect masterpiecie.
The editing is also worth noting, because something that normaly is more of a factor in movies, comes here much more into play. Depending on the situatoins you wil get blurry visions, diffrent saturations, double vision, it is all very deliberate and very crazy and dopey!
The bosses, and all around enemies are amazing in design and detail. They look so real in combination with the amazing setting, the best particle and light effects, it all really creates must see scenarios.
It is amazing how many ideas are present in this game. When you look at games like Dead Space, it practicaly is the same stuff for 10 hours...
Here you get major Level Designs changes, setting changes and gameplay changes every two to three chapters. At one time you stealth your way through a forest, dark mansions, shoot up a village full of creeps, then you solve puzzles in a church only to get to a survival scenario in a destroyed city, and a big chase through its streets… the game demands, that you adapt constantly, which can be great and frustrating at once, because you never know what awaits you in the next chapter, or even behind the next corner, and all that you learned earlier might not really be expected of you in the next few chapters. This is a gaming "best of" as much as a bag full of ideas (not always new ones mind you).
But I need to critisize the final level.. it's a kill room, after kill room, after kill room... you get to fight one more time against all of them... then you get some jump and run sections, and some pseudo stealth sections... totally out of character for the game. I think the final chapter should cut the uber lazy level design which left a bad taste in the mouth. I managed to make it throught up to chapter 15 on survivor... but the final chapter was only busy work.
Most flawes reside here… The games amazing looks come at a price… there are times where clearly the engine cannot generate a smooth experience even though my GPU isn't even breaking a sweat. These moments are frustrating, because it clearly plays much worse and there is no real reason behind it. And I am talking about a very patched up build.
Other problems are often with difficulty spikes that can get very frustrating. I have hit numerous progres walls, and although frustrating, the game pulled me in enough to fight on. (One boss I could not beat for two weaks, after two days of intense trying I started to play two attempts per day and finally did it). I have to admit though that the boss variety is amazing.
This might feel disjointed because of all the changes in settings and gameplay but it is supposed to.
It is a strange story that kinda comes together, but it seems the final pieces of the puzzle will be in the DLC. If you like X-Files, Twin Peaks, Twilight Zone or Freddy Kruger, than this might be up your alley.
In the end this is an amazing, fun, chalanging and creative game full ideas, great designs that get hampered by poor but not game breaking optimization and a rather disappointing final chapter (gameplay wise).

This is going to be a long review. for this game was longer than I expected, had a deeper story than I expected, and had more flaws than I expected.
The game deals with a massive case of identity crisis.  Is it a horror?  Is it stealth? Is it a slasher movie gone video game? Is it a shooter?  By the end of the game, I was not sure.  It's like the Frankenstein's monster of video games.
To start out, I will give praise where praise is due.  The game delivers many dark and creepy segments of game-play and rarely uses jump scares.  The sound effects are eerie, dark, ominous and nauseating at times.  They add a lot to the atmosphere of the game.  The devs also use the plot to dish out some trippy reality shifting moments that will leave you  blinking and stunned.
Some of the monster designs were spooky and can make your skin crawl.   Not all of them were original, but a lot of effort did go into that part of the game, and it shows.
The balance of skills and ammo is done well, but some of the skills feel either pointless, or like they shouldn't have been upgradable skills in the first place -- Like the fact that your character can't sprint for more than TWO seconds without upgrades.
The story, like the game-play, feels pieced together from a host of other games and leaves you scratching your head at the end with some unexplained and out of place last minute scenes that are thrown at you as the game is ending.  I understand that some of the questions are answered in the DLC, but that feels like a cheap way to get people to buy the content.  The story is too convoluted to cover in the review, but the vibe that I got is that the devs wanted free range to do whatever they wanted in the game... and they do!
Unfortunately, after the first hour or so of game-play, it was clear that many flaws were being hidden behind an ocean of blood and a promising start.  The way the devs use the plot to implement any crazy thought that entered their minds has me wondering if they all gathered in a room the first day, and the lead dev said "Okay people.  Here's a bucket; here's a stack of paper.  Everyone start writing chaotic and bloody ideas and put them in the bucket!  Don't you dare hold back!  I want an ocean of blood!  I want giant brains!  I want giant eyeballs!  I want gory, slasher like monster!  I want CoD moments that have no place in the mix!  I want the worst melee combat you can come up with!  I want a random driving segment that lasts three seconds!  I want floating hummers with heavy machine guns!  I want chainsaws!  I want poorly made invisible enemies that we only use for ten minutes!  I want stealth!  I want you to forget about the stealth five minutes later!" and that is how this game was born.
The characters aren't the worst I have seen in a video game, but they are a far-cry from believable.  The main character is an emotionless meat sack that brushes off the mental stress of human meat-lockers and fountains of blood like it's just another day at work.  The character interactions are mostly dull and don't do a whole lot for the game accept keep it moving.  There are some serious face slapping one-liners in this game.
The part that made this game so hard for me to enjoy is the fact that evey time I thought "this might be cool!" the game ruins it with clunky game-play, bad pacing, poor character development, and just outright sloppiness by the devs that made some segments unnecessarily frustrating.
The game is worth s squirt when its on a solid sale.  Otherwise, I would recommend looking elsewhere.   There are  better horror games on the market; there are better 3rd person shooters; there are better stealth rpgs.  This game wants to be all of them, but fails on all three levels in the end.

I have been looking at this game with passing interest for some time now, and only happened to notice this island creator had showed up on the workshop. It was free, so I decided to try it out. Normally I'm not a very artistic type, but I found that just playing with some of the tools actually allowed me to make some interesting, dare I say pleasant landscapes without much effort at all from mass-placement and -texture tools. And given all of the other more precise options, I can see this being a very powerful tool to others to make some really neat locales. The idea that players could make these to be in the final game is a really incredible idea, so if you're following this game, you really should try it out in my opinion.
Additionally, with the option to try out your islands as a player, it makes this a really neat insight into some of the early mechanics of the game. For once, the grappling rope actually impacts obstacles, and overall the physics seem to be building toward a fun game. (Side Note - you CAN reel in the grappling hook with the SHIFT key, took be a bit to figure that out.)
Overall, this is a really fun, free tool with a lot of impications for players, and should definitely be checked out if you're interested in this game. In my opinion, this free demo shows a lot of promise for the game as a whole, and definitely piqued my interest in it that much more.

I have anxiously been waiting for Worlds Adrift to announce a release date for the full game, since I first heard about it months ago.  I was lucky enough to get in on some NA test servers, and after getting a chance to play a version of the full game I have been thirsty for more.  The Island Creator is one of the best ideas I have ever seen a developer release to it's fans.  It's beneficial to the developers in many ways, and it allows people a small taste of the game before it is released.  It's also free, which gives me a good feeling about the developers, and the direction that they are taking for the game, and how they want to interact with fans of the game.
That being said the Island Creator is really fun.  It gives you alot of creative tools to work with, and ton's of freedom to use your own creativity.  The developers are also updating it and adding new usefull features all the time.  The other great thing is that Bossa Studios have been activly listening to their fans, and gathering feedback about the Island Creator, and ways to improve it. It amazes me that a development team is so responsive and in touch with it's fan base, that they actually care to hear opinions about a small side project of the full game.  They even have been showcasing some of the Islands on Twitch that they like.
I can't wait for the full game to be released, but at least I have something to mess around with until then.
If your thinking about downloading this, just do it.  It's free, and super fun to play around with.  If you have used any 3d modeling suite like Blender, You will understand the controls right off the get go.  It is pretty intuitive, and easy to figure out how everything works.  I have a fairly powerful computer with a 980Ti, so I don't know how well it runs on weaker systems.  It runs very well on my system.
Thanks Bossa, I appreciate you releasing this tool to the public.  It is pretty epic.

Both dates and carnal connections are represented by a playfield of iconic shapes. Initially, players might try to rely on their gem-shifting experience with Bejeweled, but they’ll likely become stymied when trying to earn the required number of points to successfully complete a date. Instead, gamers have to carefully use each of their limited number of turns to make matches of icons that correspond to each woman’s preference.
Captivatingly, there’s a number of factors that complicate this process. Removing a succession of pink hearts has the ability to raise the player’s passion multiplier. The trick is determining how often to do this. Go into the date strong and you’ll surely raise your potential to earn points, but there’s also the possibility of squandering turns on increasing a multiplier instead of actually scoring points. As such, it’s akin to the small, but significant romantic gestures that can make or break a real-life romantic outing.

Being a huge fan of horror games, I absolutely had to pick up Layers of Fear.
As described it as a “psychedelic horror” game, as you play a painter who is feverishly attempting to complete a true masterpiece, while going mad in the process.

The game mechanics are incredibly refreshing, as there was no specific villain you were trying to escape from, for the most part, which meant that the 'environment' was what you needed to fear, including several jump scares along your way.
Atmospherically, Layers of Fear is astounding from the moment you enter the house you will be exploring. Rain is falling heavily outside, with occasional bursts of thunder crackling behind you. The entire game is influenced by art and décor from previous centuries, particularly the architecture and design of the 19th century, and the visuals are very well tied together with this theme.
What also worth mentioning is the incredibly alluring and chilling soundtrack during the gameplay, that gives you the emotions the situation pulls you in.
I’d recommend the game to anyone who enjoys horror games as a genre, particularly if you don’t mind games where you can’t defend yourself and it’s all about you, the antagonist, and the spooky atmosphere.
Despite the game 'still' being in Early Access, what IS available to play is deeply engaging, if in need of a little polish here and there.
The game relies heavily on its ability to set you on edge, so if you’re the type with nerves of steel you likely won’t get too much out of it. To horror fans, however? I wholeheartedly recommend Layers of Fear to you!

I know this game has been out for quite a while, but I'm mostly reviewing it to state it's
worth getting. I have about 300 more hours from a DRM free version, so however many hours I have on here is not accurate.
If you're just curious about the "Collection" edition portion, it is worth the money based on the sheer amount of content added.
(see below if you have played the first)
It isn't important that you have played the first, as there isn't really any important information to transfer to the second. If you have ever wanted to play an RTS in which you don't have to deal with managing
your units are doing, this is likely the game for you. It requires quick thinking (or average thinking at .2x speed) and some knowledge of each guild and building, but the main campaign eases you into the game at a pace that will teach you all you need to know. Many of the missions have unique side missions to make sure there's variation each time you play.
Certain missions can be very difficult and will require you to be entirely precise in your decisions at the start (such as the mission in the King Maker expansion that sends a bunch of dragonlings at you near instantly). Clerics and Dwarven towers will quickly become your best friends.
I've played the original majesty for likely 400+ hours, and have a lot of knowledge and memories of it to show for it. I see a lot of the negative reviews and comments are based solely upon the original "being better". I personally find this one to be much more than the first in almost every way.
If you've played the first, you can expect to miss this... (cons)
However, the additions make this one worth playing. (pros)
Yes, this game is 0 to 100 on certain missions, but all of them are completely possible. You will
utilize the .2x speed button very frequently and will occassionally have to baby-sit your lower leveled powerful heroes with the heal spell.
If all else fails, you can usually go back to using two cleric guilds at the start. Clerics are the toughest unit in the game as long as you can keep them together, as they're nearly infinitely powerful as long as some mana exists. Shortly after, you will want to get dwarves for both the unit and especially the tower. One tower alone is enough to kill a werewolf or a dragon, which can easily level an entire settlement early on. By placing a normal guard tower behind each dwarven tower, you effectively multiply the effectiveness of each tower by a decent bit.
Krypta appears to be the most useful special hero for their sheer ability to stay alive while dealing heavily spread out damage with their minions.
Also, do not forget to use inns. Having a few scattered on each side can save your heroes, since often times the guild is just far enough to have them killed when they retreat.
All in all, I feel this one is more full than the first. There are some noticeable changes, but for the most part, it's just something to get used to rather than miss intensely. This game is worth your time, and will immerse you faster than you might expect.

I'm writing this review because It bothers me how little notoriety majesty gets
Majesty 1 and Majesty 2 are both incredibly entertaining games that have value that long outlives their price point. Don't let my hours played fool you. I owned these games before steam was so common place and have likely sunk over 100 hours into Majesty 1 and at least 70 or so into Majesty 2.
But what is the game like? Well, Majesty is an RTS game yes, but it is best described as being god of your own little fantasy MMORPG. Your units in the game act on their own free will, and you must tempt them to do deeds for the kingdom by setting up quests for them to accomplish in the game by way of bounties. It's an unusual system, that can occassionally be difficult to get the hang of, but once you do it feels natural.
Like players in an MMO your units will level up, learn skills, & go to the shops and buy potions, weapons, armor, and whatever magic trinkets your market might have for sale. One of them might even get lucky and come across an extremely powerful weapon early in the game and go on to become a powerful lord of your land, valliantly defending against hordes of creatures that instantly wipe out your younger units, giving them breathing room to grow in power.
I could ramble on for much longer about why I love this game, but I'll try to throw together a good old fashion pro's and cons list
Pro's:
-Beautiful fantasy art style and graphics. Every unit in the game looks great right from the start, but as they level up and purchase new weapons and armor their appearance changes in a satisfying and meaningful way. A level 1 warrior looks like nothing compared to a level 15 warrior.
-Combat, while not being super involved on the part of the player, is always satsifying and fun to watch. As your units learn new skills either from training at a guild, or from leveling up, the way they fight changes. It's always neat to see the heroes fighting in new ways as the game goes on.
-Intimidating monsters and quests that will challenge you. Because of the unusual method for defending your kingdom, it's not nearly so easy to defend in this game. Bunkering up with thousands of troops is not something you can do, so proper management is something you'll have to learn
-Great silly voice acting from the royal advisor, and many good lines from your units. The dialog is just fun, that's all there really is to say about that.
-Economics are easy to grasp, not spreadsheet material, but not♥♥♥♥♥♥easy either. You will run out of money, and you will suffer for it, but you wont need a college degree to figure out how to maintain your kingdom.
Con's:
-The game is hard, and if you've never played a majesty game before, then you're going to have a bit of a rough time starting out (Though for some this can easily be a pro)
-It's frontloaded. Many missions are only hard at the start. By the time you establish your kingdom and have several powerful heroes wandering around, you'll easily take the rest of the mission by storm. (This is more of a problem with the vanilla campaign, and not so much with the DLC's)
-Takes forever to unlock everything. You will have to complete over 70% of the in game missions to have every building and unit unlocked. This can be frustrating if your favorite unit or building is one of the very last to be unlocked.

-AI is sometimes very stupid. Generally your units will do fine without your guidance and only need you to give them a quest for something majorly out of the way, like to raid an enemy keep, or defend a trading post. But sometimes a unit will choose to go to the store when a lich is about to blow their house to smithereens, and....well that is annoying.
Control your troops as a god. Don't get killed your armies at the first step and then it'll be easy to play.

What is it about?
To sum it up: The russian devs have built a hero management simulation on top of a classic RTS basis. It plays pretty fresh, and feels damn good.
Basically, the units you build have minds on their own. There is no way to directly control them.
They do hero stuff, they wander around in search of monsters and loot, they level up just like all heroes do and can become even better with shinier armor and bigger swords.
Given some time, success and little dying they can develop from a wooden sword swinging wannabe knight to a professional murdering machine.
They misjudge their chances and die in silly ways quite often, hindering the individual progress, cost you a lot of money and ultimately, cause you to fail the map. So, the chaotic bunch needs to be directed somehow.
This is where the player jumps in. You can interact with various Spells on a smaller scale, but: What do heroes like ? Exactly, shiny things and money.
Orders are handled by issuing quests. For example, there is a wolves den which annoys you. You can create a quest for your guys, by putting a reward on it. Heroes will take on that quest if they feel like its worth it, and soon, the wolves den will be history.
The earned money then goes to that heroes purse and he will use it to buy Potions, enchant or buff himself in Guildhouses or buy new equipment if he doesn't die before he can spend it.
The money spent by heroes comes back to your purse for the most part, so its a game of give and take. With the added risk of the hero dying, resulting in loss of that money with additional resurrection costs. (These can become very very costly with increasing levels)
All Heroes will be acting selfishly on their own by default, giving little to no support to the "competing" heroes. Later on, you get the Option to group them into parties of up to four, making them work together to combine their abilities and increase in power by a lot. But also decreasing their response to quests significantly, which means, they'll consider themselves very elite and move out only for phat lewt.
After every mission you get the chance to promote one hero to "Lord", saving him for reuse on the following maps. Which is a good but costly option. Some maps can only be won by utilizing this feature wisely. All other heroes are lost on map transition.
This might sound all nice and cozy, and, yeah, when the basics are understood, the first few missions are not much of a problem.
But the difficulty rises quite fast and brutal. The maps are very different from each other and you will need to come up with a solid build order and make it work over several attemps on each new mission again. You are under constant attack from the very beginning and can fail the mission very fast if attempting the wrong way. Gamechanging scripted events can cause sudden death even later on if handled wrong.
It soon becomes a game of Chess, were you will need a clear plan of what to do when and perfect execution. The combination of this with the games occasional randomness can cause frustration at times. You've done nothing wrong, but still are wiped out brutally.
This factor will multiply when later on, your opponents have leveling heroes as well, and failure will therefore be punished twice, by losing a lot of money, and having to face more powerful enemies. Resulting in very very frustrating moments.
I'd say, the game, a couple of hours in, is a lot about trial and error and aims towards players with some dedication and will to win and has nothing to offer for casual players at all.
For the more hardcore, there is a lot of fun to be had here.
Having played the first part too, i really hope for a Majesty 3, the Game has come a long way already. I hope the developers see that too and give it another attempt. They could turn this already damn good, but underdog, game into a total blockbuster.

First of all, if you don't grinding, this game is NOT for you.
Since the Walker Update, I've been playing this game even more than before. Anyways, the game looks pretty for a free to play game, but don't let the looks fool you. Physics are kind of awkward at some places like driving a motorcycle onto a wall or some other kind of obstacle and the vehicle looks like it went through it for half a second. The infantry movement is somewhat dislikable because it feels clunky, but it is supposed to be "realistic" so I guess I'll let that pass. You can play as an American, German, or Soviet

TL;DR?
Go play SWTOR.  Same damn game, less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
I do not recommend this title AT ALL.  Trolls run free through the game, harassing roleplayers AND taking fleets (imagine a guild where you have to spend thousands of man-hours building the guild's home) from the other players.  Beside that, Cryptic, the original owner, were bought out by perfect world.  Items which were originally affordable through the dilithium-FreemiumBucks exchange are no longer, so it's impossible to get any new clothing that has come out since launch for free.  Most new, pretty ships are horribly over priced.  Don't ever expect to get the best stuff in this game.
Next, the gameplay.  Gawd the gameplay.  Imagine, if you will, a Star Trek.. that has nothing to do with Star Trek.  We're not talking 2009 the video game here!  I mean this game has nothing to do with star trek 9/10ths the time.  If I weren't green, I'd think I was in a totally different game.  Which is forgivable.  That's immersion in other games.  Not here.  Here, the gameplay itself isn't even remotely complimentary to the license.
You get your choice of Science, Tatical, or Engineering officer.  Coolio.  That's fine.  The difference is the powers you can use in the space combat and in the awayteams.  Tatical gets some team buffs for DPS, engineer can create items out of thinair, and science has some stuff such as stasis fields.  That's cool, right?  Nope.  None of that actually solves anything.  You still have to kill the targets to move on.  No diplomacy, no alternate route, you have to murder the NPCs to move on.
Okay, lets move on to out of combat stuff.  WHAT OUT OF COMBAT STUFF?  You'd think you'd get a minigame that's like "Oh, reallign these chips and then order some members of your crew to replace some plating that got blown off."  Nope.  None of that.  Anytime you get to do anything REMOTELY tech related, it's part of a dialogue tree.
Dialogue tree?  That's a bit of a lie.  The story is linear and there's no way to affect a battle.  There's no talking your way out of any combat, unlike SWTOR in which you can occassionally choose whether to fight someone or not.
STO story missions:
-We have received a transmission from deep ♥♥♥♥face space, and are sending you on a mission to one of their important worlds to do some♥♥♥♥♥♥
-OH LAWD ITS A ♥♥♥♥FACE AMBUSH!!
*3 tiny raiders against your dreadnaught*
-Ready to beam you down captain, along with the top officers of your crew because we're stupid as hell
-Woooosh
-Eyy lmao, we'd love to help but there's too many ♥♥♥♥faces here and they'll ♥♥♥♥ our faces if we help starfleet!
-♥♥♥♥FACE GROUND AMBUSH
-Ay thnx.
-Captain!  ♥♥♥♥faces have warped in!  Prepared to beam you up instead of turning on shields and handling it ourselves because we sent down all the competent crew with you!
-GO TO RED ALERT!
-Woooosh
-*one cruiser ambush*
-That'll not be the last ♥♥♥♥face we see.
-Hail starfleet
-Hai, I'm either Quinn or doing his job for him.  here's your leveeelll~
This is 95% of the starfleet mission in STO.
Imagine if in Skyrim, the only time you could use your dragon shouts is when a dialogue tree with a npc found it useful.
*insert picture of a pesant with "FUS-ROH-DAH" as one of the dialouge options*
Same goes for nerve pinch.  It disables a npc for 10 seconds in combat, then they recover and continue fighting.  Meaning it does jack ****.  Okay!  Well, when it's important to the story, then?  Once.  There is only one time in the entire game where you can use nerve pinch as a solution to a dialogue tree's problem.  Orion's seduce ability?  Same.  Except this time, it can never be used, because the npc you could nerve pinch before IS A FEMALE HUMAN.  The KDF equivelant to nerve pinch does nothing at anytime.  In combat, it's an ability that can make the target attack it's friend for 10 seconds.  But the target is always SO WEAK that it doesn't matter.
What can you do in space then?  Not a damn thing.  Ship combat is as involving as Star Trek DAC.  It's dull and colourful.  Imagine if star trek was just watching a ship shoot at a cube for a hour while the synthesised computer voice says "RED ALERT" every few minutes..  That's what this game is based on, not any star trek I know of.
Imagine if you took the storytelling from The Old Republic, slapped World of Tank's pay to win on it, then added TF2's hat system for cosmetics.  That's what you get in this disfunctional mess.  Why do I play it then?  'Cause my friends do, and it's one of the last MMOs where I feel comfortable socializing.  Not many MMOs I've played in recent years HAVE hubs designed just for socializing.
It gets woooooooooorse thooooough.
The grind.  Oh gawd the grind.  It's coming for me.
The grind is horrible in STO right now.  There is 170 levels, though you will basically max out after 120.  When you reach level 50, the game calls it "enggame" and your levels take 10 times longer.
Level 1-50 took me 3 days to do.  50-60?  I still haven't had the patience to do it on one character.
Edit: I came back to try out the admirality system.  In it, the ships your characters have can be sent out on missions.  Theoretically, this would be a fun way to get items while using your old ships.  Only problem is these ships take forever to get out of "maintence" once you're done using them.  So you'll complete two missions, then have to wait 8 hours before you can do more.
Unless you bought ships ONLY for the admirality system...
All in all, a sad result for a game that could have become something cool.

A very entertaining - if imperfect - attempt to remold Resident Evil 4. It does a better job than RE5 and 6 did, and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the Resident Evil Revelations games, or indeed the older Resident Evil and Silent Hill games. It also borrows a lot of conventions from both old and modern games like The Last of Us (sneaking and distractions), and Dead Space. Basically any fan of survival horror should be pleased with it.
The story is a convoluted mess but it does make some sense at the end. The gameplay is intense and really tough, but addictive. There is a strong sense of achievement and relief at having gotten all the way through it, but for anyone not into replaying the same boss fight 30 times, I'd recommend casual mode. Personally I prefer to be punished, and normal mode really does that.

Combine Minecraft and Counter Strike and you got Ace of Spades: Battle Builder, a block themed shooter with the ability to build cover or a stronger wall and even destroy buildings and digging tunnels, the stages are mostly themed with forests, castles, mountains and many more environments, and the ability to edit stages to your advantage on the go adds a unique touch to this shooter. Previously in "beta" this game was known as Ace of Spades but have since evolved and become Ace of Spades: Battle Builder now with a fully functional Stage editor/builder and now have full Steam Workshop functionality.
Sadly with every game there is both ups and downs and this game have received much more then expected, the game released in 2011 as a beta version but was later in 2012 picked up by RuneScape developer Jagex,
Jagex took over development of the game, making it payware on Steam and updating its game-play.
This lead many of the previous 2011 beta players to boycott the pay to play Steam version and demanded the game to once more become free to play, as this never happened and the anger and boycott was slowly dying the game still managed to evolve despite the many unbalanced updates and boycotts.
another thing is the in-game community, you will realize that much of the the in-game community is much younger and therefor unnecessary rage and swear words is part of the game.

The game has became a mess since being bought over. It has shifted from an indie masterpiece (when it was free and not available on Steam) to becoming a collection of tedious blocky minigames which have no real objective... The graphics have been destoried and replaced by cheesy, boring classes which demean the core of the game.
The older version of the game can be found here:
, it is a superior game in every aspect.

What makes it special is the third person perspective.
Super MNC brings a LOT to the moba table, but at the same time, leaves you with so little...
While other mobas are all stuck in a self-perpetuating cyclone centering around the high fantasy artstyle, Monday Night Combat is sports themed. Thats right, kids. Sports. They even have commentators and sponsorships
The world of MNC is robust with many sound assets and nice, shiny icons. However, after a week or so of playing, its easy for any gamer to distinguish a clear lack of content.
The "Pros" (otherwise known as "Heroes" or "Champions" in other mobas) all have their own unique abilities, weapons and roles making teamplay a very interesting and engaging experience. Fighting 5v5 alongside an army of lesser warriors to achieve a common, territorrial goal. Just like any other moba.
The big difference that you will see after prolonged play in Super MNC, is the clear lack of pros. Big name mobas will release new characters once a month, on average. These competitors also sport enormous rosters, all tweaked for balance. Though I will argue MNC is balanced to some degree, there is no customization outside picking from a pool of limited characters. The downfall of this game is a clear lack of community involvement in light of the limited roster.
Uber went into this with the best intentions, and for a while it was good. However, the moba genre takes an incredible amount of maintenance to keep things fresh. Especially in a market so competitive.
If you liked this game, or want to see what a 3rd person moba can do, check out Smite. Otherwise hope on DOTA2.
This game will always hold a special place in my heart. I bought the original, I played with friends. I made new friends. I laughed at many of the voices, and many of the gags in this game will always bring back warm feelings. The sad fact of the matter is that mobas cannot stand the test of time. When we look at it, every multiplayer game will eventually reach its demise.

Another game that I long put off buying because the mass of negative reviews, but which is actually a pretty good game.
It isn't
game - it has it's share of flaws - but it's good.
It's a port of a mobile game, so it has all the clunky baggage that you'd expect-
If you're expecting a triple-A game, Deus Ex: Human Revolution 1.5, move along - this is not that.
That said, and keeping it in mind, it really is a decent game.
The story - which, admittedly, is only part 1 of an unknown number of parts, and which might never be continued - is fairly compelling. Unlike Adam Jenson, Ben Saxon - the main character in this game - finds himself embroiled in the struggle against
, not because he's seeking revenge against those who, he thinks, killed his ex, but because he came across an injustice that he was unwilling to walk past. Your first objective outside of the tutorial is basic cyberpunk grocery shopping
and once you've done that, you have no compelling personal reason to keep fighting. In fact, you have a compelling personal reason not to
. The driving force behind getting involved beyond that point is just the protagonist's social conscience. I know we're living in an era when having a social conscience is seen by many as a sign that you're some kind of deviant, driven by prejudice against white people, or men, or the richest members of society, etc. but, personally, I find it admirable.
The economy is slightly stripped down, in that you can't sell any of items in your inventory that you may not wish to use, restricting your balance to those credits found in the world or earned through missions, and you buy new items through a menu screen, rather than going to any particular shop. At the same time, it is also expanded in other ways, giving you a greater variety of weapons than you have in Human Revolution. To be fair, the new weapons are basically just reskins with altered stats, but they're different enough to justify their existence. There are also bundles available, giving you the ability to buy a number of items at a lower overall price. I'm pretty sure this is a result of the original version being a mobile app, but, while I'm not a fan of in-app purchases, I actually don't mind this when it's in-game money that you're spending.
The inventory is entirely abstracted. As long as you have the credits, you can have every item in the game in your posession and not have to worry about space or weight requirements - what presence the inventory has is in the in-game store, reduced to an item being owned or available for purchase, and number of owned consumables. The RPGer in me finds that irritating, because, while I don't mind the idea that you could
all of them and keep them somewhere secure, I'm not wild on the idea that you'd be able to carry your entire arsenal with you everywhere you go.
The actual gameplay is pretty decent. The levels are pretty easily navigable, and have several available paths around them, allowing for frontal assaults, stealth, or hit and run tactics in combat zones. Gunplay feels fine for my play style, although seemingly restricted to reticle aiming, with the ability to aim down the sights being limited to scoped weapons. Hacking is essentially the same as in Human Revolution. AI isn't perfect, but enemies are reasonably smart, backing away from grenades, moving to flank you when they're alerted to your position.
If you buy this expecting a triple-A experience, you will be disappointed, but, as mobile games go, this is a good one. It's worth playing.

I never thought I'd give a negative review to a Deus Ex game but The Fall is terrible! I played Human Revolution first by accident, and all the flaws in The Fall have been fixed there so seeing things that are so familiar, but just don't work, is very disorienting. The Fall even looks incredibly like HR, but nothing works like it does in HR. Don't waste your time with The Fall, move straight on to the vastly superior Human Revolution!
I'm going to just list the problems:
- There are no separate save games!! Seriously, there is a single save and if it auto-saves after you saved manually, well, tough cookies for you.
- One power cell that recharges - that's enough to take down a single person.
- The inventory is a disaster - not only is it not an actual inventory with space allocation, your inventory shares space with a shop where you can just buy stuff, instead of finding it in the world. Very confusing and sometimes you pick up an item but it doesn't seem to be available in your inventory. One of the most thought-provoking things in Deus Ex was always figuring out what to keep and what to drop, to make the best use of your limited inventory space. A wrong choice spelled disaster. Being able to just buy anything, with apparently unlimited space, just sucks the fun out of the entire concept. It's a jumble of what you actually have and what you can buy.
- Control allocation - I've been playing for 5 hours and I still have no idea how to access half the so-called shortcuts. The original Deus Ex introduced the easy-to-use 1 through 0 button allocation where you could drag weapons etc into the slots accordingly. If it ain't broke, don't fix it! They removed something that was incredibly simple to use and replaced it with confusing nonsense. Half the time I'm lucky to find the right gun.
- Wow, the tutorials are appallingly bad. Not only are they delivered in this grim monotone, you get a single blurry picture to explain how to do whatever. In the beginning, the game actually freezes until you follow the instruction... if you can figure out what it actually wants you to do!
- Whether you kill or knock unconscious, bodies disintegrate. No bodies to alarm guards that must be disposed of, they just disappear. Which is linked to the ridiculously bad AI which decides you've left the area, even if the guards saw you twenty seconds ago, hiding behind a wall.
- You can't jump or throw things. Seriously, not at all. It sucks.
- The zones are tiny and terrible which require multiple area transitions to get anywhere - not even exaggerating, at least 4 to go anywhere.
- Hacking consoles (at least 80% of them) cannot zoom out correctly, so you can't hack it because you can't even see the nodes!
- The character of Ben is just terrible, and Anna is actually worse. The story's thin and not remotely interesting.
- Final nail in the coffin - took 7 hours to complete AND ended on 'To Be Continued'. What a waste of time.
This game basically took everything that worked perfectly and threw it all out the window... and everything they changed gets changed back for Human Revolution, and then gets improved.
I may as well finish it since I paid for it, but it is incredibly bad. Seriously, stop reading this and go play Human Revolution instead, it's really great.

I've tried this game back before it was on Steam, being a huge S.T.A.L.K.E.R. fan, and loving the games. Even Clear Sky which is considered the worst of the three? In any case, I cannot recommend this game for multiple reasons.
First of all, S-Zone is not STALKER and does not have the majority of the STALKER creatures to hunt. S-Zone doesn't have much in the way of the STALKER feel, though it has its looks. This is currently a cheap immitation, still, boasting anomaly fields, blind dogs, and STALKERs with guns running around trying to collect 'artifacts' from the fields. Sadly, the way the game is, it's not 100% STALKER, but if you want a cheap immitation to run around in for a few days to a week, be my guest and try it.
First, you'll notice the horrible tutorial. Well, back when I played there really wasn't one.  You'll notice the game's difficulty. If you don't have plenty of ammo and medical supplies, you're done for. But you only have a certain amount of carrying capacity, like in STALKER, and can't take what you can't carry. Especially if you want loot. - For people who have much experience with the actual STALKER games, this is no big deal. However. The ammo consumption, itself, is an issue since you can't sneak past most monsters. They have a massive aggro range, no apparent field of 'view' or sense. At least in the STALKER games, you can crouch and slowly make your way around a few of the mutated things. This being said; Ammo costs money. And the only way to make money? You figure that out- but all I can say is "Grinding."
Second, you'll notice how often you'll get shot once you, somehow, find your way out of tutorial city. Players out there will see you exit towns or wander through forests and they'll wait until you're far enough before gunning you down. Think a crapy version of DayZ. Except you randomly drop loot the others can pick up. No matter how hard you try to fight back, they have better gear. They win. If you're new to this game, you might as well put it down and walk away. If you've never played STALKER, go get the games. You'll enjoy them more than this pile of cheap plastic. This is, like, the chinese version of LoL - made to catch a hardcore audience into playing and paying for better colored pants and shiny guns from the cash shop.
Third- the Geiger counter and Artifact locating device require batteries. Batteries that cost money. While I do like this, it is, both, a pro and con. More realistic and another resource to keep on hand. But nothing really explained how to use the two together, nothing explained how to gather artifacts. See, this isn't STALKER. When you press Q to throw a rock in order to spot an anomally, it doesn't work. Because this isn't STALKER- See, in STALKER, you had your geiger counter you could bring up, it would 'click' as you walked. Enough rapid clickings and you were near high amounts of radiation or an anomaly. You threw bolts/rocks in front of yourself and they would either land upon the ground, bounce off something invisible that you should avoid, or set off the Anomaly like the spring-trap or gravity well. In this game, they're mostly useless, since the anomalies aren't reactive to it.
Let's talk graphics- They're kind of bad. But I guess they went for a decent immitation of STALKER. Sadly, I find the graphics ugly, yet fitting due to the fact that the games are old. So while fitting, they're not the best or the most up-to-date out there.
Community- It's an issue and a point in quality. You have good folks out there who will help you, you have bad folks out there that will just shoot you dead. Just avoid them all if you play solo. Unless you can't. Then if you die, log off for a few hours so they move on. They like to spawn camp. (Yes, there's 'set' spawn locations at certain parts of the world.)

I really enjoyed the early versions of AOS, back when it was indie and a little unpolished. The characters had real weight and didn't feel like spacemen. I will admit, this game brings many new weapons to the table. However the entire character of the original is destroyed in favor of this tf2 voxel remake. The original was so much more enjoyable for me. A HUGE factor was the usefulness of planning and base building. It was so worthwhile digging a tunnel to the front lines and trenches to cover your movements. This new version COMPLETELY disregards building incentives. There is NO REASON to build when every class can destroy your base in 5 seconds. Even the quick build options are worthless. The old game had elements of stealth and trench warefare, digging into your surroundings and slowly chipping away at the enemy across the valley. The fog of war really conveyed tension and uncertainty when crossing an open area, especially alone. All in all, the old version was extremely groundbreaking with it's suprisingly deep metagame and it's simple mechanics. Although the "real" game has smoother edges, it's fast paced gameplay completely did away with any strategic thinking and building for a run and gun voxel shooter. I'm truly disapointed with the direction the developers took.

Things I liked;
+Player character banter, good voice acting
+Good atmosphere, environments felt right, nice setting
+/-Melee and ranged combat feels satisfying (some bow and arrow hit detection is buggy/delayed though)
+Special enemies feel threatening even on Easy
+Some of the loot actually looks really cool and adds a layer of "RPG" feeling to the L4D formula the game seems to be influenced from.
Things I disliked;
-Some animations seemed poorly done, enemies sometimes stop and spin around in a buggy way
-Loot system doesn't seem great. I had equipped an item that is supposed to give me a much higher chance of getting loot for my chosen class but out of 3 games I didn't get any for the Waywatcher.
-Jumping, or whatever the spacebar is for, doesn't feel functional enough. Sometimes my character would dash, sometimes she would jump. The dashing didn't feel significant enough but would have been a cool addition.
-Last Stand looks fun, but it's locked behind a level restriction so I couldn't play it. I'm also willing to bet most groups don't want an "undergeared noob" ruining their chances of higher tiers.
Conclusion;
It's not a bad game, but it doesn't feel fully developed. The bugs that occur and the heavily RNG based loot system aren't fun to play with or look at, but if this ever went lower than $15 I'd probably buy it for some 20 or so hours of gameplay.

Utter exercise in futility.
I ground three characters to 5th level to see if "war" was any better than the first levels. The first levels are filled with hacks, trolls and griefers galore.
Someone posted a review about how the grind is terrible after the last patch. I found the grind for certain things easy enough but because there are some major failings in design and purposeful ones to create pay to drive scams it gets a poor rating from me.
The trolls like to bump a rock and make you get out of the jeep thinking they can't drive. Then you will hear a horn laugh as they leave you to walk.
Its not just the players. At first I thought "Wow, look at all the cover; like rocks n fallen trees. Then I soon realized they are troll rocks made popular in games like Dargon Age: Inquisition. Rocks desinged/placed to impede progress. They must grow troll rocks like weeds where ever this game is made.
You spend most of the first three or four levels riding a bike ( yes, that's right a bicycle into war), hitching a ride or if you're lucky an old beat up truck thats faster than a bike, bearly.
Once you think"oh boy I am level five; I can go to war in my jeep I just ground out". You are crushed by facing another grind. Incentive to buy your way to tanks, I suspect.
How, You ask? By limiting four out of five maps to no jeeps. Yep you are right again. They actually regress your character back to bikes. Oh, you get jeeps sometimes and the enemy seems to have them every time but it's ok you got your weapons.
You are imediately thrown into battle vs mostly assault weapons. That little submachine gun you ground thru the first levels? It only draws fire now, from STG44 assaults. That bolt action you thought was great for damage; hurts em but at your one shot to their three (with the same bolt action perked out).
The game touts balance as one of its major benefits. I found exactly the opposite. 90% of the games were stomps. You either had a team that was trying or a team that can't/won't cap.
There is absolutely no means to provide spawn protection in the main. The enemy can literally sit inside the buildings you spawn in at the main. Without major a design change this will forever plague the skirmish aspect of this game.
Once you get to War you find really stupid layouts, battles and spawns. Defend maps are fruitless as if you cant out attack the enemy they will roll you. The spawns to defend main objectives are (no exaggeration) 30-45 seconds walking distance away from the area and it is typically inside a building that one must weave through to defend. The attacks are no better they are typically a roll unless choke pointed by a bridge then its just a camperfest.
There was a few aspects i liked . The hitching a ride either by gettting in a seat or hanging on the outside. That was neat. The weapon realism was nice and scopes seemed realistic. The same maps but with different time of day lighting was a nice change up to a very repetitive grind through only three maps for the first five levels.
All in all; if you have time or money to waste be my guest.  I personaly found it disheartening to spend as much time as I did in the game only to get to the "war" aspect and find it a pay to drive scam. The only resolution I could see would be an intermediate aspect between the first five levels and the all out war. It would likely never happen as this seems to be their major profit plan, due to the fact, the game is mainly based and restricted by travel time.

I have to admit, I'd not heard of this game until one of my colleagues and I were talking about survival horror games and he mentioned that Shinji Mikami was involved with 'The Evil Within', which immediately piqued my interest as I've been a fan of Resident Evil since the very first PS1 game and definitely regard the (Gamecube version of the) fourth game in the series to be one of the finest games ever made - and my colleague said that 'TEW' has got a similar feel to it.
So I purchased it and have been playing it for a few days now and am really pleased to say that it definitely has all of the trappings of a great Mikami game and feels like the long lost sister game of RE4.  Yep, it's that good!  The over-the-shoulder camera angle, limited supply of ammo and health, claustrophobic atmosphere and superb music and sound are all present and correct - as are the zombie creatures and psychotic, chainsaw wielding maniacs!  New to the mix however are some nice stealth gameplay mechanics and some really trippy, almost Silent Hill-ish weird going ons.
Visually, the game is really good - although I'm pretty certain this it's an obvious port from a console version of the game as the textures are not as high quality as I'd normally expect from a PC game, but that's pretty inconsequential as overall it looks pretty nice.  The character models are notably impressive, it has to be said though.
Summing up, if you're a fan of the Resident Evil series of games (as well as Silent Hill) you will definitely want to give this a go!

Deus Ex: The Fall feels a lot like a discount version of Human Revolution, but it still manages to keep the great atmosphere and gameplay of it's predecessor.
DE:TF was first released on phones and tablets, but was later ported to PC. The port was not well received, because of its graphical downgrade from HR and some bugs. However, in my opinion the graphics, while downgraded, still look fine because of the great artstyle.  I didn't encounter many bugs in my several playthroughs either. The only one that needs to be mentioned is the click-detection bug. Sometimes you can't click buttons while in menus, and it is really annoying. Definitely not a game-breaking bug though.
The story in TF is not as good as in HR, but it still kept my interest all the way through. Unfortunately it ends on a cliffhanger, and it's not likely that we'll ever get a continuation.
The gameplay is similar to that in HR. You have many of the same weapons, as well as augmentations. The levels have many different paths to take and optional rooms to explore. The areas are smaller in this game, as a result of it being made for mobile devices.
Sound design is pretty good. Most of the music is borrowed from HR, and it really enhances the game's atmosphere. The voice-acting is also decent, with good performances from the main actors, and everyone else performs ok.
All things considered, Deus Ex: The Fall is not a bad game. It's not as good as Human Revolution, but that's ok considering the price. I enjoyed it enough to play through it 3 times and unlock all achievements, and I recommend it for anyone who like the Deus Ex series.

This game is what horror fans have been waiting for for a while now. This game is no Amnesia clone like most horror games are nowadays, but something completely different. And it really works.
Instead of facing the traditional monsters, the danger is that you're trapped in your own mind. The game offers a very plausble view of what it would be like to be insane, and sooner or later you'll find that you accept all the impossible things that you witness. It's almost like a batshit simulator.
The game does use jump scares, a fair few even, but they're not actually meant to startle you, they're more there to keep you on the edge of your seat. The constantly shifting environment the player finds himself in is actually way more unsettling because you never know what's going to happen, anything at all is possible. The realisation that anything could happen at any time is what drives the suspense here, and it works brilliantly.
The way this all ties together is how in this game the environment can change when you're not looking. Drastically. As you can't see everything at the same time, you're always vulnerable to the things that are just outside the corner of your eye. Trying to keep things in your vision makes you inevitably turn your back on something else. Nowhere is safe, and that's what the game expertly impresses on you. Just like a truly insane person.
Another thing that has to be said is the visuals. The textures are razor sharp and the models are very nice. The best thing is the artwork in this game though. Who made all this? Even if you're not a fan of the gameplay, the paintings themselves are quite beautifully made. Expert work here.
Highly recommended for any fans of the horror genre. While still in development and not the scariest game I've ever played, it's definitely among the most elegant.

Finally, the jump scares are brilliant as well because anything could jump at you, and I mean ANYTHING. Even if you turn to look from one side of the room to the other, then turn back to where you were looking at in the first place, the room could have very well changed completely.
Atmosphere-10
Jumpscares-10
Graphics-10
Overall, this game has so much potential and I can see that once it's finished and released as a finished product, it will be one of the best horror games I've played.

By far the best sword and board style fps/third person shooter out there.  There is a slight learning curve for manual blocking(the trick is to keep your camera level or use first person view).  True to it's name and former self, you can choose from many types of medieval style infantry and cavalry.  From a lancer,  horse archer, or just a walking tin can: you can choose your equipment type to fit your play style.
Graphically not the best in class, but if you care more about gameplay then eye candy, this may be the game for you.  Plenty of mods to keep you busy for years to come.  I played CRPG for several gens now (13 iirc), and it really adds another level to the game.  But the basic game is always a blast.  There are so many mods that many of the good ones come and go as groups of players migrate to the next best multiplayer mod.
Even though the game is not new, there are always players online, usually a few hundred at any given time.  Most servers will hold up to around 200 players, so battles can get rather intense.
The single player is actually quite fun as well, though it can be rather slow at times.  Takes a while to really get your warband up to speed and then it's on to capturing castles and joining wars.  It adds a nice RPG to the game, and you can go from peasant to king if you play your cards right.  So yea, there's that.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone that finds medieval warfare in a first/third person style shooter an appealing idea.  It is one of the true great games to emerge in the last decade, and just like Counter Strike, I find myself constantly playing this game year after year.
