Overture has a decent amount of potential but is a barrage on the eyes. Turning off shaking and turning down particle effects is a must.

Maybe some drop shadows or more uniform backgrounds and subtler monochromatic damage numbers could easy things up. Or maybe standardizing the base spawn rate for at least the enemies/bosses on the 1st floor would make things more bearable on beginners.
Before gameplay gets out of hand, Overture is intuitive and elements such as equipping items and getting npc buddies are instantly understandable. It’s a mildly enjoyable romp, but nothing I’d want to stick to for long term.

I grudgingly recommend this game that tried to be Silent Hill that tried to be Resident Evil 4 that tried to be Dark Souls.
The graphics are great,  minus some texture popping, and if you like gore you're in for a treat.  The atmosphere is great in many areas.
The story is actually very simple, told in the most complicated way possible.  It is also buried beneath side-plots which never resolve at all, or even connect to the main story.  In fact, it almost feels like they took every rough draft of the plot and simply shoved it into the game.
Mechanically, it's an action game that pretended to be a stealth game for a little while, then went "ah, ♥♥♥♥ it" and went full action for about 10-15 hours, then felt guilty and gave stealth another try, and then gave up its dreams and accepted what it was.  Until the Assignment DLC anyway.
The controls and the camera are janky as ♥♥♥♥.  It took less than fifteen minutes for me to switch to a controller.  Even then, the game is lazy about its cover system, and the camera sometimes refuses to cooperate.  The hitboxes on headshots are occasionally unreliable, which is just one of many instances of the game giving you the middle finger.
Many people refer to the presence of cheap deaths in the game.  Indeed, often times it feels as though the game is trying to showcase the many gruesome death-scenes, and you're there to facilitate that as opposed to being an actual player.  There are a lot of times, though, when circumstances seem impossible when they simply require some clever tactic, or perhaps a boss doesn't require as much ammo as you thought.  In these cases it is simple lack of the player's ability to read the future, or choose the correct option among several possibilities at a fraction of a second under extreme duress.  This is compounded by the game's somewhat lazy checkpoint system - not bad, but definitely not good.  It almost seems as though this trial-by-error system is simply there to artificially inflate the game's length.
The ammo is sparse.  Expect to find singular bullets at a time, of varying sorts.  In spite of this stress, it is actually very hard to fail the game entirely - unless you are absolutely terrible.  At one juncture I was so sick of the game's nonsense that I purposely expended ammo carelessly, plugging away at enemies in whatever body parts amused me at the time.  I still made it, somehow.  This deserves special mention because it implies a very carefully balanced ammo system.  You will ALWAYS beg for more ammo, and you will ALWAYS have just enough to get the job done.  Barely.
Long before the end I was ready to quit, but I didn't.  I wanted nothing more than to wipe the antagonist's smug grin off his ***hole face.  And I did.  I wouldn't call it "fun" though.  I'm sure it's a good game somehow, I'm just not sure what type of game that would be.

100/10

BEFORE YOU BUY THIS GAME please not that it was originally a game for mobile devices and this is just a PC port of that game. As such, it doesn't really hold its own as a PC game. Usually in these kind of reviews, people will mention how they have "over 100 hours" in the game to lend to their credibility. I've put a whopping 7 hours into this game, and I didn't even rush the main questline. I did every sidequest (as far as I'm aware), picked up every item (as far as I'm aware), ...you get the idea. Now, granted, I didn't do the "new game +", but all that does is increase the difficulty. On top of that, combat and conrols are clunky, and the game is glitchy as heck (especially when doing takedown moves). The story is somewhat interesting, but is of course ridiculously short and ends with a very disappointing "to be continued".
Now, all that being said, let me reiterate that this is just a port of a mobile game. Had I played it on a mobile device, I probably wouldn't have had all of these complaints. And to be fair, I've had a hard time getting the other games to run right on my computer, and I just went ahead and played this one, so maybe the "to be continued" isn't as disappointing as I think it is. Plus, I didn't even know until 5 minutes ago that there was a novel.  :-/
So yeah, long story short, just keep in mind that this is actually a mobile game, and take this review with a grain of salt.

Deus Ex: The Fall is a prequel to Deus Ex: Human Revolution, an amazing game. It has the same setting like HR and does an admirable job at the dystopian cyberpunk the series is known for. Unfortunately this is only a port from iOS and that effects on the gameplay.
You play as Ben Saxon who is trying to find the truth behind the drug conspiracy because they are very rare and all people with augmentations need them. He was betrayed from his employer, a private Military – the tyrants. Now his life and all augmented people are in danger. The story part is nothing much and not really deep.
The gameplay is the same as in Deus Ex: HR, Ben Saxon has the same augments and abilities as Adam Jensen. You need to hack objects like locked door, are able to do takedowns, crawl through vents and shoot form cover. Next to the Main missions you can talk to NPC’s and maybe they give you a side mission and/or explore the world. You upgrade your augmentations and weapons while you playing stealth or kill anyone.
As I said, this is a port from a tablet and this is a big problem. On the tablet it’s nice to play this game but the controls on a PC are terrible. They are clunky, unresponsive and the combat from cover is useless. What is very annoying is the fact, that bodies disable after a few seconds and you have many loading times. Just a terrible port.
By the way there is an ingame store which allows you to buy ammo and gear every time. That’s unrealistic and too easy. You can shoot all enemies down like Rambo, you only need enough money.
For a mobile game its impressive but on the PC it’s not very well, it looks often very ugly. The textures look a bit weak but with the lights and shadows it’s okay. The User Interface is without a Touchscreen just terrible. It’s so annoying and uncomfortable to navigate with mouse and keyboard in Deus Ex: The Fall.
The best part of the game is the Soundtrack form Michael McCann which create the amazing Soundtrack for Human Revolution. The voice acting is okay but nothing special.
Deus Ex: The Fall on Steam is for fans only. If you like Human Revolution, you can try it but don’t expect a game like this. It's not a bad game but I can't recommend it, it has too much negative points. It’s a game for tablets and not for the PC, note that. If you are a hardcore fan of the franchise, than go for it. If you are not, don’t buy it. No matter what you are, wait for a sale or buy it in a key store. Don’t buy this for the full price, it’s not worth it, also not as a hardcore fan.

HuniePop is either the single worst or single greatest impulse buy I have ever done. Going into the game all
I knew was it was a dating sim with puzzle game elements…. what the real selling point was for me was when I saw all the incredibly ridiculous steam reviews:
“Well, I didn't expect her to ♥♥♥♥ on the first date let alone squirt. And when Tiffany refuses anything other than Anal, I almost choked one out right there and then”
That was when I knew I had to see what the heck this game was about.
The game focuses on you playing as a guy who is an absolutely hopeless virgin who is utterly horrible in the dating scene. That all changes the day that you get visited by the sexy, scantily clad dating fairy who vows to teach you how to play the field and promises that with her help you’ll go on dates and get laid. From there the “Yukki”-esque fairy teaches you the core gameplay mechanics which aren’t that too different from other puzzle games in the vein of Bejeweled. You go on dates that consist of the puzzles where you connect three or more of the various colored balls and earn “Affection” points, and you can earn bonus “Affection” points by paying attention to the girls personality and focusing heavily on the color balls that she desires most. You are tasked with reaching a set level of Affection points to pass the level and have a successful date, however with every successful date you have, the level of Affection points required for the next date becomes significantly higher which certainly adds to the difficulty considering you are limited to 20 moves per date. In addition to the colored ball tokens, there are also bell tokens which give you an extra turn, heart tokens which increase your passion level that increases the affection points you get when you connect the colored balls, sentiment tear drops that allow you to use various items, and purple broken heart tokens that sap affection points from your date and can be truly devastating to a date. At the conclusion of each date both successful and failure dates, you are awarded “Munies” that you can use to spend on food, drinks, and gifts for your dates.
As you talk to the girls and successfully choose the right dialog branch you are awarded “Hunie” which is used to upgrade your traits that give you bonuses and allow you to perform better in the puzzle dates. It’s sad, because one of the games both strongest and weakest points are the dialog, for both the cut scenes and dialog trees. The dialog is really what makes this game worth playing…It will make you laugh, cringe, and blush, however it becomes repetitive very quickly, and spending time with any one girl for too long will cause the dialog to loop back around and start recycling itself.
With each successfully date; you earn a “heart” in the girls love progression bar. Once you reach either 4 or 5 hearts depending on how into you the girl is, if you successfully pass a date puzzle at night then things will get disappointingly hot and heavy. You’ll finally get laid and the sex mini-game puzzle is just merely a puzzle similar to the ones you’re used to only with no limit on your number of turns, you have to rapidly connect the colored ball tokens to combat the decreasing Affection points bar  all the while your date is moaning and egging you on. Upon completion of the mini-game you are awarded a semi-nude sexual photo of your date that gets added to your photo album. The fact that that’s as far as the game is willing to push the envelope is a little disappointing, If you are going to make a game that focuses on this type of subject matter and the entire goal of the game is to have sex…then there should have been more of a payoff than there was.
Besides the puzzles and dialog, the game also features a very large amount of “Plot”. The Plot is very well animated and the various image stills you receive in the game are all very well illustrated. The only issues some may run into with the “plot” is that the steam version is censored, but this can be easily remedied if you so desired with a patch released by the devs.
The game successfully delivers a fairly solid puzzle dating sim that is delivered with the look and feel of a visual novel. The game is held back however by its sub-par voice acting, repetitive dialog, and less than climactic climax scenes.

The Worlds Adrift Island Creator has it's ups and downs, and yes it is still in a very experimental stage.
Do I think it should have been released in it's current state? Personally, yes. I feel like it gives us as a community a good chance to experiment with the mechanics of the game and get a feel for what's to come.
Is the client still very unfinished? Yes, there are still bugs and lots of things to be improved upon, but those are things that you will always have with clients similar to this one. Like all other beta/alpha games, the client has left much to be desired, but at the same time has given us a chance to have fun and learn.
With all of the feedback that will come from this, I feel like Bossa will be able to really improve the mechanics of the game based on what the community feels is necessary. After all, the people that will be playing the game should be the people that have a voice and suggestion as to what things should be added/removed from the game, right?
Overall I like that Bossa has given us this opportunity, a learning experience, and I look forward to seeing where things go in the near future.

This is a "Game" that lets you create content for another game that will be released later and if you're one of the people who's content is selected you'll get to see it in the upcoming game. Okay? Got that? Are you Sure? Because I don't think you do.
Modding is one thing. After a game comes out, you'll see people happily plugging away at making mods for games they like. Fine. Dandy. This isn't that.
You are literally doing the work of an employee of this company, for free. Get it? You're not playing a game, you're working. This is stuff that normal game developers hire people to do. This whole thing is a farce designed to net the company free content to flesh out another product. This would be the same as Bethesda releasing the modding tools for the next Elder Scrolls game before the game was out, then taking the best mods and incorporating them into the game, then selling that game for profit while you get nothing but a pat on the back for a job well done.
Welcome to the new era of game design where you just make the community do the work for you, pay them nothing, then reap all the rewards.

Hey all.
I'm coming from Majesty 1.
Basically, to me, it's same game with a little bit advanced graphics.
New flag mechanics are satisfying (ie defend flag).
In Majesty 2 you overall have more controll on your units which is a good thing... but a bad thing.
You see, whole thing about majesty 1 was that you are a King. So you have wishes and a bunch of gold to make wishes come true and there are people who can help you to do that. If they want to. In Majesty 2 you cannot feel that atmosphere of being a king. It's more like an ordinary RTS game.
Besides, despite advanced graphics, I like original Majesty art better. I mean buildings, characters etc. They were more authentic than in Majesty 2. Here we have some genereic medieval buldings and not a Rogue's guild or Temple of Krypta.
When I'm playing the original Majesty, I always imagine myself as Vetinari, the patrician of Ankh-Morpork. Obviously the city, which I am building is Ankh-Morpork. Dunno, I always imagined Ankh-Morpork just like that.
I would like to have sequel, which have art and AI of original Majesty. Not a generic gimped RTS.
Nevertheless, if we look at this as a separate game and not a sequel, then it's pretty nice.
Conclusion is: if you want some new experience in strategy games definitely get this. If you're an old-school fan of Majesty, then I don't think that you will like this, because it's lacks the atmosphere of original game. It's better for you to view this as a stand-alone game.

Knock buildings down by cutting out the base, cut the bottom block out of a tree to destroy the whole thing, simple destruction. The building system was extremely confusing and I never did learn to use it, and other players also seemed to not fully understand the build and destroy system. I'd see players build a tower into the sky to be safe, and enemies would run at him rather than cut down his tower. I couldn't build structures over people and turrets, but when I placed turrets they'd be built over to destroy them and I'd be burried to become easy prey.
Graphics: Not much was expected, being a blocky build and shoot game, but it was actually decently done. The characters animations seemed to work around structures (no legs clipping through stairs) and explosions through out debris to bounce around.
Classes: The four classes in the game were well explained and each unique. For each game mode there was a clear superiority in a class. Open fields made sniper the best, defensive made the engineer the best (except for building over turrets being sometimes a thing), offense was the commando, and the miner was just sort of a for fun character who lacked a real strong point.
Weapons: There are few choices for each class, and then spaces that look liked locked choices, but with no explanation how to unlock them or if they are just unadded things to keep the menu aligned since some slots fill across and others don't. With such limited weapon choices, picking a class kind of locks in weapon choices and doesn't allow you to really make the character work your way.
Needs to be a little more clear on how things work, and then I might upvote it.

Deus Ex: The Fall is a PC port of the iOS mobile title and serves as a prequel to Deux Ex: Human Revolution. The game is itself a sequel to the Deux Ex: Icarus Effect prequel novel. This severely limits its chances to do its own thing, even if it does an admirable job at the dystopian cyberpunk the series is known for.
You play as Ben Saxon, a member of the Tyrants gone rogue, who is trying to unravel a conspiracy while keeping himself and former Secret Service agent Anna Kelso out of his erstwhile team's hands. Their backgrounds are briefly adressed in the game, but if you want the full story, read the book. This is not required to understand the game's narrative, largely because you'll care very little about the uninteresting Saxon and his quest. The story is hurt further by the unsatisfying 'to be continued' screen at the end, with no word on whether it actually will. You do get to interact a bit with the boss characters from DX:HR. This fleshes them out a bit and is one of the game's few saving graces.
Ok, so storywise, the game is nothing much. What about gameplay? Well, Ben Saxon is an expy of Adam Jensen, right down to the futuristic sunglasses. He has almost all the same abilities and augs. You can do takedowns, hack computers and keypads, crawl through vents, shoot from cover, .... Pretty much everything big bro Adam Jensen can, except jump. You'll use these skills to explore an urban hub, Panama City. You'll talk to npcs, some sidequests and work your way through enemy hideouts and complexes with combat and stealth, while upgrading your weapons and augs.
The extent to which developer nFusion translated DX:HRs gameplay to a tablet is pretty impressive. Unfortunately, this is also the game's downfall. The limitations of tablets really hurt the game's scope, with frequent loading times and a cramped design. Nowhere is this better exemplified than in the tutorial mission. You're faced with a locked door. You can hack the keypad or use a vent next to the door that deposits you right behind it. I'm not saying all Deux Ex entries are perfect, but when they gave you multiple solutions, you were at least got more progress than literally one meter.
Bodies dissolve after a few seconds, dead or alive. So why bother with slower pacifist stealthy when when a quick headsot is much faster. It makes little difference. No, not to conserve ammo. You can simply buy it from the ingame shop. This store is not an npc vendor, but a menu you can call up any time, including mid-combat. Need an EMP grenade? Buy one. Plenty of money lying around. Problem solved. It's an optional holdover from the microtransations of the tablet version, but it sucks out the challenge, planning and resource management.
The controls also suffer from the tablet origins. They're clunky and unresponsive. Combat from cover is a chore and often ineffective, as enemy bullets like curving around cover. Oh, and sometimes you'll clip through the world and die. Same for the UI, which has been barely converted from tablet-friendly to something suitable for PC.
OK, the story is a wash and the gameplay a mere shadow of its bigger brothers. Maybe the production values can salvage it? Don't count on the graphics. They would look great on a tablet, helped by same aesthetics featured inDX:HR. Upon closer inspection though, the ingame models and textures wouldn't look out of place on a Playstation 2, except with some glossy visual effects. The game does better in the sound department, but not because of voice acting or sound fx. Michael McCann, the guy behind the exceptional soundtrack of DX:HR, returns for The Fall and delivers music that is the best part of the game. Oh, and Saxon kind of looks like Jean Reno. I like Jean Reno.
Deux Ex: The Fall is a flawed game, hampered heavily by its tablet origins. I can't recommend it to anyone except the most diehard fans starved for more Deux Ex. With a playtime of 4-6 hours, they'll a modestly sized, but unsatisfying serving. Everyone else: maybe, MAYBE, pick it up for a buck in a sale. Otherwise, skip it, buy any of the other games or wait for Mankind Divided.
I rate Deus Ex: The Fall 2 banana out of 5.
What my ratings mean:
1 bananas - Crap. Turn around & don’t look back.
2 bananas - Bad. Not really worth it.
3 bananas - Average. For fans of the genre or a sale.
4 bananas - Good. Won't waste your time.
5 bananas - Superb. A definite must-play.

I'd like to preface this review by saying that I'm a woman who's into guys, but I got this game because it seemed very sex-positive, I like Bejeweled games, and because I was curious what the all hype was about.
The dialog has no consequences. The worst that happens is that you miss out on some points for that round, but the girls don't remember your blunders. They won't notice if you're being two-faced or if you often forget important details like their birthdays. It makes the relationships feel shallow, and it's very similar to the sort of flash card dialog that one could find in a free dating game on a flash site.
The girls don't interact with each other outside their introductions, and there are no characters besides the girls themselves. Two characters are mother and daughter with conflicting lifestyles, and I was disappointed that there's no way to influence their relationship with each other through the dialog options. It would have been great fun to help them see each other's point of view, or drive a further wedge between them. Another character has a son, but the player never gets to meet him. A single mother should care about the relationship her child has with a potential significant other.
The photos the girls send don't match up with their personalities. Why are the shy characters texting me panty shots? It breaks their characters and my immersion. If I were the sort of person whose waifu was very proper and reserved, seeing her act a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥ after we'd just met would kill my boner. I might expect that from her after her relationship bar was nearly maxed out. It would be nicer to have these characters send photos that have more to do with thier hobbies and less with their boobies. For instance, Nikki could send a picture of herself clothed normally, asking if I think that smudge behind her is a ghost.
Much of the introductory dialog is hilarious. Unfortunately, there are fewer laughs throughout the rest of the game unless you're courting Aiko; she's great. The girls have a nice variety of personalities, hobbies, backstories, and styles. I don't think there are enough options to say there's something there for
, but they did very well for having only a handful of girls. The artwork is also beautiful.
It's a nice take on the classic Bejeweled format. Having each girl prefer different colors mixes things up from the usual, and I like the way you can give a gift to change the board in various ways. Dates are untimed, letting you think and plan your moves, but when you take a girl home, you've got to keep making moves as fast as you can while still considering her preferences. The clash of those two playstyles makes a great metaphor for sex.
The $10 price point is spot on. While there are things about the game that disappointed me, I in no way regret my purchase.
If you're really into Bejeweled variants, this game is definitely within your interests, though be warned that you may find it too easy. I've found it a lot of fun, and will continue to play. As a dating game I think it's a bit of a flop, but I would love to see a HuniePop 2 in the future, with more complex relationships.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the sequel to Hotline Miami which once again features mysterious phonecalls setting you off on a rampages and massacres. This time however, there are multiple stories, perspectives and timelines involved that all revolve around the plot.
PROS:
+ Dynamic gameplay; there are many different ways to complete a level, both harsh, silent or berserker-like
+ The game is not any less shy of brutal, pixelated violence and gore
+ The story and setting are quite similar to the original: sick, drugged and merciless
+ Same as the original game: one difficulty only
+ Absolutely awesome soundtrack, and that's coming from a guy who's very picky with music; it's a variety of upbeat, energizing, relaxing and ambient tracks (more than twice as long as in the previous game (available as DLC))
+ Hard mode, which you can unlock by beating the game, is a mode that flips the levels, adds tougher enemies and limits your ammo; it adds surprisingly great replayability
+ There is a level editor and the game supports the Steam workshop very well in its easy and user-friendly use
+ Fair price/content ratio
NEUTRAL:
+/- The difficulty has been stepped up by a lot: levels are longer, feature more (tougher) enemies with guns and enemies off-screen. Especially the latter is annoying. Their reflexes are also increased. Certain levels are also difficult because you're limited to a certain playstyle or arsenal (limited ammo, melee only, etc.).
CONS:
- The story is a lot more confusing and feels less gripping than the former; it feels like a loose collection of story fragments being mashed together
- There are only 4 playable characters and a few situational ones while the original game had about 20.
This was originally a negative review because of certain very difficult parts of the game that got me going for a long while which lead to agitation. Since I was really driven to beat this game, I got past them eventually and am looking back at a pretty unique and memorable experience, Hotline Miami in its entirety.
If you like hard, fast-paced games and/or enjoyed the original Hotline Miami, buy this game.
My rating: 8/10

Following in the footsteps of its predecessor, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number capitalizes on the strongest aspects of the original game and welcomes new mechanics, new characters, new weapons, and a deeper story that aims to directly teach the player a cryptic lesson about morality, consequences, and the concept of Cause & Effect through its characters' interactions. Hotline 2 is more of the same with explosive (sometimes literally!), fast-paced, incredibly-challenging gameplay mixed with blood & guts galore. As a bonus, the game received an online-friendly level editor that encourages players to keep playing long after they've run through both the game's story mode difficulties (Oh yes, there is now a Hard Mode for people who found the game's normal mode "Too easy").
There are few drawbacks to this game, but said drawbacks are noticeable. Sometimes, the player may encounter a spawning glitch at any point of any given level that either traps them in an inescapable loop of deaths and respawns, prevents them from obtaining something they need to progress, or causes an enemy to run far outside the level's boundary lines, rendering the level impossible to complete. Additionally, players may find themselves hindered by the game's way of handling weapon pick-ups when there are multiple weapons lying in close proximity. For example, if you kill two enemies (one holding a bat or pipe and the other holding a shotgun) and the weapons are next to each other, then depending on the enemy you killed first, you will ALWAYS pick up that enemy's weapon. So in essence, if you killed the guy with the bat first, then the shotgun guy and you want the shotgun, you're forced to pick up the bat and throw it away to get the shotgun. This is often the case in levels with a lot of enemies and consequently, the result of many player deaths. This issue was prevalent in the previous game as well and evidently, did not receive an alternative.
To conclude, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is an excellent addition to the Hotline series and offers a lot in replay value, challenge, and investment that will have players coming back for more... if they haven't been discouraged by the amount of times the "You're Dead, Press A to Restart" has graced their vision.

This is a mediocre horror game.  It's ok except for some really annoying bosses.  The most frequent occurring boss is this spider-lady who appears every couple of chapters, and you're actually only supposed to fight and kill her once - every other time you have to run.  And even when you DO kill her when you're supposed to, she just shows up later in the game anyway.  She also one hit kills you.
Also, there is a boss at the end of chapter 10, who has a 2nd form that is very fast and one hit kills you - takes about 45 minutes to beat him after retrying over and over, and watching youtube strategies.  If you don't have a huge stack of ammo stashed away for him, you will be screwed.  Luckily, I had stored a huge arsenal, but if I didn't have that, I don't know how I would've been able to beat him.
There are some decent boss fights in the game, but the annoying ones really sour the experience - enough so that I don't recommend the game.
The main problem with a lot of the boss fights is the same problem with Resident Evil 6 - half the time you're supposed to kill the enemies, half the time you're supposed to run.  If you guess wrong, and try to kill a boss when you're actually supposed to run - well, you've just wasted a ton of ammo.

By far the best sword and board style fps/third person shooter out there.  There is a slight learning curve for manual blocking(the trick is to keep your camera level or use first person view).  True to it's name and former self, you can choose from many types of medieval style infantry and cavalry.  From a lancer,  horse archer, or just a walking tin can: you can choose your equipment type to fit your play style.
Graphically not the best in class, but if you care more about gameplay then eye candy, this may be the game for you.  Plenty of mods to keep you busy for years to come.  I played CRPG for several gens now (13 iirc), and it really adds another level to the game.  But the basic game is always a blast.  There are so many mods that many of the good ones come and go as groups of players migrate to the next best multiplayer mod.
Even though the game is not new, there are always players online, usually a few hundred at any given time.  Most servers will hold up to around 200 players, so battles can get rather intense.
The single player is actually quite fun as well, though it can be rather slow at times.  Takes a while to really get your warband up to speed and then it's on to capturing castles and joining wars.  It adds a nice RPG to the game, and you can go from peasant to king if you play your cards right.  So yea, there's that.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone that finds medieval warfare in a first/third person style shooter an appealing idea.  It is one of the true great games to emerge in the last decade, and just like Counter Strike, I find myself constantly playing this game year after year.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was one of my absolute favorite childhood games. I loved and still do adore the open ended 3D collectathon platformer format, and while it was no Banjo-Kazooie Ty still pulled it off rather well. I plan on revisiting the game again when I purchase the HD rerelease on here shortly. Ty 2? I thought it looked kinda cool at first but in all honesty it never held my interest for very long. Although it was supposed to be more open world it ended up feeling lesser with things divided into missions instead of big open levels to explore. Ty 3? I own it but haven't even gotten around to playing it yet, and judging from what I've heard about it I'm not missing too much.
So when I saw that the fourth Ty game was on sale for less than 2 dollars, I quickly jumped at it. Honestly I expected something fairly underwhelming, but the nostalgia alone would be worth that money I thought.
However I was pleasantly surprised. Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 4 won't blow you away, but it's a fun distraction at the very least. First off,  I loved the graphics of this game. Everything looks crisp and vibrant in its 2D animated style. Ty's use of the Australian landscape has always been something that has intrigued me and it's never looked better.
The controls were also quite great, Ty moves where you want all the time and I enjoyed that you could play the game just using the trigger and bumper buttons. (though I mainly stuck to the face buttons) Also Ty's swimming was great, it was swift and easy to control, not awkward like so many games like to make it.
I enjoyed the variety of things each level had, from collectables to time attacks to side missions to even chasing a turkey!(I always hated him as a kid) And the levels didn't just have one straight pathway, there was always multiple ways to go.
Were there downsides? Yeah. I have to admit after a while the game got a little repetitive, as is often the case for these simpler 2D platformers. It was also fairly short, not too bad but it did feel like it sorta ended abruptly. Also the final boss was quite a let down, it felt like the least challenging part of the game.
Also I didn't care for the game's audio much. I found a lot of the songs to get rather annoying over time, they were too repetitive for my taste in all honesty. And no voice acting? Mildly dissapointing.
Do I recommend Ty 4? Sure, if you're looking for decent platformer that won't tax your brain too much. I'd love to see Krome Studios try a new original 3D Ty game in the future, but for now? Ty 4 is a perfectly acceptable addition to this franchise.

The series always was a classic to me,  the music, gameplay, and characters all brought me back to my childhood, a good hit of nostalgia, and that's why I was so happy for the first to be remade for steam. That being said, I was ecstatic when I first heard that a 4th game was made, but that soon turned to disappointment. I mean I have no idea what the devs were thinking, downgrading to an arcade style game from their epic older ones. This review will be both positive and negative. The game itself is not bad, but again I bought it during the 2016 winter sale so I only paid about a buck and a half for it, so my view on the game might be different had I paid full price. When I got the game I was expected a boring mess, but it was surpisingly OK and I actually enjoyed it. I don't think it will catch my attention enough to finish it, but it definately surprised me. It was harder than I expected (not hard, but harder than I thought), and the gameplay is somewhat enjoyable. It would be a much better game had it not been a complete downgrade from it's previous ones. If you enjoy 2D arcade style platformers then this may be for you and I'd recommend it. Although if you've played any of the previous Ty games, I'd suggest contemplating before you buy it as although the characters, sounds, and feeling is similar, the game is nothing like the old ones, and recommending it for you would be harder for me. The game itself is not bad, but I'm gonna give it a thumbs down due to the utter dissapointment. I'd suggest to the devs if they continue with the Ty series they either return to the original concept of the Ty games (3D platformer) or work on putting the 2nd and 3rd games on Steam. Honestly the game feels like the devs got lazy and made a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt to profit off of the used-to-be-dead Ty series.

Deus Ex: The Fall should be taken for what it is. A mobile entry into the Deus Ex Universe. Admittedly, I'm a fan of the universe and getting another chance to play in this world, is something I am always looking forward to. So there may be some bias.
One thing that must first be noted, is that this game is a direct port from Mobile. If you look at what the game offers from a mobile perspective, it's pretty amazing. I wouldn't actually want to play it on mobile, as I can't imagine pulling off some of the stuff I do with just gestures, but hey, more power to those who want to.
As a direct port, this game did not have graphical update, the controls can be unresponsive, and the options are limited.
Graphics: for a mobile game this is excellent. As a PC port though, the graphics are okay. They aren't amazing, but they aren't completely terrible. I tried to remember where it was coming from. There are some glitches from time to time when you're climbing ladders, or performing takedowns where you will see through the scenery, which can be a little confusing the first time it happens. Yes, it will likely happen.... and more than once.
Sound: For a game that comes from mobile, the Sounds aren't bad at all. In fact, I was typically content with the music and the voice acting. It wasn't horrible, though one of the characters is a little over the top, but aren't villains always portrayed that way?
Story:  The story is rather interesting, to me at least. I liked the characters, although some of the missions seem rather structured for a Deus Ex game. Unforutnately, as the story is short, the characters don't really get all the attention they deserve. If the game had more support, we likely would have seen more with further chapters and installments in the series. Unfortunately, it's unlikely this will occur, so you get what you get and until it's decided what to do with this particular piece of IP, we likely won't see anything more for awhile.
Controls: This is where the game really shows it's mobile origins. The developers could have spent a little time smoothing out the controls for PC but unfortunately this didn't occur. Sometimes when trying to accomplish certain tasks the game will get confused as to what you're trying to do and won't allow it. I.e. if you're taking cover and you press in a direction at a corner, the game won't allow you to move out of cover, because it will only accept you taking cover again. Another major issue is when you are trying to vault over small obstacles, sometimes you will be able to walk over to them and do this instantly, and others the game will not allow it unless you are taking cover and then you can repeatedly hit spacebar to vault over the object. It can be very frustrating. Another major issue is when you are trying to interact with certain objects you cannot because the hitbox for lack of a better term of other NPCs are in the way. You can clearly see the object, you are clearly pointing at it, but the game has decided that the object next to it takes priority even though that is not the option available when you press the E button to interact. This can be highly frustrating from time to time, but fortuntely doesn't occur as often as it could. There is still one computer I couldn't hack, because the receptionist was in the way, and when I decided I was angry and shot her in the head, I discovered she had invisible bio-organic titanium shielding protecting her that seemed to have infinite regenerative properties and no matter how much I made it bleed, it wouldn't allow me to destroy it and then kill her :P
Overall: 5/10 - If you're a Deus Ex fan, go in with low expectations and you can still enjoy it. However, if you expect excellence, you will be disappointed. Take the game for what it is worth but NEVER buy it at full price. It's not polished enough for that, and it was much cheaper originally even on Android and Apple stores. I would recommend getting it for maybe $2 if you can and then in my opinion it's worth it. Base pricing of $10 is ridiculous and should never be considered.
Honestly this is one of the few games where I wish I could choose a Neutral instead of Yes or No. But because I enjoy the universe and with the above caveats, I will still give it a thumbs up... so long as you remember, it's not gonna be great, and you don't spend much on it.

Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is the sequel to Hotline Miami which once again features mysterious phonecalls setting you off on a rampages and massacres. This time however, there are multiple stories, perspectives and timelines involved that all revolve around the plot.
PROS:
+ Dynamic gameplay; there are many different ways to complete a level, both harsh, silent or berserker-like
+ The game is not any less shy of brutal, pixelated violence and gore
+ The story and setting are quite similar to the original: sick, drugged and merciless
+ Same as the original game: one difficulty only
+ Absolutely awesome soundtrack, and that's coming from a guy who's very picky with music; it's a variety of upbeat, energizing, relaxing and ambient tracks (more than twice as long as in the previous game (available as DLC))
+ Hard mode, which you can unlock by beating the game, is a mode that flips the levels, adds tougher enemies and limits your ammo; it adds surprisingly great replayability
+ There is a level editor and the game supports the Steam workshop very well in its easy and user-friendly use
+ Fair price/content ratio
NEUTRAL:
+/- The difficulty has been stepped up by a lot: levels are longer, feature more (tougher) enemies with guns and enemies off-screen. Especially the latter is annoying. Their reflexes are also increased. Certain levels are also difficult because you're limited to a certain playstyle or arsenal (limited ammo, melee only, etc.).
CONS:
- The story is a lot more confusing and feels less gripping than the former; it feels like a loose collection of story fragments being mashed together
- There are only 4 playable characters and a few situational ones while the original game had about 20.
This was originally a negative review because of certain very difficult parts of the game that got me going for a long while which lead to agitation. Since I was really driven to beat this game, I got past them eventually and am looking back at a pretty unique and memorable experience, Hotline Miami in its entirety.
If you like hard, fast-paced games and/or enjoyed the original Hotline Miami, buy this game.
My rating: 8/10

Alright, here is my review after putting in half a day's worth of time in to this game. Oh, and before I go any further, no, I did not complete the campaign, I'll get to why in a moment. So, without further delay, here is my breakdown of this game.
First of all, this game is for masochists, whether you got an unnoficial "balancing mod" or not. This is hands down the most frustrating misuse of a fantastic idea I've ever seen. The idea is pretty great, a fantasy sim city builder that tasks you with managing the kingdom by building and providing incentives for things to get done, all while your heroes do their "best" to rise in level and maybe usefullness. There's also some great voicing, at least on your side, and some pretty cool ideas that actually pan out (such as creating parties), but that's about it.
Now, for the long list of absolutely terrible crap that will continue to make your gaming experience hell. To start with, difficulty, there isn't any way to control this as the game goes from novice to advanced after two missions (read easy to holy hell wtf happened to my town?!) A lot of your completed missions thereafter are based off of luck rather than skill due to enemy spawns and constant zerg-like-rushing. Oh, did I forget to mention that? Yeah, there is absolutely zero room whatsoever for flexible strategy. Thanks to that weird developer minset you'll find that some heroes are just plain worthless, causing you to only waste your gold on their buildings for upgrades. Oh, speaking of gold, enemies don't rely on any kind of resource for whatever unholy reason, and can continue to pump wave after wave at you until you take care of their spawns. This is usually only mildly irratible however, on some later missions, you'll find yourself constantly under pressure or on the brink of ruin merely two or so minutes into a level. So if you like rushing your missions by pumping out the right heroes from the get go without actually taking the time to enjoy the game (read play for more than five minutes per mission) then this is the game for you. If you like to take your time to actually enjoy your purchase, forget this game, seriously just forget it.
So, if you've actually made it this far in my review and still wish to purchase this game AND don't consider yourself a masochist, I strongly recommend you dowload an unoffical balance mod. The one I used came from this site:
and it helped me somehow manage to enjoy myself up until a particularly frustrating mission called "Royal Feat". Honestly if game developers design it so that you have to play a fantasy/sim builder/RTS as a juiced up version of Starcraft from zerg-rush hell then they're doing something incredibly, moronically, wrong.
I get way less stress playing the Ikko Ikki on Total War: Shogun 2. And it's far more enjoyable....

It's been years, and now, I can say the following safely:
Best.  Midieval.  Game.  Ever.

While it's not exactly bug free, especially on newer computers, and the graphics are a bit aging yet wierdly laggy, these don't get in the way of the game much.  After countless hours, I still keep coming back for more.  This has earned the exceedingly rare status of games I will play forever, of which there are basically only three others, out of the hundreds of games i've played in my years.  That's saying something.
It has all the loot and items an RPG fan could desire, with a stat and ability system more in-depth and palpable than Skyrim's, a large host of memorable but not intrusive or overly-yappy NPCs with some randomly-generated aspects, and while the game is very procedural, nuances tend to make the gameplay a little different each time.
If you have even a passing interest in RPGs, war simulators, epic battles, midieval times, midieval warfare, or rags-to-riches (or maybe peasant-to-emperor in this case) story...
You owe it to yourself to get this.

I think this is one of those games that as a player you're implicitly supposed to bash, or otherwise you loose credibility in the gaming community. I can't care less about the gaming community and what people think I should say about what I play, so I can honestly tell you: I enjoyed this game.
First of all, a disclaimer: all the negative reviews made me hesitant about whether or not getting the game in the first place (that's what a Negative rating does on Steam). But I had loved DXHR, enjoyed the first Deus Ex (I'm still missing Invisible Wars, another one people are supposed to bash by default, apparently), so when I found it on sale on Humble Bundle a few days ago, I decided to buy it nevertheless.
That said, absolutely DON'T buy the game at full price. But at 2/3€ or something like that, if you're a fan, definitely buy it. At the very least, you get some quality entertainment in a world you've learned to love.
And from the experience point of view, I was pleasantly surprised. Apart from some quirky UI controls (e.g., how you're supposed to swipe scrollable text, which makes it obvious it is a mobile port) and a couple of bugs (I had to change the vsync setting to get hacking to work) I enjoyed the game. It looks and feels very much like DXHR, even though of course in a simplified way: the game is simpler, graphics do look a bit cheaper (enemies and NPCs are often recycled, less animations in general), but the sound effects and soundtracks are great, the UI is very similar, so are the minigames, and most of the game mechanics as well. I've read around that the game falls short anytime action takes place, but I've played all Deus Ex games with stealth in mind, so I never noticed anything particularly broken.
One of the greatest critics is it's short: it took me 6 hours and a half to complete it, trying to complete as many quests as possible, which is a reasonable length I believe, especially for the price. People saying it takes 2/3 hours are rushing it, which means they never got Deus Ex in the first place. The Missing Link DLC was around there as well in terms of length. It does end in an "episodic" way, and apparently we're never going to learn how it ends, but the game does end in a more or less satisfactory way anyway, with no cliffhangers or anything like that, so I can't complain.
Long story short: if you find it on sale, give it a try despite the hate: you might be surprised.

Originally planned as a DLC for the original Sniper Elite Nazi Zombie Army game, it became a fully-fledged game later on, and I can see why, there is about as much content on this game as there was on the first game. Unfortunately, this game isn't as good as its predecessor. Which is a shame, because there are plenty of new zombie types that kept things interesting.
The first problem comes with the way the zombies are animated. They often bug out, and twitch around at random. For example, sometimes, when they get knocked down, they pop back up in the standing position without any animation for a second. Another glitch is when they get stuck on each other and gets frozen in their animation as a result.
The second, bigger problem is that, the level design is far more cramped, which is to the game's detriment, since this kind of gameplay demands the ability to outmaneuver the horde to a better sniping position, and there are certain spots in this game where that kind of luxury and mobility isn't afforded. In simpler terms, this game has a lot of dead ends that are death traps, and there are some cases where the only real way out is to push through, because those dead ends are unavoidable. This is in stark contrast to the first game where any instances of being trapped is the fault of the player, and not because of the level design. Another thing to add to this is that it seems to be specifically designed to spawn zombies on top of you out of the ground, which is also poor level design.
Overall, while I do appreciate that they made the effort to make it not just more of the same, there isn't as much care out into the map design or QA done this time around. It is because of this that I cannot really recommend this game at full price. If you see this game on sale, then by all means, do pick it up, but $15 is a bit more than what this game is worth. Which is a shame, because in Single Player, it is 4 Hours worth of Zombie shooting with a solid netcode to go with the Co-op mode. If you are curious about this franchise, I would recommend that you pick up the first game instead of this, and only pick this up if you have to play more of it.

Layers of Fear is a new storydriven horror game and is thus far very well received. Speaking for myself, I didn't think it was too impressive but the overall concept is pretty neat, I'll give it that.
In Layers of Fear you play as a demented and crazy painter who lost pretty much everything in his life and now goes on to try and redeem himself by painting another picture - a project most complicated since there are very special ingredients involved. That's as far as the overall story about yourself goes.
You begin the game in a prologue narrated by your character and following that you start the gameplay in your house. You can explore pretty much everything and along the way you discover a lot of items crucial to understanding your story and why you are even that insane. At first it doesn't even seem like you're that much of a crazy person but the farther you go and the deeper you delve the more it becomes apparent that your soul is quite corrupted and shaken by what events transpired in the past.
But... what about the gameplay?
The gameplay doesn't feature combat in any way. It's purely explorative. You can walk and sort of run and of course interact with objects such as doors, little items in the shelves and all that. Interacting with doors and cupboards feels very Amnesia-esque while you can look at some items in great detail like you can, for instance, in Skyrim.
However, the gameplay does not include any sort of hiding mechanics whatsoever. Also I've discovered that you aren't being followed by any monsters and you never need to run from anything. No chase sequences. There is but one entity in the game that can probably kill you but as long as you pay heed to the hint written on the walls upon first encountering that entity this won't happen. Avoiding death is very very easy.
But since this is a horror game there's got to be some horror in it, right? Well. There is I guess. Let me convey it this way: I can certainly see why some people would be creeped out or even scared by the game at certain points. Speaking for myself, to me it felt like the game tried really hard to scare me or make me feel uneasy. I never had that feeling tho. I was quite relaxed, actually. Nontheless, as far as actual horror goes I will give the game credit for not using any blood whatsoever but rather utilizing cleverly placed jumpscares that are not over the top as well as some very neat effects.
Anyway, the music of the game is quite alright. Nothing too special and nothing we haven't seen before so overall it's okay but nothing I would really marvel at. The sounds on the other hand are quite nice though. If you are vulnerable to such games the sounds will do a good job at creeping you out at times. Combined with some of the visual effects the game provides in certain situations I can certainly see how people would become uneasy.
Now, in conclusion: The horror in this game feels a bit loosely patched together and didn't scare me a bit. Most of those scenes rather invoked a feeling of "O-kay... whaaat the hell is going on?" but nothing where I'd go "Oh mah GAWD I wanna go home! ;~;". This is because you never feel watched, you don't feel chased, there is nothing that actively engages you ever, nothing to run and hide from and after playing the game for about an hour that becomes very apparent very quickly and beyond that point you pretty much lose your fear of the game because you know for a fact that nothing will ever come and get you unless you come to it. And you never need to actively engage said entity. At least not as far as the game goes at this point in time.
However, let's look at something else: the way they've crafted the overall aesthetic of the game along with the story.
The aesthetic of the game is rather brilliant to me and for a game powered by the unity engine it looks very very polished and neat. Looks are quite fantastic for a unity game. So good in fact that even the dirt looks natural. And the visual effects the game provides are marvelous at times. You'll see a whole room just curling up and deforming directly before your eyes while you can move around it and interact with stuff - it's not a cutscene in which you can't do anything. That's rather brilliant. Also there are some other neat effects and ideas in the game that are pretty cool to look at. Nothing shocking and fear-inducing but nontheless a work of art.
The story itself is also pretty well-crafted. You only get bits of your character's history by reading letters from third party people or diary entries, newspaper articles. It's nothing too new but it is done quite nicely. Personally I wanted to know more about the guy I'm playing as. Not that his character is anything new within this genre of video games but it was interesting enough to keep me playing.
Also, even though I find the actual horror to be lacking in this game I found it interesting enough to play through. I wanted to know the end of it and I was quite interested in the solution the protagonist came to to ease or erase his troubles. Because he's mad like a cow, psycho bonkers crazy in fact.
To conclude this:
Overall the horror is lacking, there are some neatly placed jumpscares and it has some good sound design but overall I wasn't impressed with how it felt in relation to how it presented itself. However, the visual effects, the aesthetic and story are pretty interesting and kept me playing because I wanted to know more and see the end of it.
Would I recommend this game?
Depends. If you are very susceptible to horror and easily scared by stuff like this you will probably enjoy it as a horror game. However if you walked through Amnesia like it was a relaxation session you will be bored by the horror. If you are interested in a story driven exploration game with a beautifully crafted environment and a protagonist who's completely out of his mind and exploring his madness a little, then this game might be quite right for you.
I can not recommend this game at the current price in relation to its current stage of completion - about half of the content is still not present and needs to be added for the game to feel complete. Grab it while it's on sale (like I did) or buy it when the full game comes out. In this stage it's not worth the full price.

A good mix of different flavours of horror, all contained within a late 19th/early 20th century style stately home. What do I mean by "different flavours"? Well, it's not all jump scares, though it does have its fair share of them (with some of them being quite "cheap" if I'm honest. i.e. Stuff randomly flying off a table with a typical scary audio cue), but there's a lot of impending dread, psychological elements, mind ♥♥♥♥s, you name it, the developers are really trying to touch all the bases on what scares us.
They're doing a great job, and I thoroughly look forward to it being finished. My only criticism design-wise are some of the jump scares, as they're pretty obtuse and bring out more of a groan from me after the initial shock. There is a difference between something suddenly happening accompanied by a loud noise, and the player making themselves jump due to their own seemingly innocuous action. Don't get me wrong, there is plenty of the latter as well, and one of the best scares I've had resulted from me just turning around and spotting something. No loud audio cue or fast/sudden movement. I won't spoil what it is.
The story is quite intriguing as well,  piecing it together via the various snippets found throughout the set pieces and audio clips from our "protagonist", with everything slowly building a mental image as to the events leading up to the current moment.
The trailer did give me a different impression of the game from what it actually is however. Each moment in the game feels disconnected from one another (probably intentionally so) after the short beginning, making it feel like one, incredibly drawn out hallucination. Whereas the trailer gave me the impression it would be a bit more... Progressive. The protagonist still interacting with the outside world in some ways such as phone calls, perhaps wading in and out of psychotic episodes, but is ultimately anchored to the house, returning to "normality" for shorter and shorter periods of time, building up into a climax that would leave you questioning whether "normalcy" is even a possibility any more.
But that's probably not going to happen with what we have so far, and that's fine, it's still a great (and terrifying) experience. You just kind of drift from moment to moment constantly, like you've just gone full whacko right off the mark and fallen into a neverending nightmare coma, spasming on the floor of your workshop.
On the technical side of things, my only complaint is performance issues. Running on an i7 3770k @ 4GHz, GTX 980, 16GB RAM and an SSD, I get some pretty bad frame drops when looking in certain directions in some areas (even though it appears I'm just looking at a wall). Settings maxed out except for Chromatic Abberation (I find it annoying in any game that is seen through a character's eyes, and not a camera). With this being Early Access, I'm sure it's something they'll address before the game is released.
Overall, VERY recommended for horror fans. The story DOES cut off a couple/few hours in (depending on fast you are), so be aware that (as with all early access titles) you're not getting the full product, though what's currently available is definitely in a very "finished" state.

If you're a Star Trek fan, then you'll want to play this. Obviously, PW makes their money by having microtransactions. However, despite this, it's still equitable for the F2P player. As the game description says, it's like being inside the show. Sector narration is done by Leonard Nimoy, Michael Dorn reprises his role as Worf and there are other familiar characters. If you're a Star Trek fanboy like me, then you'll see this game as a time suck. It's not the most visually stunning game out there but it's a lot of fun.
Edit 1: Recently, Tim Russ reprised his role as Tuvok during a Dyson Sphere event.
Edit 2: Now that I have more time on record, I can add a few things. My view about the game above is still the same. However, I will take the time to add a few things. As I said before, it helps if you're a Star Trek fan to begin with. You get to play with the ship types you saw in the different series and you get to visit the places you could only see on TV. I will caution you that the story takes place some 30 years after the events of the last Star Trek movie (no, not the new ones...I mean Nemesis). If you take that into consideration, you'll realize that it's a whole new take on the franchise.
Edit 3: I mentioned before that there are microtransactions. Really, the best ships are there and it wouldn't hurt to drop some money on Zen to get a few of them. That being said, you seriously don't have to. What you're really paying for are the consoles that come with them that give you some neat abilities. When you hit max level, you can get all kinds of equipment by running PvE/PvP queues that evens the playing field. So, you don't need to buy anything at all.
Edit 4: With the Legacy of Romulus update they did, the current mechanics seem to favor the Romulans since you can choose a side. Their ships seems to have the advantage in fights and function in multiple capacities. That being said, the disparity isn't actually there. Each race has their strong suit and each race is deficient somwhere.

Majesty 2 (and the expansion packs) build upon the experience of the first one, that is, a strategy game where you cannot control any of your units. Instead you supply them with potions, new weapons, enchantsments etc. In order for them to do your dirty jobs, you'll have to place bounty flags on targets (whether it's for killing or defending).
Now, for the actual review; I found myself drawn into this game rather fast - I was a big sucker for the first one, and even though this one gave off a different 'vibe', I did end up falling in love. It wasn't this "love-at-first-sight" dealy like with Majesty 1, but rather a more of a rebound type of love. You know the feeling. She looks like your ex, she talks like your ex, even somewhat similar personalities -- but at the end of the day it's NOT your ex.
For all intends and purposes this *is* Majesty - but without the British accent - without the extra edge and charm.
The Campaign was interesting, and I'm fond of the fact that they mention the acheivements of the previous rulers (you). The Expansions were... Meh. I mean new missions - yay - doesn't help that they are rather bland. Don't even get me started on the Monsters-pack, so many spelling errors etc.
What I'm trying to say is... Don't fool yourself into thinking this is Majesty. It isn't. It plays the same way, and it's great as a standalone title. Just don't be blinded by the title and the shiny "2" after it.
For this kind of game it's quite nice. 7/10.

Following in the footsteps of its predecessor, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number capitalizes on the strongest aspects of the original game and welcomes new mechanics, new characters, new weapons, and a deeper story that aims to directly teach the player a cryptic lesson about morality, consequences, and the concept of Cause & Effect through its characters' interactions. Hotline 2 is more of the same with explosive (sometimes literally!), fast-paced, incredibly-challenging gameplay mixed with blood & guts galore. As a bonus, the game received an online-friendly level editor that encourages players to keep playing long after they've run through both the game's story mode difficulties (Oh yes, there is now a Hard Mode for people who found the game's normal mode "Too easy").
There are few drawbacks to this game, but said drawbacks are noticeable. Sometimes, the player may encounter a spawning glitch at any point of any given level that either traps them in an inescapable loop of deaths and respawns, prevents them from obtaining something they need to progress, or causes an enemy to run far outside the level's boundary lines, rendering the level impossible to complete. Additionally, players may find themselves hindered by the game's way of handling weapon pick-ups when there are multiple weapons lying in close proximity. For example, if you kill two enemies (one holding a bat or pipe and the other holding a shotgun) and the weapons are next to each other, then depending on the enemy you killed first, you will ALWAYS pick up that enemy's weapon. So in essence, if you killed the guy with the bat first, then the shotgun guy and you want the shotgun, you're forced to pick up the bat and throw it away to get the shotgun. This is often the case in levels with a lot of enemies and consequently, the result of many player deaths. This issue was prevalent in the previous game as well and evidently, did not receive an alternative.
To conclude, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is an excellent addition to the Hotline series and offers a lot in replay value, challenge, and investment that will have players coming back for more... if they haven't been discouraged by the amount of times the "You're Dead, Press A to Restart" has graced their vision.

Hotline Miami 2 is nowhere near as good as the original. First of all the story tries to have several levels and characters to it, but I just find it uninteresting. I can't say if the story in the original was masterpiece either, but at least it gave you that psycho-delic feeling that made you wanna kill more. The music also does not hold a candle to the music in the original even though it is alright.
The main problem with Hotline Miami 2 though is the fact that in almost every level the corridors are so long you cannot see what's at the end even with the look-action (Shift). This means if there's an enemy there with a gun, he will shoot you. This same annoying problem is present in almost every level. I constantly have the feeling the camera should a bit higher, or that I could scroll higher to see more of the surroundings. This just ruins the fun. I don't recall this ever bothering me in the first game.
There's other smaller issues that are either bad game design or just buggy. One of the new characters/masks is a pair of two men, one with a chainsaw and another with a gun. You control the one with the chainsaw and the gun guy sort of follows you around, just slightly late, which makes sniping enemies from behind a corner needlessly arduous. Half of the time the gun guy gets stuck on objects like tables and door frames as well. This just sucks.
Then there's the military levels where you pick one gun at the start of the level and also get a knife. You cannot pick other gun in the level although enemies still drop their weapons like normal. When you run out of ammo you have to find an ammo container to refill it. However, you never get a full clip, just a few bullets. For example, if you start the level with a sniper rifle you get 2 clips with 10 bullets each. When you use them up and get to the ammo container, you only get 4 bullets. When you use up those 4 bullets, you can go back to the container for another 4 bullets, ad infinitum. This is artificial and tedious as ♥♥♥♥. What were they thinking? Why can't you just pick up the enemies' weapons? Marine's honour?
On top of all this, playing Hotline Miami 2 gives me a headache. Probably due to the screen shaking and stuff. So, no I don't recommend this game.

The Fall is not as bad as most reviews imply, but with its greatly simplified mechanics, small map, and half-finished story, it falls short as a Deus Ex game. At least it is cheap and has a few enjoyable missions.
Deus Ex is like Zelda: the first game only received one sequel, and every subsequent entry builds backwards in time: The Fall is the prequel of Human Revolution, which in turn was the prequel of Deus Ex 1.
While technically this game is supposed to be a direct sequel to the first and only Deus Ex novel, Icarus Effect, it does a mighty poor job at that, because it only references events without any real context or background. We play as two agents on the run from one of the main antagonists of Human Revolution, Belltower PMC, but their tale just hangs in the air both in the beginning and at the conclusion: the game ends in a ‘to be continued’ screen, but Square Enix long ago abandoned all plans to make any sequel after this game flopped.
Since The Fall was originally an iOS title, naturally a lot of sacrifices were made in game mechanics: there is only one city now – Panama, which feels like a bad attempt to merge the Detroit and Hengsha maps of Human Revolution – with a set of small missions and no role-playing whatsoever. The infinite inventory space, omnipresent shopping menu, lack of jumping, and the automatic vanishing of downed bodies all push the player towards a more aggressive play style opposed to the focus on stealth in other Deus Ex games.
Still, frankly, I wouldn’t say The Fall is a bad game, because it is enjoyable as an almost indie quality (and indie price range). It’s just if you expect it to measure up to the Deus Ex name… then it cannot deliver.

Stronger combat? Whatever you like. The object of the game is to explore the island, gather food, fend off predators, and let your pack thrive.
Once you have a good surplus of food, you can go to the beach and move to another island. Generally, any island you move to will be larger than the starting island. However, each biome has it's own unique challenges, weather, diseases, and predators.

3) There are no steam achievements. (I WANT ACHIEVEMENTS.)
I definitely recommend this game though, it's a ton of fun and it's a great way to kill time. 9/10.

Just like Dead Space and Resident Evil 4, this game gets a divisive reception from gamers.The ones who like it, and the ones who didn't.
Most of the ones who liked it usually loved Dead Space and Resident Evil 4, and probably older school RE games. And the ones who didn't are usually in this tiers:
-tier 1 is composed of pretentious idiots that thumb this down because of this generic copypasta argument: "I have gun therefore isn't scary, this doesn't scare me blablabla I have balls of iridium" but in the end they coulnd't even play real horror like Amnesia or Outlast because they found it boring or scary or pretend to don't own a PC.
-tier 2 are the action nuts that picked the wrong game and expected gunplay like killing floor or CoD in their game, also using the lack of multiplayer as a valid reason for a thumb down.
Look, the game isn't perfect but most of it's shortcoming are technical in the end. Is solid, and with no doubt a great addition to horror themed games and great ride in it's own terms.
The best things are the combat, the atmosphere and how the devs had the balls to actually make it more opressive than just shadows, gore and sounds: if you don't thread carefully or puts your wits in use you'll have a very hard time. There's traps, scarce items that make resource management key, and vicious unforgiving enemies. All of this combine in, for example, fooling enemies to fall in a trap, and other moments to give you a very tense experience that I knew in the end Mikami could provide.
The worst? The story may need a visit from a wikia to get a better understatement. I'm sure giving the it more insight could have worked against the uncertainty that works so well with horror genre. But that's more my opinion on horror themed games than an actual fact.
The game will play with you and your head a lot, and maybe you'll  feel for moments it's overdoing it (like in Bioshock Infinite or Mario world) with moments like "Princess is in another castle". Again, this is on purpose and works with horror because it makes you feel that you're never in control, but sometimes they overdo it so much that you might just take a pause out of frustration.
If I have to put it bluntly, this is a Dead Space game with vintage weapons, working headshots and a story that sometimes goes too much 'out there'. As I recommended any Dead Space without hesitation, I also do it with this one.
Just finished the main campaign. Definitely some story telling problems, but in the end it works. Great gameplay, spooky, and leaves you thinking. Would recommend

The Evil Within is an old-school survival horror by the creator of Resident Evil: playing as Detective Castellanos as you try to survive the various nightmarish places and enemies put in front of you is quite fun overall but sadly its old-school roots can sometimes get in the way of your enjoyment.
-the art style of the places and creatures you'll meet is exquisitely surreal and disturbing
-the game mantains an eerie and dreadful atmosphere for its whole length
-memorable antagonist
-good sound design
-the survival aspect is well executed, enemies can be quite damaging and come at you suddendly or in waves, ammo and health items are never plentiful forcing you to rely on stealth kills/distractions
-provides a good challenge even on its basic difficulty level
-overall story is pretty interesting and engaging
-the upgrade system for weapons and skills works nicely and lets you customize your character to fit your playstyle
-good length
-certain enemies, mini-bosses and bosses with instakill moves can be annoying for some players
-the game progressively shifts from horror/stealth sections to more action/combat oriented scenes and this might not sit well with everyone
-clunky controls for fine movements and aiming, expecially with a controller
-graphics are a bit too washed out and shadows can be, at times, way too saturated in black: there's also some noticeable texture pop-in
-there's some weird mouse acceleration in menus, mouse wheel was also never fixed and so can't be used in them
-while interesting the story is a bit too cryptic for its own good
-having to break countless boxes/jars to gather items gets boring fast and also detracts from the overall atmosphere
-having to go back and forth to the savegame hub (accessible through mirrors scattered around levels) to save, upgrade or open lockers gets annoying in the long run
The Evil Within is truly a throwback to the good old days of the survival horror genre and it provides a good experience overall with a strong (albeit cloudy) story, disturbing enemies, challenging boss fights, collectibles, a good amount of weapons and several upgrades to choose from.
Its old-school roots also mar the experience a bit though, movement is clunky, fine aiming (even with a fully upgraded weapon) can be a bit off at times and the fact you are required to pull off headshots most of the time- while evading enemies trying to grab you- can make things frustrating at times. It can also get a bit aggravating on certain bosses, where you have to dodge their moves and then frantically try and adjust your aim to fire properly without wasting too many shots.
But persistence in the face of certain design faults is rewarded by one of the most enjoyable horror experiences I've had this year and, while The Evil Within isn't the masterwork that Resident Evil was, it's nonetheless a quite good game that survival horror fans'd have in their library.

The Evil Within is one of the most frustrating and also most rewarding horror games to hit the PC since the dawn of time. When the game first came out, I absolutely hated it and if I reviewed it then, I'd have never recommended people buy it, let alone play it. However, multiple patches later, 60fps and removal of the black bars opened up a gaming experience which is the closest thing to Resident Evil 4 that you can get so far.
Having said that, in my opinion, the first 3 chapters are a bit lack luster, with annoyingly forced scenes where you have to flee, mixed with the TERRIBLE accuracy of the starting weapon, the pistol. This leads to a very frustrating experience, as mentioned previously. The lack of ammo (its a survival horror so this is expected) would be fine if the pistol didn't have a 5 degree cone of accuracy on it to start with, which means you never get rewarded for accuracy. This takes a lot of skill away from the player sadly, which lets the game down.
HOWEVER, chapter 4 onwards is like playing a different game. The first real horror experience for me was in chapter 4 with "Laura", who is the best and worst of Japanese horror cliches merged into one creature. The game then sets you up right after that moment with an equally bad part, literally throwing you out of the hot frying pan and into the fire. This is the pace the game then continues with for the majority of its 15 chapters.
PROS
+ closest game to Resident Evil 4 in terms of approach and style
+ Interesting story
+ nice setting
+ impressive visuals
+ genuinely hard encounters
+ INSANE level of difficulty if you're brave enough...
CONS
- Still needs a very powerful machine to run it properly
- "Boss" creatures aren't explained and you have to repeatedly die whilst learning their mechanics
- Storyline isn't explained at all, instead it was left for the DLC!!!
- Pistol accuracy is an absolute disgrace and even after 5/5 maxing out, it still has a 2.5 degree cone...
- Matches mechanic seems to fall by the wayside the further you get into the game, especially after Laura.
- Some chapters are vastly longer than others for no apparent reason, almost like they were developed by different departments.
