Someone is trying to create their Magnum opus, while simultaneously being haunted by his past.
This simple premise somehow draws you in, and compells you to see this painting to completion and also discover the story of his past.
When playing this game you will be enveloped in the atmosphere, due to its well use of color pallete and lighting, as well the soundtrack, which is a nice use of somber piano and higher pitched points for added tension. There are clever uses of sounds used throughout which is something that I personally appreciate and consider very creative.
Something I personally believe adds to this games atmosphere is its actual use of NO SOUND at some points. It will actually utilize something that often isn't anymore and playing portions of the game and noting the sudden dissapearence of all noise whatsoever immediately gets your attention to look a little harder at your surroundings to see what is wrong.
The pacing is good; nothing ever feels too short nor too long, but some scenes are slightly emphasized more than others due to more time occasionaly being required for some areas than others.
The clues in-game are great and finding them is not too challenging but none the less rewarding as they are your gateway to the main characters past and a little bit into his physche.
Overall, upon completing this game you will most likely feel an appreciation towards it, and yearn for finding that 'next piece'.

I honestly don't think I can ever write a review good enough for what I think this deserves. The second game improved from the first in my opinion, but this review applies to my general obession with both.
PC Gamer did a good job though recently, have a look 'cause it's probably a lot better than what I wrote:
The two games together are possibly the most unique and memorable singleplayer experience I have ever had. Although I admit it has a pretty limited audience, as this isn't something you play for fun. The intricate plot which demands curious players to investigate further, is hidden in the dialogues, level details and , all of which are tightly packed into a "high-octane" campaign which takes about 5 hours through on the first try. Becoming both extremely frustrating and deeply moving as it progresses, you are pushed forward mostly by sheer determination to finish each level, as the game explores a storyline so unusual of choice (who the ♥♥♥♥ makes a game about late 80s sociopathic hitmen in animal masks...) and twists that it demands more than a single playthrough for a full understanding. Coupled with a compelling retro art style and matching soundtrack from fantastic independent artists, which introduced me to an entirely new artistic subculture, these titles trump my experiences in ~90% of other singleplayer games I've played, from Far Cry to Age of Empires. The gameplay itself can be extremely unforgiving and not as smooth as others, especially with the AI modifications in the sequel make being shot offscreen much more annoying, but it has left a deep impression on me and my experiences with video games.
After playing this I have become obsessed with the series, which may skew my review slightly. Falling in love with the title seems to be incongruous with most players of Hotline Miami, but
to any other mildly depressed, introverted ♥♥♥♥♥ out there with strange inclinations in video-game choice, I wholeheartedly recommend this game and its predecessor, in any order.

This was the game I was looking for.  I discovered Majesty as a mobile app, and when I read that it was a port from PC (a well-done port, in my opinion), I decided to get it here on Steam.  I also got Majesty and Majesty HD, and while fundamentally similar in gameplay, they don't have the polished graphics that Majesty 2 has, and have that feel of a game a bit too old to get into in 2014.  If only I had played it a decade ago and had nostalgia driving me to return.
So in short, if you're looking for something different in RTS, namely a game where you don't directly control the heroes you've created, this is well worth some play time.  You build buildings and train adventurers of various classes.  You choose upgrades to stock the stores you've erected.  The adventurers you train will go out and explore and kill stuff, then buy items from the stores, provided you've researched the items they can afford.  When you want something killed or an area explored, you set a bounty and the adventurers decide who goes to collect.  The graphics aren't going to blow you away, but they're well-drawn and the game mechanics are a lot of fun.
One thing I've struggled with a bit: I haven't found any selectable difficulty options, and the levels are all laid out linearly despite being displayed on a map as though you could just select what challenge you're ready for.  When you progress to a difficult level, it is difficult and there isn't a lot you can do about it but retry until you figure out what you need to upgrade in what order.  This makes for a bit of tedium as you play for ten minutes and figure out that you lost in the first minute.  The only thing you can take with you between levels are heroes you've promoted to 'Lord' status, and if you've got some lords who are of a decent level but not too good you might be able to get a jump on a tough level, assuming you have enough starting gold to pay for the Hall of Lords and also to hire the lords, (the better they are, the more they cost, which limits the number of times you can do this as they will inevitably level up and cost more the next time you need them).  Outside of that, most levels require you to figure out the exact order to upgrade the exact right type of troops for each map, which removes any illusion of free will in how you approach each level, and a bit of the fun.
Bottom line: very challenging, bit more linear than I was hoping for, but a solid RTS-with-a-twist.

Seeing so many negative reviews its a shame I can't add my review to Majesty 2 since I own the Collection edition. So here will suffice. I rate this game 8.5/10 and I played the original Majesty too (rate:9/10). M2 is a sim  RTS+RPG game, Like RTS games you have create an economy, research, create armies and destroy the opponents. The sim part is because you don't control the units (caled heroes). You assign rewards to kill a monster or destroy a building and depending on the reward 0 or more of your heroes will go achieve your task (more money = more heroes). There are soe 5 different kinds of tasks you can assign to heroes. The heroes will buy themselves upgrades provided that you created the necessary buildings and invested  on the research (which cost gold). Placing the buildings is your task and its important. There are defense towers and many other kinds of buildings (15+). Heroes level as they gain more experience (RPG component). I love this whole concept of the Majesty series.
Plus points:
- Unique take on RTS
- A variety of heroes: gnomes, archers, paladins, monks, necromancers (some 15+ types)
- Rock-paper-scissors system. .
- Varied gameplay in the campaign.
- RPG element s great. You can check each of your heroes and see what spells/powers they have learned.
- Game is well polished.
Minus points:
- Some of the latter missions are way too difficult. Basically, large number of monsters are thrown on your base before you even got the chance to set your economy. This frustrates the last 1/3 of the campaign. The first 2/3 are great. Its a shame. Maybe they should have add difficulty levels.
- So there are cheats and the player is forced to either spend hours figuring out how to beat each of these later missions or use the cheats, which is a shame either way.
- The concept is so amazing, one can't help feel that they could have designed a better campaign. One of the (hard) missions is to defeat two opposing kingdoms. It is incredibly cool as each of the opponents is using different armies. They could have thought other missions like that.

So far I'm really enjoying the game. I've played for 10 hours and feel like I've barely scratched the surface of the available content. Trying to breed for specific genes while avoiding the complications that come with inbreeding and mutations makes for interesting gameplay.
I really like the direction the development seems to be headed. I've spent most of my time playing on the experimental mutations development branch and I've really enjoyed the new gameplay features that they're building towards.
Overall, the game seems to be really stable. I didn't experience any game breaking bugs or glitches. There are a few minor annoyances that don't seem like much, but add up over time.
The biggest annoyance, for me, is that you can navigate using WASD or the Arrow keys. I prefer WASD but if I press more than one key at a time (which frequently happens when switching from one direction to another) it immediately begins renaming the currently selected creature. Because of this, I have quite a few creatures named "sssssss" and "asa." There's already a mechanic in game where you click on the name and can type in a new one so I'm not sure if this is a feature or a glitch. If a glitch, then I hope it's fixed. If it's a feature then...I really hope it gets fixed.
Another annoyance is that, as your pack grows, it becomes more difficult to manage each individual creature. While that is as it should be, the problem arises when creatures die and I have no idea why. I think they're dying of old age, but sometimes it might be because they were sick, or wounded, or they starved to death. There is a notifications panel that informs you that a creature died, and you can zoom to the skeleton, but it doesn't tell you who it was or how they died. It's not until two or three turns later that I realize that the creature I was planning a breeding program around was the one that kicked the bucket.
The other issue is the notification window itself. You get a notification for each sick creature, for when it rains, for when a creature gets a parasite, when they die, and I think several others. The problem with this is that you have to go through and clear each individual notification by hand. I often find myself just closing and ignoring the window altogether because I can't be bothered to clear all of the warnings manually every single turn.
Really though, these complaints are just annoyances. The game itself is adorable, challenging, and a lot of fun. The thing to remember though is that it is a Sandbox. Meaning there are no goals save the ones you set for yourself. There is nothing to tell you what to do or where to go. You learn by experimenting and figuring things out. You learn from your mistakes and you make mental notes for next time. You start to plan ahead and come up with strategies for how to tackle specific goals. The longer you play, the more you learn.
If you're the type of person that likes sandboxes, setting your own goals, experimentation, and playing god then you'll probably enjoy this game.

A few new enemies were implemented to help mix up the game-play.  None of them are ground breaking or innovative, but they do add to the game.
It all comes down to how much you enjoyed the first game.  SE:NZ2 is a fun, but it is not an epic title.  I personally found the achievements fun to hunt with a group of friends.
One other thing to take into consideration before getting this game is the lack of players.  The match making, like the first game, is dreadful.  If there are any public players on, you'll be lucky to find a team anyways.  Be sure to have a group of friends to play with if you are looking for a good co-op experience.

For those of you who are horror buffs and are sick of zombies and the like, for those of you who mourn Konami's stupidity about PT, for those of you who are looking for the very pinnacle of horror... I literally cannot recommend one more highly than this.
What it does right, it does extremely right, and brings a lot of fresh ideas to the table, even while giving nods back to older games of horror legend.
What it does wrong, it does wrong out of an experimental spirit that works rather well. For those of you who loved PT, this is a worthy extension of its ideas, mechanics, and story (not verbatim of course, but you can't deny the parallels).
Pros:
-MANY, MANY SCARE. WOW
-Wonderfully rendered fever dream
-Looks great for the Unity engine
Cons:
-It's basically PT (though I don't know if this is really a bad thing, considering PT was awesome)
-While they have a fresh way of dealing with death in the game, they also repeat it to the point that it feels a bit pointless
-I can't help but feel that, in an experience this long, it's a little disappointing that there isn't more GAMEplay. It remains a walking simulator of sorts.
But honestly, if you're looking for something really extremely well done, beautifully atmospheric, complete with wonderful tense moments AS WELL AS jump scares, this will not disappoint. I guarantee it!

This is a kinetic multiplayer deathmatch game, done in 2.5D. The movement in this game is great, you feel it control of your character at all times, and can use dives tackles, dodges, jumps, wall jumps, wall hangs, flips and slides to navigate the wonderfully detailed levels. As for the combat, you have seven basic weapon types, all of which behave differently, and you can bring two into a fight, so theres plenty of mix and matching and experimentation to do. Or you can only use your fists if you like. Different characters have different personalities, and also different special abilities like temporary invulnerability or  health on kill, and so far they all seem well balanced.

Of course, the combat goes hand in hand with the movement, and its all about using all these weapons and abilites on the move while dodging enemy fire and by god it all combines into one hell of a game, it feels great to dodge artfully around a room chopping up enemies with a sword, or winning a match by tossing your empty gun at a fleeing opponent or gracefully sliding under an incoming rocket while blasting the shooter with your pistol or dive tackling an enemny off a cliff just as theyre about to land the killing blow.
Its just great fun! A more than worthwhile investment at 10 euro.

The Evil Within is one of the most frustrating and also most rewarding horror games to hit the PC since the dawn of time. When the game first came out, I absolutely hated it and if I reviewed it then, I'd have never recommended people buy it, let alone play it. However, multiple patches later, 60fps and removal of the black bars opened up a gaming experience which is the closest thing to Resident Evil 4 that you can get so far.
Having said that, in my opinion, the first 3 chapters are a bit lack luster, with annoyingly forced scenes where you have to flee, mixed with the TERRIBLE accuracy of the starting weapon, the pistol. This leads to a very frustrating experience, as mentioned previously. The lack of ammo (its a survival horror so this is expected) would be fine if the pistol didn't have a 5 degree cone of accuracy on it to start with, which means you never get rewarded for accuracy. This takes a lot of skill away from the player sadly, which lets the game down.
HOWEVER, chapter 4 onwards is like playing a different game. The first real horror experience for me was in chapter 4 with "Laura", who is the best and worst of Japanese horror cliches merged into one creature. The game then sets you up right after that moment with an equally bad part, literally throwing you out of the hot frying pan and into the fire. This is the pace the game then continues with for the majority of its 15 chapters.
PROS
+ closest game to Resident Evil 4 in terms of approach and style
+ Interesting story
+ nice setting
+ impressive visuals
+ genuinely hard encounters
+ INSANE level of difficulty if you're brave enough...
CONS
- Still needs a very powerful machine to run it properly
- "Boss" creatures aren't explained and you have to repeatedly die whilst learning their mechanics
- Storyline isn't explained at all, instead it was left for the DLC!!!
- Pistol accuracy is an absolute disgrace and even after 5/5 maxing out, it still has a 2.5 degree cone...
- Matches mechanic seems to fall by the wayside the further you get into the game, especially after Laura.
- Some chapters are vastly longer than others for no apparent reason, almost like they were developed by different departments.
See my entire playthrough here on my channel if you so wish!

This game is actually quite good.... if you are playing melee only. I really liked the first hotline miami and the difficulty never seemed to bother me too much, and dying over and over was usually my fault and not the game's. I did rage at one level where the level design was basically a square, but that was the only one really. Also, I was able to play melee exclusively. That's what is bad about hm2. I am a melee guy and melee is more rewarding anyway. The reason I do that is because THE GUN PLAY IS GARBAGE. It just doesn't work with the simple control scheme. This was ok in hm, but in hm2 you are sometimes forced to use guns, which is annoying as hell. Being accurate is hard as hell in the chaos of the game, and the lock on doesn't work half the time, but that is mostly player fault. The fault from the game is the controls. When losing stealth and having to do a shootout (which happens a lot), the controls just lose all use. Picking up another gun is necessary while fighting, and since so many times there are weapons grouped up in the same place, you probably won't pick up what you want. A lot of the time you will pick up an empty gun when a full one is right next to it. The same mechanic is ok with melee since any melee weapon works fine. The throwing will also screw you over. You have to throw what you don't want anymore, which is horrible. You can't just put it down with a different button, but instead you throw it like a pro pitcher that takes steroids wherever you are pointing. So during a gun fight you may not be paying attention to where you hurdle the weapon, and it may fly into a window and attract more guys. Or during quick stealth you may throw it into a window and be exposed. Death Wish was the most infuriating of the levels with the zebra mask. I get it is supposed to be a really hard level, but it always felt like the game's fault when I died. The dumb zebra mask makes you roll with space, which is the same as finishing a guy. So I rolled so many times into a door when I was right over a guy, which got me killed many times. All my complaints about guns came into play too, since you have to get into a gun fight. I felt so good after I beat that since I got to play as the killing punches mask guy, since he could only do melee. Simply put, there needs to be more controls and configuration. A simple control scheme is always better, but this is too simple. There also needs to be a better prioritization of what you pick up.
Small grievances that are meant to be annoying: I hate dogs and how gunshots don't pierce doors, but that is part of the game and meant to be part of it.
Again I do like this game a lot, but hotline miami was much better and tighter as a game. I am really just saying some negative stuff since all the good stuff is known.

As the king, you decide what gets built, what heroes get hired, things to research and upgrade, and are allowed to spend some of your cash on spells for more influence on the course of the game.
Unfortunately, just like the first game, this one suffers from the problem of needing to be lucky for the first few minutes and hope that the den of mini-dragons that can kill every hero in one attack doesn't decide to send a wave towards you before you've even built a single barrack or guard tower. But the times when you don't get imediately ♥♥♥♥ed from the start are what make the game great. Do you invest in upgrading the rouges guild so that all your heroes have their weapons poisoned? Maybe build a guard tower next to the sewer entrance so that the ratmen that come from it don't ravage your marketplace? Or do you research better spells, equipment, and potions for your heroes to use? Coming to forkroads like that  and then playing them out to see if you made the right choice are what gives the game so much character, if you can bear the 10 failed attempts beforehand where a boss teir dragon decided to attack your palace as soon as you loaded the level.

===1. The game was a complete problem to even get to work right.===

The credits told me I can skip with the b button so I pressed that on my Xbox controller and it did nothing. I then clicked on the keyboard... nothing. I was stuck and thought something was wrong so I closed the game and start it back up again.
I decided to once again try the controller button and went to the character screen via mouse and then tried to move around with the controller.. still nothing.
I was playing games earlier with my controller so I know nothing is wrong with it, but I decided to just unplug it and replug it back in... I started to hear the notification noise of my controller bleeping over and over and over as the game's menu for the controller started to flicker and I got worried. Unplugged and replugged again and it's the same bleeping over and over. I then didn't unplug the controller and just closed the game... the bleeping stopped...

Oh I must mention as well that that horrible lag stopped on the first few floors too after restarting the game those 6 times.

G'day mates! Ty the tazmanian tiger for the xbox was, and still is, my favorite video game of all time. So needless to say that I was very hyped for this game, that being said, I will try to leave as much nostalgia and bias out of this review as I can.  So for any Ty fan who is concerned that because this game is 2D it's "Not a Ty game"...don't worry, this game is still a Ty game, and chances are, if you liked the originals, you'll like Ty 4.  Ok so first off, the story. As much as I miss the voice actors and cutseens from the first games, the cool comic book style of cutseens work fine and I enjoyed them. I also enjoyed the characters and their personalities. As for the actuall story itself, it's not absolutely amazing, but I still thought it was enjoyable, something goes wrong somewhere and Ty has to come and help. I did however find the twists and turns about a few select characters, such as Sly and "I thought you were dead!" Fluffy where really cool. They were nice supprises. I did feel that the ending kinda came out of nowhere and the final boss was just a bit too easy, but it was still fun.  As for the gameplay, it works absolutely fine IMO. The controls felt solid and I had a blast with it, you never feel like your slow or slippery. and the platforming is fun because of that. My only SLIGHT nitpick is that gliding feels a bit nerfed from the other games and you lose altitude  at a much faster rate,and whenever Ty is in the air you are always moving forward,which made it to where I had to tap left and right a bunch to land where I wanted to, but again, it's really no big deal, and rarely ever gave me a problem. Now as for the soundtrack, Ty 1 has one of my favorite, if not my number one favorite soundtrack in any video game, and in general, I was happy with this games music, especially since compared to todays ost's for video games, this game has some seriously good tunes that should be listend to even when not playing it, I loved most of them, thought some where just alright, and only disliked one. The level design and the music always complement each other nicely, and each one felt just right for it's level. I ESPECIALLY loved the remixs from past games.  So to sum this review up, if your a fan of Ty, you should ABSOLUTLY buy this game, I can almost guarantee you will have an absolute bonzer of a time! And for those who are new to the series, I would seriously recomend you get this game, its a super fun 2d platformer collectothon, with some great characters,levels,and music, do yourself a favor and buy this little beauty of a game.  And who knows, we may even see a Ty 1-3 port or Ty5 in the future, which would be a dream come true for me, anywho hope you have a bonzer of a time with this awesome game!!

I absolutely adore this game, granted I don't have as much time as others to devote to it. The developers keep it updated pretty regularly and are active on facebook. My only critiques are generally things that they intend to address as the game expands anyhow, like being able to move off my island to somewhere else. Again, not something that will likely be a problem in the finished product.
The game is not easy, but it's not impossible either. It does require you to plan and think before making a decision; meaning you can't just let it run, come back later, and be set. You have to be active, and you have to consider the ramifications of your actions. Because you also have to plan for food, each action you take with your creatures has to be well thought out or you'll end up starving. As much as you might also want to inbreed to quickly build your numbers, you might find them all dying off due to illness.
Overall the game is fun, really considers genetics on a level that those with limited knowledge could still understand, and it keeps you entertained. When I -do- play, I tend to lost time pretty easily.

A slightly above average survival horror game which does just what this genre is supposed to do and I believe is expected from horror fanatics like myself...but nothing more.  Uncharacteristic of a majority of 'horror' games recently, Evil Within does a solid job at providing (in most combat situations) just enough ammo to get by which makes the survival aspect of this game true to its word.  Combat is more or less acceptable in that you have a variety of weapons at your disposal along with tools in the environment to use against enemies such as glass bottles for distractions or hand axes for one-hit kills.  It's fun and fast paced despite a few sluggish controls.  A notable example is during intense scenes where you have to fight in enclosed spaces, it would have been nice to have a 180 degree turn like in Resident Evil 4.  Another minor complaint I have is that I wish there was some sort of reticle when aiming bottles at enemy heads; Sometimes I would aim right for their head and miss completely. Kind of annoying.
The money dropped after killing enemies to purchase weapon/ability upgrades can get rather frustrating because it takes a few seconds to pick up, and there are moments in the game where if you don't pick up the money you can't return for it because you are essentially on the clock to get somewhere and are being swarmed by enemies.  It would have been preferable for there to be an auto-pick up for money.  I think the lack of this feature takes away from the fun in combat.    The environment is beautifully rendered and at times I have stopped myself to take a few screenshots, however, the textures popping in and out from the distance is distracting and the immersion wanes.
The AI in this game is remeniscent of Resident Evil 5 where Sheva would be pretty much useless in the heat of battle.  Here I can be at low health with no ammo, lure an enemy near the AI and he just stands there against a wall or walks a few meaningless steps until I'm pinned on the ground.  The best thing about the AI is you can heal him for free.  They are at most a distraction for you to bide your time/reload/heal.  My biggest issue of all is the atrocious fps inconsistencies throughout the entire game so far.  I can go from ~30fps or lower to 60.  It does not matter how much I play around with the minimal graphic settings available, fps doesn't change.  There are some scenes which look amazing where the fps is consistently good but others that are of similar quality where the fps is consistently horrible.  I have not encountered any other game where my fps behaves this way and I have played similarily demanding titles.
I'm on chapter 6 currently and while I don't regret buying this because I caught it at a decent price, it is something I could have passed up.  The Evil Within started out as a promising survival horror but was quickly overshadowed by a number of design flaws ranging from controls or lackthereof, sluggish aiming, optimization, and poor AI mechanics.  I hope my opinion on this game becomes more acceptable as I approach completion.

Layers of Fear takes you on a terrifying journey through the tragedies of a painter and his late painist wife. As you play, the presence of your wife grows stronger as you make your final painting of her. It uses the standard Unreal 4 engine fare and excellent sound design to boost the game's atmosphere. The gameplay itself is a little lacking however, with the only actions with purpose is walking through the game, but that is supplemented with the Amnesia like interaction with physics and lore through the world. The movement is a little clunky but easy to get used to.

Well, let's just say... I enjoy games of all types, horror games in particular have always held a special dark place in my heart.  This is especially true for Layers of Fear.  There are many great horror titles out there but...  THIS game... WOW.  You may think the idea for a painting game is odd... but please, listen to these reviews, it's dark, visceral, unequivocally mind-bending and yes it's terrifying.  It felt like I was losing grip on reality.  If only it were possible to experience it again for the first time.  And even at that a second playthrough still holds great value.  So turn the lights down, crank up the headset and you're in for a real treat(trick).

This game is just amazing in every regard. The sound design is completely on point, bringing you into a deeper sense of immersion as you play. You may not notice the subtle pattering of rain outside the house, the crackle of thunder, and the creak of floorboards underfoot. You may not consciously notice, that is. Every creak and groin and thump in the house just drags you intot he creepy atmosphere and really puts you in the setting.
The graphics are amazing, and really show what Unity can actually do as an engine when put to task by a developer who is willing to put such detailed environments together. I was amazed when I found that this was an engine that a few years ago would not have been remotely considered capable of such feats by the general public. But in this game we get to really see the engine showcased, and can appreciate the great detail of artwork put into this game.
The environments are limited to one area, but are varied despite this, even with the house appearing to have loopbacks and backtracking. The maps are just that well done, and really permit the scares of this game to hit you suddenly and with consistency.
I played this with someone else and we were genuinely impressed and creeped out at every turn. I cannot recommend this game more highly, to the point where other scary and impressive games that came out this Halloween season were left with us comparing them to Layers of Fear and effortlessly choosing Layers as the superior scary game. I can't wait to see what comes as more of the final product is released.

HuniePop is puzzle game with a few dating sim elements. You play the game on a day to day basis as a hopeless dude (or lady!) looking to date one of many women in the game. It is a quirky game with the art style of a Japanese visual novel and the writing of one of the many flash based, dude-bro western dating sims.
2D- Japanese Visual Novel styled art
+Surprisingly decent production value for this style of game.
+Surprisingly accurate lip sync for all characters.
-Art style is inconsistent between character stills and collectible CG. (Honestly of the three characters I have completed so far, none of them really looked entirely the same as the in game stills. The art isn't bad, but it can be a bit jarring.)
Mixed- The character art. The art style itself will be highly subjective but many of the characters felt generic when it came to character design. This will be a matter of opinion however and you can easily check the characters before you buy.
+Surprisngly good soundtrack. My personal favorite is the Spanish guitar tune that plays during certain romantic dates.
Mixed- Voice acting. I found the voices hit and miss. Some of the characters sound VERY similar due to sharing voice actresses and can be extremely noticable at times. My personal favorite is the main hostess Kyu.
The actual writing in the game takes some getting used to. It uses, in the developers own words, a highly abrasive western style of writing. So expect some "ladybro" speak, club girls, and the like. I personally found it very entertaining but it might be a shock to those who are not used to this western style talk coming from Japanese style character art.
+ You are bound to find someone you like in this large cast.
+ The writing maintains a consistent quality. If you like the story, you will be pleased to know it maintains it style and quality throughout the whole game.
- There are very few "events" in the game. Girls have an introduction scene, and an ending scene. Otherwise all character dialogue comes in the form of question and answer. You will ask them questions, and sometimes they will quiz you on what you asked. You can see some character development through this but it feels like reading a Flash card and it repeats often.
The puzzle aspect of this game is a simplified bejeweled. It starts of easy and then with every victory it increases in difficulty. That is to say ANY victory will make EVERY puzzle hard. So if you complete one girl and then start another, her introduction date will be much harder than the previous girls.
In between puzzles you will go around talking to each girl. Talking earns experience, which is called Hunie in this game, which is used to increase traits that make certain block more valuable. A useful thing to improve as each girl has a preferred color of block to match. If you are succesful in impressing a girl you can earn dating gifts that do cool things like turning all the bad blocks into good block, or cashing in on multipliers to help complete the date.
Girls have a stamina bar that keeps you from talking to her too long. You can increase the stamina using food which is bought with cash, called Monie in this game. Monie is earned by dates. You will get monie even if you fail, so it is still worthwhile trying a date no mattter the difficulty.
Overall I find this to be a fairly fun puzzle game that is light on content. If you like Bejeweled, cute girls, and abrasive humor I would say the game is worth the asking price. I do hope that in any sequel they will expand on, well, everything. It is a very simple game but with some fleshing out I feel it could find a good niche between the puzzlers and the dating sims.

I haven't played Star Trek Online since it launched back in February of 2010. I can say without a doubt that I was excited for this game when I first pre-ordered it. And then I played it. It wasn't the worst MMO I had ever played but it definitely didn't live up to my expectations. The ground combat was clunky, the early story and missions were boring and there was little to no voice acting. About the only thing I did like was the ship to ship combat. But that couldn't save it for me. I just couldn't bring myself to buy the full version.
Now, 4 years later, I find myself picking it up again after hearing about how many changes have been made. It piqued my curiosity so I began to play last week. Trust me when I say, this isn't the same game that I decided against buying 4 years ago. Pretty much everything has been revamped. The game is now in it's 8th major update since launch, so there's quite a bit of new content.
Starting out, the first thing I noticed that the whole intro has been scrapped and is now completely different. Instead of finding yourself in the middle of a Borg attack, you are now an Ensign at Starfleet Academy, who has just graduated and been given his (or her) first assignment. You have been chosen to be the First Officer aboard a not-so-new Miranda Class ship. Your first mission is to go out and collect some data samples with your cadet crew. Then things go wrong.
The story is engrossing from the very first moments. It's a major step up from what used to be.
Then there's the C-Store. Currently, the game is Free To Play, which is good for someone like me, who's on a budget. Usually I hate the Free to Play options in games because I feel like my version is severely diminished. That's not the case in Star Trek Online. As a matter of fact, aside from some nifty cosmetic stuff and things like different styles of ships, I haven't really seen anything different between the Free to Play stuff and Paid subscribers. There are a few things, such as more costume slots or extra Duty Officers, which are nice but not necessarily hindering you if you don't have them.
What really impresses me about the C-Store is the ability to buy Zen (the currency used in the Cash Shop) with in-game Dilithium. Admittedly, it's at a pretty steep cost. About 125 Dilithium per 1 Zen. That means that if you want to buy the cheapest item in the C-Store, you'll need about 31,000 Dilithium saved up. Which is going to take you quite a bit of grinding. But still. The option is there and that's more than most other games will give you.
Overall, I have been having a blast. Currently I've only made it to Level 20 (Commander) and I have yet to join a Fleet but that hasn't stopped the fun from rolling in.
The only thing I could really ask for is some good PVP or better PVE Instance queues. But that's not to say I wont keep playing.
At the moment, I am going to give it a 7 out of 10. I've seen some bugs but those are nothing that can't be fixed in later patches.

Excellent game, in my opinion, despite it's flaws.
Some Pros:
- Beautiful vistas
- Engaging Ship-to-Ship combat
- extensive content, with no need to spend real money in the cash shop
- active community
- Missions can be skipped if high enough level
- XP is easy to earn, via Duty Officer Assignments, which allow you to set up "over night" missions for experience and resource gain.
- Well-Balanced gameplay and PVP combat.
Some Cons:
- Dilithium (used to buy ZEN coins for cash shop) rates are extremely high... 120-130 Dilithium = 1 ZEN Coin = $0.01 USD
- Away Missions seem to take forever, and aren't nearly as engaging as the Space Combat.
- For a game that takes place during a time of war, there isn't a lot of war going on... not even between players of opposing factions. A PvP Territory Control Wargame would easily fix this, and while there are unofficial versions made by fans, I'd rather have one that doesn't require me to keep track of updates on another, third-party website.
- Fleets (Guilds) are difficult to get up and running when you're only a few members strong. Either pray you have a lot of friends, with lots of friends, or get ready to spend real cash on getting your fleet up and running properly.

I bought this game thinking that it would be like Killing Floor, you kill a whole bunch of
rattos, and as you play you will gain experience and levels and even gain new equipment.  I was partially right.  Vermintide has been described in a lot of ways, many of them negatively, and I can understand the people who make those negative comments.
If I had to describe Vermintide using two games, I would describe it as Dark Messiah of Might and Magic meets Left 4 Dead 2.
In Vermintide you play as one of 5 adventuring classes (Human Witch Hunter, Wood Elf Waywatcher, Dwarf Warrior, Human Bright Wizard, and Human Soldier of the Empire).  They all have their own advantages and weaknesses, such as the Bright Wizard's magic allowing her to bypass armor, but at the cost of her needing to watch her consumption rate so she doesn't risk being consumed by the warp (if she does, she will explode and it will kill the enemies around her, but also her).
Your enemies are the
Skaven Empire, which is a horde of rats who seek world domination (or at least, to eat everything).  Your typical skaven wields a sword or spear and has an attitude, but among the Skaven are the
elite skaven.  These include
gutter runners,
pack masters,
poison wind globadiers and of course
rat ogres.
The game is fairly fun, and if you want even more Left 4 Dead-like action you can also play Versus mode.  Or just play Last Stand, as it's a fairly good gameplay mode too.

The story has also grown into a layered multi-character saga that spans several years and involves a serial killer, a Russian gang war, and even an actual war. It’s less of an ambiguous mystery, but just as bizarre and fun to piece together. The more plot-driven approach means we don’t get as much freedom to choose how we tackle each level, because most are tied to a specific character. The upside is that it also allows room for Hotline Miami 2 to present new situations, interesting characters, and unpredictable events that break away from the typical expectations of a sequel.
Hotline Miami has always been known for its mindless killing, but in Hotline Miami 2, the dozen playable characters are defined by their personal motivations. You can play as a soldier who kills because he’s in a warzone, which is a very different reason from the copycat killers who recreate the crimes of the original Hotline Miami character. This saves it from falling into gross repetition or suffering from style over substance. It also means that Hotline Miami 2 can explore new scenarios, thanks to character-specific goals.
One character, in a shocking twist for Hotline Miami, can actually get through a level without killing anybody (unless you manage to send him into a murderous rage). Knocking someone down and picking up their guns results in an animation of you rendering the weapons non-lethal. Playing through these levels is very close to the lethal ones, mechanically speaking, but it’s still an interesting example of a character’s personality changing things up.
While many levels are bound to a particular character, there are a few that do offer some choice, either variations of a mask or other accessories that grant different abilities. The carnage wreaked by the chainsaw- and gun-wielding brother-sister duo in Swan masks was especially fun to play, but I also enjoyed the sequences featuring characters who don’t even wear masks at all. In terms of story, a restraint like this makes sense and is a great way to get us closer to what’s happening and why, but in terms of gameplay, it can feel limiting. It’s a trade-off; a negotiation between some of Hotline Miami 2’s more arcade-like aspects and a more fully fleshed-out story that allows for the exploration of several different tones and moods.
Fortunately, an unlockable Hard Mode prevents some loss in replay value. This new difficulty mode mirrors level layouts, adds more enemies, and removes the ability to lock on – all excellent tweaks if you love a challenge. An early version of the Hotline Miami map editor is also included, which is already easy to use and is a great way for the community to expand the life of Hotline Miami 2.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

The game tries too hard to be like Resident Evil, namely the first one and the fourth one, but while Shinji's newest entry may not be his best, it is definitely not a bad game by any stretch. The atmosphere of the game is spot on and gives you a horror movie vibe, as for the black bars and the 30 FPS, it didn't bug me as much as it has bugged others, but there are ways to fix them if you have any issue with either of those. The camera was a bit of a nuisance at times in the game, not giving you a full view of the action and leading to some frustrating deaths where you get hit out of no where or when trying to look behind you leads to an unfortunate attack by an enemy trailing after you. The creature designs are well done, creepy and grotesque, but there isn't a TON of variation, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it does drag on you after a while after killing a Haunted enemy for the 500th time.
The story is hard to follow and very vague and mostly feels like a set up for a sequel and in some ways it is nonsensical. Not a terrible story, but with a little tweaking it could have been a lot more satisfying and interesting. The characters you meet are very emotionally dead and have no real personality, but despite this you sort of connect and begin to enjoy their presence despite their characterizations and plain bad AI, as they give you the comfort of companionship. Some chapters feel like they go on too long, but the game offers checkpoints and save points that won't frustrate you as they might in a game like Alien: Isolation. The game also took me a sizable amount of time to complete.
The game also feels like it trails from the whole survival horror aspect and begins to feel a bit cheap or more like an action game as hordes can suddenly be thrown at you when you least expect it to surprise you and lead to quick thinking and intense fighting or enemies will automatically know you are around a corner in a scripted fashion. These things aren't bad necessarily, but it gets annoying when you want to go a more conservative approach towards the game and see if through patience and smart planning you can overcome your enemies and obstacles which feels thrown out the door when these encounters occur, and frequently so throughout the game.
Overall, The Evil Within is a good game, even great at times, it isn't the scariest game out there, but its atmosphere helps build an overarching suspense as you journey the twisted version of Krimson City. It has shortcomings for sure, but if you are a fan of Shinji or survival horror, you may not be dazzled as you may have been with games like Resident Evil 4 or the original Resident Evil, but you'll still find a thrilling experience that keeps you coming back for more.

Sonic the Hedgehog 4: Episode 3 is what many people are calling Shinji Mikami's swan song; a culmination of everything he's learned over his career. Episode 3 features the most radical redesigns since Sonic Boom. They even have new names: Sonic is now known as Sebastian Castellanos, Tails is Joseph Oda, and Amy Rose is also in the game as Juli Kidman. Sonic also keeps talking about his dead wife, who I assume would be Sally Acorn, but I'm not sure she's ever pictured.
Episode 3 has plenty of running sequences, and even opens up with one against a chainsaw-wielding Knuckles the Echidna, but it also throws in aspects from other games, such as Shadow the Hedgehog. This may feature more guns than any other Sonic game I've ever encountered, and Sonic frequently has the option of either fighting enemies or trying to stealthily handle things. The ring system has been replaced by a health bar that can be replenished by using health kits. I'm not sure that it really coincides with the series' idea of speed, but it does address criticisms previous games have had wherein you win the game by holding right.
Dr. Robotnik has really gone out this time, and all of the gang has been trapped in some kind of bathtub mind trap machine. The main villain actually seems to be Shadow, renamed Ruvik, as he tries to find Christopher Thorndyke, who is now a white-haired fellow named Leslie. Those that aren't fans of Chris, don't worry too much, as Leslie is much more useful than his Sonic X counterpart; he can open doors and stuff sometimes.
Overall, I'd have to say Sonic the Hedgehog 4: Episode 3 is a sort of spiritual sequel to the Shadow the Hedgehog game. It's weird that they chose to follow that route instead of going for a more classic Sonic game, but I guess it's still better than episode 1.

This is of course a sequel to
, just a collection with all the DLC (think expansion packs, not just small additions though there are a few). I recommend picking the original up if you can handle dated graphics, the gold edition is available on Steam as well but that's not what this review is for.
Like the original game you play as the King of Ardania, who with your trusty comedic aide/advisor you build a fairly simplistic kingdom of a market, blacksmith, guardhouses and various guilds to train Heroes. Heroes are the key to this game as they are the characters that will fight your battles and you have the most
over. Influence is the best word because you cannot directly command them to do anything, just merely suggest they do some tasks by setting bounties (attack, explore, defend) as well as a fear flag which while it isn't a bountie in the true sense, they work on the same mechanics.
The campaign chronicles the journey to become the undisputed King of Ardania, as time progressed from the first king (from the first game) each king has tried to secure their place in history with grander feats of bravery. Lets just say the last king didn't do so well and you should watch the opening cinematic to see the bravery your forebearers had. The campaign is missioned based and you generally need to complete each mission to progress to the next ones, they generally unlock one or two missions at the same time and for replay value the tutorial is completely optional. Be warned, it does start simple but you do get a large difficulty spike later.
I recommend
Majesty game to anyone who is remotely interested in the premise of the game, this is a worthy sequel but the changes made sort of balance out the improvements made to make it equivalent to the original. The biggest difference from the original (for me) is most heroes will not respond to your bounties quickly unless you put some real money on them, not necessarily a bad thing because it does seem you get more gold income but it can be slightly annoying if you're used to the original. If you want this as an updated version of Majesty you won't be dissapointed, though you may find yourself wanting a bit more.
This is a trap, don't be fooled. It really isn't as good as the first one, as a matter of fact, it's worse.

I bought this game because I had seen two different Youtubers play it and I instantly fell in love with the graphics and the atmosphere.
I knew my computer wouldn't be able to run such high quality graphics (lol what a sad little 4 year old laptop) but I got it anyway--there actually is a nice menu and some quality controls, though they are a little limited and mostly allow control over shadow quality, bloom, texture quality, and so on. No LOD control, or anything, so I still can't play it because LOD is the main issue my laptop has running games. Or, rather, I can technically play the game but it runs at a low framerate. (I expected this when I bought it, so it doesn't bother me much.)
But that's fine! And once I have a better computer for games, I'll play it through and enjoy myself. :) For an early access game, the graphics are amazing. Actually, they'd remain great outside of early access. The game is, in my opinion, super beautiful.
And watching it, it's definitely spooky. I am a big fan of "walking simulators" and exploratory games that don't have a lot of skill-based puzzles or combat, so I know I'd enjoy this. The sound design is pretty good, too. The game, as a whole, has such a great atmosphere and I love the surrealist touches and the use of sort of... oil paint-based imagery. The melting doorways and pictures, I mean, with that sense of layering and texture that comes with thick oil points. (Layers... haha..... layers of paint)
Even though I can't run it on my computer, I think it's great, and I can't wait to really be able to play through it all. I also cannot wait to see how it will be when it's a completed game. I trust that the rest will be just as good as what there is now.

Layers of Fear is by far the best experience I've had with a "horror" game. It isn't too reliant on jump scares or creepy music or any one thing but rather manages to blend these elements into a delightfully delectable spooky smoothie. If you're not good about exploring the environments this game is not for you because through the exploration the story unfolds a lot more. I seldom found myself scared (until I got towards the end) but the game doesn't really go for that, I think the developers are focused more on an examination of the troubled human psyche and it shines in that respect, the atmosphere is hauntingly beautiful with a piano composition that returns throughout the game and the Victorian interior design. My only complaint is that the last section it lets you get to is in the middle of chapter 5. I understand that this is early access and not finished yet so it is excusable but it was a bit disappointing. This has been by far one of the best polished early access games I've played and I think that is due to the wonderful developers who are working well with the community they have accumulated and listening and acting accordingly. I have one last thing to say, pay attention to the writing on the walls. Thank you :D

The other reviewers have said Ty 4 is too easy. Well, if you only plan on running through the main game, from points a to  b, sure, it's pretty easy. But if you want to complete all the sidequests, it's quite challenging. And as there is no guide on here, so far, that is a bit of a tricky task.
The gameplay itself is pretty smooth. Controls are responsive. The game looks great, plays like a playstation 1 or 2 era platformer (as it should), and has a wonderful soundtrack. While it was short (I arrived at the final boss at what seemed to be out of the blue) the replay value is relatively high: there are plenty of sidequests and items to find, minigames, leaderboards, and an assortment of suits and rangs to buy, so really you can't go wrong with the price for this one.
I found Ty to be a relaxing game--only as hard as you want it to be. I would definitely recommend it to fans of the series or fans of the old Spyro and Crash titles, but it may not deliever as much to the Steam crowd who likes extremely difficult games that turn old conventions on their head. Still, I had a great time. Big thumbs up.

That's it. That's literally all this game has going for it: it bleeds Australia from every orifice like it's some continent-specific hemmorhagic fever, and it's a much, much worse Blade Kitten mechanically, probably because it's a port of a Windows Phone game. I've been a fan of the Deus Ex franchise since the box art for the original game caught my eye some 15 years ago.  I pushed through Invisible War and thoroughly enjoyed Human Revolution.  I knew The Fall was an iOS port and tried to take that into consideration, but that excuse can only stretch so far.
The tragedy of this game is that it's episodic--Steam makes no mention of this--and development has seemingly ceased on the next episode.  For an episodic game that original came out in July of 2013 to have no mention of when the next episode is due is unacceptable.  The developer's website for the game leads to a 404 and
has removed all mention of The Fall.  How Steam can sell a cancelled game is beyond me.
There's been no up-scaling of any of the 3D assets for the PC port at all.  The character models themselves, while angular, do not look terrible.  The buildings of Panama have a brutalist architecture vibe which fits well with the game's themes and low poly requirements.  The scenery pieces (e.g. rubbish bins, vending machines, fences) needed to be freshened up for a PC release.
Music and sound design in the game is perfect and takes many cues from Human Revolution.
The GUI is atrocious in it's overly large icons designed for a touch interface.   The worst aspect of it is your inventory; gone are the days of managing what you carry.  You can have every weapon and item in the game (though only assign a set amount to quick keys) magically appear in your hands just by clicking "buy" from the store.
There's an incredibly annoying glitch were being in cover while using a takedown will randomly result in your character being unable to move.  This happened about once an hour for me.  How this got past QA in what is a stealth title baffles me.

Keep in mind, this is a mobile [phone] port. That means the graphics aren't great, and there are a few control oddities here and there. That said, going into it knowing what it is, its serves its purpose well. A fun, minor, Deus Ex entry.

The game is really fun (in a group). Also I notice that the dev team really put a lot of love (sometimes misguided) into the game. I mean, we're talking about a game where you can look at a character in game and see what direction they are looking at based on how their head has turned, see what equipment they brought along down to all their trinkets, and each character has collision detection so if you all decided to stand on top of a chandelier for some reason you can push each other off.
It has some of the best melee combat in any game I've played bar the M&B / Chivalry style games. However, it's at least several factors more visceral than any of those games as there's so much meat and force behind your blows. When you wield that two handed axe and just cleave through hordes it feels UMPH! so good!
The voice acting and visual style is great too. I like the characters quite a bit and have grown quite attached to my dwarf ranger. My team and I love hearing our characters banter over the games and we'll often quip stuff like "shut up elf" or something like that as we hear them talk. Also, elves suck♥♥♥♥♥♥those stupid namby-pamby tree-hugging too-perfect cream-faced worms.
However, with all its pluses it has so many flaws. The loot system is dumb and too RNG with way too much grinding required. I mean, I'm a guy who likes Disgaea and Harvest Moon and all those kinda other worthless grinding games and even I think this has way too much useless grinding. It's because almost all the time your grind gives you completely garbage crap and you can't progress due to how you actually need useful stuff to do the higher difficulty levels. So you throw things on the forge and throw things in the altar but every single thing needs RNG and even the RNG rolls need RNG themselves. It's just so infuriating. Sure they added the new quest system to help alleviate some of that, and to its credit it does to a degree, but even that is more RNG for your RNG to RNG the RNG.
And the game can get repetitive. I mean, it's obvious that it will because it's a L4D-style game. But it has to be said. I've lost count how many millennia I've spent climbing the stairs to the Horn of Magnus. How many centuries of my immortal life have I used ♥♥♥♥ing defending two worthless wells (why are they even there? Who puts two wells next to each other?).
There are lots of other little quibbles too. Low playercount. Game is awful if you're alone. Bots are pants-on-head-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Difficulty just spikes all over the place. Lots of levels are just straight up mazes and are confusing. I don't actually like Skaven to begin with. Etc.
At the end of the day, I'd probably only recommend buying it to people who have a good group willing to play it. However, I do recommend trying it during a free weekend because there is quite a lot to see and it's worth seeing at least once. You gotta do the two handed massacre at some point. It's just so good.

I started off playing just for the TF2 awards, but I ended up really liking Super Monday Night Combat.
Super MNC is a fast, fun, competitive, and often difficult third-person shooter where you play team-versus-team in a handful of game modes. In ways, it's very similar to Team Fortress 2 and DOTA 2. That might sound strange, but once you try a round or two and get a feel for the play, which involves lots of wacky characters escorting waves of robots to the enemy goal (while blasting the opposing team's robots yourself), you'll see what I mean. Through quirky humor and loads of character upgrades, Super MNC does manage to carve out its own place, however.
I found Super MNC to be a bit hard to get into, and not just because other players seem to be godly at the game, but because the tutorial is confusing and doesn't really explain well how everything works. I suspect this is an area the developer had to skimp on, due to the game's odd (botched?) release, and subsequent issues. It's worth it to read up on things and put in some time though - the game is fun and rewarding once you figure everything out.
It's a shame the game's maker, Uber Entertainment, has seemingly abandoned this game, as it's still fun to play, and there still seems to be enough people around to find a game to play at just about any time of day. The core game is free to play, however, and there's lots of fun to be had without having to buy in, so it's hard not to recommend Super MNC, even in it's somewhat neglected state.

The Showdown Effect is a fun little brawling shoot em up that manages to include and parody tropes and cliches from various films in both it's aesthetic and, more impressively, it's mechanics.  Playing a match is like watching the action scene of several movies welded together in a hilarious chaotic mess full of snappy one liners and bullet riddled sets.
Each character has unique abilities, such as, I kid you not, the "out his own time Austrian kindergarden teacher with a stolen identity"  's ability to shield himself from damage, allowing him to stand tall in the face of oncoming gunfire whilst wielding massive machine guns!  and ... well, you get the idea.
Though simple, the game manages to incorporate a high skill cap in it's mechanics, guns will only hit the target, rather than the surroundings, when your cursor is over them, allowing for the various rolls, slides, jumps, flips and tackling dives to come into play, there is also a large variety of weapons, including various guns and melee weapons, each with their own strengths.
The levels are designed in a way reminiscent of a miniaturized metroid mania
with large rooms interconnected by passages ranging from corridors to airducts, with various environmental objects strewn about them
The developers decided to go with a large number skins over the same stats
allowing for a large amount of personalisation, which also stretches over to player customisation, which extends beyond hats and into chest and leg wear as well, allowing you to add to your character or create something entirely different, like a kung fu master in full plate.
All in all Showdown Effect is a solid game, combining elements from shooters and beat em ups into a fast paced, unique and entirely amusing experience
I'd recomend it to anyone who enjoys games like Super Mario Bro's or action flicks of any sort.
-Az

First of all, this is not a simulation.  The game calls itself a Fantasy Kingdom simulator, but that's wrong.  Majesty 2 largely lacks the elements of a sim game.  If you're looking for a sim, look elsewhere.
This is an RTS.  It applies the same basic principles of RTS games: build buildings, acquire resources, build troops, fight.
To the game's credit, though, its RTS mechanics are fairly unique for the genre.
Instead of commanding troops directly, like you would in Command and Conquer, Starcraft, and to a lesser extent Kohan, you control them by trying to incentivize them.
So if you want an enemy destroyed, you post a quest flag on the enemy's base, along with a reward.  Your "heroes" (they are called heroes but they are both as numerous and as functional as troops might be in other RTS games) will then gravitate towards the flag, at a pace depending on the size of the reward offered.
There are diffferent kinds of quests to use, and different heroes have different preferences for them.  A ranger hero, for example, prefers exploration quests (basically just removing fog of war from the map, like you might do with an Observer or Zergling in Starcraft), but will still do other quests (with priorities based on reward).
So some people might find that interesting.
Unfortunately, most of the game consists of taking out "lairs."  Lairs are creep spawning buildings littered across the map.  Destroying lairs is important, because it generates revenue (much like in Warcraft III, where destroying as many creeps as possible was crucial to the early game- here, though, the entire length of a game requires you to destroy lairs).  There are many lairs.  The monsters they spawn are relentless.  There is no grace period at the beginning of the game for you to build up your base and army.  It is both difficult and tedious to fend off the constant assaults, while also staging your own attacks against lairs and AI opponents.  Compounding this is the fact that as your base grows, indestructible lairs spawn amongst your buildings.  These are the sewers and cemetaries.  The sewers endlessly spawn hordes of mutant rats (and you will get more than one sewer), and the cemetary spawns constant undead.  These are complete weaklings, and can't be taken care of by the paltry automated defenses available to you.  So you have to devote heroes (and gold, because heroes pretty much never go anywhere without gold) to kill off waves of enemies coming from within your own base as well as without.  This is very tedious.
You also have to ensure your heroes' survival, because they need to level up and acquire better equipment.  If they don't, they won't be strong enough to survive.  That's some catch, this catch 22.
You can bring in heroes from previous scenarios (these are called Lords), but they are extremely expensive and you can only have a maximum of four.
There are no difficulty settings in Majesty 2.  If you're thinking "Well, I can just play on Easy Mode," tough luck,  There isn't one.  There's no downgrading the crapstorm.
The story and setting are silly.  The game is intended to be humorous, but I didn't laugh at a single joke.  Maybe it's better in the original Russian, maybe I'm just a joyless git.  Some people find the game hilarious, I'm not one of them.  A staple of the game's humor is the odd take on the fantasy setting, and frequent jabs at the trope.  Barbarians are all Conan-types, complete with Germanic accents.  You never see Dwarven women.  Nearly everything is at least slightly silly.  Might be amusing for some, but not for me.
For those of you still interested but concerned about the difficulty, there is a fan-made campaign with adjustable difficulty settings out there.  I haven't tried it, and can't speak to its quality.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 4 is a direct 4th title of the original series. Yes, the original three games back on the xbox and PS2 between 2002 and 2006! This was one of those games that was hidden somewhere in my childhood and was on the brink to be forgotten with time. Luckily though, Krome Studios were awrsome enough to make a 4th game and get it up on Steam!
The game is really sweet, albeit very short, and for a good reason. This was made in hopes that Krome can get funding big enough to help port the original three games to PC on Steam! If you would like to see them port the three masterpieces to PC and play them for yourself, you can help these guys by getting Ty 4, and perhaps even the artbook and soundtrack!
Now on to the actual review of the game itself.
The gameplay is very smooth and swift. It's a 2D platformer with a hefty focus on adventuring, completing objectives and mini-games, beating others to the high-score. The original cast is back, with characters across all three games featured and all of them playable(as costumes Ty can wear). The movement and actions Ty does are all familiar moves from the original games and bring a sense of nostalgia to those who have experienced em'.
The graphics are well made and nice! The game runs at a perfect matched fps depending on your monitor, giving it a nice and buttery smooth experience. The controls complement this nicely as well. The art-style itself matches the way it was in the previous titles(most notably the first in the series).
The sound and music is top-notch. Throwing the boomerangs, hitting the enemies or objects, it all sounds great(although throwing a power-shot can be a bit anticlimactic :P). The music is very reminiscent of the very memorable banjo-plucking tunes you hear from the first game and it follows the same style over here.
Gameplay time avarage at about 4-5 hours, depending on how much you speed through the game at first or look for collectibles/farm for opals. The replay value revolves around getting all the collectible items and rangs, additionally the costumes if that fancies your taste!
Now I'm gonna say this one more time. If you would like to experience the amazingness that is Ty 1-3 fully ported for the PC, support them by getting this game! Ty is one of the few mascots back in the PS2 era that still have the living licenses of today(compared to other titles). Help them help us gentlemen!
Thank you for reading my review and hope you get a clearer view at what's goin' on here!
~Melee

While on a lower budget, and after about nine years, the most significant video game character from my adolescence came back with a STRONG attitude. Yeah, there are still plenty of concerns about whether this game will be good or not, or the ponderers who will criticize Krome for breaking the style of the game. Technically, they already did that with that Game Boy Advance port for Bush Rescue (Ty 2), which, while I never played [that version] myself, I know it was a 2D game.
But again, I understand the questions and concerns. Yes, all the characters—and more—are here, with a bit more to their personalites and such. They have evolved, such as how Dennis the Tree Frog is no longer just obsesed with those crazy Thunder Eggs; as now he's his passion for them has gotten him into the study of them and other things like it (I'm so embarrassed that I forget what the actual word is). It's like all the characters have aged well during those nine years, so it feels like a GREAT reunion. Mount and Blade: Warband is one of the most classic and iconic games of the RPG genre. Unlike many other titles in the genre, MB:W does not hand an easy life to the player from the very start. The games makes you work for every single soilder in your army, and will not hesitate to take all of it away in one battle. But this is what makes this game unique. Once you finally put together a reputable fighting force, it is one of the most rewarding gaming expeirences you will ever encounter. Going from small skirmishes against 10 bandits to massive line battles against 250 highly trained knights adds such a unique contrast that really makes you feel rewarded for actually making it into the late game. But as I said, your entire army that you have amassed over the past 15 hours can be wiped out in a matter of minutes.
Another thing that turns a lot of people off of MB:W is the fact that MB is a fairly old game. And like many other old games, MB is not rich with beatiful enviroments and engaging character models. I know that when I first tried to play, this is exactly why I was turned off from this game. But where MB:W lacks in graphics, it makes up for in rich and rewarding gameplay. Sure it is not full of features that most AAA titles have today, but a major part of this game is how much of a badass it makes you feel like. Just imagine it. You are a Nordic man who is the son of a retired soilder. Your name is Fjordenhiemer and you are the strongest Nordic boy on this side of Fjordintown. Tragically you are thrown into the middle of a 6 faction conflict that spans across an entire continent and are forced to raise your own rag tad army to take the entire kingdom for yourself. Time and time again, you are beaten by packs of bandits, and time and tme again you find yourself having to scrap together another army. But once you take a foothold, and once you amass a force to be reckoned with, you stare those bandits in the eye and they run from your holding their panties as they try and not trip.
But seriously, if you are looking for a game that is extremley rewarding, makes you feel like a badass, and one that you can spend many hours on, MB:W is a very good choice. But BEWARE if you are easily bored, or find it frustrating that you actually have to work for once in your life and not be a lazy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Overall MB:W is a great choice for the more patient gamer who does not dwell on graphics and focuses more on core gameplay features, and is one that I would highly recomend to people who meet those requirments.

My goodness...don't be deceived by the (currently) mostly negative 30% positive reviews.  Most of these were written by people who played Human Revolution and compared it to that-- or who dinged it for not being sufficiently complete or couldn't get past the fact that it has mobile origins.  Of course it's not going to be as good, or as complex, or as satisfying.  But for the price point, it gave me the opportunity to return to the Deus Ex world for a little augmented stealth fun while I wait for Mankind Divided.  It's basically a simplified, possibly even dumbed-down Deus Ex.  But it still the same world and *feels* like Deus Ex.
So if you're looking for an HR experience, note the following differences:
- No jumping or lifting!  But oddly, you get used to it.  You stop wanting to jump on every crate or move it to access a secret area and get your explorer XP.
- No vendors.  You basically can buy anything anywhere just by going to a particular screen.  Yes, I'm sure that shows its mobile in-app purchase roots.  What this also means is no *selling*, so having to run around picking up and selling every gun for extra credits.
- Infinite inventory.  Packrats rejoice.  Coupled with "no vendors," you permanently have anything you pick up, unless you consume it.
- Bodies disappear after a few seconds.  No having to drag them around the corner and hope they don't mysteriously switch to dead during your Pacifist play-through.
- No boss fight!  Depending on what you thought of the boss fight (especially in the original DX:HR), you might consider this a good thing.
Some of these changes may seem jarring.  It really is a dumbed down Deus Ex: HR, but that doesn't mean it's not fun.  As long as you go in knowing this, you can actually enjoy the game.  Because here are some things that *are* like DX:HR:
- Play with stealth or with guns.
- Lethal and non-lethal takedowns.
- Hacking minigame almost the same
- Rummaging through trash looking for credits or beer.  ;-)
- Augs are a subset of DX:HR, but most are there.  Hacking, stealth, social enhancer, armor, cloak, aim stabilizer, etc.
- Art style...graphics looked fine to me, not as good as DX:HR of course but still "credible."
- Writing: main/side quests are in the same vein, as are NPC interactions and dialog trees.
- Trading cards and achievements.  Easier to 100% than HR.
So give it a shot if you're waiting for Mankind Divided's eventual deep discounts and price drops.

It pains me to say that Deus Ex: The Fall is so disappointing as to be nearly unplayable.  It's Human Revolution just... less.  It looks like a third party came in and just made every aspect of the game worse: buttons often have to be clicked multiple times to work, cover works differently, the inventory/shop systems are completely different, and even hacking, which was super minimalistic to begin with, is now quite a lot worse.
I put in two hours and I just can't keep going.  If you're hardcore enough to push through for the sake of the story, good on you, but I simply can't say that this game is *fun* in any way.  The graphics are similar to the original, but the voice acting is poor, and even the storyline is shoddy.  If you're looking for a good gaming experience, don't touch this with a ten-foot pole.

I don't see a valid reason not to get this game if you are a fan of survival horror.  Unlike many horror games, it is atomospheric, enthralling at times,  and consistently strives to avoid cliche jump scares.  The gameplay is satisfyingly challenging with ammo being scarce and the enemies taking a lot of lead to be put down.  Never during the game did I feel as if I never had enough ammo, however, although it did have a tendency to punish inaccuracy, ie. if you missed 5 shots you might not have enough ammo to kill an enemy, but, as most enemies are quite slow and the aiming system feels pretty natural, this is usually never a problem.  This game managed to scare me on more than one occasion, the enemies are essentially zombies, aim for the head, keep clicking, and they die.  There is a good mix of bosses that consistently managed to be tough enough to generally require a number of tries, the only exception being the final boss, which kinda changes the game into an on-rails shooter rather than the tense third-person game you spend 13-25 hrs playing through.  The gameplay is, as I've said, solid, but the story is generic and, while it is a fine enough story, it is nowhere near as good as the rest of the package, leaving me feeling let down at the end of the game but, at the same time, satisfied.  One of the most unfortunate parts of this game are the plethora of ways that you can instantly die; bosses, normal enemies, and traps littered throughout the world all have the ability to smite you in one shot (although this doesn't apply to all of the aforementioned or, indeed, to most of their move sets) which can lead to some silly deaths that can leave you kinda salty.  But, that just makes you try harder to get through the obstacles, and take every fight slowly, thoughtfully, not rushing through it like many other games. Thus the instant-deaths enhance the game and give it a deserved old-school feel with a modern look.  I believe that this game is a staple in the library of anybody looking for a good horror game that is just as much about the scares and atmosphere as it is about the actual gameplay, two categories where this game has few real rivals.
