VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED...only after you play Hotline Miami 1.
Hotline Miami is one of the most memorable Independent games in recent memory + actually ever developed - loaded with a thrilling soundtrack, old-school style of gameplay (with its diffuculty) + visuals; an absolutely insane story; action galore; & tons of violence. Hotline Miami 2 is the action-packed, top-down action-packed shooter/steatlh game, which follows this up with more of the same, for the most part - and then some.
HLM2 feels much bigger (took me around 21.2 hours in my first playthrough, BTW); much more sprawling; much more ambitious; & much more epic of an endeavor. While the original game was quite difficult at times, HLM2 definitely ups the ante here in difficulty much quicker & expands on the original game in many ways. In some ways, HLM2 is a much better game - but in some "ways", it's just not. Those few "ways" shouldn't stop fans from playing, though - Hotline Miami 2 is a great sequel.
HLM1 mostly had you play as Jacket & Biker, two characters who were getting mysterious phone calls from somebody to basically go off + kill certain people & groups. HLM2 serves as both a prequel + sequel to the game, as well as filling in much more explanation as to some of the things left vague, ambiguous and/or unexplained from the original. HLM2 doesn't tell these events in order + the story does jump around quite a bit, as you will be playing as numerous different characters from numerous different groups and/or agendas to give this whole crazy story a much-much larger picture.
HLM2 experiments here with often much bigger, wider, & more open-spaces for levels. Levels, in general, are much more varied in locations + the actual scenery in the game. You won't always be wearing a mask, as you will not always be a serial killer here. Sometimes, you might have a group of characters you're with. Instead of selecting a mask, you might be given the option to select from one of a few different members from a certain group; or go into a level with two members from a group. You might even have to in one level be forced to be all the different members in the group, at different parts of the level. You might not even be allowed to use weapons in a level. The game is constantly changing these things up, to keep things fresh + interesting.
This is just a start of the experimentation in HLM2. You might be forced with a certain weapon throughout the entire level + find ammo within the level. Some characters even have their own special skills (like rolling/dodging or you control two characters at one time where you have the option to shoot as one or melee as the other). HLM2 varies so much in its gameplay, style & scenery - that it's easily the much more ambitious title of the two games.
One-shot kills is the name of all the HLM games, as in if you take one shot, you're dead + you will have to redo the entire floor you're on. If you finish a floor, you can go to the next + death results in you restarting your current floor. Finish an act, and you move onto the next. You will be scored + graded on how many combos + quick kills you make, which will make the game replayable for those who want to replay the game and/or its levels/chapters.
I played with mostly the XBox Controller here, BTW - and it played absolutely fine, for the most part. Locking onto enemies worked fine + firing away was absolute bliss + often a rush in adrenaline, when you get into big shootouts. When playing stealthy - which you can + should do when necessary, BTW - it can be very satisfying to take enemies down strategically, thanks to the game's overhead/top-down viewpoint.
Not everything is paradise-like here, for the gameplay. Sometimes, locking on didn't lock onto the enemy I wanted + sometimes b/c levels are so massive & open in size + space, you might get killed from an enemy way off-screen cheaply & have to redo the entire floor. Frustration that can arise b/c of the game's difficulty can set in, but there's the other hand here that when finishing a level, especially some of the later levels, it can be extremely satisfying once you finally take care of business.
Just like the original game, the soundtrack here is absolutely amazing. Pulse-pounding electronic beats will fill your eardums + often get you into the action, with an overdosage of caffeine that can absolutely get your adrenaline going, perfectly going right along with the intense action. It is nothing but sonic + musical bliss here, with tracks from the likes of MOON, Megadrive, El Tigr3, Scattle, Perturbator, El Huervo & the even more extensive list of musicians that contribute to this tour de force of a soundtrack.
If HLM2 isn't enough on its own, with this game also having a Toolset + being on Steam Workshop - there is likely more HLM2 for the player to experience, even if its not from the game's developers, to actually keep them going. That, or one can build their own HLM2 levels, if they so desire.
Hotline Miami 2 is much more difficult - especially early on even + it really ramps up even more later on, too - and the story pretty much requires knowledge of the original, as this game serves as both a prequel + sequel to the original. If the player can get past these minor hurdles & actually sink their teeth into this game, they're in for much more ambitious sequel here + a real treat here, to say the very least.
Hotline Miami 2 is a great game, even despite its very few flaws. While it might not have the freshness + "new-ness" of the original here, it does try to out-do it in many ways. Not only that, but the amount of variety in scenery + gameplay is excellent, especially when compared to the original. It succeeds in some ways, doesn't in others. But, the failures here are absolutely very minor here - and that just shouldn't stop you from playing this game, if you've already played the original. Hotline Miami 2, even despite its very few flaws, is a very ambitious follow-up & succeeds in most fronts, making it a very easy to recommend to fans of the original masterpiece.

I can wholeheartedly recommend this game. As a fan of survival horror games, this game did not disappoint. The action approach this game takes is very reminiscent of Resident Evil without it impacting the immense tension and atmosphere this game brings upon the player. Everything about this game, mainly gameplay, is well executed minus a few hiccups here and there when walking.
The story, as many have complained about, is good but many expected the story line to be spoonfed to them in cut scenes. This game basically takes the perspective of Sebastion Castellanos and the player meaning you both have no idea what's going on. All that you know is that you need to do your job as a detective to figure out who's behind the foul play while protecting those alive. The story unfolds as you progress and pick up assortments of documents spread throughout the game. The only things the cutscenes provide in this game are the situations you will be facing at the moment and a little bit of story behind the antagonist. This is a story where most of the back story is being told by documents in the game rather than cutscenes.The DLC is also great in it's own right because it further explains what is actually going on while Sebastion is trying to fulfill his duty as a detective.
Overall the game has tons of elements to scare the player and keep them on their toes. With the Akumu difficulty, the tension only rises because one hit is an instant kill. If you're looking for a great survival horror experience much like Resident Evil 4, without all the ammo, then this what you should play. As a fan, this game did not disappoint!

The Evil Within is a horror videogame developed by Shinji Mikami, the man behind the famous Resident Evil series. The story of the game revolves around police detective Sebastian Castellanos and his two partners as they visit a mental hospital where a murder occurred only to find themselves trapped into an allucination world of some sort controlled by a very deranged mind, with no apparent way out.
While the Evil Within has been heavily advertised (especially by its director, Mikami) as a return to the survival horror formula, as it was to be expected by the creator of the Resident Evil series, the game is in fact an ACTION horror game: you are pretty much tasked to destroy the various monsters blocking your path and not elude or hide from them.
Unfortunately for the player, however, Sebastian, the playable character, is indeed a typical survival horror protagonist, with his limited movements, low health and scarce resources. This great gameplay design flaw really ruins the Evil Within as a whole and is the source of many, far too many frustrating moments through the whole experience. While frustration and a general sense of hoepelessness are core elements of a horror game, they are less acceptable when they are due to bad design choices. I'll try to list the most glaring issues below:
- The first and second chapters of the game introduces stealth mechanics to the player and stealth is indeed vital to overcome them both, regardless of the difficulty. Starting from as early as chapter three, however, stealth is tossed out completely from gameplay in favor of straight fights with the monsters. Generally speaking, stealth doesn't serve much of a purpose if enemies spawn directly onto your character and the bosses are straight combat-oriented. Also (but fittingly, in a way), no update whatsoever allows stealth to be more viable through the various chapters
- The game is very survival horror-ish when it comes to resource managements: as to say, you will find little resources through the various areas. While you can somehow deal with few healing items or grenades, the same cannot be said for the ammo of your weapons, which you will ALWAYS find yourself in need for more and more. While this issue can be somehow mitigated by specific updates (like headshots being more prone to outright kill enemies or a weapon being able to carry more bullets), correct ammo management becomes essential. Relaying on your melee attack also doesn't work as an ammo-saving strategy, since, on top of being remarkably weak and expose yourself to a counterattack, most of the time it'll just put enemies down just for them to stand up again moments later (something that can be negated with headshots or setting them on fire with matches)
- The checkpoints in this game are very incosistent, to say the least. In the first chapters you pretty much have to clear huge areas from enemies stealthly without any checkpoints in-between: so if you get spotted or killed it's back to square one for you (and you have to collect all goodies along the way again). Later in the game, checkpoints have a nasty habit to place themselves just before unskippable custscenes or just before a puzzle: in the latter's case if you die by an enemy attack just moments after solving the puzzle, you have to solve it again
- True to Japanese horror videogames fashion, this game spots very cheap deaths from time to time, as to say instances where, be it because you don't know what to do right off the bat or the game decides to just ambush you, you are going to die and have to restart from the last checkpoint. This becomes increasingly frustrating as the checkpoints start to appear far away between each other
- The game features a variety of traps that will blow up and inflict massive damage on you if you don't take steps to disarm them beforehead. The issue here is about you needing to place yourself in precise spots near the wire traps to disarm them (else, they will go boom) and the mines being extremely difficult to set off (and should you fail, the mine will explode). It's also worth mentioning that there are far too many instances where said traps are right behind a corner and undetectable till you run into them and turned to pieces (see above)
- The bosses in this game have a rather unique design and are more akin to puzzle bosses: instead of just shooting them to death, you have to figure out how to arm them first and cheese it for all it's worth. The issue here is that said weaknesses can be rather obscure at times and, more importantly, all the bosses are downright damage sponges, capable of eating several pounds of ammo each. Given the above mentioned general scarcity of it for the whole game, it's not uncommon to find yourself in the middle of a boss fight without anything else to throw at the boss. It also doesn't help that each boss have its own one-hit kill attack that can and WILL use with gay abandon, and youc character's control scheme makes dodging and evading painfully slow and unrelayable
All the issues I listed above can't be somehow mitigated choosing the right difficulty level. At the beginning of the game you can choose only between Casual (which is the easy difficulty setting, althought that isn't saying much, given it had to be nerfed after launch) and Survival (the normal difficulty). After beating the game, on top of bonus overpowered weapons and a sort of New Game +, you can play on Nightmare (hard setting) and AKUMU (one hit and your character dies).
Another glaring issue of the Evil Within is the way the main story goes along as you go deeper in the game. Several hours in the game there is really no plot to speak of: you know for a fact the characters are trapped into an illusionary world and there is a sociopathic killer pulling the strings, but the whole things just seems to keep going by itself and nothing more. The game does add more plot elements later on, but even in the end several questions and important plot points are left in the dark and the characters' interactions minimal.
To its credit, the Evil Within spots some incredible and genuinely unsettling environments and enemies design most of the time, althought they seem to both lose their consistency towards the final sequences, where the game decides to reuse several assets from previous levels and everything drags on far longer than it should. The final boss is also more atmospheric and bombastic than it is challenging and/or satisfying to beat and throws the game's general gameplay out of the window.
The Evil Within remains one of the most frustrating videogames I've ever played and a very poor attempt at mixing together action and stealth in a horror game, with results that do nothing but to frustrate the player every step of the way

I'm of two frame of minds about this game.
On one hand, I believe that it's a fun game with some interesting potential.
On the other hand I feel let down by the dating part of the game. I might have been misguided in this, but I was expecting something a bit more... like a Visual Novel or Dating Sim, where talking to the girls would branch out more or allow for different events to happen.
I would love to get to talk more with Jessie about her work, her situation with her daughter, maybe help her mend that relationship.
I'd also love to get to actually look at Aiko's web browser history, or get it down and dirty under her desk.
And what about taking part in a yoga class with Beli, or go on a space trip with Celeste?
The girls are interesting, but apart from filling a fact sheet and getting some glimpse about their personality and life, the whole talk part of the game feels somewhat shallow and something that could be improved greatly, hopefully in a sequel.
The match 3 part of the game is fun and somewhat addicting. I'm not a great match 3 player, mostly because it's not the kind of game I usually play, but the gifts part lends itself to some interesting choices to strategically take on the puzzles.
The art for the girls ended being better than I was expecting, especially for the naugthy event images. I wish there were more of those event images though, both nsfw and sfw since they do work in framing the background the girls a bit more.
All in all, even with some reservations about those parts that I think could have been done better/made them have a bit more depth, I believe this is a fun and nice enough game, definitely worth the asking price, especially with the release discount.

-Sequel to the Deus Ex novel, Icarus Effect
-Expands on Human Revolution's story
-True pacifist option
-High level of character customization
-Poor standalone game
-Port of a phone game (see Overall section)
-Poor storytelling
-Finnicky controls
So let's start with what this game is.  This game is a Deus Ex game made for mobile phone, to be used with a touch screen.  Thus, many of the more refined aspects of Human Revolution were dumbed down so that the game itself could work on a mobile phone.  This shows in the game's graphics, the controls (which show their touch-screen mindset), and most of all in how several of the abilities work.  And for a phone game, this was actually really great.  I played it there first, and thoroughly enjoyed myself.  It's one of the best games I've ever played on my phone.
So why don't I recommend it for computer?  Because Human Revolution is what this game was based off of.  This game took all of Human Revolution's gameplay and dumbed it down so that it would work on a phone.  And then, for some god-awful reason, they ported that dumbed down version made for phone back onto computer.  I just... I don't understand.  I literally have no idea.  In no reality does this strike me as a good idea, because people go in expecting Human Revolution 1.5 and they get a bad port of a dumbed down version of the game they wanted more of.  Of course people are disappointed.
Now that that's out of the way, here's a bit more about the game itself.
It follows the story of the novel Icarus Effect, and picks up shortly after the novel ends.  The game itself is fairly short with a plot that isn't all that fantastic - and nowhere near the level of Human Revolution - but it has one decent twist in it.  The characters are mostly forgettable, especially if you're coming in with no prior novel knowledge, but the game does a good job of recapping the relevant events of the novel at the beginning.  If you start the game thinking you'd love to know more about poor Anna Kelso, who has like zero scenes past the first section, read the novel.  She's much more interesting than Ben Saxon in my opinion.
Anyway, the game ends poorly, with the obvious intent of continuing the plot in a later sequel.  It's very unsatisfying.  The plot is barely serviceable and the characters are all thoroughly forgettable.  If you want more Deus Ex, this
give the Deus Ex experience, but not like you're probably hoping.  This game was an experiment to see if Deus Ex could work on a phone, and they really did the best they could with it.  And it's not that the game isn't fun on computer.  It just falls a little short on pretty much every front.
Not really worth it, unfortunately.  Maybe get it on a heavy discount, or just buy it for your phone.

Compared to other games in series, The Fall is no good. But for something that was made for smarphones - yes, you can enjoy it. Everybody know it doesn't met with so many nowadays standards. That doesn't matter. Also, maybe I'm alone, but I think it's nice to see good smartphone games avaible also on PC, so even people with nomrla cellphones would be able to enjoy it.
So, that's probably everything I can say is positive in Deus Ex: The Fall. I'm not fan of mobile gaming, it's good for little games, less for something more "serious". It's well made SMARTPHONE game, which surprised me few times. While I played The Fall, it reminded me with not so good fps games from many years ago. Yup, it was almost same. It's not a bad thing, a little nostalgia while playing something not so old. Sometimes AI acted foolish, boss fight (if you can call something at the end like this) felt like a joke and same goes for ending. What I really enjoyed were making takedowns, maybe because it's a Human Revolution things. Graphics, music, UI and many others are fine - for a SMARTPHONE game. It's rather decent if you would want to compare it to some PC games, even those 10+ years older than Deus Ex: The Fall.
If you want it, get it on sale, or maybe on your phone (if you have a powerful one), so you will have your little Deus Ex universe in your pocket. I can't truly recommend it or not, so I guess it leaves me no other option as mark it negative. There is no harm in giving it a chance but you need to be rather prepared to be dissapointed with this one.

This game...is very deceptive. On the surface it looks like a basic cookie-cutter Hack n' Slash that will take no time at all to win but it is actually quite extensive, rather difficult, and very addictive. It is (or used to be - the most recent update seems to have slowed things down a bit) one of the most fast-paced Roguelikes I have ever seen, and that is the rub because you need to play it in order to know what it is really like so I am not surprised that it doesn't get mentioned very often. I found this game because I wanted something cheap that I would only play every now and then but I keep coming back to it and that is saying something. Again, nothing spectacular or mind-blowing here, but Overture is definately a very underrated game. Roguelike fans will appreciate how intense and sometimes downright futile the levels can be and newcomers will enjoy how well Overture teaches them about the genre straight away. Nothing fancy; no elaborate opening or intricate plot. You just choose your character and go at it. The graphics are clear-cut (which I think is important in 2D games) and the soundtrack is fantastic. Simple mechanics and absorbing gameplay. Black Shell Games knows how to make a game that does nothing more than what it is supposed to do.
Two thumbs up.

TL:DR: If you like sidescrollers, or the ty universe as a whole, definitely pick it up! 8/10
Ty the Tasmanian Tiger 4 is the forth installment in the Ty series, this one departs from the original 3D platforming game to a more traditional 2D sidescroller. As a huge fan of the first three games, I was worried about whether this one would hold up, but it smashed my expectations thoroughly!
This game manages to take all of the features from the first 3 games and fit them into a sidescroller without feeling forced or out of place. Classic gameplay mechanics such as boomerang gliding and biting your way through flying eggs return as well as collectables such as koala children and thunder eggs! There's a whole host of unlockable boomerangs and costumes to pick up with your opals and every tassy tiger from the game is represented.
Whether you're a seasoned Ty veteran or a newcomer to the series, there's plenty of content in this game to enjoy the graphics and music are reminscent of the original trilogy and the gameplay mechanics are both easy to learn and satisfying to use, definitely pick this game up!

Beautiful game, bringing back an old classic! Reminds me a lot of the good ol' days, when I played games like Crash Bandicoot and Ty the Tasmanian Tiger on my good old Xbox. I really wasn't expecting any new TY game anymore. Ever. I didn't even know the original creators (Krome Studio) still existed. The old three Ty games were 3D platformers, but this one has the graphics and gameplay style of games like Rayman Origins and Rayman Legends, where Rayman also got a make-over from his classic 3D platform gameplay. I have to say, I love the graphics and music in this game, it's very beautiful and everything runs smoothly on 60FPS. Also there's a lot of content in this game, that will keep you busy for a pretty long time. There's 40 levels, but these are all very big and well developed levels, which takes you about 10 minutes to complete for each level, if you just rush through them. Then there's also hidden collectibles you can find scattered through every level. And on top of that there's also minigames hidden in each level like Time Attack or "Kill as many enemies as quickly as possible". There's also a currency in the game (opals) which you can exchange for new boomerangs with special powers, or a dozen of skins/characters to play with. This game will surely keep you busy for a while, and I can say it's definitely worth that 5-6 euros! I would even pay 15 or 20 for it. Now, let's hope for the return of the first three games on Steam, especially my favorite, the second one. :)

Steams recommend or not recommend system makes it a bit hard to review things..  If you aren't looking for a hard-as-balls (or even challenging) platformer because even I (terrible at platformers) had a fairly easy time with this game then you may like this game. If you're actually familiar with TY then the nostalgia may also be worth it. Besides that I can only really recommend this to younger gamers. For someone like me who has never even heard of the series this game neither has the plot nor the challenge required to keep me invested.
Options and controls: Fairly barebones menu, you have a couple basic options and the ability to change resolutions. There is no real way of adjusting the game quality besides a single button which lets you choose between the nicer looking default and a lower quality one for weak pcs but I honestly doubt that even most low end machines built anywhere in the last few years would need it. The game does offer full controller support and doesn't break like some other games do meaning that you can start off using the keyboard and mouse and switch to controller whenever you want unlike some games where if you accidentally click with the mouse and it registers you'd have to restart the entire game.
Gameplay: The game controls fairly well no matter what you use but this is one of the only platformers I'd recommend using the mouse and keyboard for because of 2 reasons. The first, less important one, is that using a controller doesn't offer any actual benefits because there's no sensitivity in the movement, the speed is the same whether it's a slight tilt of your joystick or if you have the joystick jammed all the way. The second being that the game is too damn easy on controller. Granted, even with the mouse and keyboard it's still pretty easy but at least you have to somewhat aim. With a controller the boomerangs are auto-aim meaning you just have to spam the crap out of the attack button for most of the game (with the exception of rare boss battles, immune enemies, and enemies that are too strong for early game boomerangs). Most enemies are very easy to kill and have a set aggro range where if you leave it they'll walk right back to where they were so you can kill most of them without ever having to take damage. The game is also very slow, there is no run or dash button (excluding a sonic flying dash-esque ability where you hit multiple targets to get somewhere) and the levels are straightforward making for little challenge. There's some very basic platforming for the most part on large maps with a lot of side paths but these paths are only really for collectibles which don't matter besides the eggs which are used to unlock the epilogue of the game. The rest is just for the purposes of 100% the game and are a bit tedious to get. As you have an unlimited amount of lives and the enemies that you've killed before dying remain dead there will rarely be times in the game where you have to put in much effort besides fetch-quests where the only challenge really comes from having to actually explore the map. Main quests that aren't the fetch type even have big yellow arrows telling you where to go.
Plot: As someone who has not played this series before the plot seems very weak. As I am not familiar with the characters it's hard to feel anything towards any of them and the nature of the plot resembles a childrens cartoon in that it's very all over the place from section to section without much of a larger coherent plot going on (there is one but it has barely any impact and rarely even comes up). Again, if I had played the series as a kid I would have probably enjoyed this much more. A bit of voice acting for the major points may have helped people new to the series to know the personalities of the characters.
Audio: The music is alright, kinda funky but the pacing of the music is strange. It's a bit too calm and relaxing for platforming and also sometimes speeds up for no reason for a single riff (whether or not you're in battle or just walking around). The sound effects are quite nice and would be much more satisfying if the game was more challenging and thus you'd hear some of the sounds (rewards, dying enemies, etc.) less.
Overall impressions: An okay game for me. It's not amazing but it's not a bad game either, there just isn't a real challenge even with manual aiming. Not recommended if you are unfamiliar with the series or want a challenge. Possibly recommend if you grew up with the series and want a nostalgia trip (after all it's quite cheap) or have a young gamer in the family who would like a colourful and easy platformer. There was also a crash at one point in my 3 hours playing the game but it was minor and no real data was lost besides the weapon I had just purchased.

I don't know about you, but I don't need my games to be super complicated. I mean, my favorite games are ones with plenty of depth and discovery to them but I'm also okay with a very simple loop if it's fun enough. Overture kinda toed the line with me for the first few minutes, and I thought I was ready to put it down after a few runs. And then, an hour and a dozen runs later, I realized it had more of a grip on me than I expected.
Overture is a 2D arena twin-stick shooter based around traditional fantasy classes and monsters duking it out. There's no story whatsoever here, you pick a class and you go kill things. Every floor is a big open square full of randomly-generated terrain, items, and monsters for you to traverse, collect, and murder respectively. Once you find and defeat a giant slime miniboss you are ushered to a boss arena, and if you are victorious you move on to the next floor to repeat your rampage.
The first thing you need to know about Overture is that it goes fast. Your character can cross the screen in an instant, your weapons are rapid-fire like machine guns, and enemies will swarm you with only a moment's notice. Barrels explode their contents over the entire screen in great chaotic flashes and the blood and corpses pile up until you can no longer recall what the floor looked like. While it has light RPG and roguelike elements this feels most like a bullet hell game, with you weaving in and out of enemy hordes as you eviscerate, perforate, or incinerate everything in sight.
You'll need to be pretty on point with your reflexes to keep from getting overwhelmed, because the many denizens of whatever this place is are relentless. Spiders, trolls, skeletons, necromancers, knights, and more fill the levels, and once you wake them up they will hunt you until you are dead. There's a huge variance in how fast they are and how they attack, with spiders being just as fast as you and melee-focused, while cyclopses are incredibly slow but hurl flurries of difficult to dodge projectiles. It's important not to get trapped and move intelligently, because you move faster in the direction you're firing so backpedaling or circle-strafing is not going to save you here.
Killing monsters earns you experience towards leveling up, making your basic attack and your special attack more potent and you a little sturdier. The equipment you find also helps with this, split into five slots and conveniently swapped with one button when the simple comparison prompt appears. Items pop out of bosses or racks or chests, and there are even NPC minions you can free from crates to battle for you. You'll also pick up health and mana vials to replenish your bars, and gold to unlock more of the game's two dozen classes.
This is where the game actually hooked me, because of the impressive variety to the classes. Each of the four archetypes (warrior, thief, mage, shaman) have half a dozen specific classes within them, like barbarians and templar for the warriors and rangers and bandits for the thieves. Everything about these classes, from their attacks to their speed to their stats, is wildly different. Whether it be the constant piercing attacks of the peltast or the endless deluge of poison bubbles from the witch, every time you start the game with a new character you'll be treated to an entirely new experience.
I haven't even finished unlocking all the classes, but I got hooked on trying out each one and pushing further and further with the ones I liked. The allure of new gameplay helped me overlook the small frustrations of getting mobbed or trapped by particularly difficult attack patterns. Overture is a tough game, though ultimately fair because if you find yourself taking too much damage or not doing enough, you can keep killing easier monsters and hunting loot until you feel more up to speed. It's not exactly the prettiest game either unless you miss old 8-bit RPGs, but the graphics keep things as clear as they can in the chaos. I doubt you'll be spending dozens of hours plowing through the hordes with new characters but the frantic fun is good enough to keep you busy for awhile, and that's all I really ask of games like this.

Overture is a neat little indie game. It is a brutul, fast-paced action-adventure rogue-like game in the likes of Realm of the Mad God or Binding of Isaac. It boasts 24 playable characters, all with unique attacks, and randomized levels with hundreds of enemies.
Visuals - The art of this game comes from Oryx Design Lab (very skilled reto-styled graphical artist. RotMG also uses sprites from here) and fits very nicely with the style of the game. The UI is efficient, but the gameplay can get quite messy with all the flying numbers and particles and projectiles. Overral, the visual aspect of this game is decent.
Audio - The sounds of this game give approproate feedback for your actions, and killing enemies is satisfying. This game features a great chiptune soundtrack (available as a DLC OST). The music is pretty good; nice electronic sounds and very catchy.
Gameplay - This game is a very challenging perma-death bullet hell. There are 10 levels, and dying sets you back to square one. You gain money to use on character upgrades, which are permanent. These upgrades are essential for making it far in this game. Getting far is something I've failed at, with my highest level reached being 4. The combat is polished and refined, and there is a great variety of randomized gear. The gameplay of this game is fun, though a tad bit punishing.

Note: I didn't review Deus Ex: Human Revolution & The Missing Link DLC due to having the original versions of the game instead of the Directors Cut edition, which contains both. But if you must, I rated Deus Ex: HR a 8.75/10 and Missing Link a 6/10.
Deus Ex: The Fall is a prequel to Deus Ex: Human Revolution and it takes place in 2027 following Deus Ex: Icarus Effect's ending. The protagonist is Anna Kelso and Ben Saxon and the antagonist is Jaron Namir. Namir is the leader of the Tyrants while Saxon used to work for them, but was betrayed by them. This game is a iOS port. Due to this, critics have hammered the game with very negative reviews.
Campaign: The campaign is solid. As normal with Deus Ex, this game's storyline was solid and fits into the world of Deus Ex. The story starts off bland at the beginning but becomes increasingly enjoyable as the game progresses, however the game is subject to an anti-climactic ending, ruining the atmosphere. There is a DLC tab in the game, so it seems as if there was meant to be more missions, but stopped after the poor reviews. Regarding Saxon, as the player, you can invest into him as the story progresses due to uncovering mysteries. In saying that, the story and investment of Saxon doesn't hit high gear, rather it progresses slowly passing average territory. The game is relatively short clocking in at 4.5 hours playtime. There was only three main missions in the game and five side quests, so wasn't in-depth by any means.
Gameplay and Graphics: The technical aspect of this game was awful. I will state a few notable issues. The game looks zoomed in due to the port despite being 1920x1080 resolution. The graphics are pretty bad compared to Human Revolution, especially for a 2013 game. There are noticeable frequent FPS drops, but are relatively minor drops. Actions and movement tend to be delayed, for example, moving against the wall. The gameplay also feels limited with no sprint button, no jump button, and only one kill/knockout animation. There are speech issues with dialogue between characters. Basically, there are few good things about the gameplay and graphics, but are plagued by numerous issues, glitches, and bugs.
Positives: Of course, the negatives outweigh the positives. However, the campaign and storyline was solid. I overly liked the revamped inventory system. Comparing to HR, now you can buy weapons, upgrade those weapons, buy grenades, etc. essentially you can use your credits more frequently. Despite liking it, buying weapons is unnecessary due to making the game easier. Another positive is the usefulness of hacking. In Human revolution, if you hacked a computer, there would be relevant information for the player that the game would not find useful. Whereas in The Fall, if you hacked a computer, it would contain very useful information to help in the game.
Overall: The game had its moments in the campaign and through the few positives I just mentioned, but frankly, the game is a bad iOS port. I bought it for $2.49 on sale and I wouldn't recommend it, especially at full price. 3/10.

VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED...only after you play Hotline Miami 1.
Hotline Miami is one of the most memorable Independent games in recent memory + actually ever developed - loaded with a thrilling soundtrack, old-school style of gameplay (with its diffuculty) + visuals; an absolutely insane story; action galore; & tons of violence. Hotline Miami 2 is the action-packed, top-down action-packed shooter/steatlh game, which follows this up with more of the same, for the most part - and then some.
HLM2 feels much bigger (took me around 21.2 hours in my first playthrough, BTW); much more sprawling; much more ambitious; & much more epic of an endeavor. While the original game was quite difficult at times, HLM2 definitely ups the ante here in difficulty much quicker & expands on the original game in many ways. In some ways, HLM2 is a much better game - but in some "ways", it's just not. Those few "ways" shouldn't stop fans from playing, though - Hotline Miami 2 is a great sequel.
HLM1 mostly had you play as Jacket & Biker, two characters who were getting mysterious phone calls from somebody to basically go off + kill certain people & groups. HLM2 serves as both a prequel + sequel to the game, as well as filling in much more explanation as to some of the things left vague, ambiguous and/or unexplained from the original. HLM2 doesn't tell these events in order + the story does jump around quite a bit, as you will be playing as numerous different characters from numerous different groups and/or agendas to give this whole crazy story a much-much larger picture.
HLM2 experiments here with often much bigger, wider, & more open-spaces for levels. Levels, in general, are much more varied in locations + the actual scenery in the game. You won't always be wearing a mask, as you will not always be a serial killer here. Sometimes, you might have a group of characters you're with. Instead of selecting a mask, you might be given the option to select from one of a few different members from a certain group; or go into a level with two members from a group. You might even have to in one level be forced to be all the different members in the group, at different parts of the level. You might not even be allowed to use weapons in a level. The game is constantly changing these things up, to keep things fresh + interesting.
This is just a start of the experimentation in HLM2. You might be forced with a certain weapon throughout the entire level + find ammo within the level. Some characters even have their own special skills (like rolling/dodging or you control two characters at one time where you have the option to shoot as one or melee as the other). HLM2 varies so much in its gameplay, style & scenery - that it's easily the much more ambitious title of the two games.
One-shot kills is the name of all the HLM games, as in if you take one shot, you're dead + you will have to redo the entire floor you're on. If you finish a floor, you can go to the next + death results in you restarting your current floor. Finish an act, and you move onto the next. You will be scored + graded on how many combos + quick kills you make, which will make the game replayable for those who want to replay the game and/or its levels/chapters.
I played with mostly the XBox Controller here, BTW - and it played absolutely fine, for the most part. Locking onto enemies worked fine + firing away was absolute bliss + often a rush in adrenaline, when you get into big shootouts. When playing stealthy - which you can + should do when necessary, BTW - it can be very satisfying to take enemies down strategically, thanks to the game's overhead/top-down viewpoint.
Not everything is paradise-like here, for the gameplay. Sometimes, locking on didn't lock onto the enemy I wanted + sometimes b/c levels are so massive & open in size + space, you might get killed from an enemy way off-screen cheaply & have to redo the entire floor. Frustration that can arise b/c of the game's difficulty can set in, but there's the other hand here that when finishing a level, especially some of the later levels, it can be extremely satisfying once you finally take care of business.
Just like the original game, the soundtrack here is absolutely amazing. Pulse-pounding electronic beats will fill your eardums + often get you into the action, with an overdosage of caffeine that can absolutely get your adrenaline going, perfectly going right along with the intense action. It is nothing but sonic + musical bliss here, with tracks from the likes of MOON, Megadrive, El Tigr3, Scattle, Perturbator, El Huervo & the even more extensive list of musicians that contribute to this tour de force of a soundtrack.
If HLM2 isn't enough on its own, with this game also having a Toolset + being on Steam Workshop - there is likely more HLM2 for the player to experience, even if its not from the game's developers, to actually keep them going. That, or one can build their own HLM2 levels, if they so desire.
Hotline Miami 2 is much more difficult - especially early on even + it really ramps up even more later on, too - and the story pretty much requires knowledge of the original, as this game serves as both a prequel + sequel to the original. If the player can get past these minor hurdles & actually sink their teeth into this game, they're in for much more ambitious sequel here + a real treat here, to say the very least.
Hotline Miami 2 is a great game, even despite its very few flaws. While it might not have the freshness + "new-ness" of the original here, it does try to out-do it in many ways. Not only that, but the amount of variety in scenery + gameplay is excellent, especially when compared to the original. It succeeds in some ways, doesn't in others. But, the failures here are absolutely very minor here - and that just shouldn't stop you from playing this game, if you've already played the original. Hotline Miami 2, even despite its very few flaws, is a very ambitious follow-up & succeeds in most fronts, making it a very easy to recommend to fans of the original masterpiece.

In all fairness this IS a good game, in story and gameplay... its only the frustrating game level designs, and plot elments that hold it back.  I would give it a "Mixed" but that is not an option.  I wont get into the gameplay differences between HM1 and HM2 which makes this game much more frustrating, dealing with more blind corners, windows, and long hallways so get used to getting shot from enemies you cant see on the map, but its the story and how much effort the devs put in to give the audience what it DIDNT want.  That is where I draw the line.
*SPOILERS*
They know we wanted to see Jacket return as a playable character, they teased us with him showing up in the background in several cutscenes, throughout the game.  You never do, he's a big FU.  And worst of all, they know "The Fans" are the most interesting characters, the most visually flashy, and play almost completely different from the rest of the game!  You not only are they unique and interesting individually, but they come as a team letting you pick between them for each mission, that is after you unlock them one by one... you spend a total of 1 mission where you have all 4 unlocked on your first playthrough before they are taken away from you.  Not only are they no longer available to play as, but they are gone early on, less then halfway through the game, forcing you to try and care about Manny Pardo, the journalist and Richter to carry the "story" through its final leg.  Each of these characters play very similiar to one another, the only dramatic difference between the three is that the journalist doesnt like killing which gives him a unique non lethal approach unless you chose otherwise.  But this just forces you to play a game, where your favorite parts were gone before you got a chance to truly enjoy them, and now you have to play hours and hours of frustrating levels with characters that are less interesting both plot and gameplay mechanics wise (Until The Son levels which are indeed amazing, so the finale does end with a bang)  Which brings us to the ending cutscene.  They know we would want a sequel... they ended the game with that all but impossible, so the world wont even live on.
So this all begs the question, why did they do this?  Why did they make their game less satisfying in both plot, style AND gameplay?  It seems like its purely to be unexpected.  That everyone would EXPECT them to make a game the people who bought it wanted, so they did the opposite to be... creative?  I dont find that to be a great reason, and I personally stopped caring about the plot half way through the game, only to pick back up towards the end, then saw the world and lore I truly admired go up in flames.  It all felt insulting, and since there's no "Mixed" Ill give it a thumbs down.

Hotline Miami 2 is now a much loved game, and one that often left disgruntaled and confused players in it's midst, at first. However, when people came together, and pasted together the events of the game, the game revealed a much deeper quality orginally glazed over, like it's precursor, and proved it's worth as a sequel to one of the best indie games of all time.
Hotline Miami 2 starts with a twisted interpritation of the first games events, in which you start the game playing as an actor of Jacket in a slasher flick made just 3 years after the events. Things quickly fall apart though, and soon you're jumping through time, playing as a menagerie of disgruntaled and flawed individuals, all sharing some connection to the animalistic violence that underlies the story like Miami's beating heart. A angry racist. A unemployed man taking care of his mother. A oppritunistic journalist. A tired hitman. A corrupt detective. A thoughtful spec-ops soldier. A livid mob boss. Four disillusioned war vets. And each with something they want, very, very, badly. Hotline Miami 2 shows us what lit the flame of Jacket's rage, and how it spread, and presents us with a subtle commentary on violence itself. But, as before, no consideration is made for your comfort, your understanding. Hotline Miami is what it is, and it is your job to draw your own lines to understand what it all means.
Hotline Miami 2 has some considerable differences from the original which you will recognize quickly. Dennation has decided to include detailed and high quallity pixel art, which is, as a pixel artist myself, absolutely exeptional in it's quallity, and looks great. However, some may rightly be alienated by the shift from the first game's minimalizim and strict adherance to 80's aesthetic to a more detailed approach. That said, it's still recognizibly Hotline, and should absolutely not deter you, because the game is more like the first then it initially appears. Controls are MUCH smoother and less is up to chance now. The music is exeptional too, though I miss M.O.O.N, Pertubator and the others did a great job.
On a final note, I was initially concerned with the game's difficulty prior to release, as I felt like I was pretty good at the first and no longer found it very difficult. The second game had absolutely no problems with this and in fact left me feeling much the same as I did at the start of the first game. It should be played AFTER the first and is a continuation of it's difficulty. People also say it feels much more gun based then the first. It does have levels based around the charecther abillities, and Pardo and Nicolas are certainly pretty gun based, but there is much more room for melee then it first feels like, and in fact, melee generally will get you farther as always. Not to mention that the charecters like Corey and Alex are melee-based and really, its pretty ballanced in the end. So if you enjoyed the first game, buy the second. It answers your questions and is a worthy sequel.

Through constructing buildings in your fantasy city, you attract adventurers. Warriors, rogues, clerics, mages, etc. They earn gold by completing quests you give them, like attacking monsters and clearing lairs. In turn they spend that gold in your buildings, buying items such as healing potions and weapon/armour upgrades, which in turn gives you gold to buy or upgrade new buildings. It's a unique concept for an RTS. The game is a little dated now and it doesn't quite realize it's full potential, which is a shame. I'd love to see Blizzard make a version of Majesty.

Niche is a very unique game. It is an adorable turn-based strategy game where you play as a tribe of squirrel-esque animals gathering food, avoiding or defending against predators, and breeding to evolve more adapted creatures. Difficulty is controlled by the player based on which habitats you choose to migrate your creatures to from the relatively safe meadows to mountain tops full of predators waiting to eat those who avoid freezing to death.
Where Niche really shines in the "realistic" genetics system which controls the abilities your animals have to help them survive - such as the ability to crack open shellfish or dig for food - and includes various genetic defects and penalties for inbreeding. Combined with the migration system which limits you to a small number of creatures migrating to each new world it forces you to plan ahead. In addition, many abilities are mutually exclusive forcing you to choose which niche your particular creature is going to fill.
One draw-back at the point of writing is that some abilities/resources are unbalanced. I've managed many successful cautious berry-picking species and some omnivorous coastal creatures but I've yet to make fishing be worth the effort.
Overall Niche is an enjoyable relaxed game, with adorable art and sound effects. However, if you are looking for exciting action or deep story-telling this is not the game for you. (8/10)

This game is one of the most addictive I've played in over a decade. I've yet to finish a game, but that's because I keep bouncing between the myriad of great mods and I have a problem with not finishing games. First/third person combat feels smooth and responsive in either mode and the game (having no voice acting or real story) is very open-ended. Whether you start as a poor dirt-farmer's daughter or the squire son of a veteran warrior, you can become a King's Lord/Lady in command of an army and castles, help a dethroned Prince or Princess reclaim their stolen land, or just take over the world yourself and make all your friends lords.
Warband takes place in a fictional continent (sub-continent?) stretching from the deserts, mountains and steppes in the south to the plains, tundra, and Nordic riverlands in the north. The Nords, led by King Ragnar have the best infantry, but with little archers and no cavalry. The Swadians are your basic medieval French/English/Holy Roman Empire sort; heavy knights and men-at-arms. The Veigirs to the east of the Nords in the north are, by all accounts based on the medieval Rus. Funny hats but heavy, HEAVY armor and hammers. In the steppes you have the the Kerghit Kahnate and Sarranid Sultinate, who represent the Kahns and middle-eastern sultanates respectively. To their east are the Rhodoks in the mountains, with their polearms and crossbows. Can't take  a castle worth♥♥♥♥♥♥but can absolutely keep you from taking one of theirs.
Jesus Christ the mods people make for this game. I will mention and give a brief description of three here.
1) Brytenwalda: sets the game to a historically accurate 8th century Britain, divided under the numerous kingdoms. Massive overhauls to the map, combat, party system, diplomacy, literally everything is different. These guys did such a good job that they were hired to make the Viking Conquest DLC (which was met with mixed feelings upon release, but I can personally vouch for Bytenwalda).
2) Gekokujo: Set in 17th century Japan, the overhaul adds matchlock guns and most of the smaller mods that are in most overhaul mods for Warband; namely Diplomacy, Freelancer (join lords' armies as a soldier for a weekly wage), among many others.
3) Floris Expanded Mod Pack: Along with the aforementioned Diplomacy and Freelancer mods, this pack boasts great graphical improvements and a complete (optional) reworking of the in-game troops. I highly recommend it if you're looking to improve the game more than completely change it.
4) L'aigle: While currently in alpha and slow going in development, it takes that game to the Napoleonic Era in singleplayer (the Napoleon DLC being multiplayer only) with great line infantry controls and units with a wide variety of factions and weapons.
Now for the ugly (nothing bad about this game, jut a little ugly). This game is not pretty without mods, but the game is so modable, and has so many mods that, on top of massive overhauls or just gameplay improvements and enhancements, improve the visual quality, it's not even an issue. And modding the game is as easy as could be. Drop a file in a folder, launch the game, sellect the "module", play.

Very few games have left me with as many conflicted feeling as The Evil Within. It swings from being a genuinely scary game to feeling like a decent-if-forgettable RE4/5 clone and back again. There are hurdles to jump over in understanding how the gameplay works before you can get into it and then the game never leverages the strengths of that system. There's a creepy element of psychological torment that pervades the game and story, but when it pokes it's  head through the story is, quite frankly, kinda stupid.
The gameplay takes the Resident Evil 4 route, but where Leon Kennedy was a badass and thoroughly capable of handling any situation Sebastian Castellanos is a wuss who's not particularly great with a weapon and whose physical attacks are hit an enemy like a weak gust of wind. You'll quickly find that open combat is a terrible option as enemies are tough and even headshots that blast away large portions of their skull only seem to moderately annoy them. It's easy to burn half your ammo on one enemy. While it's not particularly scary the early sections are like a playground where you slowly stalk enemies and carefully choose your point of attack.
Then you find out the game has an upgrade system. Suddenly you're given a lot of options for improving you physical prowess and the usefullness of your weapons (of which you'll get a small arsenal of) The game begins to force you into open combat more often and it become obvious that ammo conservation isn't important because the game is regulating how much ammo is dropped by enemies and from crates. I just blasted my way through the stealth sections at the end because they're just set in boring corridors that are a pain to navigate carefully though and there's not particular penalty for going rambo through it.
What really saves the game is the middle third of the game which slows down the pace and uses the game's atmoshpere to good effect. You'll traverse torture chambers, crypts, a deserted mansion, and caverns and that pacing, sound design, and enemies just feel right. I constantly felt on the edge of my seat waiting for something horrible to happen.
Then you hit the city and the game loses momentum through to the end. It lacks both the atmosphere of the middle third and the well designed stealth sections of the first third. You're too well equipped and upgraded for the action sequences to feel like a desperate fight for your life or the stealth sections to feel imposing. The big bosses are silly rather than imposing. It's not bad, but it's not the type of horror game that The Evil Within should have been.
If you're a fan of horror games it's worth it to pick up on a sale because when it works The Evil Within works really well and when it fails it's never bad, it's just disappointing. Despite everything I still liked The Evil Within even if I wanted it to be so much more than it was.
Some further thoughts if you're still reading.
- The game is very linear and features little exploration. The idea was to constantly warp you around and keep your bearings off, but I don't think it worked that well although I respect the theory behind it. Interestingly one of the best and creepiest sections is set in a mansion that you have to explore.
- Has a Dark Souls thing going on graphically where most of the architecture of the buildings looks great, but any thing natural looks like doo-doo. There's a part where you walk through a field of sunflowers and the texture on the ground looks like it was ripped from an N64 game.
- Jennifer Carpenter (who played Debra on Dexter) gives one of the most bored and unenthusiastic voice acting performances you'll ever hear in a game. Fortunately she only gets a handful of lines.
- I really like what they did with the RE style save room by making you question the safety that it provides you.
- Textures are constantly loading slowly. Scenes cut to aother angle of things that don't have textures loaded. At one point a gate drops revealing a boss monster whose textures pop onto him a second later.
- (SPOILER ALERT) If you want to be overly analytical about things you could certainly draw parallels between Ruvik's story and the nature of game development when surrounded by corporate culture. How he both has control of his creation taken away from him while simultaneously being trapped by it. As a game developer Shinjo Mikami is both typecast as "The Horror Guy" as well as having a lack of ownership over Resident Evil and being forced to watch it taken in directions he may never have intended. Ultimately, as this is Mikami's last game in the Director's seat (allegedly) Ruvik is ultimately looking for escape (and to try and scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Sebastian/The Player along the way.
But that may just be me looking too deeply into things.

The game is decent fun, if you would like a Dark Souls/Left 4 Dead merging.  The controls share some similarities to Dark Souls, with dodging, blocking, heavy and light attacks, timing things correctly, reacting to your opponents, etc.  They are simplified to fit a FPS format, with the exclusion of parrying.
The game's loot system is based on dice rolls, so you're hoping on luck to get items.  However, you can craft items (still luck based), upgrade items, and complete daily missions to acquire guaranteed loot (my preferred method).  This can be frustrating, especially for DLC weapons, which cannot be acquired any other way than rolling the dice at the end of a mission.  I'm still lacking DLC weapons months after purchase, so I would not recommend getting the DLC.
The game is quite challenging.  It has about 20 maps (including 8 DLC maps).  There are about 50 weapons spread out between 5 characters.  The rats are modeled very much like L4D's zombies, with a tank, specials, and trash rats.  The game does have events during holidays, with free gear handed out.  For example, an item is given out freely upon logging in each day during the winter holidays (it can be very rare loot).
Overall, the game has moved in an upward direction over time, and I think the devs mean well.  Sometimes we need to be vocal and steer them in the right direction (currently working on DLC weapons to be included on purchase).  This game is getting better, so it's worth keeping an eye on, if you're interested.

This is an Early Access game.  Keeping that in mind, this game has a LOT of potential, but is still missing a really big part of what makes survival horrors so terrifying - a real threat.
Before I go into that, I want to highlight some things I thought were extremely well done:  You start off in a pretty snazzy home that eventually devolves into a horrible nightmare mansion.  The graphics are pretty and make some killer terror sequences.  The story is revealed to you (well, mostly, since the game is still in development) through newspaper clippings, drawings on walls, audio flashbacks, and journal entries.
My first impression was that this was a typical horror scenario - man has great life, man loses great life, man goes crazy and does terrible things.  I'm pretty over that storyline, BUT I was pleased to discover that this isn't exactly the case and not everything is as it seems, which was a huge relief.  The sound quality is great, the music is haunting, and, like I said before, there are some very well done terror sequences.
However, there was a lack of real fear when I played that can be attributed to a complete absence of any real threat.  The game is very linear - and as many spooky scares as there were, knowing that they wouldn't actually HURT me took a lot of the power away.  There was a moment when I thought I had died (a very PT moment) but I woke up somewhere else and carried on as though that moment was all according to plan.
Actual fear and dread is a really important part of a survival horro (duh), which I pretty much just said this game lacks, but I still recommend giving this game a shot because this is NOT FINISHED!  The potential for this to be a fantastic, scary game is very high and I am looking forward to seeing what the developers do next and finishing up the story.

The good: As a fan of the Deus Ex universe, I enjoyed having more story content. There are some new and some returning characters to get to know. The bad: This is a port from mobile platforms, and the controls were poorly done IMO. They just seem very finicky and timing for quick movements is difficult. The game was intended to be the first in a series, but the others have not yet been made, so the ending leaves you hanging.
General info: The player character, Ben Saxon, was introduced to the Deus Ex universe in the companion novel The Icarus Effect, which takes place just prior to and during Human Revolution. If you enjoy the lore of Deus Ex, this is a nice little addition with some more info on one of the Tyrants. The game gets a lot of hate, but I think most of that is due to the poor PC port. If you know what to expect going in, I think it can be enjoyable for fans of the series.
Overall: Would recommend it to those who are already Deus Ex fans; if you've never played a Deus Ex game before, start with the original Deus Ex or Human Revolution first.

While Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number adds a great deal of depth to the storyline of the franchise, its combat and playability are decidedly lacking.  Wrong Number definitely believes in quantity over quality.  The storyline will easily take double the amount of hours to complete that of the first installment and truly does add some interesting characters and plot developments.  It's a shame they are tied to such poor gameplay and level design.
The controls are finicky and and designed for the small levels with relatively few enemies seen in the first installment.  Wrong Number features much larger levels which cripple the player by limiting the scope of view.  The number of enemies demands that one be able to switch targets in rapid succession but with the controls being mostly unchanged since Hotline Miami 1, it's always a crapshoot trying to lock on to a specific enemy closing in on you among several.
I enjoyed many of the new play mechanics involved with each character but some of them are more gimmicky than useful.  The ability to combat roll is offered with such little frequency that most players won't have the chance to become proficient with it and the ability to dual wield is a joke.   On the other hand, playing as a character who is limited to blunt weapons and nonlethal means of dispatching enemies adds an edge to an otherwise bland experience.  Unfortunately, Wrong Number never manages to achieve the same intensity of the first installment.
Fans of Hotline Miami will be dissapointed to find that the frantic, reckless combat has been supplanted by much more strategic and stealthy mechanics.  Given some of the characters' motives, this does make sense in a few levels but it often turns into a game of trying to figure out a way to exploit the nature of enemies rather than truly engaging them.  This is especially true when playing as Alex and Ash with combined melee and ranged attacks.  Their combat style has potential to be frantic and relentless but the large levels with multiple open spaces and firearm wielding enemies put an end to any hopes of an intense experience.
Many of the levels will become frustrating after a time and players will start to look for ways to trick the system and progress tediously through each level.  Many levels even demand techniques like this.  I'm not sure if this was intentional or if dreams of a bigger badder sequel got in the way of practicality. Overall, Hotline Miami 2 feels like a hyper-violent puzzle game with some glaring loopholes.

HOTLINE MIAMI was like lightning in a bottle. Vicious fast-paced gameplay, brutally low room for error, a striking visual style, and a fantastic synthwave soundtrack. HOTLINE MIAMI 2 promised to bring back what you loved and more - bigger levels, badder weapons, more variety, better music... and did it deliver?
No.
What is so frustrating about HOTLINE MIAMI 2 is that it feels so close to a good game but is fundamentally held back by infuriating design decisions. Frustration and reloading (again and again) was one of the hallmarks of the original HOTLINE MIAMI, but 2 pushes that frustration into feeling like it wasn't your bad move but rather a cheap ineviatbility that you couldn't have forseen.
Remember
in the original game, when there were a bunch of small, windowed rooms surrounded by hallways? HOTLINE MIAMI 2 is basically that but for the whole game. There is a much bigger emphasis on gunplay, with long hallways, big empty rooms, and sprawling levels that even a shift-look can't entirely reveal. The upshot of this is that you will very, very often be shot by an enemy from offscreen and/or through two windows that you weren't even aware was there.
"Recklessness is rewarded" was the mantra from HOTLINE MIAMI. Thinking by the seat of your pants as you strung combo from room to room was often the best way to go, it all clicked as you suddenly started throwing bats and picking up shotguns to blaze through a level and only afterwards realizing how it all worked. HOTLINE MIAMI 2 forces you to slow down as peek-a-boo becomes the name of the game.
For instance, remember the Tony mask (killing punches)? It returns, but with a twist: You can
kill with your fists and cannot pick up guns or weapons. Seems like an interesting twist, but instead leaves you feeling like a fool as you see a big room with three gunmen inside and no easy way to get them. So you inevitably end up cheating the AI - popping open the door and ducking out, or running past the open door, until one of them runs at you and you punch them. Rinse and repeat. No longer a tense, bloody fight, it's a slow tedious way of gaming the system that feels at once cheap and yet the only way to succeed.
Speaking of gimmicks...
Jacket in HOTLINE MIAMI had a basic setup (he could use everything) but the different collectible masks would give him a little boost in each area - longer combos, more ammo, further reach, etc. HOTLINE MIAMI 2 takes a different tack, instead you often are forced to switch between different characters with their own built-in twists and limits - a pacifist who dislikes guns, an army man who will only use his issued equipment, and so forth. But in the end these end up feeling frustratingly limiting rather than encouraging alternate playstyles. Tony (as mentioned above) leaves you feeling gimped as much as he makes you feel powerful. Switching between a knife and a gun (army man) is nice, but when you run out of ammo and encounter an enemy that must be killed by a gun - and you can't pick up any of the guns lying around nearby - you feel cheated. Some tricks are of dubious use - I've yet to find a use for Corey's rolling dodge. Others simply don't work - a duo of geese (one with a chainsaw, one with a gun) sounds like a great combo, but the trailing gunner is so rarely lined up that the only thing to do is shoot the wall to draw enemies in and saw 'em up.
The music is good. The artstyle is good. New weapons are good. But unfortunately, the
just isn't there, and without that excellent balance between
and
I cannot recommend HOTLINE MIAMI 2.

I've just completed my second playthrough of this game over a year after my first playthrough and I have to say, this game is really something.
You play as several different characters and experience their play style and perspective - some of these perspectives take place before the events of the first game, and others take place after. Some of the playable characters interact/cross paths with each other across the story as well. In my opinion it's a solid improvement on the first game, the levels are more challenging, take longer to complete, maps/rooms are bigger and many require frequent use of holding shift to look further (coming from the first game, you may find you're being shot a fair amount by enemies you couldn't see in normal view), and enemies generally seem quicker in their reaction times. The only bad thing I can say about it is that I sometimes find I go into a sort of autopilot mode on harder levels if I die several times, as I end up replaying the same part continuously to the point where everything feels rehearsed, and for me that can ruin the enjoyment a bit. There are also a few gameplay issues, like enemies never react to finding their allies dead on the floor, randomly they don't appear to react to hearing gunshots, picking up weapons when there are several around you can be a bit clumsy and sometimes interferes with your combo (plus enemies seem to be able to pick up empty guns and use them), and occasionally you might find human enemies or dogs spinning rapidly in doorways, corners, etc.
Despite this, I think this is a very well done sequel with prequel elements. The first game was good but it was much more fast paced gameplay wise, and what it offered in regards to a story, I initially didn't pay much attention to, and I ended up approaching this game in a similar way during my first playthrough. Playing through a second time however, I really came to appreciate the plot, the characters, the fantastic soundtrack, and the overall attention to detail, and it's given the Hotline Miami series a place in my favourite top 5 (maybe even top 3) of all time.

DO NOT believe the metacritic rating. This game is an excellent game that does exactly what it sets out to do: Allow you to blow the heads off Nazi Zombies.
Much like the first game, the weapons are varied enough despite their initial similar appearances. I can only imagine how identical all of these rifles look to a layman. Despite that, they offer enough variety and are, quite surprisingly, EXTREMELY well balanced. There is no one loadout that breaks the game, nor any that is useless. Between me and my three teammates, we all chose totally different sets of gear. One of us chose a long-range, bolt-action rifle with a high powered scope, two of us more medium-flavored but with totally different secondary weapons and the fourth (me) with a VERY short-range carbine and shotgun. They all work and are all a barrel of fun.
The maps are MUCH MUCH MUCH more varied than the first game with some interesting set-pieces that really added to the game. They are gimmicks on the surface, but I thought they were cool. One thing to note is the difference in maps from NZA1 to NZA2. The first was very open 90% of the time, with only the occasional really close-in tense fights, focusing more on massive hordes than proximity. The second was practically the opposite. Almost totally close-in and with few distant engagements.
With those in mind, think of NZA1 and NZA2 as the same game with some good variety and differences between the two. Both are quite good at what they do and deserve praise for it. When they go on sale, buy 'em. They're still a lot of fun on your own, too.

This is one of those games I'd see on sale every now and then, but just didn't buy.  I finally read some reviews.  When you see several players that have played a game 1000-2000 hours, there must be something to it.
Can't really compare this game to another game as it is very unique.  There is definitely a strategic aspect to the game, but also a very solid FPS part as well.  You do quests and fight battles to improve yourself and your ability to rule.  Through this you pick your friends and enemies (not always directly) which will affect how the game will unfold.  There is no right or wrong way to do things.  There are several options on how to earn money - killing bandits, getting involved with trade, building businesses, raiding villages.  You can marry, and become a king yourself.  You can be a saint to everyone or a rude $%#%& and fight everyone if you want.  Completely up to you.
It is a very rewarding game.  The feeling when you win that first battle, especially when undermanned.  That feeling when you win your first tournament, raid your first village and score tons of loot, help take over a castle, or join in a massive battle of several hundred.   Great stuff!
On top of the basic game (called "Native") you can install mods.  I'd recommend playing Native for a while first though to get a good feel for the game.  I'm now playing the Floris mod which adds some great enhancements to the game (especially with Diplomacy and overhauling tournaments) while keeping it close to Native.
I have yet to try multiplayer, but plan on doing that soon...
Be warned though - this game is very addicting.  I have over 70 hours in just a couple of weeks.  Since I still have to work to pay bills, I sacrafice sleep.  :)
Highly recommend you buy this!

Wow. Just wow.
Gorgeous.
Engrosing.
Immersive.
Frightning.
Amazing.
When they say psychedelic horror, they ain't kidding.
If you're looking for an action shoot 'em up or hack 'n slash, keep looking. If, however, you appreciate carefully crafted storytelling that sucks you in like a great book that you can't put down, and plenty of jump scares, look no further!
Best experienced at night, with headphones!

The Good:
--This is a publishing company that knows its horror, and knows enough about horror to know that the scary♥♥♥♥♥♥is not monsters, it's what humans are willing to do to themselves and others.
--This is also a publishing company that understands the use of symbolism, which is what distinguishes the individuals who really "get" horror and people who throw gore around like a food fight in Hell's cafeteria.
--If you're an art and horror buff like me, the game is stuffed full of completely sensical allusions to classical art, to the artistic process, and to the kind of person many of the old Masters happened to be.
--The spare set design allowed them to reuse scenes over and over, with slight changes, in a way that never gets old and actually enhances the experience of the game.
--I have never been so strongly reminded of the actual process of painting (yes, I actually paint.) The game was incredibly full of insider references and experiences native to being a working artist. It's amazing to get the chance to see video games embrace the arts and the fact that video games are a form of art.
The Bad:
--The plot was a bundle of seriously recycled horror themes. It's easy to lose track of this in how beautiful the game is, but don't go in expecting anything new in terms of horror. I saw the plot coming by chapter two. In some ways, this means that the foreshadowing in the game was working exactly as it should have been. However, it ruined the scare factor for me entirely. I spent the first three chapters giggling at the effects.
On second thought, that worries me a little. May need to gargle holy water.
The Ugly:
--One playthrough took me two hours, including the time I spent playing the Halloween special. I bought this game, and the end thanked me for playing the "sample" game. Perhaps that's just a bit of code that should have come out, but between the really damn short play time and the message at the end of the game, I'm a little.... meh about it. I am aware that it was intended to be short (I browse forums before buying), but two hours is pretty damn short.
I'm willing to recommend it because the visuals and a few of the not-quite puzzles are just that damn good.
The best value for this game lies in thinking of it as an interactive horror movie. That's pretty much exactly what it is.
edited to add: Yes, I'm aware this is an EA game. However, I can't review what I can't play.

The game is decent fun, if you would like a Dark Souls/Left 4 Dead merging.  The controls share some similarities to Dark Souls, with dodging, blocking, heavy and light attacks, timing things correctly, reacting to your opponents, etc.  They are simplified to fit a FPS format, with the exclusion of parrying.
The game's loot system is based on dice rolls, so you're hoping on luck to get items.  However, you can craft items (still luck based), upgrade items, and complete daily missions to acquire guaranteed loot (my preferred method).  This can be frustrating, especially for DLC weapons, which cannot be acquired any other way than rolling the dice at the end of a mission.  I'm still lacking DLC weapons months after purchase, so I would not recommend getting the DLC.
The game is quite challenging.  It has about 20 maps (including 8 DLC maps).  There are about 50 weapons spread out between 5 characters.  The rats are modeled very much like L4D's zombies, with a tank, specials, and trash rats.  The game does have events during holidays, with free gear handed out.  For example, an item is given out freely upon logging in each day during the winter holidays (it can be very rare loot).
Overall, the game has moved in an upward direction over time, and I think the devs mean well.  Sometimes we need to be vocal and steer them in the right direction (currently working on DLC weapons to be included on purchase).  This game is getting better, so it's worth keeping an eye on, if you're interested.
