When a new Deus Ex game comes out, fans of the series gobble it up like baby ducks.  You can bet gamers were salivating behind their monitors when they saw there was a new installment in the series.  Unfortunately, they will have to endure the never ending wait till Mankind Divided, because the Fall just does not carry the banner.  With the exception of some decent shading and lighting effects, graphics that might look halfway decent on a mobile device barely look better than the 2003 graphics of Invisible War.  Although The Fall has a faux version of the signature look of Human Revolution, it is simplified, and scaled down so far in detail that the level designs suffer.  It feels more like you're running through mazes than playing a modern FPS/RPG hybrid.  The salt wouldn't sting so bad if it had the same signature stealth system we knew from Deus Ex Classic.  In The Fall, enemies are so sensitive they practically have eyes in the backs of their heads.  Also, the movement is pretty clunky, so running around shooting everyone isn't always the best solution either.  There is some good writing along the way, but the overall plot is fairly simple, with much fewer side missions than there are in the mainstay Deus Ex titles.
I would bet that absolute diehard fans of the series might be able to force themselves to play this for the sake of completion.  Then again, we don't get much of a sense who these characters are within the scope of the Jensen, Denton, and Denton team.  Those who are not familiar with the series but looking for a fun stealth shooter with  RPG elements would be far better just to start with Deus Ex Classic, then work their way up through the Invisible War and Human Revolution.

Above was my original review in which I gave The Fall a thumbs down.  However, after playing the game more, I actually decided to revisit my assessment of the game.  While all of the things I said at first still apply.  There are a few really annoying things, like the addition of a persistant market instead of having NPC vendors located around the world.  It is designed for mobiles devices, and I think it would look better on a tablet than on a PC.  Was Eidos lazy in pushing out a game that could have been quite a bit better if they were willing to invest a little more into it?  Yes!  But in the end, if you can get past the dated graphics and bugs the game does feel like a Deus Ex game at heart.  Because of that, I would have to say it's worth playing for any fans of the series.

This game shares a lot of qualities with left 4 dead. Yes it does have the same gameplay style, however there are some things that make it different.
Graphically the game looks much better than left 4 dead. While not crysis level jaw dropping graphics, the game is polished and makes my gtx 970 work hard on extreme settings. Still getting 60-100 fps at 1080p.
What is different is really in the extra parts of the gameplay. The levels are just like left 4 dead. You move from cheakpoint to checkpoint or just survive endliess waves of the horde. However as you go through the maps you must pick up dice which give you better odds when rolling at the end of a successful mission for better loot for your character. The more higher qaulity dice you pick up the better chances for rarer loot.
After you start collecting loot you can break down the ones you don't like at the forge or fuse a bunch of low level stuff together for better iteams. You can also enchant or pray for better stats. These concepts will give you a reason for replayablity.
There are a lot of levels. I have about 10-11 unlocked, not sure how many there are in total but that is what i have so far with just the base game and the survivial add on.
So should you buy this?
Do you like left 4 dead, then YES! Do you like warhammer? Maybe depends if you like shooters as well. Decent warhammer lore and conversations between characters but not an in depth full warhammer experience.
Cost 30$ for the price of the game without add ons or dlc, so it's half the cost of a full title. Well worth the investment in my opinion.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This game is a fair bit of fun. Especily for a Trek fan, like me. The setting is nice and you'll find yourself saying "Kirk or Picard? Nope, I'm better!"...up untill the Borg have you for breakfast in your first Elite STF. Which brings me onto one of the main things that you'll need to know. Progression/Endgame.
The race to max level can be done very quickly, but without finishing all of the story arcs in the game, which sorta leaves you away from the generaly well-designed missions (Some are a bit goofy, and a couple are nothing more than the old kill 10 rats thing) and not enjoying the full story. This ends up dumping you in an endgame in which you may not understand why such and such a thing is happening, not to mention the practice you get on deciding how to setup your ship. You'll get gear througout your missions (Which you can replay to get better versions) that you can (And should) experiment with so you can set up how you like at the end. This does bring me to a slight pont of controversy - The dreaded C-STORE! (Or cash shop...whatver you wanna call it.)
Whilst you'll hear "Oh god, it's a cash shop! It's Pay2Win LOLz OMGBBQ ect, ect" You can very easily match up with the best captains with everything you earn in game. Yep. I've seen it myself. You can (and will) get an edge with the ships and crew on offer, as well as the lockboxes in which you buy your keys from (Either C-store or from the exchange for high amounts - You are warned). These can make a bad captain semi-decent, but you'll die alot anyway without the skills and gear to back it up. Whilst it sems to be slightly on the steep side for these edges, this is made better by the fairly often sales that are thrown on. Or, by earning Dilithium (A premium currency), you could get it all and pay nothing! ..With a bit of work.
One last thing to mention is that the game still has it's bugs. Some from right at the start, sadly. As well as "bugs" which turned out to be quite useful and conferred no real game bonuses, which were fixed while these still exist! The bugs and somewhat bad UI (As a Science officer that wants to heal.....ARGH!) can make this game a bit of a nightmare for the newer player.
In time, I found that the setting and the gameplay has outweiged the bugs and issues I've ran into. Others may not agree, but you've nothing to loose by giving it a go. If it's not your thing, then no problem! Leave your own review and say what got you. If you like it, then great! I think you're playing a good title. Not perfect mind! If you look at your Steam and see you've sank close to 2000 hours on it like me....then I'll see you out there, Captain!

UPDATE: 3 years later, I've reinstalled the game recently and while 90% of my review still stands, and I haven't played much due to my addiction over the last year to SWTOR and WoW (all hail Legion), I do want to add in a few points:
- The story. My god, the story. Even though there's not as many new missions as I'd like to play through (I appreciate the devs want sleep!), since Legacy of Romulus the writing has drawn me further and further in. I've really enjoyed the Iconian War so far and I look forward to finishing it on a new character.
- New half-faction(?), where you can start as a Starfleet officer from the 23rd century (original serious nostalgia and film grain intact!) but after the first bunch of missions you mainly follow the standard Federation story. I only did a few and they were really fun to play through, even though it's not my thing.
- Although the engine got a few upgrades recently, it's really showing it's age. I've played it on both Windows and Linux (through Wine and PlayOnLinux) and it just gets... slow. If you can put up with some rough edges it's no issue, though I wouldn't want to play it on a low-spec PC like I used to.
- The cash shop is just... depressing. I got this feeling when I reached endgame a few years back but now it just feels worse. You either need to waste countless hours mining resources and dilithium or fork out the £20-30 for a competitive ship and gear at endgame. Some have argued that it would cover the price of picking up a new game anyway, but it still feels wrong. I suppose that's the tradeoff of a free-to-play game.
- If all else fails, Q's Winter Wonderland will always pull me back in. Murdering snowmen and skating around Star Trek is an odd coupling, but quite satisfying.
Anyway, that's me done. My original review is below.

[[ First reviewed Nov/Dec 2013, Season 7/8 ]]
Good fun for Star Trek and non-Trek fans alike. Some of the lore and story could be worked on (seen mainly in the episode missions) but the more recent stuff is much better. Unfortunately the game is heavy on combat, although there is a diplomatic option it's very limited - a shame considering the source material. There is a variety of combat to enjoy however - from the story missions to STFs ("raids" of a sort) to patrol missions to the new Battlezone (one of Season 8's highlights).
Also the lock boxes and other pieces from the cash shop feel really overpriced to me, but you can earn ZEN (the cash shop currency) by trading in Dilithium (another in game currency), meaning with a lot of work you don't need to spend much, or anything.
It's also good because you can play as one of three factions (with more rumoured to come - Cardassians look to be the fan favourite at the moment) - the Federation (Starfleet), the Klingon Empire (KDF), or the Romulan Republic (a hybrid similar to Pandaren in WoW - you join either the Federation or the Empire at level 10 while keeping some faction bonuses). You get 3 character slots free with an account so you can keep one character of each or a mix of the three.
Other highlights are the customisation (from your character - you can be any canon race, or make your own and control every aspect of their look, and your ship - colours and pieces from different ships can be mixed), the bridge officer (who accompany you on ground missions and give extra abilities in space) and duty officer (send extra officers on assignments that complete in the background over several hours - even when you're offline) systems, and the events (Winter and Summer - you can easily use these to make extra money or even get a new top-level ship, plus they're just fun to join in with). Along with the cool buzz when you think of yourself as a starship captain, or even admiral.
Overall I'd recommend it, after all it's free so you don't have much to lose by trying it out.

A very good, though highly underrated game, The Evil Within uses concepts from great horror titles, such as Dead Space and Outlast (also Silent Hill and Resident Evil), while adding a flavour of its own, to create a thoughtful and quite enjoyable experience. It does have its flaws, mainly of which that it is a bit too action-oriented, so fans of Amnesia-style gameplay might be a bit disappointed with it. Its strongest points are its story, its setting and some of its characters, which may stick with you long after you finished the game. The focus tends to fall more on tension, especially due to a clever, though not necessarily original ammo management system, than on genuine fear.
Pros:
+original setting  (includes a combination of very diverse environments)
+interesting and original story
+ammo conservation system is very well-done
+difficult, but satisfying to complete exactly because of that reason (just wait until you see Akumi mode)
+a lot of replayability value
+some amazing boss fights
Cons:
-story is pretty confusing (It does get explained in the DLCs though)
-except for Ruvik, characters are insufficiently developed (The DLCs will catch up on that too)
-lacking real jumpscares
Neutral:
*a lot of gore, this might be decent overall, but in some points it feels a bit exaggerated
*perhaps too combat-oriented. Some people, who are fans of the Resident Evil or Dead Space series, might not mind, but others, who enjoy a more stealth-based approach, typical to games such as Amnesia or Outlast, may not enjoy it. (The gameplay completely changes in the Kidman DLCs though)
Note: Notice that I kept mentioning the DLCs in my review. The reason for it is that, storywise, they aren't exactly expansions. Though in terms of everything else, they are completely different from the main game, the DLCs are actually necessary to understand the story of the main game (except for The Executioner, which is an expansion from all points of view). I noticed that many negative reviews complained about the poorly explained story. While I agree that it cannot be grasped just by playing the main game, I thoroughly recommend buying the DLCs. They introduce tons of new stuff and change the game from combat-oriented to stealthy/get-ready-to-be-jumpscared/what's-lurking-behind-my-back style.
Conclusion: Despite its weak points, I believe it deserves an 8/10.

Sometimes, when I'm on Steam, I'm not really even sure what the Hell I'm looking for. I know what I like in games, and I just sort of flit around trying to find something that appeals to me. Well, Mount & Blade: Warband has just about everything that appeals to me in a game; strategy, combat, customization, as well as some RPG elements.
To me, MnB is the child of an RTS and an open-world RPG. While the RPG elements and story are not at the forefront of the game, it doesn't matter in the least. It has an empire-building feel along with fantastic battles. The combat, while at first felt clunky, now feels pretty damn good. Check out my list of bullet points below:
(TL;DR - This game is a fantastic mix of strategy and actual combat. There are endless optioins when it comes to customization of your army's units. Do yourself a favor and buy this right now.)
Combat
-Pros-

-If  you like to get into the thick of combat you have your choice of melee weapons both 1handed and 2 handed; swords, axes, polearms, and the like.
-There are also some ranged choices if you prefer to slay your foes from afar; bows, crossbows, throwing axes and javelins.
-The combat engine is pretty great, once you get used to it. You can block and attack directionally, from both sides, above-head swings and thrusts with a myriad of weapons. These attacks come in very handy depending on the weapon, as all melee weapons have a 'reach' statistic, which allows you to plan battles accordingly.
-You can gear yourself up to be a heavily armored mounted knight, with a lance, sword and shield or rather you can be a quick and nimble ranger, bombarding your foes with a rain of arrows.
-Cons-
-There is a slight learning curve to the combat, however, the developers have AUTOMATIC settings on directional blocking which can help a rookie immensly. Also, there are difficutly sliders for the AI, both in combat and in the world that can help you get started.
-Occassionally you can get stuck, typically while defending a castle where the AI on both sides just sort of slams into each other in some sort of chaotic slug fest, which can, at times, leave you on the edge of a battle, looking for a way to satiate your bloodlust.
Unit Customization
-Pros-
-You can level and outfit your character however you want. You can go full blown combat and become a Master at Arms, or you can dedicate yourself to more financial pursuits and focus on leadership and trade skills. It's completely up to you.
-Units in the game can come from a few different nations, each nation has perks that are beneficial to each unit type. A quick example is that the Nord Huscarl (an upgraded Nord footman) is by far one of the best melee infantry units in the game. Meanwhile, the Swadians have the best cavalry with the Swadian Knight. So train your troops accordingly to maximize their potential.
-Heroes can be acquired to your party throughout various towns and cities on the world map. How you outfit them, and level them, is up to you.
-Cons-
-Sometimes outfitting a hero NPC can be cumbersome, forcing you to switch between various menus to make sure that you're equipping them properly. Not a huge hinderance though.
Strategy / Empire Building
-Pros-
-There are so many ways to strengthen your standing in this world it's unreal. You can align yourself with the various nations or strike it out solo and conquer the whole damn map.
-Actual battles can play out VERY differently based on your individual playstyle. You can organize a healthy mix of units, cavalry, infanty and archers and strategically attack your foes, or just charge right in, completely up to you.
-All of the major cities and castle in the game can be captured by laying seige to them. You can align yourself with a nation and join their war parties to do this, or raise an army of your own and claim everything the sun reaches. Just be sure to train your units accordingly before attempting a seige.
Overall
-Pros-
-Great combat.
-Excellent customization
-Wonderful use of strategy in and out of battle.
-Endless replayability. Seriously. You could play this game 100 times and have a different experience each time.
-Cons-
-Slight learning curve, not too bad.
-Dialogue is pretty ridiculous sometimes.
Long story short, it's an excellent game.

I've only played this game for about 90 minutes, but considering there's only about 2 hours of content for an unfinished game, I thought it would still be prudent for me to share my thoughts on it so far.  The best way that I can describe this game is that it's the game that many of us THOUGHT Gone Home was going to be like.  Granted, Gone Home depicted a very well-crafted story in its own right, many people who saw early game footage imagined that it was some sort of horror game, and it wasn't.  Well, good news, Layers of Fear most certainly IS that horror experience.
The description of this game labels it as a "psychadelic" horror game, but I think they meant "psychological."  I suppose one could see walking through a Victorian house of horror as a 'groovy' and 'funky' sort of experience, though, so who am I to judge?  Regardless, it does a fantastic job of drawing you in ever so trepidatiously, constantly feeling as if something is going to jump out at you.  The game relies heavily on its ability to build suspense, and to that end it does a fantastic job.
Traversing the house is a farily linear affair.  Often times, you will walk into a room only to have the door slam shut behind you and lock.  For those of us gamers who suffer from an extremely obsessive compulsive gameplay style; constantly feeling as though you must have forgotten something in the previous room, this does an excellent job of shoving us along.  It also help to control the pacing of the game, so as to not let the player dwell too long in one place, and keep the story moving.
Speaking of story, there isn't too much to glean just yet, as the game is still unfinished.  What can be summised so far, is that the artist has suffered a series of tragedies, which have left him distant, despondent, and increasingly disturbed (sorry for the alliteration). I'm curious to learn more about this character and the game does a terrific job of being able to blend the narrative with the physical appearance of the house, which is visualized by paintings that change shape, bleed out, and even fly off the walls.
I would strongyl recommend this game, despite it being in early access, as it presents a lot of promise and I'm excited to see where the story goes.

I give this a rating of 8/10.
Reasons To Buy:
1.) Gameplay: 9/10
The gameplay is phenomenal. Very smooth, extremely gory, and powerful feeling. When you connect your hammer or sword to a rats head...the feeling is wonderful. I play with a controller, as I do for almost every game that isn't a top-down RTS, RPG, ect. The ranged combat is super powerful, and can turn the tide of a battle. The skill level of players DOES matter, as in any mode but easy, you will die without a good team.
2.) Graphics: 7.5/10
The Graphics are great. No it's not a fully-polished AAA title, but the visuals are awesome. The game is extremely dark, but it's fitting; the damn world is ending! You won't be paying too much attention to the minor details anyways...this game is a constant fight for survival.
3.) Matchmaking, Loot system, Story: 6/10
This is where the game falters...and may cause many of the negative reviews you see. Trust me, they are not enough of a factor to make the game bad. Honestly, the matchmaking is awful. No dedicated servers, lag, connection problems...but hey, the game isn't AAA, remember? The loot system is different, this may be good or bad depending on who you ask. I personally do not care for it, although it has been kind to me. At the surface it is luck based, but with enough grinding you can eventually get what you want. The story is meh, but this game isn't designed for a story anyways.
4.) Price: 8/10
I see many complaining of the price point, but come on guys! It's half an AAA title, and one can get many hours of entertainment out of it! I think that it is worth the cost, although the developers could be a little quicker in adding new content...*cough* *cough*.
5.) Replay-ability: 7/10
Not a whole lot. Once you complete all the stages you will most likely play the maps you like 5 or 6 times, then only play the first stage for grinding purposes. No, not like strippers you sick bastar*s! Well, kind of...you will be dancing around, dodging death, instead of cat-calls...
Final Summary:
Buy it! Have fun! Kill Vermin!

It's impossible to review Vermintide without mentioning Left 4 Dead, so let's get that out the way: Vermintide is Left 4 Dead with elves and wizards. If that's not your cup of tea you're probably not going to find much of interest here. But while the comparison is inevitable it's definitely not a criticism: Vermintide is a fantastic 4 player first person hack'n'slash adventure that brings all the best bits of Valve's seminal zombie shooter and adds a whole lot more: ugradable weapons, a selection of customisable player classes to play, and melee.
With each class having a range of weapon options you get a lot of choice about exactly how you want to play: my role of choice is the Dwarf Ranger, with a shield to hide behind that grants a secondary sweeping stun attack and a hammer that stuns enemies in an arc in front I excel at holding packs at bay while my friendly Wizard charges his slow-but-deadly fireballs. The group dynamics are pretty good, with the special enemies requiring a decent balance of builds to combat, though player choices roles could have done with a little more variety beyond "hits one thing hard/many things less hard at range/up close"
But above all the group dynamics and customisation it's the combat that really shines for me (ranged combat less so, some occasionally glitchy movement and animations can make aiming trickier than it perhaps ought to be.) Melee attacks feel solid, visceral: Blunt weapons clang futilely off heavily armoured enemies and connect with meaty thuds on their less armoured companions, blades whistle and slice as they cave through packs of rats. First person doesn't tend to be a perspective that works well for melee combat, but Fatshark have done great work here: every attack just feels damn good.
It's worth noting that at the time of this review I haven't played enough to unlock a wide variety of gear for every class, so take this all with a pinch of salt if you're likely to invest the time to get into the deeper customisation. However this factor is one of my major issues with the game, and its existence is worth discussing: Progression through the difficulty levels feels very much gated behind gear rather than skill and, for me at least, thats a little offputting. I don't put a huge amount of time into games, and knowing that the higher difficulty levels are out of my reach unless I'm willing to grind just makes more likely to put the game down rather than try to achieve them with what I've got.
That's not to say the progression and customisation are badly implemented: there seem to be plenty of mechanics in place to negate the frustration of an inherently random loot system, but it's not really for me.
Overall Vermintide is a highly enjoyable hack'n'slash, especially if you're playing with a group of friends. While the progression system feels a little bloated it doesn't detract from the minute-to-minute fun you'll have mowing down hordes of rats.
Definitely recommended.

TL;DR: Concept is intriguing, execution is lagging.
Overture purports to draw inspiration from Zelda, Binding of Isaac, and Diablo.  I am not sure which versions of those games the creators were inspired by, because I don't recall any of them throwing hordes and hordes of monsters at you as soon as you start play.   There is no strategy, no hidden doors or secret treasures, no mazes, no...well, anything that resembles those games.  It bears a larger resemblance to Smash TV than any of the games mentioned.
The game doesn't teach you how to play- not only is there no real tutorial, the learning curve appears to be non-existent.  You select a class, the game starts, and you're off to the races.  The mechanics aren't difficult in and of themselves, but the massive number of projectiles, enemies, and other obstacles on screen remind me more of the bullet hell genre than a "roguelike".  The biggest downside to that, however, is that your hitbox is MUCH larger than a single pixel.
The graphics come from a tileset (fine, they serve their purpose), the music is repetitive, and the control is surprisingly crisp.  None of this, however, saves this game from it's biggest flaw- the gameplay.  It is just...bland.  Sure, this game might work for 15 minutes of mindless play, but games like that are a dime a dozen, and there are much better out there than Overture.

Waste of $5
Honestly, I would have enjoyed myself more buying 5 candy bars than playing this game. It seems like the developer(s) of Overture were planning out the mechanics before a torrential bee storm assaulted their home and the last thing they could do was upload this. My two largest points are that the game has no plot and it seems that the game is a smashed together Krabby Patty concocted by Jenkins.
Delving deeper into my first point; Overture's story couldn't be more uninteresting had they hired the Kardashians to write it. The reason being that there is no story. Story in a game is an important component in keeping the player there. Story gets the player invested in the characters and the components and in turn the player will continue to play and discover new game mechanics and content. However, in developing Overture, someone must've spilt coffee on the script. As you can see by my playtime, I was not too inclined to continue playing after an hour simply because I asked myself: "Why do I care about this game?" and "Am I getting new content by continuing to play this game?" I couldn't find a reason to care about this game, much like no one can find Malaysia Airlines. The answer to the second question is simply no. Within 15 minutes of play I played all the first level maps, fought most enemies and got bored.
Much like I am doing with you most likely. However, never fear, my second point is fairly short. I learned a lot about game mechanics in high school. This game seems like something I would have made when practicing my skills as a game designer. This is why I feel like this is a waste. To give an example: As a GFX designer I'm still an amateur, so most of my work for other people is done for free. To apply this concept to this game, why should we pay $5 for Overture when this seems like amateur work? Simple, we shouldn't.
Dev. of Overture, my advice to you: No shame on you for publicizing your work. Shame on you for making us pay for it.

Around 1% of the people who bought this game have actually beat it. I am the 99%.
On the one hand, the core of Overture's slash-em-up fantasy bullet hell gameplay (with a great soundtrack to boot) is incredibly addicting. Heck, I'll probably go back to playing it after I finish this review. On the other hand, there's not much else to it. The level are all randomly generated squares where the enemies slowly rush you. The bosses (all of which are simply scaled-up versions of normal enemies) all require exactly the same strategy: kiting in an extremely confined space. The upgrade system is one-dimensional and gets very expensive very fast. Some of the classes are unique and fun, but others are only slight variations on other classes and many are simply not viable if you want to get anywhere in the game.
If you buy this game, you'll probably have a few hours of fun with it. I did. But as you play more and more that feeling that you'll never get beyond the first three floors and are stuck grinding more infinitesimal stat increases that you know, deep down, will never give you the edge to win the game, gradually eats the fun out of the experience.
So, how would I improve Overture?
-Better boss designs that required more dynamic strategies and larger, more varied boss rooms (perhaps with traps?)
-More coherent enemies and map combinations to combat the utter randomness. Being rushed by armies of skeletons, spiders, oozes, yetis, ogres, necromancers AND minotaurs in a single level is ridiculous and completely immersion-breaking, especially when the game has several clear map themes (forest, dungeon, lava, etc.)
-More varied enemy behavior and skills, especially for melee enemies
-Permanent stat increases beyond attack power (health, mana, etc)
-Stat and mechanical improvements for the game's less viable classes (Knight, Invoker, Bandit, etc.)

Jagex Ruins Everything
---
So, for those who don't know, before Ace of Spades was purchased by Jagex, it was a free game on the internet that you would download and select a server to play on the Ace of Spades website. Back then, the graphics weren't amazing, but the maps were great and the gamemods were fun to play and compelling. There weren't any classes, only three guns you could choose from: the rifle, the SMG, and the shotgun. Back then, it was a fun game that I would recommend to all of my friends, and I considered it to be as great as games of the same genre such as TF2.
Now, I can't say that anymore. Instead of having a choice between three guns, which was simple and balanced, now there's four different classes you can choose from, and one class that is practically designer for griefers: the miner. The miner is equipped with dynamite, drill guns, shovels that dig out huge portions of blocks, and can destroy a spawn in a matter of minutes, ruining the match for everyone. Of course, the community and its players are the ones who do this, but it's Jagex that made the class practically designed for the destruction of a spawn.
While the feature of being able to destroy and create blocks to turn the tide of battle is cool, when paired up with all the happenings of this game, it just becomes boring and rage-inducing. Honestly, Jagex should have just updated the graphics of the origianl AoS, and then the world would've been a happy place. When they "renovated" the game, they got rid of amazing game modes such as Arena and a free for all mode. And they even got rid of some of the best maps such as Hallway.
Also, the classes are way too OP, and very unbalanced, unlike all nine classes in TF2. TF2 has nine classes, five more than AoS, and yet they were able to balance each and every class' weapons so that the game at least feels fair. In this case, that was never considered. The sniper can fire multiple shots without reloading, unlike the sniper in TF2 which can only take one shot then must duck for cover as he reloads. Also, sniping just feels easier in this game for some reason. I don't know why, but there isn't much challenge to it. Anyway, the Engineer has the ability to fly at the cost of fuel, but also has a SMG. So, he can easily come done from the sky and rain death upon many people quickly. And the miner, as I've already explained, is just a griefer that came from the depths of Hell.
The commando I personally haven't had any trouble with. Anyway, this game would have been much better if it was just an update with better graphics. If they want to make money on the game, that's fine by me, I would pay for it. But it's not a good game. Do not give Jagex a single penny, as this game just sucks, as I give it a score of 2/10. Not even one dollar would be fair to pay for this game, and Jagex should rethink their entire AoS situation. Thank you for reading my review.

The gameplay is a little monotonous in single player, but get three of your friends, turn the difficulty up to sniper elite and multiply the zombies X4 and you'll never look at a zombie apocalypse the same way again. This game can go from laughably easy to downright impossible depending on how hard you want it to be. The guns all feel similar, with only one having notably less damage (M1 carbine) and the obligatory shotgun (and the preacher) and magnum (called the webley). The game is in a sort of 3rd person mode but zooms down a scope when you fully aim with any rife. In addition to the three classes of guns (rifles, subs, launcher, shotties and pistols) the game gives you 5 options for explosives: two kinds of grenades, land mines, trip mines, and dynamite which explodes when shot. What this game doesn't do is tell an in depth story. what it does do is blow away boredom along with several hundred zombies at a time. If you see it on sale, I heartily recommend picking up a four pack (as this game is best played with 4 players) and sharing it with your fellow zombie shooter loving friends.

Storyline: 8.50/10
Graphics: 8.50/10
SoundTrack: 9.50/10
Overall: 9/10
Given the original only came out around eight months ago, Rebellion’s sequel to their supernatural zombie sniper festival is most unexpected, having popped out of cover just in time to cash in on Halloween and no doubt extend the finances of the studio as they work on Sniper Elite 3. Nazi Zombie Army 2 continues the template laid down by the original almost to a tee, offering a series of corridors and open levels in which to snipe and lay down traps for the incoming hordes, wrapping its premise around the loosest and silliest of plots. It’s still basic and slightly awkward, and it’s still 100% more fun when played with other people.
Trading the Nazi soldiers for those of their undead cousins, Zombie Army 2’s combat takes shape as a series of shooting galleries, sometimes confined and sometimes open, often requesting the gang of four combatants to defend a specific location from assault on multiple sides. Physical barriers block progress until each and every last zombie has been dispatched back to the underworld, and a neat scoring mechanic allows for competition between groups as players vie for the highest tally of grenade kills, headshots and long-range bollock-busters (or the space where they used to be, anyway).
My local Tesco has gone downhill
The plot, for those of you that are interested, takes into account Hitler’s plight in the original game, with his ‘Plan Z’ now in full effect and overpowering even his own bunker. In order to put a stop to the undead hordes you’ll need to find three pieces of an ancient artifact stashed away in various hellish locations far removed from the original’s re-used World War II assets, with the majority of the new environments swathed in devilish flames and lit with hues of orange and red.
Just like its predecessor and the original V2 however, the sniping and gunplay mechanics remain largely the same in Zombie Army 2. The go-to weapons are unsurprisingly still a variety of WWII sniper rifles augmented with a steady-aim breathing gauge that recharges during combat, with secondary slots available for a machine gun and pistol. The latter two begin as fairly useless options as each level slowly unfolds, but soon become invaluable for popping groups of zombie heads whenever the shufflers breach defences and begin to swarm your position. A swift kick to the guts will also put them down in a pinch, but that solitary melee attack still lacks the crowd-control utility of alternatives found in the likes of Left 4 Dead, making it a little limp as a last resort.
The planning and trapping aspects of Sniper Elite are also still in full effect here, played up to the maximum in the all-new levels designed specifically for Zombie Army 2. The array of options remain the same, encompassing two types of grenade, trip-wire explosives and dynamite. Working as a team to successfully booby trap a location and take down swathes of shuffling zombies is a satisfying experience when a well-thought-out plan comes together, and the frantic corridor-clearing when things fall apart is just as frustrating or enjoyable depending on your luck. And Rebellion obviously knows its onions regarding the elements players responded to best the first time around, as the level design in the sequel is far more accommodating. Siege locations are more prevalent with numerous cover spots and opportunities for funnelling the undead into carefully-laid traps, whilst machinegun ammo is found with a greater frequency, enabling more of those last-gasp firefights or desperate runs to revive a colleague. The range of special zombies are also augmented by a couple of new additions to the mix, with a fiery, fast-moving variety proving particularly tricky and the “summoner” constantly resurrecting fallen foes unless you take him out.
That’ll be a tricky shot with a sniper rifle
It’s also very much still the case that if you’re playing Nazi Zombie Army 2 alone, then you’re in for a pretty dull experience. Despite the additions, the extended waves of enemies and narrow shooting galleries can still become a frustrating slog in singleplayer. In four-player co-op however, Rebellion’s title sputters to life with a satisfying blend of preparation and on-the-fly tactics, made all the better when you have to backtrack or wade into a crowd in order to help up a tardy or over-confident comrade. Being part of a well-oiled four-player sniping team is a huge amount of fun, and even the chaotic mess of an incompatible unit is good for a giggle while it lasts.

Disclaimer: I'm incredibly biased when anything involves monster girls.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game. It's a card-collecting, turn-base strategy game where you explore a world inhabited by both humans and monsters (who all also happen to be cute girls). Monsters are contained in cards, some humans are the masters of said cards, exposition, exposition.
The main appeal of this game is of course the art on the cards that you collect, which are all great to look at. I always got excited when I recieved a new card I didn't already have, and immediately started rubbing it. Oh yeah, you also rub your girls to make them stronger, just like real life.
The gameplay is realatively simple: You or your opponent go first, lay down your card, then your monster moves up one space every turn until it reaches the opponent's castle where it will saccrafice itself to deal one point of damage. However, it gets more complicated as you dive deeper into the mechanics and strategies of each card, as all good games of this genre do.
The majority of the game is easy enough, but near the end there is a noticable difficulty spike. And although it's optional, the final final boss after you beat the game is incredibly difficult.
I relly enjoyed Monster Monpiece. If you're as big of a monster girl fan as I am, I really reccomend this game. If you don't care, it can still be a fun game.

It's impossible to review Vermintide without mentioning Left 4 Dead, so let's get that out the way: Vermintide is Left 4 Dead with elves and wizards. If that's not your cup of tea you're probably not going to find much of interest here. But while the comparison is inevitable it's definitely not a criticism: Vermintide is a fantastic 4 player first person hack'n'slash adventure that brings all the best bits of Valve's seminal zombie shooter and adds a whole lot more: ugradable weapons, a selection of customisable player classes to play, and melee.
With each class having a range of weapon options you get a lot of choice about exactly how you want to play: my role of choice is the Dwarf Ranger, with a shield to hide behind that grants a secondary sweeping stun attack and a hammer that stuns enemies in an arc in front I excel at holding packs at bay while my friendly Wizard charges his slow-but-deadly fireballs. The group dynamics are pretty good, with the special enemies requiring a decent balance of builds to combat, though player choices roles could have done with a little more variety beyond "hits one thing hard/many things less hard at range/up close"
But above all the group dynamics and customisation it's the combat that really shines for me (ranged combat less so, some occasionally glitchy movement and animations can make aiming trickier than it perhaps ought to be.) Melee attacks feel solid, visceral: Blunt weapons clang futilely off heavily armoured enemies and connect with meaty thuds on their less armoured companions, blades whistle and slice as they cave through packs of rats. First person doesn't tend to be a perspective that works well for melee combat, but Fatshark have done great work here: every attack just feels damn good.
It's worth noting that at the time of this review I haven't played enough to unlock a wide variety of gear for every class, so take this all with a pinch of salt if you're likely to invest the time to get into the deeper customisation. However this factor is one of my major issues with the game, and its existence is worth discussing: Progression through the difficulty levels feels very much gated behind gear rather than skill and, for me at least, thats a little offputting. I don't put a huge amount of time into games, and knowing that the higher difficulty levels are out of my reach unless I'm willing to grind just makes more likely to put the game down rather than try to achieve them with what I've got.
That's not to say the progression and customisation are badly implemented: there seem to be plenty of mechanics in place to negate the frustration of an inherently random loot system, but it's not really for me.
Overall Vermintide is a highly enjoyable hack'n'slash, especially if you're playing with a group of friends. While the progression system feels a little bloated it doesn't detract from the minute-to-minute fun you'll have mowing down hordes of rats.
Definitely recommended.

Fun game with some extremely satisfying melee combat...until you realize half the party is using legit autoaim features (Bright Wizard Bolt staff and Elf Trueflight bow). You don't know bad design decisions and frustration until you wind up the big, juicy Dwarf hammer for the thousandth satisfying, crunchy hit on a Skaven, only to have an arrow fly from around a wall and kill it as an Elf shoots wildly into the air. Then the next Skaven explodes into fire and blocks your screen with flame effects from some Bright Wizard bouncing their shots around in the most boring, uninteresting, trivial gameplay since mobile games.
The bad dev choices don't end there, as the game had a rocky launch, still has loot frustration issues, suffers from performance issues, and is way too overpriced for what should be an accessible coop game.
BUT if you can find a good melee party and are on a challenging enough difficulty, you'll have a hoot. And that's why I keep playing and ignoring glaring design issues. Because at the end of the day swinging a huge hammer, or amazing mace and shield, or slicing with a rapier, are all super fun and well done.
And with the community made Grimalackt Quality of Life mod you can finally enjoy Vermintide comfortably solo with bots, as well as control your own lobby and kick without a vote. Great for tailoring your play experience.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I am generally pretty sceptical to horror games because they tend to consist of a bleak plot and lots of jump-scares, without adding some consistensy to the "horror" part of the game. About 90% of all the horror games i've personally seen did not provide any interesting scene or experience, so Layers of Fear does stand up in that way.
«Layers of Fear» has some things that it does good, like using environment to reflect the mental state of the hero, pretty good voice acting and overall mediocre plot (which is good in comparison to others, because it does not try to introduce something absolutely new or fantastical, but rather to reshape the image we have in our head of "the usual") and an incredible atmosphere, that keeps triggering the feeling of being lost and at the same time led "by yourself through yourself".
However there are some things too familiar to horror genre that "Layers of Fear" uses in abundance: the element of surprise which at first looks pretty well, because it's the environment that astonishes you instead of some monster, starts to feel redundant as you see it times and times again it. It had also actually upset me to see some jumpscares in this game. Even though still pretty rare, they make Layers feel alike all the other horrors.
So if you prefer horror games, this one might feel refreshing. While being comparatively short it still presents some pretty good moments and scenes, which were never or barely used in other horror media. To crown it all I should note, that this review is based solely on my personal opinion, and some points may very well be affected by my personal preferences and/or thoughts about game design. In no way i think them to be absolutely true so if you have some thoughts to prove me wrong and show another side of this game, that i might have missed, i'd be glad to hear them.
Update after the game release:
Now that the game is out and full i cannot recommend it more. Some content was added, various bugs were fixed and the game is now overall finished.
I still can't make up my mind if i will ever come back to this game for another round, but that is not because of the dullness or anything, but because of the feeling it leaves you with. On various occasions it shows you such obscene, such crazy scenes, so that you start questioning your own sanity.
It is amazing how very few games managed to do that properly. Yes, some people may say that «Layers of Fear» copied some scenes or elements from other games and in some cases that may be true, but the way these scenes form a full complex image is just amazing. Every single room, action, piece of dialogue fits right in to such a degree that i can think of very few things that i'd change in the game if i had the power.
To top it all, i'd like to note that this is the best horror and psychological thriller i've ever seen and/or experienced. I suggest for oversensitive or mentally weak people to stay out of this one, because "the spooks are real", but every other person is more then welcome to try it out. You will find yourself scared, interested, disgusted and fascinated all at the same time, while roaming the labyrinths of painter's mind.

Does Deus Ex: The Fall deserve all the hate? My answer; yes and no.
On some things I have to agree, bugs ever present, gameplay a husk compared to Human Revolution. Those aside, it was still enjoyable, albeit lacking the amount of depth and content HR had, but what were people expecting from an iOS port. I myself never expected the graphics to be stellar, all I've ever cared about when it comes to ports is optimisation, and frankly The Fall ticks that box, running flawlessly minus a few minor bugs; never experienced lag nor any crashes whilst playing.
As a game itself I'd argue it is one of the weaker entries to the franchise, but it's decent enough to warrant at least a single playthrough. The story continues from where the Icarus Effect novel left off, as such you may be confused going in without having read it. Seeing as the game ends on a cliff-hanger it can be assumed a sequel was planned, up until the massive backlash and as such, it's unlikely we'll see the end of Ben and Anna's story. I'd recommend against buying at full price, buy on sale instead if you're considering it.

Deus Ex: The Fall is easily one of the worst games I've ever played, and it breaks my heart to write that.
I'm a huge fan of the Deus Ex franchise, having ritually played the original at least once per year for the last decade. I eat up news and announcements about the games like a rabid fanboy, and I was onboard with Human Revolution as soon as they announced it.
What a shame, then, that The Fall (a port of a mobile game) is so terrible in just about every conceivable way. Broken game mechanics, stiff AI and level interaction and an equally lethargic and boring storyline combine to make this one of the worst games released in 2014, system be damned.
To talk about this game, we first need to discuss the expanded universe. When Human Revolution came out, there was a tie-in novel called Icarus Effect that was released too. That novel was a prequel/interquel that had the dual duty of setting up events from the original game and telling its own story within the framework of Human Revolution. A British SAS soldier-turned-mercenary named Ben Saxon allied with a Secret Service agent named Anna Kelso to attempt to stop the Tyrants (the antagonists of HR) and working to expose the Illuminati for their crimes.
The Fall is a pseudo-sequel to that book, and either retcons or reframes certain events so that they fit in line with this game's storyline. It does such a poor job with it that I wondered why they even bothered. The rationale for why Jaron Namir (the leader of the Tyrants) brought Saxon onboard in the book - that he was largely doing it as a way to acknowledge the guilt for all the crimes he's committed over the years - is largely ignored here. Anna Kelso, a level-headed and strong character in the books, becomes a woman who practically stays in the fetal position throughout the whole game. The death of Saxon's friend in the book becomes a retcon where he miraculously survived and became a new member of the Tyrants. Memorable events (like Saxon leaping out of a cargo plane and using his Icarus Landing System to survive a fatal drop into the ocean) are so buggy and half-finished that they become laughably bad.
Nearly every facet of the gameplay is counter to the franchise's design philosophy. Levels are disappointingly linear, with only the barest attention paid to the world-building and characterization that's so famous in other installments. Guns feel like pea-shooters, and the oft-mentioned zoom-in-while-aiming is incredibly frustrating. There's no sense of martialing the story with the gameplay - you can buy extra ammo and guns whenever you feel like it, trivializing the role inventory plays in these games.
The worst part is that this game sets up a sequel hook that will probably never be addressed, concerning characters we have no reason to care or be interested about.
I remember when this game was first announced, and the scorn it reaped on the internet. Incredibly, the final product was even worse than I thought. I still feel like I was ripped off, even after buying the game at 75% off.
Don't waste your time with this. Go back to the original game or Human Revolution for a far better experience.

"Roguelike" was never intended to mean "unbalanced."

It leads to monster projectiles you cannot see to avoid, thus causing death. It leads to loading into a level with monsters already swarming the entrance. The first boss is overtuned for the beginning of the game and creates a situation where you must get lucky with the random item drops to defeat it.
The class upgrades need more meaning (such as added hp, defense, etc). The incremental price increase smacks of lazy development.

This game is pretty good. It's graphics are terrible, but the gameplay and shop upgrades are there. It's a decent rogue-like.

One game mode - spawning in a floor and killing the giant ooze, then another boss, and repeating (well, I assume, I only ever made it to the 3rd floor). Has potential but a lot of issues right now. Spawning of enemies is too eratic (I've pretty much died before my screen was fully visible) and it's way too difficult to see anything, especially when you die in only a few hits. There's not much of a tutorial and the game starts at a pretty fast pace without a lot of explanation about anything, but it's fairly intuitive so that's fine. It would be nice if there was a health and mana bar that wasn't right below your character, because it's almost impossible to see when you're swarmed. Could also be improved if there was a simple replay button instead of bringing you back to the main menu when you die (which you will do a lot). A more complex upgrade system would be nice, I only got my ranger to level 6 or so but from what I saw it only increased damage, but being able to upgrade armor, health, and mana as well would be nice. There are 5 item slots that are nice for a little bit of customization but each type of armor slot all provide the same buff (weapon is attack, armor is def, etc.) and maybe a random chance buff (8% more gold or something). There are 24 total characters I think, and there is enough variation between them where for the most part they feel unique, but ultimately the gameplay is all the same: hold left click and dodge, with an occasional right click; how oftten you right click is probably the main difference. Overall it's decently fun but it doesn't seem to have much depth and as others have pointed out, it's just a bit of a grindfest.

The Evil Within is a tough game to review for me. Since I still feel somewhat conflicted about it. I want to love it since it comes from Shinji Mikami. Creator of the Resident Evil series which was my favorite survival horror franchise until after 4. I went into this game hoping we might see a return to those old games style. I ended up being disappointed though. What you will find with the Evil Within is you don't get the classic Resident Evil style or even the more modern third person shooter style of the post 4 RE games. Instead it's more like a less polished RE4 that tries to shove in stealth elements that are not all that well executed.
The game is at times frustrating. Since it forces you to fight yet doesn't always provide much ammo. Like it's not sure what game it wants to be. It's also filled with traps, and cheap boss fights that will instantly kill you many times in a row until you finally figure out exactly what it is they expect you to do. Yet despite these considerable flaws it's still an interesting game. Filled with very impressive visuals. Exploring the world itself is a strange ride as environments constantly shift into ever crazier horror scenarios. Like a mixture of every horror movie you have ever seen. I admire the artistic visuals yet at the same time they draw me out of the experience, making it harder to take the world seriously, and be scared strangely enough. Ultimately I do recommend the game. Just perhaps not at full price, and only if your willing to put up with some frustration from less than perfect game design.
On the DLC front the Assignment, and Consequence are both expansions to the main story that keep the same high production values. Be warned both of them cut out the gunplay nearly completely focusing entirely on Stealth, and story. This is unfortunate since the stealth mechanics in Evil Within just are not very good. But if you like the game you should definitely pick up these DLC's as the round it out nicely. However do avoid the Executioner as it's pretty bad. Feels cheaply made, and adds little to the experience.

I don't know why this game has gotten the bad reputation is has, I can only assume that much of the negativity stems from a poorly executed and buggy release.
However, having completed the game recently (may 2015) I can say that the Evil within is a pretty decent game. For those who loved the likes of resident evil 4 and to a lesser extent resident evil 5, the evil within provides a wholesome 15 hours of similiar game play.
Now don't get me wrong, this game is not going to redefine the genre and we aren't going to be talking about it in 10 years time. However for the price and the amount of support the game seems to be getting it is a reasonable purchase and an excellent one if in a STEAM discount sale.
This game while clearly fitting in the horror genre, is about as scary as the likes of Resident evil (so not one bit). If you need your adrenaline fix then I heartily recommend you go play alien isolation. However, what the Evil within does very well, and I would say even surpasses resident evil, is make you very aware of your ammunition. Ammo does not drop from every other enemy or in nice convenient boxes of 15+ bullets. To that end, the game is a very stingy version of resident evil 4, which is great for reminding you how vulnerable you are.
If you liked Resident evil 4/5 and that style of game-play, then please pick this game up at some point and show your support.

Super Monday Night Combat is a class-based, free-to-play third-person multiplayer shooter.
The game is a televised futuristic death-sport that has two teams of five fighting each other in hopes of escorting bots to the enemies’ base and destroying their coin-filled moneyball. Doing this will require teamwork, upgrading your players, protecting your team’s bots and destroying the enemy’s turrets.
During play, you will level up and are allowed to spend your points on upgrading your three abilities or your defense and attack power. You will also gain money for purchasing stat boosters, jump pads to reach higher places and waves of bots to send at your opponents.
After a game is over, your profile will gain experience points.
Super Monday Night Combat is well worth your time if you are looking for a free shooter. It has a large variety of characters, great maps and is not a pay to win game.

I'm shocked how this 2nd expansion is identical to the first one: released half a year later Zombie Army 2 suffers from the same mistakes the first game had. Glitches, bugs, only 5 chapters (again, a relatively short game you can complete in a mere 5-6 hours) and a horrible algorithm that makes it extremely difficult for you to find players.
I know for a fact that there are a lot of people wanting to play this game and finding hosts is very, very difficult. And even if you manage to start the game from Chapter 1 with 3 friends who are willing to play it till the end disconnections will be common between the chapters.
Gameplay-wise the game is the same so in case you do not encounter any issues it is pretty fun. There are some new enemy types and some scenes when you can mount a gun turret having unlimited ammo at your disposal so you have no issues with gunning down hordes of enemies. And of course bullet time is still very exciting.
Also, the environments now look different: this game is darker, more creepy and there's fire almost everywhere. I liked this as the 4 soldiers' mission to get rid of the zombie menace seems to be more desperate.
Still, playing it without issues is difficult and it is a shame they could not correct the problem related to the game session finding.

Me and a friend snagged this when it was on sale, and played through it over the course of 3-4 days. The individual missions are few, but very long. There's a few annoyances (If you die, you can't rejoin a game in progress, and you can't save in the middle of the missions between sessions). But overall, the experience was tremendously enjoyable and entertaining.
The game play is mostly of the form "go from A to B, through a horde of zombies". Sometimes you have to do "seiges" in which a bunch of zombies spawn and you have to kill them. At all points it felt pretty organic - you just go around killing zombies as you see best, and you're not really locked into any given strategy most of the time. There's a variety of weapons (Sniper Rifles, SMG's, and pistols are your guns, while you have trip mines, land mines, grenades (2 types) and dynamite for your explosives and traps. You can also get two types of shotguns (though only off the ground in some missions). The gun handling is superb, as you'd expect.
I recommend it, especially if you like zombie games, or sniping games (though there are few chances for real long-range sniping).

You haven't played a game like HuniePop. Sure, you've probably played countless match three games. And that's what this is, make no mistake. It's a big, well developed match-three with a lot of clever mechanics and abilities cast against a decent ramp up of "required points vs. X turns" with no stupid Candy Crush puzzle games or pay to win nonsense, nor the limitless grind of Puzzle Quest.
But the other half of it, the theme, the story, that's something you don't see very often. See, the match three here is cast as the act of dating one of the game's many lovely ladies, from the socially inept shut-in to the ♥♥♥♥♥y party girl to the sweetheart lady to the studious cheerleader. You go to each of these ladies and give them gifts between each puzzle to earn currency to upgrade your stats, so you can do better at the puzzle game, succeed at a date, to win money, to buy gifts, to get stat XP.
There's no "dating" here in the classic dating sim game sense like Fate/Stay Night or that one with the girl in the washing machine. Just a few philosophical questions from each girl and a "do you remember my [X stat]?" type things that dole out more XP if you nail them and do not penalize you at all if you don't. You have to go from girl to girl. You're a player, not a white knight out to fix their problems. You enjoy their company, wine and dine them, and move on. The basic game flow is just "meet girl, buy gifts, level stats, complete date puzzle, unlock CG, meet next girl."
The characters range from outrageous to sweet, and there's something charming about women written as women, flaws, neuroses, kinks and all, rather than the pure perfect waifus of the Japanese dating sim.
If you complete the whole of the puzzle campaign for a girl, you get to... er... copulate with her and get an appropriate, yet censored CG.
That's a lot of effort for porn. But this is a terrible buy for porn. It's also not a great buy for a romance geek either. But what you do get, a solid puzzler, to spend some time with interesting women, the sort you very seldom see writers in any media want to commit to. Not because they're offensive, there's really nothing in this game offensive (Yes, boobies are prominent and some of the characters are a bit ridiculous but that's simply their character. This is the sort of game that makes even a crass, drug-loving ♥♥♥♥♥y party girl actually seem pleasant to be around if you can keep up with her. I don't see how you could take offense from this game unless you went looking for it.), but because very few writers want to risk the toes they step on displaying the whole gamut of the feminine personality, from the sweet and charming and shy to the energetic go-getter to the catty hedonist to the insecure to the awkward to the inept. It isn't especially realistic but there's something pleasantly human and unique about the whole thing, the sort of thing Rockstar tries to write somewhere between making everyone a goofy psychotic clown set in an ugly nihilist-filtered world.
But, at the same time, remember, it's all from top to bottom an excellently realized veneer atop a solid puzzle game framework. You are here to match three and every interaction serves that match three. The theme is just so well-realized that you could easily forget and want to actually spend more time with the girls than you're given.
On the whole, I think it's absolutely worth trying out for something unique. That the gameplay is pleasant is a huge plus.

Ace of Spades is a very unique twist in the FPS Genre, mixing in elements like Minecraft and Call of Duty to make an experience that hasn't been done by many other games. The main features in a nutshell is that the terrain is destructable and you can build bunkers and bases or sniper towers and so forth. The game is very fun, especially when you get good at it and change a few of the controls but it does have some problems like that some maps have the issue of one side clearly having the upper hand and that there will almost always be a camper on a server. There are no classes that are over-powered or unbalanced and you have to train with them for them to be any good on the battlefield.
It is practically a multiplayer-only game but servers are far from empty and there are a lot of game modes to try out and you can create your own maps. The Steam workshop for this is very basic but still good and fun to try out fans' maps. As every game has, the game suffers from bugs but the game-breaking ones have been removed. Graphics can be altered as well for better frame rates.
Overall, this game is a must buy if you want a FPS with a interesting twist and I give it a 7.5/10.

Ace of Spades: Battle Builder... where do I begin?
This entire game is nothing like the original. Jagex took the perfectly good Ace of Spades that I loved and played for hours on, and sawed off everything good that it had. Those who did play the original know what I'm talking about. The slow yet fun paced action? Gone. The use for building large trenches to the other base? Worthless. The building of large forts made for sniping or defending your flag? Nonexistent. But I'm not going to lable that, because some people may be confused by what I'm saying in this review. Lets begin, shall we?
The good things Jagex has added;
New weapons, which is nice.
Class based warfare. The original partially did this, but not very in depth.
New modes. Some are more famous then others, but thats not exactly a bad thing, since games usually have a lot of modes that most people enjoy than others.
Now, lets move on to the bad things.
The bad things Jagex has added;
Fast paced combat, which feels nothing like the original.
The complete removal of the use for building, mostly since the Rocketeer can fly over all cover.
Small maps. I mean, Jagex messed up the easiest part of the game, and that was making decently large maps. Classic mode tries to make up for this, but just utterly fails at it.
Now, the biggest sin of all time in this game;
Classic mode. This has to be the worst attempt at rebooting a original aspect of the original game, and heres why; hardly anybody plays it, very limited maps instead of random generation, like the original did, one weapon, OUT OF THREE OF THE ORIGINAL WEAPONS THEY CHOSE ONE! Now, I know what your thinking, you can enable these settings to include the shotgun and SMG, but that should not be an option, that should already be enabled, I mean, if your going to name it classic, MAKE IT FEEL LIKE THE CLASSIC.Don't make it to where you can toggle the original weapons on or off, make them permanently on all the time, JUST LIKE THE CLASSIC, don't slap on the name classic just because it has some little features of the original game, make it feel like the actual CLASSIC. Oh yeah, and random generated maps like it had on the original game, GONE. I mean, a simple feature that can be added in, is not even implemented? Although the classic maps are large like the original game, it just doesn't feel like the original.
I cannot explain how mad this makes me. But, I'll leave out all the rest, just for your sake, in case you never played the original, because thats what the rest of my review will be complaining about.
My final verdict;
My rating for this game is 3/10. This is not the original. Nothing close to it, and thats the exact reason why I bought this. I thought it was an advanced version of the original, but was extremely disappointed in the end, and so are the many others that also bought this. Also, Battle Builder is not a correct name for this. Its just another Call of Duty clone, since nobody builds because there is no more point in it. If you've never played the original, you may not know what I'm talking about, but those who have may agree with me. Please, I beg of you, go waste your money on something better than this. $14.99 is enough to buy games that are much better then this. Also, $14.99 is a ridiculous price for a game that used to be free. I beg of you, do not waste your money, and instead go to this website for the free, original, and better game;
I'll meet you on the battlefield.

What is it: a generic roguelike with a focus on grinding and some very, very small RPG elements.
Goal: go over 10 floors populated by slight variation of types of enemies and end-of-floor bosses to win.
Pros:
+ Game mechanics are very simple to learn
+ You can spend a few minutes/hours mindlessly killing your time.
Cons:
- The game has zero depth
- Looks apparently impossible but is actually extremely simple after learning two tricks
- After that, it becomes a long, tedious journey keeping the left mouse button (attack) clicked all the time.
- Graphics are very generic
- Monsters can spawn and stay out of the boundaries of the level
- When you win, you are rewarded by a ``victory'' writing enclosed in a square. Really.
At the beginning the game looks very challenging because thousands of enemies come to you and you die very quickly. It looks like the only purpose of the game is you accumulating ``money'' to invest in better characters. However, after you realize that leveling up makes you way stronger than investing money in your character, you can just obtain the right objects to level up fast and grind your way through the floors.
It does not help that, every time you save, you lose your progress on the current floor and have to kill all the enemies again, but keep your level. Thus, you can actually trick the game and become insanely powerful just by loading, killing monsters for a while, saving, starting killing monsters again.
I spent several hours on this while thinking about something else, just for the sake of beating it. So I guess the joke's on me.

Overture is a rogue-like game in which you kill hordes of enemies by just walking around, holding your mousebutton and aim in the direction of where the enemies are coming from.
Basically a game doesn't get any more simplified except if you count 'clicker games' but when playing this game you are not far off from that level.
I guess this game could best be described as a combination between 'Hero Siege' and 'Real Of The Mad God', which are not my favourite kind of games but at least they gave me some kind of enjoyment. Overture is unsatisfying to play and feels like a chore.
Apparently it seems this kind of game is considered 'fun' nowadays if you look at the Very Positive rating but I doubt anyone who has played games with more substance would enjoy this one. It surprises me the developer even dares to say this is inspired by games like Diablo, Zelda and The Binding Of Isaac because I don't really see the connection there.
If you get enjoyment out of grinding for hours and hours this might be a game for you. If not, I would stay away from this one.

Overture is most likely a grinding game, as you have to put a lot of time in this game in order to attempt to finish it. However, considering the fact that most of the indie games are not having quite a big action, Overture is very dynamic as in each floor you have to kill hordes of monsters, which in not quite easy as the number of incoming monsters is quite big and you have to pay a lot of attention to the game in order to not die, cause if you die you will have to start the game all over again from the very first Floor. Also, the Boss Battles have a certain difficulty level which makes the game progression much interesting.
So, which are the Pros for this game?
- A cute and colored design, design which changes from a floor to another
- A big variety of enemies
-  24 heroes to choose
-  The possiblity to upgrade your hero
-  The player can collect items during game progression
-  Entertaining soundtrack
- Traps which hide extra hordes of enemies
Of course, there are some Cons for this Overture as well:
- Some visual effecs might be disturbing (for example, when your hero takes damage from enemies there is a kinda strong visual impact on the screen)
- Perhaps there would've be nice if there was a story line for this game
So Overture is pretty much funny to play and I recommend this game to anyone.

Directions:

2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Great game and very addictive. Well worth the money for the amount of time you will spend playing this. Lots of different blocks/parts to use to create almost anything you could imagine. Let your creativity go crazy. Building rockets and robots is always fun. Has everything that i wished minecraft had. This game has replaced minecraft for me. Looking forward to the "survival" mode where the farm bots etc are involved.
Only problem i have come across is sometimes you can accidentally make a run away rocket/car. If you accidentally delete the drivers seat depending on how you have setup the activation for the thrusters or engine it can run away on you. If you are lucky it will get stuck in a tree and you can retrieve it using the lift to capture it, other times it is gone for good such as in the case of a run away rocket dissaprearing into the sky. This can be funny as you try to chase your runaway creation but othertimes it can be frustrating if you have spent a long time perfecting it. Lesson learnt though, dont delete the drivers seat unlesss its attached to the lift.
Theres some interesting features that make the engineering side of things more realistic. Such as needing to consider weight vs power. For example one thruster may be able to launch a small craft, while if you build something heavy out of steel blocks then it will not and you will either need more thrusters or to reduce the weight. I have also noticed this happening with bearings used for moving parts such as doors etc. If it is a big heavy door made of steel blocks the single bearing may not have the power to lift it. Your options are then to create some sort of assistive mechanism or to recude the weight by replacing some steel blocks with something such as the medium weight beams or the light weight wooden blocks.
The weight balance can also affect your creations in other ways too. For example having lots of heavy blocks at the front of a flying craft and not much weight in the rear will cause it to nose dive. These little details mean you need to think more about balancing things out or adding counter weights.
All these extra features are not immediately apparent, and while the game can be simple, if you choose to optimise your creations then it can actually be quite deep thanks to these extra physics elements. Since there are ways to optimise your vehicles it would be nice to have a speedometer perhaps as part of the HUD when you enter a drivers seat so that there is a more measurable way to see what difference you may be making. eg. If you were trying to make the fastest car possible.
