On A Roll is a short, low budget 2.5D platformer with obvious Sonic the Hedgehog influences. To the game's credit, it manages to incorporate elements of the Sonic games without ever feeling like a clone. It's definitely more inspiration than copying wholesale. The controls are also spot on. Movement with a 360 controller feels very tight and precise, and I never had trouble getting my character where I intended for it to be. Graphics are a big area where this game falls short. It doesn't look quite as bad in motion as the trailer makes it look, but that's not exactly a big compliment. The use of simple shapes for characters feels lazy, and the background elements aren't much better. On top of not having well put together graphics, I've also encountered some very obvious shadow glitching through large sections of the game. Not sure if this is a universal problem or specific to my rig, it doesn't break the experience, but it definitely doesn't add to the feeling of this being a well made and polished game.
Level design is actually quite solid, surprisingly so given how low budget the game feels. There's a mix of straightforward platforming and light physics puzzles. I'm not generally a fan of puzzle platformers, but here those elements are pretty innocuous. It's genuinely a fun game to play and there's far worse platformers on Steam. Music is decent too, if repetitive. The light and cutesy tone of the soundtrack fits with the feel of the game. The game only has partial controller support out of the box for a 360 controller, which is hard to forgive in a 2015 game, especially a platformer. The majority of the game can be handled with a controller just fine, but using menus and resetting the positions of movable objects both require a keyboard.
On A Roll made me smile, which is more than I can say for a lot of games in my library, even ones that are objectively better than this. If you grew up playing 2.5D games like Pandemonium, you should get a kick out of it. The game touches on nostalgia buttons that I didn't realize I had, and while the execution could use improvement, seeing an homage to that style of game feels good. It's only a few hours long, but for the very modest price that seems fair. For many people, the low quality graphics and being yet another puzzle platformer on Steam is going to be a dealbreaker, but if you've read this far and are still actually interested, you could definitely do a lot worse for your money. On A Roll may not be winning any game of the year awards, but it is enough fun to be worth looking past the flaws, especially if you're nostalgic for PS1 era 2.5D platformers.

Your typical AAA title nowadays - good graphics, awful game in every other way.
My brother purchased this for me as a birthday gift. We have played a good few hours together now and I have concluded that the game is somewhat enjoyable. Not because it's a good game, however, but because it is absolutely hilarious to witness such sh*t.
The story:
Absolutely ridiculous story with incredibly boring characters. At the beginning of the game, after visiting an asylum, you leave to find what looks like the beginning of an apocalypse. Buildings are on fire and sh*t and there is even one of those giant cracks in the earth (I have no idea what they're called, but its used in loads of those stupid action/thriller movies). The story is just so far fetched that I assume the entire story happened in his imagination (I am yet to finish the game). Nevertheless, the devastatingly bad story does have its advantage as it provides several hilarious and cringy moments for you to laugh at.
The voice acting:
All of the voice acting is atrocious and extremely bland. There is no character development at all and the character you play as sounds way too calm, considering the situation. Also, the script is extremely amusing because it is, like the story, awful.
The gameplay:
Your character, despite being in the police force and, therefore, having completed demanding physical endurance tests, can run for about 2 seconds before stopping to catch a breather. Literally 2 seconds. This is not an exaggeration. However, fortunately for him, he can teleport through magic mirrors that take him to a hospital ward with an electric chair that injects green sh*t into his brain. He willingly chooses to take part in this process. After all, this injection of green filth directly into the brain can produce additional clothing pockets that can store extra ammo. Also, his stamina can be increased so that he can run for a remarkable 4 or 5 seconds without stopping.
In addition to this, the combat is appalling. Did you know that you can shoot half of an enemy's brain out with a weapon of your choice and he will continue to show signs of perfect cognitive ability. Well... I take that back. At times the enemies will run straight past you and stand around in a corner for a while. Also, the melee combat with bare fists consists of punching the enemy twice, then running away as he swings a really powerful backhander at you. Rinse and repeat that process about 3 or 4 times and you kill him.
Conclusion:
A bad game that's only real positive aspect is the comedy that can be found in its flaws.

The Evil Within is an old school kind of horror game.
Story 7 out of 10
You play a detective and are drawn into a strange world of gore and blood. The story is okay. Not really ground breaking.
Graphics 8 out of 10
I really like the graphics .The rays of light of a flashlight, the shadows, the water, the blood, even the pictures on the wall of just some random room are all done with a whole lot of love for detail. You can tell that somebody hat fun designing and programming the game.
Music 8 out of 10
There really is not a lot of music. But the sounds are perfect, the cracking of a door, the sizzling fire of a grotesque "bonfire" and the wood floor when you are trying to speak past an enemy.
Gameplay 7.5 of 10
I liked the fact that this game wasn't as easy as some other horror titles. There was a point in the game, when I faced a "boss" and had only 3 (!!) bullets left ....that was some tough battle! And I absolutely understand when some other gamers rate this game lower because of the sometime ridiculous difficulty. But that's how it is .Bullets are scarce, you are never going to be able to go gun wilding into a battle and it's always advised to sneak your way through the levels. I advise you to play with a controller, because it's way easier.
Overall Rating 8 out of 10
The game contains gore and blood and some really twisted and disturbing scenes that probably won't leave you unaffected. And may even stay with you after you're done with the game. The games difficulty might be a big turn off for some, while others may enjoy it (probably Dark Souls Gamers  ^.^ ) .Overall I would suggest this game for all mentally stable gamers over 18 years of age.

Disclaimer: I got into the beta and so received this game for free. I was never asked to make any sort of review and thus am reviewing it of my own free will.
This is a game where you use monster girl cards to battle your enemies. Battles take place on a 3x7 grid, where the left 3x3 grid is yours to freely place any card, and the right 3x3 grid is the enemy's. The cards represent a unit which means when you place the card on the board the unit appears. All units travel on the same row they are placed and cannot change rows. Your goal is to get any unit to the other side next to your enemy's base thereby damaging it by 1, regardless of the unit. At the end of your turn all your units move forward by 1 (except for newly placed units unless they have a certain ability). There are melee units, range, healers, and buffers which raise the attack of the first unit in front of them. You have mana which is needed to place cards and regenerates by 3 every time it's your turn. Placing cards of the same aura in a row is a must use tactic because of the great bonuses it gives. These battles are fun and tend to vary wildly depending on what cards you and the enemy use. This is really the only reason to play the game, therefore if battles don't look interesting then you probably should pass on this game because the story is forgettable.
The story is simplistic and not really that interesting until about the halfway mark. Something bad happens that threatens the world, so you have to go to the different cities to get a certain item before the villain does. Sometimes they agree and give it to you, other times they understandably don't give it to you so the villain comes and takes it just like you told them would happen. I found the characters uninteresting and the dialogue underwhelming; it's not bad by Compile Heart/IFI standards but not as good as say the Neptunia games (which aren't very good either in this regard compared to other JRPG games like Tales Of...).
How the gameplay works outside of battles is you have points you can move between on a map. You don't actually control a character and have them walk around. Moving to the different points on the map will initiate a battle, start a story event, give you an item, give you a card or card pack, give money, or give rub points.
Speaking of rub points, that's how you upgrade your cards. It's a minigame type thing where you click with the mouse or controller button on the picture of the card you are upgrading. It's best to look up a Youtube video of it... On pc it's rather pointless and just a waste of time. A skip button or something would be nice instead of an item you have to buy with real money (you can find it ingame but it's very rare). This game was originally on the Vita which had a touchscreen which makes this minigame have a little more sense there where you are rubbing the girls with your actual finger instead of a mouse pointer. Pro tip: use an ahk script (Google it, it's a safe and legit program) which causes you to rapidly click with a toggle. I'll link the script I use at the end of this review. Your click finger and mouse button will thank you. Also, when you upgrade your cards the girls lose more and more clothes :D, but nudity is never shown :(.
The problem with "upgrading" cards is that it's often not an upgrade at all. Attack and health will go down in favor of a useless skill or an ability you don't care for. However you can pass an ability from one card to another by fusing it with an already placed card of the same type. So that weak card that has awesome abilities (counterattack)? Fuse it with a strong card that has high attack and health and create an unstoppable unit!
Many cards will have skills on them. Skills cost mana to use and are automatically used when you place a card (but not when you fuse it with another card). So if you have 5 mana, a card that needs 3 mana to summon with a 2 mana skill, that card will use 5 mana when placed. It doesn't matter if the skill has no effect, it gets used anyway. And 9/10 times the skill will do nothing for you thus wasting mana. On the sort of plus side if you don't have the mana for the skill it won't get used. Therefore it's advised to place those cards when you have low mana so you don't waste it with worthless skills. I have no idea why they designed the game like this, fortunately the enemy is bound by the same rule.
+Battles are tons of fun and really the only reason to play this game.
+The music is nice as is usual for Compile Heart/IFI games.
+The card art is great, especially the newly uncensored cards.
+Plays well with either K&M or controller.
+-The story and characters are nothing special.
-Online multiplayer was not included for some reason. A real shame.
-Being unable to NOT use the skills on your cards thus saving you precious mana.
-The AI cheats just a little bit because in the mid game at the start of every match they always place certain cards that have skills which increase their mana, and in the late game they start also using cards that decrease your mana, always at the start. You too will be able to get those cards after you beat the final boss.
-Not a fan of the microtransactions to get rare cards using real money. It's not needed or anything and is easily ignored so that at least is good.
-You can't increase the resolution beyond your desktop's native res.

As a player of some previous Star Trek titles (among them Star Trek Voyager: Hazard Team and Star Trek: Starfleet Command Orion Pirates) I was relieved to see this finally come out as a free to play (mostly) game.
To be honest.... It's a good ST combat sim SHIP-wise.... It was reminiscent of STSFC: Orion Pirates, but with a 3D environment, and changeable ship components.... Which is pretty damn cool.
The downfall to this game is the somewhat clunky environments otherwise... like ship interiors (which are massive... Hallways feel more like gymnasiums) and the combat mechanics... It works somewhat like KOTOR, but not as well. You constantly beat down a barrage of enemies that are all the same, and just clustered to get in the way of your objective... And the missions are always linear...
In the series, ship captains are always making life/death decisions, finding diplomatic ways to resolve things, solving puzzles and trying to keep their crew alive in the face of danger. In the MMO, you are forced to either follow the ONE path, with no decisions on your part, or shoot all the enemies in the area to death before they do the same to you. No choice in the matter.
Regardless, the ship customization (name whatever you want, even) and having that customization stick, and be displayed... As well as the tedious but flexible system that allows you to earn in-game currency and use it to acquire things without breaking your wallet is pretty awesome. For the customization of characters and ships, as well as the ability to engage in good ship to ship combat (for the most part), I'd give this game a good rating.
...I'll just be staying off-planet for battles as much as I can.

Mount & Blade: Warband (along with its predecessor, Mount & Blade) is a game so unique it is difficult to fit it snugly into one category. It's an action RPG, it's grand strategy, it's a simulation, it's open world. This game is a whole bunch of things that melt so perfectly together, and it is unlike any other game I've ever played. For anyone who is even the slightest bit interested in medieval warfare, this is the game you never knew you wanted.
You start out by answering some simple questions about the life your character has lived thus far, and critiquing the way your heroine (or hero) looks. You are thrown into the large continent of Calradia which is split into six unique factions that are constantly at war with each other. The world map is familiar to those of us who enjoy grand strategy games; you can view the land and the castles/towns/villages/hideouts etc. that exist on it at any one time, while your character and her horse moves along it like a pawn on a gameboard. The colors of the names tell you which faction currently owns and controls each piece of land. What you begin to do from here is ultimately up to you. You can try doing favors for lords and kings to win their favor and ultimately work for them, whilst building up a small army of ragtag soldiers that you recruit and hire from various places, or you can be bold and try almost immediately to begin taking over land yourself (which I wouldn't recommend for the first dozen or so hours into the game).
Battles in this game are nothing short of amazing. Both warring sides start out on opposite ends of the map (I've never seen the same battlefield twice, by the way, so I believe they are randomized based on the terrain type you are currently traversing). You can issue commands to your army, and this is fun to mess around with. For example, you can tell your archers to stand their ground and your cavalry to charge the enemy, while giving a different order to infantry. It's all up to you. By default, all units will charge, and for the most part, this is sufficient. You will then meet your enemy in the battlefield, where cavalry can run over infantry, archers can shoot riders off of horses, and you can kill horses while their riders are still living, making them fall face first into the ground before swarming them. Basically, if you've ever seen two opposing sides charge in a movie and have felt that intensity and awe, you can actually play as one of those people involved in Mount & Blade, and each and every time it's amazing. This game is fantastic for nerds like me who love anything medieval; not only are there full out battles like this, but you eventually (and your army) get strong enough to take over castles, towns, etc., and you get to be one of the units that is a part of this, each and every single time.
The goal regardless seems to be to take over the entire map of land, whether through an existing faction or through your own, which you may create once you have a strong enough army to begin taking over land by force. Lords will double cross you, downright insult you, and even beg their respective kings for the rights to a castle you may have taken over yourself, and depending on the circumstance, you may or may not be jipped out of a piece of land you worked hard for. You can then, however, decide to accept that or give a one fingered salute to your king before renouncing your allegiance and going your own way. It is entirely up to you.
I would highly, highly recommend you play as a woman character, even if you are not a woman in real life. The game is fantastic at reflecting the negative attitudes toward women at the time, and those mentalities can highly influence you during the game. For example, I created a woman character and named her after myself, much like I did for the first Mount and Blade. I set about leveling up my character and recruiting soldiers, and picked up a mercenary contract for a faction. After taking over three castles single-handedly for the faction's king, I spoke to the king, introduced myself, and asked to be promoted to being his vassal. He told me outright that he didn't care what I had accomplished. Because I was a woman, I could not be his vassal, and I couldn't own land. I asked him what would happen if I took an enemy castle by force, and he replied that he would "think about" letting me keep it. This sexist attitude (although very realistic for the time) got me so fired up that I promptly cancelled my contract with the king and began taking over his land by force. After about 40 hours of in-game time, he was exiled from the land, his faction was extinct, and all of his land belonged to a new faction appropriately named "Rosie's Kingdom of Awesome." About 40 hours after that, I was Queen of Calradia. But it all started because of my motivation to overthrow an arrogant and sexist king as the woman he insulted, and no other game has done such a great job of inspiring me to create my own grudges and follow through on them until I conquered all.
This game is one of the most perfectly put together pieces of work I've ever played. I've seen people question the graphics, but I think the game is simplisticly beautiful (also, I grew up in the 90s--graphics don't matter to me). The game runs perfectly on my older non-gaming laptop, so that's also a plus for those of you looking for a large scale warfare game that can play on a toaster. There are some glitches, although nothing game-breaking (people spawned on the outside of a castle wall in 2/500 or so sieges I played, and I once had to sit out one siege because I fell through a crack in a floor of a castle tower and floated perpetually until my soldiers won the battle without me and I could exit). The character animations are a bit stiff, but I actually like them that way; it brings humor to the game for me, and if any future Mount & Blade doesn't have the stiff animations, I'll miss them.
Mount & Blade: Warband took 90 hours of my life away in the past week, and very few games can pull me in so relentlessly. This game is one of my personal favorites, along with Mount & Blade (I haven't tried With Fire & Sword yet, but it's only a matter of time). A solid 10/10 from me. Buy this game. Buy it now, and let it consume you. :)

Highly recommend this game as it is yet another example of the potential games have to immerse the player in a world unlike their own. And in Layers of Fear, the world you're taken to is full of darkness and insanity that lingers in the walls and bleeds through the carpet, beckoning you onwards throughout the game to taste its sweet horror.
Many of the comments point out how scary this game is. Personally, I agree it is scary but not like Amnesia scary (which on my scale is utterly terrifying). This game has a constant undertone of darkness and a nightmarish quality that bares its teeth all throughout the game, with moments of heightened terror which truly make the experience worthwhile while not being too terribly scary to be unable to play through it.
The voiceover, trinkets, and pieces of correspondence that you discover throughout the game provide a very well-rounded way of understanding the madness that struck the artist and how his colleagues around him reacted. The soundtrack is superb, and at one point I had to stop momentarily to enjoy the piece that played over a particular part of the game.
Overall, Layers of Fear overflows with beauty and tragedy, and I'm glad to have been able to experience this piece of art. To the developers: You're one of the good ones. Thank you for your ongoing contribution to indie games.

Nearly jumped right out of my tree from fright on several occasions, all in only a couple of hours playing. It's clear from the start where the game draws it's influences, and yet the inventiveness of the horrific imagery is consistently some of the best I have seen in a video game, so it really ends up setting itself apart from PT in the end. Where PT felt like a slow-burning horror mystery, Layers of Fear is the video game equivalent of a jaunt through an avant-garde haunted house. There are a few cheap jump scares that seemed to be thrown in randomly to get that "Five Nights at Freddy's" effect, but more often than not, you're just trudging through the fractured psyche of a hopelessly disturbed man, taking in his tragedy and feeling like your going through a bad acid trip. The story becomes pretty clear almost immediately, which I think is just fine. Though I like the story in a very...macabre sort of way, I respect that the developers opted to lay it out very quickly and openly so it didn't get in the way of the freaky set pieces, which is where the real strength of the game lies.
So all in all, Layers of Fear represents quite an impressive feat of design for such a small indie company, and I'm more than a little eager to play the rest of the game once it hits it's retail release. Even in it's current state, I would say give it a try. It's only going to get better.

HuniePop - A Dating Sim with full english VA?
For those who  are wondering what they are getting themselves into when purchasing such a game, I'd like to point out that the main gameplay element in HuniePop is it's Candy Crush style minigames where you align orbs (vertically or horizontally) in order to gain points. Unlike most date sims, you're not given dialogue during the actual dates themselves. Instead, you must reach a certan amount of points by completing the previously mentioned minigame in a certain amount of turns. While this detracts the game, the voice acting is suprisingly well done and it seems a fair amount of effort was put into the characters. Also, asides from the small conversations that you have when first meeting one of the eight female (love interest) characters, the chatting becomes rather monotonous once you've realized all you can do is ask these women about their personal information and background, and all they do is ask you seemingly random questions or quiz you on the information you've found out from them. Every now and then you get a text from your magical Hunie phone device, and these contain interesting or querky pics of the females (Great artwork!)
Pros:
Great art! You'll know what I mean when you see the texts messages ;)
Good voice acting! It's awesome to see a date sim with actual VA.
Unique characters! Each female has a different personality, with varying likes and dislikes which can take advantage of.
Cons:
You're constantly quizzed on information you've learned from talking to the ladies.
The dates (Pretty much the main part of a date sim) involve you winning a repetitive minigame.
Doesn't seem to be any other objective than just maxing out your relationships with the females by completing dates.
Important note: While the game is ecchi, it's definitely not eroge. If you're expecting H-action, don't go on steam.
TL;DR - Overall I'd give this game a 7/10. It's definitely worth checking out if you're into these kinds of games, but unless you reallly enjoy candy crush style minigames, it'll get boring quickly.

I bought this largely as a joke expecting a total wreck of a game but it's actually fairly entertaining.  I mean, you can't take it seriously; all the girls are basically caricatures and the conversations never rise above ludicrous but the mechanics are entertaining, there's some laughs to be had and the puzzles ramp up to be challenging (mind you, I never play puzzle games so maybe the Candy Crush masters will find this easy).  You meet girls, ask them questions, get asked questions and go on "dates" represented via the match-3 bubble puzzles where the personality of the girl affects the value of each bubble type (so one may value "Flirting" matches more and another "Talent" matches).  Your conversations are tempered by a constant need to buy food and gifts to keep her talking and the dates oddly give you the money you'll need to start all over again.  Eventually your night time dates can lead to bedtime frolicking represented by a "lightning round" style puzzle.
The game is unabashedly what is is and if you think you might be offended, you certainly will be so save your money.  If the trailer makes you laugh at either the dialogue or voice acting, you'll probably enjoy yourself for at least a while.  I don't know if the game will have a ton of staying power from a gaming standpoint (unless you want to collect a bunch of semi-naked pictures) but it's fun while it lasts.
Of special note is the musical score which is very catchy and well done.  It's rare that I notice game music enough to realize it and I found myself enjoying it multiple times throughout my playing.

The graphics are wonderful and the world modelling is simple but effective, the physics is tight, which for early access speaks volumes about the developer commitment.

Well done, this is exceptional, I look forward to whatever direction it is taken in.

The Evil Within is an old school kind of horror game.
Story 7 out of 10
You play a detective and are drawn into a strange world of gore and blood. The story is okay. Not really ground breaking.
Graphics 8 out of 10
I really like the graphics .The rays of light of a flashlight, the shadows, the water, the blood, even the pictures on the wall of just some random room are all done with a whole lot of love for detail. You can tell that somebody hat fun designing and programming the game.
Music 8 out of 10
There really is not a lot of music. But the sounds are perfect, the cracking of a door, the sizzling fire of a grotesque "bonfire" and the wood floor when you are trying to speak past an enemy.
Gameplay 7.5 of 10
I liked the fact that this game wasn't as easy as some other horror titles. There was a point in the game, when I faced a "boss" and had only 3 (!!) bullets left ....that was some tough battle! And I absolutely understand when some other gamers rate this game lower because of the sometime ridiculous difficulty. But that's how it is .Bullets are scarce, you are never going to be able to go gun wilding into a battle and it's always advised to sneak your way through the levels. I advise you to play with a controller, because it's way easier.
Overall Rating 8 out of 10
The game contains gore and blood and some really twisted and disturbing scenes that probably won't leave you unaffected. And may even stay with you after you're done with the game. The games difficulty might be a big turn off for some, while others may enjoy it (probably Dark Souls Gamers  ^.^ ) .Overall I would suggest this game for all mentally stable gamers over 18 years of age.

Deus Ex: The Fall started as a mobile game back in 2013, exclusive to iOS, implementing touch screen controls and mechanics that fit a first person shooter well enough to be entertaining on a phone or tablet, but it was never meant to be played with a mouse and keyboard. The later Android version offered the same experience, and with a great success on the mobile market, it wasn't long before a PC version was announced, a version that comes with almost no improvements, which for a PC title end up close to a catastrophe. You play as Ben Saxon, ex-military at Belltower who ended up joining a secret squad known as the Tyrants, with the mission of keeping balance between organizations and eliminating possible threats. It won't be long until Saxon will realize that most of the things that the Tyrants told him were lies and soon enough his departure from the team will put him on the most wanted list, forcing him to go into hiding. The adventure begins when Saxon and his partner Anna run out of Neuropozyne, a drug used to prevent Neuroprosthesis, a build-up of scar tissue that blocks electrical signals between augmentation electrodes and human tissue, making any augmented human being unable to live without it. The whole plot rattles around Saxon's search for Neuropozyne, following gang leaders and completing different tasks for people who might be able to supply them with Neuropozyne in exchange. Even though all those details will be unravelled in the first five to ten minutes of the game, that pretty much sums up the entire story, as it is a short one to begin with, taking no more than three hours to complete, and even worse than that when it does get to a point where it seems like its action will change and the story will move on to the next plot point, it just ends, leaving you with a true sense of disappointment as if you accomplished nothing.
As mentioned before, this was originally a mobile game, and in that environment it would play decently; on the big screen however, things change as almost no improvements have been made to adapt this title for a keyboard and mouse control scheme. The movement is pretty much limited to what a phone or tablet can offer, and there is even the lack of a jump button, even though this version clearly needed one. Navigating through the menus is a nightmare, as it was meant to work under swipe movements, now having to use the mouse in order to drag the menu items and get where you want, and even worse than that there are no shortcuts for important things you might want to access more frequently such as your Augmentations or your Inventory; instead the game uses the Esc key to open up an enormous menu and letting you choose what you want to do from there whether it's a simple Save command or upgrading one of your weapons, which proves to be difficult to do at times. This rushed port of touch screen mechanics makes your life even harder when it comes to things such as hacking, where you might not be able to move the screen to the point where you want it to be at all, making it challenging to solve the hack or just forcing you to spend your credits on an autohack just so you can move onward with the game. The cover mechanic is just as bad, refusing to work properly at times, making it hard to switch cover and make your way past some guards undetected, but since the AI is almost absent that is the least of your worries. On top of the terrible AI that allows you to take multiple enemies in a row down with a melee attack as long as you time it right, there is a long list of bugs and glitches that came with the port, starting with unreachable items and ending with the fact that I inexplicably fell through the map more than once by doing nothing apart from following the instructions.
This is just an upscaled version of a mobile game, which makes it a terrible looking game on the big screen, as the graphics seem outdated by an entire generation. On top of that we have the horrible animations, almost non-existent lip sync and facial animations of such detail you'd think this game was released on the N64. The visual effects are basic and even though they don't stand out as horrible since everything around them looks just as bad, they are still part of the same engine that looks outdated by a decade.
The voice acting is a really bad joke, as it lacks basic concepts such pitch and tonality, and sometimes it will switch volume inexplicably, probably to wake you up because everything that comes out of a character's mouth is so boring and pointless. The dialogue is just as badly written, and for some reason subtitles kept disappearing from time to time, even though the character was still talking right in front of me.
One simple playthrough can be completed in roughly three to four hours, add two more if you're staying for all the side quests and achievements, and since there is a New Game+ mode you can replay the entire game without starting all over again if you've missed some achievements on your first playthrough, but even with that in mind, there's isn't much else to do around a second time.
Deus Ex: The Fall was a pretty bad game to begin with, but on the small screen of a phone or a tablet it somehow seemed bearable and the actually working touch screen mechanics made it fun to play despite all its other flaws, but on PC that simply isn't the case as those flaws are still there and on top of that, the gameplay mechanics are not optimized to work on a mouse and keyboard, and sometimes not even optimized to work at all.

Let's be frank here.
This is Left 4 Dead.
An incredibly pretty Left 4 Dead with a stronger focus on melee combat, set in the Warhammer universe.
This has its ups and downs.
You kill rats. You kill rats across a bunch of stages, with a  cadre of I-hesitate-to-say 'stereotypes?' including an alcoholic soldier, a woman with an unhealthy appreciation for fire, a height-disadvantaged marksman, a sour well-dressed man, and 'an elf.'
These five-minus-one bop around (It's left 4 dead, remember?), killing rats with a menagerie of weapons ranging from eight kinds of bows, things that stab rats, things that cut rats, things that shoot rats, and things that burn them.
These are organized under a familiar tier system and, with the inclusion of a free DLC (Grab those, you really want those.), are recyclable and functional enough.
The good stuff :
- It's reaaally pretty. I like Skaven, I play them all the time in the tabletop, and you really have to admire just how 'good' they look, in that wonderfully
sort of way. You'll admire it when you're spinning around, decapitating and disemboweling too-friendly ratfolk by the dozen. Blood sprays and splatters, heads come off, and they have a wide variety of responses to their slaughter -- it really is like a sociopathic carnival ride.
- The combat works. It's fairly simple, but there's some nuance to it. Big frack-huge hammers and swords work on crowds if you do charging attacks, knives and rapiers turn slaverat 'ambushes' into something akin to dropping a handful of rodents in a large, angry blender. Certain weapons can off rougher targets quickly by nicking the head, some weapons couldn't care less. Bonus tip, for play as the Witch Hunter - go into the options, and check the controls for 'weapon special.' It'll be relevant.
- It's fun. Get four folks together, roll to which schmuck does what job, learn how to do said jobs. Forget how to do said jobs immediately, and wade chest-deep into the Vermintide shouting like mad-folk. Go on, get some blood on you, champ. You'll like it.
The less-good stuff :
- The loot system. It's janky. The free DLC attempts to aid this a bit, and it does. But it's still...janky.
Finish a mission, and you're rewarded with a chance to...play a dice game. You roll dice, you get a thing.
More accurately, you'll roll the dice, and get a thing for a class you aren't even playing.  Now you can turn this into 'other stuff,' but the recycling mechanic can also give you a thing for a class you're not even playing...that's pretty good.
You could argue it's to ease you into all the classes and keep you from dedicating yourself to just one like a spoilsport. You can also argue it's stupid and dumb, and you wouldn't be wrong. It's really up to you, you just have to ready to say "Oh, thanks for that white Dwarven hammer, game, especially as a reward for my hard-mode bot-only double-grimoire run."
- The physics, sometimes. They're janky. Sometimes. They're either a bug or a feature, depending on how hard they make you laugh, or if you ever see them at all (you'll probably see them.) I've see them a few times.
- The levels. From what I've played so far, the quality of stages can range from "Alright" and "Bretty gud" to "backwater fairground corn maze from Hell." You're going to memorize them or you're going to play them once, per difficulty, and never touch them again. Also, the Point-of-No-Return™ is sort of dumb; slightly-tall wall, broken stairs, inconvenient rock? Can't go back. Sorry, too bad. Usually it's no problem -- until the game decides to drop a Packmaster behind you and grab the last person over the ledge.
Trust me.
The really bad stuff.
- Bot AI.
Grab your friends, or make new ones, because the AI for private matches doesn't wanna be your friend. It doesn't wanna do anything, for that matter.
I'd compare it to Payday 2 Bots, but that wouldn't be fair to this game - they're almost as stupid, but they CAN get things done; in combat, you'll be fascinated by their incredibly sporadic competence. One moment, they're unable to deal with three basic rodents shivving their ankles. Next, they're triple-headshotting Special vermin before they can even engage your group. And then they stare at a wall, blankly, as you desperately try to get them to pick up a collectable, or getting caught by 'disabling' enemies after you've passed a Point-of-No-Return™ with frightening regularity.
It's pretty good, if it goes on sale be sure to grab it. Bring friends, you need those. Grab the free DLC, you need that.

This game isn't as bad as everybody is making it seem. Sure if you expect a whole new game with upto 30+ hours of gameplay you are going to be dissapointed. The game isn't perfect and it has it's share of good and bad issues. Which I shall go into.
The game runs smoothly at a pretty decent rate. (I have a plebtier PC) and there wasn't any framerates issues throughout the entire game. The game was smooth from start to finish.
The HUD is pretty clean. It's got a few obvious touch screen elements that shouldn't really be there. Drop down menu's and a rather unusual ingame store (using ingame money). Overall the HUD is better than I've seen from other ports.
The audio, the ingame music is pretty decent. Fairly similiar to Deus Ex:Human Revelution. It's very close to DXHR although it's not exactly the same. It's a very much welcome addition to somebody that enjoyed the soundtrack to Deus EX.
The voice acting is so-so. It seems to fluctuate between the characters, depending on how important or the screentime they have, The main protagonist I feel has a decent amount of quality. However the training mission instructor is absoluetly terrible. She's rather dull and boring. Speaking with one tone. Just readling lines off of a script with absolutely no emotion what so ever.
However sometimes the audio in game skips and jumps. Sounds get repeated or the audio mutes itself for two seconds. I also personally found the ambient sounds to be annoying but that's just a niggle I have.
The background music was also louder than everything else. I guess they wanted to cover up the bad voice acting. Luckily you can change that in the menu settings. The setting aren't great either to be honest. It's got audio setting and reset your data but there isn't one for brightness and this game really needs that. I was bumbling along for a bit in some places.
The levels are split into short sections, this requires a lot of loading, luckily the loading only takes a few seconds but it all adds up. It could've been better but at least it's short.
The cutscenes are pausable which I haven't seen too often in games, so it's good that you are able to pause the game and it's slightly difficult to accidentally skip the cutscene if you want to resume the game. The orange glow used for items and 'hints' are still visible in the cutscenes which is really distracting and I personally find it annoying. You maybe able to overlook it though.
Unless you turn the Autosave feature off. Due to the fact that there is only one save slot that both you and the autosave is supposed to use.
Technical problems.
Whilst I was playing I found that the mouse would get stuck in the centre of the screen which then made it impossible to look or aim. Minimizing the game helped fix that issue.
The buttons in game for the menu aren't always responsive, sometimes you have to click on it more than once and some times upto 3 times.
Whenever I performed a takedown the entire world would flicker and drop out (during the cutscene) this happened mostly in tight places but seemed to be entirely random.

Once you kill or knockout an enemy they just fizzle away into orange triangles and then vanish. Which makes stealthing this game so easy that it's a joke. If you are used to playing MGS on the hardest whilst going for a complete stealth run. This is going to be like 'Baby's first stealth game'
This isn't really an issue but it's pretty damn lazy, all of the animations have been recycled from DX:HR. The game also ends on a cliffhanging telling you that more is coming. Which I highly doubt by now.
Overal, it's a nice little package. It's not great and it definetly has it's fair share of issues, However if you can get it cheap during a sale and you like Deus Ex, I'd suggest picking it up.

The first Hotline Miami was inspired by many things, such as a documentary of "Cocaine Cowboys" giving them the inspiration to do the game in a Miami setting. The movie: "Drive" that was released in 2011 and the use of masks came from the film "Kick♥♥♥♥♥"
Unlike the first game, some characters don't wear masks. Not only does this help make the levels more interesting (and incredibly hard), but it makes sense narrative-wise.
It took me almost 50 hours to complete the game normally, get A+ on all normal levels AND complete the game on hard-mode. I was shouting and cursing at my screen so much over this game, that I can't even count how many times my mam has had to ask my to be quiet. But since I like games that challenge my abilities, it has only made me want to go back to it! 100/100!

While it may not be to many people's liking (FOV issues, the letterbox format, etc), I must admit I enjoyed the game.
The story itself ranges from "passable" to "quite impressive", with many of the latter chapters making up for the terrible writing at the beginning. If you stick with it, you will probably quite like it!
Gameplay wise, it is very close to RE4, albeit not as well-balanced as that, and on occasion you will die purely because of the controls being a tad "slow", but in many cases your death will be because you didn't watch your surroundings, you didn't hide in time or you simply got a bit too careless.
The soundtrack leaves a lot to be desired, sadly, with many of the chapters making use of the same background music, or on occasion none at all, which doesn't necessarily make sense and it just missing.
The environments on the other hand are mostly really well done, some of the levels are really well thought-out and tie in together very well. There are a few instances where textures are still loading in (due to the game, not the hardware) which distract a little, but other than that the environments are great.
The game has gotten a lot of mixed reviews. Personally I liked it a lot once I got towards the middle of the game, so I urge you to stick with it and you'll hopefully enjoy it.
The single player campaign can be completed in around 7-9h, it is worth replaying in my opinion, you get a couple more decent weapons, and you can collect a lot more hidden extras. I urge you to find all the map pieces, you might like the outcome ;)
The DLC itself is okay and adds a bit more to the main story as you are getting to know the main characters a bit better and see their experiences in this nightmare. It can be finished in a few hours.

So after watching the game through an LP-er, I couldn't believe all the things that I missed that makes this game soooo much worse than I originally thought. I mainly missed these as I was playing through this game personally and was too focused on the fact this game was so boring, i wanted it to end asap. I just cannot let it go and must write something about it, such as this review. Lets get down to it, if you are a fan of horror games and haven't played this, please pass on this; you already have played this game. Otherwise, get it on sale or even better, watch a longplay of it online, you'll get the same experience.
Pros:
Graphics are pretty sweet (awesome asthetics and cool effects here and there)
Cons:
Combat is very clunky (Take over-the-shoulder but make it worse)
Plot is all over the place and very unoriginal, even illogical at times (It actually makes no sense whatsoever)
RPG and crafting elements are kept to a bare minimal (crafting only affects one weapon, and the RPG elements involve just getting upgrades)
Gameplay is very repetitive (go from point A to Point B and shoot people, barely any puzzles in the game and the bosses all feel the same)
Extremely Linear
A lot of this is inspirripped from other games (Almost all of it is like: Silent Hill, Resident evil, Cry of Fear, Dark Souls, etc.)
Checkpoint System.... enough said
Neither Pro/Con:
Voice Acting is ok (Some bad spots, some good spots)
Atmosphere is there for a bit (A lot of graphical, scary looking monsters are in the game but they aren't scary)
Extensive Review begins here, Shorter version down bottom:
Their are 3 core things (personally for me) to making a good horror game: Gameplay (Can you scare the player?), Atmosphere (Can you provide a dreaded setting for the player?), and immersion (Can you get the player to be involved and invested into the world?). If you fail in all 3, then its not a good horror game. You can fail in 1 or 2, but not all 3. Lets start with Gameplay.
Gameplay:
Gameplay in this game boils down to a single thing. Run from Point A to Point B, shoot some dudes or run away from some dudes. Their are too few, simple puzzles throughout the game and essentially, you'll just be running and gunning throughout. You have your same generic, cloned zombies for minions with boss fights that are similar throughout the game. They are huge, and have insta-kill moves. Its hard to feel like you have an actual health system unless you are fighting zombies. The only uniqueness in the bosses is their use of the environment and how they interact with it such as using mines or destroying hiding places. Overall, you'll just be running in a straight line from point A to Point B, shooting some zombies and moving on to the next chapter. This game takes repetition to insane levels. A lot of the boss fights are reminiscient from other games like safebox man (pyramidhead), chainsaw man (other games), generic spider boss...ughhhhhh, can we have some originality please? Checkpoint system is very poorly done alongside a saving point that is only accessed through mirrors placed throughout the game. Literally, you'll have done the parts necessary to progress, you die to those instant kill moves and you are FORCED to go through all that same part again....WHO DOES THIS ANYMORE? Come on... how does that equate to a fun experience? That is only going to cause more frustration than you want to bring to a player that is trying to enjoy the game.
The Crafting/RPG system is very small and minimal. RPG boils down to simple upgrades while crafting is just making more ammo for the crossbow.... sooo creative. They literally went sooo bloody basic on everything here, its ashame to even bother including them. Would have been better to just give set numbers. Oh, lets mess with the protagonist's head and he'll suddenly realize he can carry more ammo or sprint farther... Yes because messing with the brain increases the strength of your character and makes your weapons stronger.... not like making custom parts for weapons or other ways of crafting or including RPG elements. Nope, got to do it basic and bland way of magically making everything just work through one button press and some juicy green gel... Lame and lazy.
Plot:
This plot has to be one of the worst plots I have ever experienced in a game. A lot of it is just, why are you doing this or why is this happening? None of this though is even explained until the very end where you will probably have lost any interest in caring by that point. You'll be invested to start with, then be confused for the next 14 chapters until the end where you find out that the plot is completely stupid by that point. The plot twist will make you wonder how this game even exists to begin with. A lot of the characters are very bland, uninspired and not much developed or cared for throughout the game. They will be there one chapter, then disappear for the next 5 chapters, then just die or do something stupid later for plot convenience. Honestly, just forget this game even had a plot to begin with and just continue walking in that straight line until you hit the next chapter... oooh so scary -_-.
Atmosphere and immersion:
A good horror game can get you involved in the game and make you fear your environments, making you dread what could be out there. This game fails at this sooo poorly with its frustrating mechanics, its horrible plot and its underdeveloped characters. Its very hard to be even involved or invested into the game when you are too busy just wanting the next chapter to just show up so you can complete the game as quickly as possible. Without investment, you aren't gonna be immersed into the game and the scary/horror parts are just gonna be huge nuisance. Overall, it has some horror elements but they are the same thing as any other horror game. Oversized humanoids, strange looking creatures, mixed-creatures like the spiderlady or Dog-looking creature.
Everything Else:
Graphics are pretty which is where I think all the money went. Making the game look as dazzling as ever while giving little attention to the gameplay sections. Honestly, did the developers ever play through their game and think "Hmmmm... does this equate to a fun, good gameplay?" Don't think so.
Shorten version (didn't realize reviews had a character limit ;_;):
If you enjoy walking down long hallways while occasionally fighting an enemy or 2 with the same tactics coughcoughFFXIIIcoughcough, that throws in random horrific looking enemys, then wait for a sale and try this game then. Otherwise, its just a very weakly developed game that should have spent more time in development to polish out those weak parts. Gameplay is just so bland and weak and the story needed better writing.

A masterful game and a refreshing title in a very confused genre. Mikami revolutionizes many ideas present in Resident Evil 4, and brings back a great, sinister, brooding world, ready to end you at any moment. This is not a return to classic survival horror, nor should it be. It is the next step forward in the ideas Mikami intially created. In my opinion, this is a high quality game, and I haven't enjoyed a survial horror title of this caliber since Dead Space 2. The Akumu difficulty does show some flaws in the gameplay, that if fine tuned a tad more, would cause less frustration on the higher difficulties. However, it is still extremely rewarding upon completion. This game may not be the "scariest", but it has some incredibly tense moments and chapters (ie Chapter 4,7,9 etc), that are blended very well with the less intense moments. I highly recommend this game and hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

Overture is the first roguelike I've ever played (excluding about ten minutes of NetHack) and it is definitely an amazing first foray into the genre. Overture's gameplay is fast-paced and demanding; though boss fights can become frustrating, the joy received when the boss is finally killed is unparalleled. The class variety in this game is also appreciated. There are four class groups (the classic RPG archetypes; warrior, mage, rogue, and shaman), each of which contains six classes making for a grand total of 24 classes. While the classes are all fairly basic (one primary attack, one secondary attack) and some feel similar, they're all just varied enough to give the game a different feel when you play through it with different classes. All in all, this is an outstanding game and well worth your money.

I have had a blast playing this game. I started playing because of the similarities to left 4 dead, but there are so many other features unique to this game that have grown on me as I've continued to play. The setting is much more thematic than Left 4 dead. Rolling and getting a new weapon is always kind of fun.  The Patrols add an added level of alarm, especially if they show up in a tight hallway, and it makes you feel accomplished if you come out on top from one of their attacks. The uniqueness of each playable character adds a bit of importance to how you play with your team members. I would say the difficulty is a step up from that of Left 4 dead as well. Perhaps the only complaint I really have is with disconnect during game play. it's not a deal-breaker for me, but it can be a pain to be fairly close to completion of a campaign only to have the host disconnect. The community is pretty friendly from my personal experience, and it's fun to be able to share strategies back and forth with other people.
I would recommend not playing on easy your first time through, ultimately easy will probably be harder for you. I don't see much difference in difficulty from easy and Hard, (except for better loot options upon completion in hard.) I would suggest starting at a bit harder difficulty because you will  be able to more easily find players willing to join your game. (They want better loot too.) This will help you learn strategies from slightly more seasoned players, and you are more likely to finish the campaign playing with these players.

I'm one of the many mourning the loss of P.T. and Silent Hills, but after multiple playthroughs of Layers of Fear, I have to say that it is truly the 2015 replacement for P.T. at the very least. What makes this game so special, is that it doesn't NEED P.T. or Silent Hills to be an amazing piece of art, it just is!
Excellent gameplay, beautiful visuals and plenty of spookiness make Layers of Fear more than just a clone, and even in its present short form, it has plenty of story and mystery to go around. I've been intrigued with the ever shifting environment, and am thrilled to see that in a game, because so many horror games rely on "Boo" scares rather than eerie images and situations.
I'm anxiously awaiting new areas and new frights, but believe me, I'm loving what's there so far! Talk about pushing Unity to its limits!
One minor gripe would be that the 9/30/15 update took away one of my favorite features wich was using the left mouse to pick an object up, and right mouse to put it back (it was also like that for reading documents, although I loved the addition of text, because there were a few notes that I couldn't understand the handwriting!). But honestly, I can live without it!
All in all, it's the best horror game I've played since P.T. and believe me, coming from me, that's saying something!

Unfortunately, this review won't be filled with references to ♥♥♥♥♥s, hos, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥hos, and nobody's ♥♥♥♥♥-feelings are going to be hurt. I've taken a serious look at this game from every angle, and it's a disappointment.
Basically the goal of Huniepop is to have sex. This is accomplished through a combination of telling women exactly what they want to hear, giving them gifts, and then playing a match three puzzle game until their panties drop. There are nine women, all with their own occupations, personalities, nationalities, interests, and so on. Compared to other dating-sims however, this game is amateur-hour.
One of the notable things about the Huniepop video that gets passed around (you know which one), after Audrey has her spit-off with Kyanna, she demands that you take the receipt and get her money back. This isn't in the actual game! Also, a menu appears where you had various options (like working a job). This is common in dating-sims as there's a schedule, time-management, etc. This also isn't in the actual game! Let's consider this:
Audrey: "Take the receipt and get my ♥♥♥♥in' money back from that ugly ♥♥♥♥♥-♥♥♥♥♥."
You: "Okay fine" (walk into the salon)
Kyanna: "Hello! Can I help you?"
You: " Yes, I...   (Now you can choose between arguing over the receipt, using the opportunity to flirt with Kyanna, maybe you could talk crap about Audrey behind her back)
Nothing remotely close to this happens in HuniePop. This why they're called missed opportunities. Aside from a brief introduction, there aren't any more character interactions. There isn't any character-development either. I'm probably expecting too much from a "digital waifu" but what can I say? It's appealing to see someone (however fictional) grow as a person. Audrey has a drug-problem, Nikki is anti-social, two of the women are single parents, and absolutely nothing is done with it. All you have to do is memorize their likes and dislikes, buy the appropriate items, and you're in there like swimwear. Nothing ever changes, and after the first hour you're just going through the motions.
The puzzle game is what it is. There's not much to say about really. A bit of strategy is required, since you must collect a certain number of points with a limited amount of moves. There are also special items that cause various effects, and they're awarded through finding the right gifts for the ladies. It's entertaining, but nothing special.
Admittedly, I've played some weird games. The one thing they all had in common though was that there was always some sort of challenge, a goal that couldn't easily be met. In True Love (NSFW PC Game, not unlike this one), I had to manage my schedule, work out, do my homework, and know what to say to raise a person's affection level. Style Savvy: Trendsetters basically required that I paid attention to details, thought outside the box, and made intelligent decisions. Even Dead Or Alive Xtreme Beach Volleyball required serious effort or else my expensive gifts would get tossed in the garbage. I couldn't care less if Tina wore the million-dollar-postage-stamp-bikini I purchased for her, but I'll be damned if she's gonna do me raw by ditching it the very next night. What makes a dating-sim -- or a game with dating-sim elements -- work is that you're not playing for the fanservice, the cheese-cake, or the naughty bits. You're playing to win.
I guess that's why I can't appreciate HuniePop for what it is. After you look past the f-bombs you're stuck with a bog-standard experience. Nothing ever really changes or becomes interesting. Just once I wish Jessie would stop asking questions about me and mention SOMETHING about her 20 year-old daughter. Instead all I can do is ask about her weight, her age, or her cup-size. I mean WTF..I...ah forget it. I better quit before I start drinking again.

I spent a lot of time deciding whether to give this game a positive or negative review. Overture isn't a
game, but it definitely isn't a good one.
Overture is a hoard-time grinding game. No, not a dungeon crawler. No, not a puzzle game. No, not an RPG. This is a grinding game. Progressing in this game isn't determined by skill, choices, or even luck, but how much time you're willing to put into this game, which honestly isn't worth it. You will NOT be able to clear this game without grinding for what seems like forever.
You collect gold in each stage, gold is used to unlock/purchase or level up a character of your choice, which becomes more expensive each time. I've only put a little over an hour into this game and even then, I had to force myself to keep playing. The only difference between floors is that enemies have more health as you progress.

When you think of a shooter game a medieval-theme is the last thing you expect.. But that's exactly what Black Shell Games's game Overture is: a roguelike bullet hell shooter game where you're tasked to destroy legions upon legions of monsters while things constantly fly across your screen. It's a high action, fast paced game that'll leave you blinded by damage scores and the amount of chaos going on screen.
The objective of the game is to get through the floors while fighting amidst countless enemies such as skeletons, dragons, blobs, and minotaur. There's an insane variety of creatures throughout the game. Occasionally you'll see named creatures, which have the chance of giving the player special gear, health potions and a bonus in gold which also acts as your XP, doubling their values. The named creatures do have slightly more health and are often guarded by a cluster of creatures, which means they're hard to get to, but they're worth it in the end. Each creature has a comically randomly generated name like “Hilda the Disgruntled” or something of that nature, leaving this bullet hell style game a least a little humorous.

An absolutely fantastic horror game on par with the likes of P.T. and Amnesia
Definitely worth the price.

Incredible horror experience :D Loved every minute of it! I've been playing this game since it went on Early Access and have now played the full version beginning to end.
GRAPHICS
Absolutely superb. Brilliant use of lighting and shadows. Simply put some of the best interior graphics I've seen, perhaps only beaten by the legendary P.T.
However playing with a triple screen set up (5760x1080) isn't perfect. For one getting close to walls with 3 screens causes the camera but not the player to clip through. This does not happen with traditional resolutions.
Also with 3 screens microstuttering is a serious issue and the game can't hit 60 FPS (Intel Core i7 4790K, GTX 980 Ti, 8 GB RAM). It hovers in the 45-50 FPS range but feels like 15 because of the stuttering. Again, not at all an issue at normal resolutions. Microstuttering remains an issue in the full release as well even at 1920x1080.
SOUND
Mostly good, very rarely rather bad, often exceptional but honestly 95% of the time it's just generic horror game type sounds. Lots of sudden loud sounds used for jump scares. However there are maybe 4 or 5 sound effects that really sounded bad to me. Fortunately they're quick and non-looping sounds. The music is exceptional and sets the mood brilliantly. They actually do some really cool stuff with music in the game.
CONTROLS
They do the job well but are a bit erratic. You'll be looking around steadily then suddenly it accelerates really fast. It's really not that bad but these are not CoD or Halo controls. Also it's not uncommon to get stuck on small objects.
SCARES
A nearly even mix of psychological and jump scares... and man are there a LOT of both! This isn't your traditional horror game where you'll have to wait an hour or two for the scares to start. It's pretty much right off the bat with Layers of Fear. There's plenty of really messed up imagry that works REALLY well. There's also a lot of jump scares that are surprisingly well crafted given how common they are in this game. Even at the very end the jumps feel fresh and unexpected.
Regrattably I don't get that sense of dread I get with games like P.T. and Amnesia. Layers of Fear is more like a very colorful and really bad acid trip. Also, while creepy (monster spoilers ahead) the ghost feels like a direct copy and paste of Lisa from P.T. in both the way she looks and moves and in the way she kills you but with naked boobies (I seem to recall reading that this was deliberate but I'm not sure)
One problem that I had with the game prerelease was that the scares were just packed WAY too close together. This has been mostly fixed but not completely. Particularly towards the end it feels like the scares are happening one right after the other diminishing the effect.
GAMEPLAY
There really isn't any. There are some relatively simple yet clever puzzles and a few scavenger hunts but that's it. There's no combat, no hiding, no inventory ect. This game is definitely a "walking simulator" but damn is it a good one!
STORY
Decent. It's told almost completely through hidden and optional newspaper clippings and notes so what you get out of the story depends on how much you like to explore and read. If you DO take your time and look around I thought the characters were very interesting. The story isn't going to blow you away but I did find that I wanted to know what happened and the story definitely added to the messed up mood the game is going for.
REPLAY VALUE
Limited however this game is just PACKED with detail. Even more detail than P.T. It's the type of game where you will definitely notice something different each time you play. I played through each of the prerelease versions multiple times and it always felt fresh even though it was the same. And with the full release they've added a TON more content. There's also quite a bit of notes, newspaper clippings and drawings to find.
WHO IS THIS GAME FOR?
For: P.T, Amnesia, SOMA, Paranormal Activity, Blair Witch, Haunted House fans.
NOT for: Dead Space, Walking Dead, Alien Isolation, Slasher, Action fans.
RECAP
Definitely loved going through this and will do so again... and again and again and again! There are better, more complete horror games out there such as P.T, Amnesia: The Dark Descent and SOMA but this game is miles ahead of most AAA "horror" action games and quite a few steps above most of the indie offerings on Steam. 4.5/10 An absolute masterpiece and a must have for fans of less actiony horror games.

This game was absolutely amazing. After trying other horror games and be outright disappointed or uninterested this game finally gets it. It has the perfect mix of an erie and detailed story but just enough to leave you hanging and every “clue” unravels a piece of the puzzle. As stated before, I’ve tried multiple other horror games and was very unsatisfied however this has the perfect blend of not being too much of a “try hard” (In which there are very predictable jump scares at every corner and usually not creative ones at the least) and having very ingenious and unexpected scares. This game is also very, very atmospheric with eerie things such the rooms changing (I know this doesn’t sound scary now but just wait, this becomes such a mind ♥♥♥♥!) and paintings altering in some way. The “monsters” of the game are very explained through the story (unlike multiple other horror games like Amnesia) which adds to their overall creepiness and makes you blend with your characters thoughts, guilt and anger throughout the story. And the monster, where most horror games fail to do well at is in no way a disappointment to an incredible lead up. Now relating back the overall story, this is possible one of my favorite things about the game because it gives you an outline; a fuzzy portion of the truth that YOU can focus into and what YOU want it to be. This game makes you cringing at every corner. Constantly on the edge of your seat, nervous as hell for the next thing, whatever it may be and turning around every 10 seconds to see if the world around you is still familiar. This game is beautiful and being in EA it’s great to contribute to its work (and don’t forget to mention that it’s only 10 dollars when it’s worth more than 60) I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is interested or wary about spending money on a horror game. This one is nothing like you have ever played. At the end you feel your character's insanity, their guilt and problems like they are your own and leaves you wanting more. I would like to also thank the creators for making this masterpiece. Keep stuff like this coming guys, it’s amazing!

It's, uh. How do I put this.
I showed this to my friends because I thought it was a train wreck of a game, yeah? Turns out one of them had enough disposable income and enough deep seated hatred of me to actually buy it out of the blue for me.
My screams of anguish echoing through the house, I installed it while he cackled maniacally in my ear. Then, through Steam's wonderful beta features, I streamed it and he watched me play.
I won't lie: It's a funny game. Throw all the logic you've got stored in your brain case out, and it's good for that at least. The puzzles ramp up strangely well, though really, I'm ♥♥♥♥ing awful at games like that and am not a good metric for the difficulty of them in the slightest. There's racism, specifically from your bubblegum fairy friend, and all the girls are less human beings and more charicatures of what certain human cliques are supposed to be, but that's alright: It makes it even funnier, as long as you don't take it seriously. By the time another friend started watching me play, I was invested, and the three of us laughed our asses off constantly (partially due to our own commentary, partially due to the game).
It's not BAD. But then again, I'm the kind of person who sits on Newgrounds playing ♥♥♥♥♥♥ flash games all day, so I'm not exactly smart. I will say, however, that it's not some kind of spectacular rainbow coated super game: It's funny. The puzzles are challenging, for lobotomized dickmonkeys like me, and what more do you want? I mean, it's got blatant objectification of women, but we've already established that if you're going to play this you need to turn off the logical and reasonable parts of your brain and basically just go with it.
If you're the kind of person who's open minded and doesn't get offended easily and you desperately need something to do because, like me, your standard hobbies are slowly becoming less and less fulfilling as you descend into the maw of inevitable insanity, go for it.
If you're literally anybody else, then take any recommendations with a grain of salt: It's certainly not something everybody will find as amusing as I did.

I was hoping to see something like Stalker, but in the form of MMORG. What I saw was a horrible parody. Aiming sucks badly, especially in the "shoulder view", there are no iron sights at all. Everything including ammo is overpriced in the shops. Quests mostly send you to some random map area full of monsters, then you have to come back on foot through the respawned monster legions. Loot is very hard to find, almost impossible if you don't know where exactly you have to look. Tracking of quest waypoints is very bad and works only during few quests. Movement is stiff, jumping is a joke - you have to step back from an obstacle to jump on it. You can get stuck inside watch towers, so you will have to jump from the top. There's no fast travelling, so you have to walk and walk and walk until you are killed by a pack of dogs that spawn like hell. When you are badly hit, you have to spend 30, 40, 50, etc. seconds lying unconcious on the ground looking at your own body and other players who try to finish you and get your loot. If you decide to abandon waiting and to move to a safe zone, they take some of your items - this sucks @ss! Animals spawn out of control almost everywhere and can re-appear right after you kill the previous horde. Dogs can bite you from behind a barbed wire fence or through concrete walls. Graphics is much worse than in Stalker. Ambient noise does not work almost everywhere. No background music at all. In the station's bar instead of music they play (possibly) stolen audio dialogs from A. Tarkovsky's "Stalker" movie. A lot of unclear things in the game - crafting, repairing, skill usage and so on. Last, but not least - why the game requires local admin rights to start every time? There's something fishy about this...

This is the kind of game where the things certain people love about it are the same things others will loathe.  When starting, it will very often have a very slow beginning, but due to the inherent unpredictability of how the kingdoms interact at times each playthrough is bound to be minutely if not entirely different; the character background customization interacts with this in a very tighly done and highly polished, intriguing fashion, with certain backgrounds and character makeups resulting in playing the game in a largely or entirely different manner.
The combat is... awkward, at first.  Perhaps the greatest failing of the game when first getting into it; while it's easy to adjust and become accustomed to, it also has an issue of overall responsiveness which leads to extremely frustrating moments of the game punishing the player for happenings that are the game's own fault.  And that is the crux of what may make new players turn the game off; the game is difficult for the inexperienced.  Once the player character falls in battle it's quite common for the player's personal army to be utterly crushed by virtue of Random Number Generation (RNG), and that leads to capture.  This kind of failure leads to a slippery slope kind of play, with a defeat leading to  players struggling to pick up the pieces of the life they'd been building for themselves.
Once the player has begun winning battles, however, is when the game begins to get its shine; winning battles and tournaments increases the player's power and reptation, which will in turn make it possible to ingratiate oneself and align with one of the many factions vying for control over the land.  Beginning as a wanderer, then becoming a successful mercenary in the service of a nation, then eventually earning pride of place as a lord or lady of the land; it is at this stage where the game's political and developmental aspects come into play, where battles can more easily be left to the soldiers under your command to allow you to manage the larger parts of the army, such as equipment, training and campaigning.  But getting to that point of the gameplay, the truly meaty aspects of toppling nations and climbing the ranks of social prominence and power, is an exercise of climbing up a greased mountain.
I very much reccommend Mount and Blade as a series, Warband especially so, but with the caveat that it can take a very long time before the game truly opens up to the player and demonstrates everything that it has to offer.

Cossacks: European Wars is Ukrainian Game Developer GSC Game World's foray into post-Age of Empires warfare (I was about the Classical Age, II ranged from the Dark Ages to the late Medieval Age and III was about the Age of Discovery), i.e. warfare taking place in the 17th and 18th century.
The best thing about this game is the building set: unlike Age of Empires, EACH civilization possesses its own, unique set of buildings, all of them very detailed and true to their real-life counterparts unlike the rather generic and fictitious ones from Age of Empires II.
This really is the game's biggest strength, paired with the fact that you get to see their construction process. While in Age of Empires all you see are tools lying around the building's foundation till it is complete, in Cossacks you can see the buildings get built up bit by bit.
Otherwise, there are many similarities between the two game francises - you start with some villagers, build a town center, build a mill for farming, market for trade, barracks and stables for your army, shipyard for your navy, foundry for your siege engines, blacksmith and university for technology upgrades, and towers and walls for defence.
Thats where the similarities end. In Cossacks, priests can only heal and not convert. The convert mechanic is instead put on the shoulders of your military units, who can effortlessly capture enemy buildings and peasants if there are no enemy soldiers nearby. Same goes for you - so it is vital to guard pretty much everything, from your villagers tilling the fields, chopping wood, breaking up rocks or working in the mines with soldiers, as well as your buildings. This includes towers!
Speaking of towers, these need to be built OUTSIDE your walls as they cannot fire over the wall, which is very annoying and contrary to the mechanic in the AoE series.
Cossacks has more resources than Age of Empires - apart from food, wood, stone and gold, you also have iron (needed for ranged units) and coal (needed for ships). Food is also constantly depleting, and the rate increases the more units you have, so famines can break out and your people get killed off one by one if you arent careful!
You have the diplomatic centre, where you can recruit units for gold really quick. Useful if you need to defend your areas from being captured by the enemy quickly, or recruit cossacks for quick exploration of the map (and capture enemy mines for example), but these units are otherwise subpar compared to units trained from the barracks or stable.
The units you train can then be upgraded several times, each costing more than the previous one. These upgrades increase their attack and defense, or in the case of siege equipment, reduce their cost and recruit time. Infantry units can march in formation if an officer is recruited, but you need a minimum amount of soldiers to be able to create a formation (which gives attack and defence bonuses).
You start in the 17th century and can advance to the 18th century about mid-game onward, giving you access to more technologies and an improved barracks that lets you recruit better units. But again, you need to train these from scratch, so if you have already spent a lot of resources into training 17th century units, this will be an initial setback.
The downsides of this game is that you cannot have AI players play against one another in skirmish mode - the more enemies you play against, the harder it is because they are all allied against you. The campaigns are quite tough and not nearly as enjoyable as the ones in the AoE series.
The music is AWFULLY generic and more of an earsore than anything worthy of remembrance like the AoE scores.
The graphics are a bit rougher/coarser looking than AoE, but they're otherwise fine. I don't like the fact that your villagers never manage to fully chop a tree and move on to the next one, so the presence of vegetation is of almost no strategic importance whatsoever and merely aesthetic, as the trees, rocks and mines near your base will last you for the rest of the game. The game supports many resolutions out of the box which is great, and its speed is very scalable which is also neat. You will need to run the game shortcut on compatibility settings (e.g. XP SP 3) so that it works on operating systems like Windows 7 or newer.
3.5/5.
