Overture is honestly fast becoming one of my favourite games.
Firstly, I'd describe this game as being simple to control, but nigh on impossible to master. The control scheme is as straightforward as they come, only using WSAD and the mouse, but the difficulty lies in coping with the colossal amount of enemies on each level (supposedly up to 10 levels, but in my first couple of hours, I never got past 2). There are 24 different classes, divided between warriors, archers, mages and shamans, and I found myself using mainly the standard ranger. I did also try some of the others, and it's clear from the get-go that used properly, you can get through swathes of enemies regardless of which class you choose.
There are also power-ups scattered around, which can either be better equipment (letting you deal more damage, increasing mana regeneration etc); or NPCs who follow you around and help you deal damage. As well as this, you can collect gold as you go through the game, and use it to buy new classes or upgrade the ones you already have.
My only slight complaint would be to do with the bosses, which must be killed to progress from level to level. Given that no class has a huge amount of HP, fighting such absurdly tough bosses in such a small room can become frustrating.
Ultimately, this game is brilliantly fast-paced, very punishing (although rarely unfairly so), very well presented in a 16-bit style, and utterly painfully addictive. For £4, you can't go wrong.

If you like Overture, you'll call it a fine example of the action-roguelike genre. If you dislike Overture, you'll call it unremarkable and derivative. Both reviews, I think, are absolutely fair.
As is standard for the genre, you're a pixelated fellow with far too little health and far too many foes, and it's your job to wander through a series of monster-infested fields to find and murder a miniboss guarding a staircase, which will take you to a boss fight. It's played from a top-down perspective and feels at times like a hack-n-slash and at other times almost like a bullet hell.
Gear drops occasionally, and with the exception of the occasional item with a special ability attached to it, each piece of equipment does the same thing; a sword, for instance, will always increast your attack power, while a ring will always increase your mana regeneration. Though shallow, this is good; you absolutely don't have time for any deeper item comparison than figuring out which number is bigger and going with that.
Each class has a (usually) fairly generic left-click main attack aimed towards your mouse cursor, typically some variation on the theme of either a fired arrow or a sword swung mercifully halfway across the screen. Each also has a right-click ability that consumes mana and is unique to its own class; the rogue, for instance, becomes invisible while right click is held, while the Ranger fires a spread of arrows. It's all quite straightforward and follows the equipment system's example of not being a lot, but just enough.
As a longtime fan of Roguelikes, Roguelike-likes, and whatever else you want to call procedurally-generated games that hate you and want you to die, I can tell you that Overture doesn't do anything particularly unique. It's a variation on the themes of its predecessors, and if you've played the Diablos, the Realms of the Mad God, the Zeldas, or the Bindings of Isaac it cites as its inspirations, you're not going to see anything you haven't seen before. However, whether or not it does anything new, Overture does what it does very well.
Ultimately, if you feel like you have enough action-Roguelikes, you can pass this one by; while good, Overture is by no means unmissable. However, if there's room in your life for another entry in the admittedly crowded genre, Overture is a good choice, and I heartily recommend it.

Summary: A flawed horror game that is slow to start, but once it does it firmly establishes itself as a horror classic
Pros:
- Very atmospheric with a genuinely high creep factor
- Top quality effects, graphics, animations, environments etc
- Voice acting, music  and storyline is high quality if not perfect
- Comprehensive skill tree that feels satisfying once you progress past the 1/3 mark
- The game feels cohesive, i.e. all elements feel consistent e.g. gameplay, sounds, etc..
Cons:
- After a ripping, exciting start the game drags through the first couple of chapters
- The storyline is a little bit non-sensical, but personally I didn't find it too bad
- Movement is clunky, although not as bad as the original RE series
- The camera is pretty awkward esp. in tight spaces
- The nominal game price is too high
I've played just about every recent horror game (Alien, Dying Light, etc) and I have to say although it's not my favorite game, The Evil Within (TEW) is still a top quality one.
If you enjoyed the original Resident Evil series of games, you will be right at home with TEW.  It features clunky combat and heavy atmosphere.
A lot of people seemed to complain that the story was too illogical and that the protagonist was cliche, but I didn't have a problem with it personally.  I felt that it all worked pretty well.
With most horror games, I usually ask the question: is this game spooky, and can it keep me engaged?  The answer here is a definitive yes.  It is firmly an action horror, as you can fight back, but there are many fights you have where you aren't able to outright kill certain creatures.  You have to find other means in the environment to keep them at bay while you are running away.
These moments are tense and terrifying especially when you lose sight of those creatures and you can still hear them.
I have to give kudos to the developers for the top-notch quality for the entire game - the environments are believably dirty, run-down and gross.  The sounds and music are critical to horror games.  These are also top notch.
So while I can't totally recommend this game at it's full price, if you do see it on a discount, and you are a hardcore horror fan as I am, you should get it right away.  Although it has its flaws, it is still a solid must-play entry into the AAA horror genre.
Rating: 7.5/10 Brains

S.T.A.L.K.E.R The Zone
This is one of my newer reviews, and prefered to play this game for a couple of hours first to try and understand what is going on and how the mechanics work.  Firstly I will write down a short list of the Pros/Cons, and if it is worth the game time.
Now as you are aware, S.T.A.L.K.E.R Is quite a good game, if you have played Chernobly or Clear sky, then you may know the story already. sZone-Online is a more MMORPG style game based on the S.T.A.L.K.E.R Series, but capable of building your character more and develop him, the games were great, this however brings out a all new meaning to "Are you ready to face the zone, Stalker?" Experience.
PRO's
- It is Free-to-play
- It has quite a lot of content already
- Follows a basic story line, features English and Russian
- The economy in my opinion works out quite fine
- A lot to do.
- Contols are easy to manage
- PvP Arena, and PVE Sessions.
CON's
- There are parts in the game were it features only in russian, e.g. some quests. But they will probebly fix it up
- Graphics are not the best, but doesnt mean the game is bad
- A couple of bugs which relate to the NPC's or having your character vanish for a moment, this can also relate too walls you can see through in PVP.
- NPC's tend to glitch out, meaning their shadows show up near you when you are attacked.
- You seem to get kicked from the game for standing around only for a couple of minutes.
Now I know a lot of people might suggest this game is crap, everyone has a opinion and everyone prefers something else.
Result:
The game is quite fun, it is boring at the start, but once you get to the second stage you begin to earn more items and rubles the more you do, I earned at least 7 Thousand rubles in just a hour, and managed to get myself some decent amount of stuff. Items may look expensive but they are not, following from the games the good stuff are one of the most expensive pricey pickens you may encounter, but with the amount you get you can easily collect some interesting things.
Arti's produce some good quality Currency if you find what you are looking for, even though some items have a Day limit on them, there are quite a lot of good items that do not, so really it is a WIN/WIN situation.
My suggestion: Take your time, read the dialoge if you can, it takes time to get used to it. But once you start to spend another hour on it, you will know it is worth it. It may be free-to-play, but I noticed a lot of items are balanced and how they should be placed. PVP matches you do not really encounter a man with a OP gun, this time it is your skill, not the weapon. So I thank you for reading this, and hope it will change your mind on the game.

This game is a hollow attempt at cashing in on popular culture. It offers very little as far as innovative gameplay goes, and has extremely broken mechanics. Perhaps in time it will improve, but as it currently stands the gameplay can be described as tolerable at best.
The worst part is how hard it is to actually hit. You know it's bad when you can abuse BASIC MOVEMENT to become invincible. Basically, you have an extremely small reticule, and when you attempt to hit an enemy you won't actually hit them unless it is directly on them. It causes combat to feel extremely clunky and frustrating, especially when you can clearly see that your axe or sword is being swung in a wide horizontal arch. It's like everyone is wildly running around trying to hit pointlessly miniscule hitboxes. The whole time I played this I was mashing the mouse button while circle strafing as the player in front of me did the exact same thing, both of us locked in a perpetual circle of uneventful combat.
On top of the terrible combat detection regarding weapons, the cursor itself is wacky. It really isn't possible to explain controls unless you experience them yourself, but I can try. The default sensitivity is way too slow, and when you increase it the inertia of looking around just feels clunky and too tight. The broken controls on top of not being able to hit a damn thing on top of not understanding why you can't hit a damn thing even though your sword is literally passing through the enemy's body make for excessively poor, unsatisfying, and uneventful combat. Even when you do kill someone, you just feel like you were the one who got the lucky hit in first.
Aside from the controls, the UI could use some renovation as well. In my case, I encountered some ignorant goon spewing sexist and offensive language riddled with grammar errors and profanity. I did not want to hear this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so I tried to mute him. I asked in the chat how to mute, no response. So, I type /mute (a typical mute command) and get the message "you do not have permission to use this command." Wtf. Do I have to unlock the ability to not have to listen to annoying♥♥♥♥♥♥heads? "Being able to focus and play the actual game instead of listening to some idiot" DLC for $4.99 out soon! That is crap. Give me the freaking mute command. I looked on the menu and I saw it, "mute players." I thought, oh, ok, I can just do it from here. WRONG. It opens a list of ALL the players in the lobby and makes you hand select the players you want to mute. Great. The best part is that the mute menu gives no feedback as to who is talking at any given time. You have to unpause, wait for the trash talkers to speak, memorize their names, open the mute menu back up, and mute them. What a goddamn hassle. How unfriendly can the UI be? So, I am sitting there waiting for these idiots to speak so that I can see there username and mute them, and it takes about 5 minutes because they only speak periodically, you know, short bursts of speech is all they can muster, when lo and behold some curious little fellow with a seprano triple C voice joins and starts giving the typical squeaker cringe dialogue we all know and hate. About 30 seconds into trying to find his name in the list of 20 or so small font usernames, I forget that I have to see it in-game because no mic icon will appear next to his name in the mute list. I thought "this game is♥♥♥♥♥" left the lobby, closed the game, and started this review.
The inventory sucks, too. To swap weapons you have to press the corresponding number on your keyboard and then left click to select it. This sounds minute, but you try it. It doesn't even make sense the way they did it anyway. Why can't you just press the button to swap weapons? If I press "1" I obviously want to take out my polearm, otherwise I wouldn't have pressed it. I am a big believer that details make a game, and all the little details like that add up to a horrid and rusty experience indeed.
Furthermore, some of the classes are just broken af. Suppose everyone is just swinging at the air every 3 seconds (combat is THAT slow, I am not exaggerating) having a good ol' time when all of a sudden a viking berserker comes up and starts mauling everyone with the fire rate of a P90 submachine gun. I know these warriors were historically ruthless and hardy, but why did you have to make them literally overpowered in every way? The knight has 200 armor, but it doesn't make a♥♥♥♥♥♥when he is stun locked by the thousand axe attack of death you can pull out of your♥♥♥♥♥ IF YOU ARE GOING TO HAVE♥♥♥♥♥♥MECHANICS AT LEAST KEEP THEM CONSISTENT.
My biggest complaint, however, is with the Man-at-Arms class. He is described as a "pantless Frenchman whose insults are as sharp as his polearm." His voice is literally the most stereotypical French voice of ALL TIME. He has a mustache that would put the pringles guy out of business and goes around in padded leather armor, a metal helmet, and no freaking pants. Do people really make "Oui oui" jokes anymore? Isn't that like a dead joke by now? Also, did any Men-at-Arms you have ever seen just refuse to armor an entire portion of a critical section of the body? Me neither...
By the way, "Oui oui!!! Hon hon hon!!!" is an actual in-game dialogue option. Seriously...Great content, developers, just alienate the second or third largest gaming demographic by making your content offensive and ignorant. It MIGHT be funny once, but after a thousand times?
In conclusion, this game is clunky, irreverent, frustrating, unbalanced, has a UI that resembles a 4 year old's LEGO creation in terms of design, and is simply not enjoyable.

So, just take that into account. But for what it is, Deus Ex: HR Lite Edition, it's okay. Not phenomenal, but I had an itch for more Deus Ex: HR and didn't want to reinstall that game, so this little diversion did the job just fine.
Something funny worth mentioning is that graphically, this game is on par with Human Revolution. That's a testament to both the evolution of mobile gaming graphics and how underbaked HR was. Not to mention that 300+ fps with maxed anti-aliasing is always nice.
So, to reiterate, if you can snag it for $2 during a Square Enix sale like I did and are CRAVING more HR gameplay, get it. For any other situation, disregard The Fall.

Hotline Miami 2, or the Juggalo equivalent of a coffee table book, is nothing if not apparently intended as a centerpiece for conversation about what the hell is going on with it. I found the experience extremely interesting for the following reason: it might be the very worst game I have ever played.
For the sake of fielding a coherent argument for why this is, let's grant Hotline Miami 2 a few feet of slack--let's say the superfluous deaths from off-screen and the inconsistent AI that never misses a shot are intentional design features that are meant to challenge the player. Let's just say all of that is fine. Now, remembering back to Hotline Miami 1, what made that kind of gameplay work? Could it have been the versatility of approach to its levels? The tight quarters of said level design? The bite-sized floorplans that encourage speed and improvised brutality to accompany the infectious driving soundtrack and splashing neon lights of an interactive reptilian murder-ballad? Absolutely--it was a game that presented a horrific domesticity to a Smash TV model of excruciating violence, and it was tough to put down for its two-hour runtime on a sweltering summer night.
Almost none of that is present in this game. You are forced to carry weapon loadouts and essentially die if you run out of ammo, to pause for full seconds to gawk down hallways far longer than you can see only to be shot down by an offscreen shotgun sniper standing doubly-invisibly under a potted fig tree, to forget about the fourth building-patrolling Rottweiler blended into the black carpet, or to continually run linear gauntlets of barbaric memory-games that accrue itemized lists of 50 Potential Deaths per floor that you can almost never account for beyond waiting for blind circumstances to deliver you alive at the end. The floorplans are huge and you will repeatedly die for inconceivable, unseen reasons, having learned many valuable lessons of some kind.
It's such an obviously stupid direction for this game to have gone that I can't help but suspect that it was done on purpose, not to challenge players with "new" mechanics, but to punish them with worse ones.
Imagine you're in biology class, and every time you make any kind of incision on your bullfrog specimen, the teacher throws a wad of firecrackers at your hands. "Did I do something wrong?" you ask the teacher. The teacher laughs maniacally and screams "PRESS R TO PICK UP THE SCALPEL AGAIN." You do so, and this time you try to cut open the specimen from a different angle, but once again your knuckles are blasted open and singed by firecrackers. "HAHAHA YOU IDIOT NOW PRESS R TO TRY AGAIN AGAIN AGAIN AGAIN AGAIN AGAIN AGAIN" the teacher roars, drooling and lighting another string of explosives to hurl at your eyes this time. You do eventually work the thing open, and the teacher gives you a C- for your hour of suffering. ("DO YOU ENJOY TORTURING ANIMALS, YOU SADISTIC CREEP CHILDREN?" the teacher crows himself to sleep, night after night)
This is not how you train somebody to do anything. This is how you tell people that what they're doing is a stupid waste of time. This game's design philosophy is worse than incoherent, or even that which you'd see in a cynical cash-grab--it persistently negatively reinforces absolutely everything you do in it.
Is there a lesson here? Who knows? Hotline Miami 1 asked why you found its genuinely satisfying formula -fun-. There was room for conversation there. Hotline Miami 2 is not even close to fun--it's a hyperstylized, hyperviolent form of waiting. Waiting for the 66th attempt at butchering an entire building of gangsters to finally save your stupid idiot life before some other maniac shoots your incompetent, purposelessly savage character in the face at level's end.
The story isn't about anything--it's at best a bunch of dialogue that samples idiomatic petards you'd find in a third rate techno track. Maybe it contextualizes the original game in some way, like the marketing claims, but all it really does is show a bunch of crazed faces mouthing words words words. Dates, times-of-night, and locations flash by, but the events are told out of order and nothing sticks apart from a sense the designers like to imagine what would happen if Quentin Tarantino made a dream-logic movie about the Cold War. Enchantingly, zero of the story arcs add up to anything across some 13 playable characters, nothing is wrapped up, and the whole damn thing kind of just get whisked away by a big drug dream and an apocalyptic cleansing by the end. You can read the Wikipedia rundown of what supposedly happens here for whatever reasons, but I'll be damned if I was able to make heads or tails of anything that was being said as it was being said. There's no draw. There's nothing to root for. It's just a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that sort of just happens.
Can you smell a little bit of contempt? I really don't think I started it--I'm more than a little convinced Dennaton hated making this game and hated that people liked the first game so much. But I'm projecting awfully hardcore, as there are piles of evidence to the contrary--be it the animal-mask-murder-themed footie pajamas you can buy at their merch store or their design blog in which they explain how deliberate and crucial all their choices are despite the critics never understanding the intracies of the AI that honest-to-god does not actually work.
Maybe this is was an attempt to push twitchy score-attack gaming to a new apocalyptic extreme, but do not count me among the many apologists willing to pretend its mechanics actually hang together as a game that is seriously playable. The mess it makes is at least extremely memorable for the sole reason that I didn't know I could hate a gameplay experience as much as I hated this one.
The music, as you'd expect, is the one glowing positive in the whole experience--the voracious savagry and enormity of the soundtrack far and away outclasses everything else, almost like the game is intended as idle background decoration for it rather than the other way around.
All in all, this game's ideas are terrible and its presentation varies from vagely cool to completely stupid, and if your blood-powered pachinko murder-game is going to start us off with a brutal, interactive sexual assault that is so meaningless in the overall meaninglessness of the story that you immediately present the audience with the option to skip it before it happens, you've more than lost me. You're not even phoning it in at that point--you're being a no-class jackass with nothing to say. You're a deranged Melvin desigining a game to preoccupy dull nine-year-old sociopaths who would otherwise spend all afternoon stuffing fireworks into bullfrogs.
Maybe this is their way of repaying a secret sense of debt to society. Maybe it was just something to do for a big fat paycheck. Whatever the case, this is without a doubt the most serious contender for Worst Game I've Ever Even Heard About, which I never could have expected for how much I liked the first one.

This game is truly addictive.  The game is a great dungeon crawler retro type.  You can play as many different classes - Warrior, Rogues, Mages, and Shamans.  Each category has several character types with their own unique weapons and perks.
Each dungeon or level, I should say, is generated randomly.  Here you rescue NPCs who will fit with you and you collect gold and mana and health from killing enemies and destroying vessels.  The enemies are all unique, some move slowly, some sneak up really fast, some have ranged projectiles.
The game is simple, but made of the best possible ingredients.  And the game is challenging!  The game ramps up it's adrenaline as you do.  When playing it can get to an insane level of enemies requiring accurate attacking while moving and seeking safety.  There are no true safe areas and thus the skilled player must be alert and quick.  With the gold, you can upgrade your character(s).  You also use the gold to unlock other characters within a class.
It has the feeling of retro goodness.  It surpasses retro goodness in my opinion.  It's one of those games that could easily eat through many stacks of quarters with no regrets.
The original soundtrack is great.  It is hard to please everyone with a soundtrack, but I think they did a great job and I enjoy my Overture sessions with headphones on as great detail was put into the audio.
I highly recommend this game.  It takes no complications to start playing, but to master it will take some real skills and many addicting hours.  This game will make you happy -- buy it!

Hotline Miami 2 is a sequel to a hit that was Hotline Miami. It's very brutal and looks pretty much the same, but... the devil is in the details.
Where HM was a visceral puzzle killing simulator where you eviscerated people using melee, projectiles and firearms, the sequel is basically a shooter. Yes, it looks the same, you can chop people up, let their intestines run wild and do lots of gore stuff. Visuals are pretty much the same. Yes, you hear the same amazing audio and proper sound effects. Oh that superb music... And yet, it plays nothing like the first. Where in HM you basically went through kill, die, adapt, repeat, HM2 lacks that adapt step. Where in HM you planned your trick shots, bounse the knife here to kill that guy there and grab another brick here to stun that one there, in HM2 it's shoot the wall to attract guys and shoot them all dead. There are a few levels that are as good as the predecessor's, but they are few and far between. Which is a shame because HM was great and HM2 is not even close.
I liked:
* the music
* several levels that reminded me of the first Hotline Miami
* seriously, the music
I disliked:
* how the game became a shooter
* dying from of-the-screen enemies
* how anything not shooty-shooty was non-viable
* the fragmented story
Get this:
* if you're ok with Hotline Miami becoming a shooter
* if you're looking for a shooter with amazing music
Don't get this:
* if you expect puzzle murder sim
Easy to learn, hard to master.

Some levels you're forced to play with specific masks, in other levels you play as a character that can't perform lethal eliminations, in some levels you're stuck with specific weapons, and in my least favorite levels you're forced to play as this god awful double character - one with a gun and one with a chainsaw - and trying to position your corner shots is a living nightmare. However, there are a few levels where you choose a mask - but they're much less frequent than the levels where you're forced to play as someone else.
Having played the first and the second back to back, after playing the first a little over a year ago, I can say with certainty that while the second one is more frustrating in the fact that the mechanics are constantly switched up on you, tremendously throwing off your groove, it is much easier. The melee hurtboxes seem larger, and some characters you play as can even take a few bullets before going down.
All-in-all it's a Hotline: Miami game, but if you're coming in looking for more levels of the first game (as I did) you're going to be let down.
As for the upside, it's still a controller clenching challenge that's not entirely bred from frustration, the excellent soundtrack is still there, and this one has some semblence of an understandable story. There are much larger levels than in the first game, making for some interesting new encounters in different styles, and there's even a bit of sexual violence if the regular headsmashing katana-slicing gorefest just wasn't enough for you.
Being forced to play as other characters, which I personally found to be derailing, does force you to tackle situations in different ways and can keep you from grinding through levels by redeploying the same tactic all the way through. All the old enemies are there; melee guards, gun guards, bosses, and dogs, but there's a few new additions in the form of unqiue enemies that are given a few lines of text upon entering the area and have completely unique fighting mechanics.
The story it tells is fairly interesting, and is definitely a step up from the previous game which basically just confused my♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
No silver Delorean in this one, but there is a sweet van.
I recommend this game while on sale, but just be aware that while it is very similar to the first game it is vastly different in that it doesn't just hand you levels and tell you to pick a mask (which for some people, myself included, was my favorite mechanic of the game).

Great Warhammer game that is a pretty dang good successor to L4D. Though has a declining player base, which sucks, and doesn't run well on lower end machines (I get 60 in some places, and fps as low as 15-20 on low settings with the high cpu usage items off). Loot system is a joke, but Fatshark has addressed and is improving it. All in all for a small studio and dev team as Fatshark, they managed to make a pretty damn decent Warhammer game, with surprisingly smooth melee combat (seriously, not many games nail this for some reason). Nothing more satisfying than my hammer bouncing off the skulls of skaven heretical filth!

Though due to the small playerbase, finding a game can be troubling at certain times of the day. I advise if you want to actually find a game, don’t use the table, press “L” to bring up the lobby list and find a game that way. Loot table as I said is not the greatest, and Fatshark is trying to fix it (though you can increase your chances of rare loot by collecting grimoire books hidden throughout the missions). They release one free DLC for every paid DLC, as of this reviews publishing, we have two free and two paid for, so the third should be free. Also worth a mention that there is zero backtracking, which is a con for me, since you may overlook a grimoire book which will mess with your loot success rate (that is receiving a rarer item), as well as a team member getting pinned by a special in the previous area.
The game does have it’s issues, but they don’t seem to be giving up on this title yet, just be patient if you do buy this. They are a small dev team, working hard on updates, fixes, and content releases.

Vermintide is basically Left 4 Dead in Warhammer universe. Which is actually great, because I strongly believe L4D was the best cooperative shooter out there, and Warhammer is one of the best settings out there. It doesn't feel like plagiarism too; in fact those who played L4D will be happy to see some familiar interface elements and concepts, while new players will undoubtedly like how simple and clearcut everything is. Plus the gameplay is vastly different since it's mostly based around melee combat and it's pretty good at it.
The very important part is the characters. I actually believe that having more than 4 characters and having different characteristics for them was one thing missing from Left 4 Dead. This feature is implemented very well here, and I actually found all characters very fun to play as.
The game has great atmosphere, created through pretty eye-catching dark visuals and solid acting (one of my favorite parts of the game).
You can upgrade your characters with new equipment, thus providing some variety and randomization, but at the same time there's no need for annoying grinding, and players without good equipment can still be useful, so you don't have to worry about that aspect.
The developers of the game are also pretty great, they take feedback into account and keep providing new content.

Vermintide tells a tale of Triumph and Tragedy, of defiance and survival in a world, drowning in ratlings.
Vermintide is a challenging, satisfying cooperative survival game oriented around missions, and set in the end times of the Warhammer setting. The focus upon melee combat and spatial awareness yields an exciting, active experience which you would do well to share with three of your friends. Each of the characters has a distinct personality and style of play, so there is choice without a glut.
At present, there are less than a thousand players online in a given day, though the game has not been out for a full year, and over half a million people have bought it. This is the product of a long, steep difficulty curve. In order to participate, one needs appropriate experience and equipment. Both require time, as rewards are randomized, and their quality limited.
If you enjoy challenging cooperative games, Vermintide is worth your time. The setting and mechanics are novel for the cooperative survival genre, and well paired, with melee heavy combat embedded in dark fantasy. Find a friend or three, and face this doom beneath us!

Today we take a look at Shinji Mikami's/Tango Gameworks The Evil Within downloadable content 'The Assignment' which comes in at just £6.99 and comprises of two extra chapters to add to the already lengthy game. Players assume the role of sidekick detective Juli Kidman as she fulfils a shady role alongside the protagonist of the main game Sebastian Castellanos. This time round Juli is alone as we learn what happens to her during the events of the main game, which if you haven't played there's moments where the three investigators get split up. It's a great opportunity to experience the horrors from another perspective except unfortunately the game switches up the gameplay style to make things less free form and more taxing. What was great about the main game as Sebastian was the eclectic mix of stealth and action gameplay to tackle the many levels. Unfortunately, this has been stripped back here with an over reliance on pure stealth which in many ways would be fine but not if you're expecting more of the same gameplay from the main story. The stealth mostly works but there are some dodgy moments where trial and error rather than skill comes into play which is a bit of shame. Unlike Sebastian, Juli is unable to attack her enemies whilst sneaking about until half way through the game which means a fair bit of unhindered sneaking which might not suit all players. The enemy AI system is a bit hit and miss here where it's not always clear what their direction is or to predict movements to sneak past. When coupled with some awkward key prompts and camera angles makes things a bit harder than what it should be. Players can use lures to good effect but when faced with invisible enemies it becomes all the more fiddly. Perhaps this is deliberate to heighten the tension, but in reality is cause for some frustration. Negatives aside though and there's some excellent audio visuals moments throughout the three hour campaign which is divided into two chapters. The visual elements are second to none with a real flamboyant approach to warped mindsets and imposing twisted character designs. The locations are suitably dreary, but also drenched in some fine details - especially during the opening of chapter one making the game sparkle at the right moments and keeping the player hooked despite an abundance of dimly lit tight spaces. There's some issue with performance though as the framerate tends to dip quite often even when using a high end system. This isn't a major issue but is noticeable when it occurs. Luckily players are given a few options to tinker with making the game more bespoke. To conclude, The Assignment serves as a decent addition to the main game offering more madness from the depths of Shinji Mikami's great design process. There's some truly wonderful set piece moments that could have you screaming at the display, but by and large the game's pacing is pretty consistent and well suited to a more methodical approach. Action gamers really need not apply here and it's pure stealth with a little bit of aggression thrown in during the latter portion of the experience. If you're keen on expanding on the original game and can ignore some slightly wonky controls, camera angles and frustrating enemy encounters in places then you'll find much enjoyment here especially for the reasonably pitched asking price. If trial and error fused with slow paced creeping about isn't your forte then you might struggle a bit but will undoubtedly be bowled over by the excellent visual quality. Score - 7.5/10

Layers of Fear is a very innovative, interesting take on the newly revived Horror genre. It grips the player from the very first minute, and doesn't let go until the end. I'm very eager for the game to release in full, as I'm chomping at the bit to finish the story and reveal everything there is to know about the main character. If you're looking for something to practice having a heart attack with, Layers of Fear is it.

This game is solid proof that mobile platforms are time machines. This game's quality is at least from 10 years before its release.  It's just not up to snuff compared to what I'd expect from Square Enix and its subsidiaries, especially after playing Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
I hesistate to say this because I'll have to accept its existence, but I'm pretty sure Invisible War's character models look better at times than those in this game released for PC in 2014!  The best examples are the NPCs that pepper Panama. They have a polycount for a PSX game.
As for the gameplay, it is a toned-down version of that in Human Revolution.  For example of how the gameplay has been reduced, there is no jumping. You can fall off of things, climb latters, and vault over those designated as acceptable, but no free jumping.  The player also cannot pick up and move items, like boxes. That's not entirely true. There is an aug to move heavy objects, but it has been reduced to shoving scripted XNG crates from preset position A to preset position B. Aside from those examples, it's pretty much HR. One more thing and spoiler warning!
The level design is still complex at the very least. Lots of possibilities for the player to explore, mostly through man-sized vents. The designers did make more breakable walls, which I appreciate as well.
The voice acting is probably the most impressive feature of this game.  I really hope that the assets are reused because they are a waste on this game in its current form.
The writing is a mixed bag. I find the method Namir was planning to employ Ben Saxon to be ludicrious and the twist to be pants-on-head. Doesn't make a lick of sense. That said, I think Ben Saxon and Anna Kelso to have potential as good characters with some depth.
It should be apparent that I cannot recommend this game. It is not good enough for the consumer and not good enough for the franchise. The best thing the developer and publisher could do is drop this whole idea of putting this kind of game on a phone or tablet. Since The Fall is part of an episodic series, they would be wise to remake this installment with the existing Human Revolution tools and assets as well as the next installment. Then, stitch them together like DX: HR Director's Cut. As a consumer, I would advise you to wait for that to happen or, if you cannot hold back your curiosity, wait until this version of the game is very cheap. I bought it for 2USD and I did get my money's worth.

I wish there would be something between "Recommended" and "Not Recommended" for this.
In all honesty, Deus Ex: The Fall didn't deserve all the hate it received. Yes, it certainly has obvious flaws and it's riddled with questionable to outright laughable design decisions. But even after that, it did not fail to deliver the Deus Ex feeling to me personally, and especially its story is quite enjoyable.
I picked it up on a sale for less than two bucks, and I felt that it was worth it for a few hours of fun (50% having fun with the actual gameplay, 50% laughing about how bad some of its aspects were).
I can perfectly comprehend why many (non-trash-loving) people would be angry about The Fall; the graphics are somewhere around Quake 3-level (yes, that's a game from 1999), the level design makes absolutely no sense, the AI is as intelligent as a piece of burnt toast, the quality of the voice actors ranges somewhere between okay-ish and awful, and you can just feel that it is a half-hearted port of a mobile game - to name just a few points. Yes, that sounds god awful if you list it up like this, and it probably is, but if you are a fan of the Deus Ex universe and you want to have a few hours of trashy fun (that hopefully isn't destroyed by a game-breaking bug), you may as well pick this one up on a sale for a few bucks. You might say that Deus Ex: The Fall belongs in the "so bad, it's good" category in this regard.

I find this rather peculiar. Because this game tries. it really does. Each season that progresses with this game it seems to add significant more details and features. While the MMO features a few insulting tropes (crates, horribly imbalanced PVP, Loot systems) It manages to maintain what it wants to be: an exploration of all things Star Trek. If you want to explore things in your own ship, have a few fun star trek themed missions with friends or even by yourself (since some actually DO that apparently), The game adapts to your tastes. you can have a crew of NPCs that serve as your bridge officers (and powers in space) that can reasonably supplement human players. So long as you equip them right. It's regretful that ground combat is ultimately shallow and immensely dull, as there are only so many planet types and spaceships you can stomach before it gets old. what REALLY makes the game shine is the space combat. It's a logical evolution to what Star Trek: Legacy was from long ago. Instead of four vessels, you pilot one extremely specialized craft. I've tried nearly every ship type, and cross classing, meta-building, as well as customizing are highly encouraged by a fairly straightforward user interface. I bought this and played it way back in beta release. It's a delight to see cutscenes, textures, classes, ships, everything transform this game. Seeing as it's free. why not give it a try? you might find yourself enjoying trophies on your bridge.  My only reccommendation is avoid PVP. Starfleet is extremely underpowered against both romulans and klingons, and very little has been introduced to counteract the cloak ambush. Honestly the PVE missions against borg, the crystalline entity, and the dominion are an absolute delight when you see massive high level vessels backing you up. At the very least, give it a try. I'm sure that there will be something that will catch your attention here in contrast to all of the medieval sword slashing and magic potions that plague MMOs these days
Very good, fun, multiplayer experience Star Trek fans will be attatched to, wether you like combat or roleplay.

By far the best MMO on the market today... if you are a Trekkie/Trekker.
I once found myself playing WOW as my only source of MMO and was fairly pleased with the game until changes made to it, caused even the most enjoyable tasks to become mundane and tedious.
Thus I quit MMOs altogether for years. Then along the way my friends want to play Neverwinter, so I started playing it, and in my visit to the PerfectWorld site I was struck by something that caught my attention, "Star Trek Online." I was curious and being a Trekker myself, I downloaded the game and installed it.
Now I'm not going to tell you it's perfect, far from it, and I will list all the problems I have with the game, there are many. But for all its problems I just keep playing. So first let me talk about some of the things I really like about it, before I list my complaints.
The Galaxy they have created is rich with content, after all they have probably the best lore to work with and the game doesn't dissapoint on that front. The game allows you to choose from an assortment of race types within two major factions (Federation and Klingon), three if you count the romulans. The romulans become a race that can be added to either of the major factions.
Once you have chosen the race you'd like to play, then its to the editor where you have an almost endless of choices when designing your character. Although I have seen better character editors in games, this one is pretty good, and it only takes a few minutes in the game to see how many different kinds of aliens people can design using the same editor.
You may start off flying a ship that looks like it came from the 22nd century but it doesn't take long to start earning your way to better ships and weapons.
Now the space combat in the game is amazing, and although it has some problems, over all its one of the best combat systems I've seen. Considering you can kill borg cubes, I mean seriously who's going to complain about that?
Ground combat, leaves a lot to be desired. Compared to ground combat in other games like WOW it's missing a lot of the elements that make ground combat fun. Even with a phaser in hand, it should be something enjoyable, but instead it feels like a stiff controlled figure running about with a gun in hand. Also because of the nature of the combat system, it doesn't take much to die, a couple of hits, which can make some missions very difficult and not much fun.
But the good news is you do not have to do much of it, if you do not want to. Unlike some MMOs that rely heavily on the built in campaign or missions to build your levels, that is not really required in this game as you could level just by getting into battles with your ship or doing foundry questing. I was able to take a character from 1 to 50 just by doing foundry missions.
One of the things I really enjoy is that almost every star system has some kind of interaction, and this allows you to fly anywhere and do something if you so desire. As a new player you will find yourself flying everywhere and getting into random enemy encounters just to hone your skills, but the random borg encounters are the most fun.
Joining a fleet the equivalent of joining a guild in wow, is where I really learned how to play the game, and I would recommend it for anyone interested in playing this game seriously. While it would sound like being in a fleet means the same thing as it does in WOW, it does not. There seems to be a more laid back feel to fleet life, though I'm sure there are those who take it quite seriously. And as the game does not have any 25-player instances, you can throw an easy 5 player together and go shoot some tholians or borg.
Much of the best content doesn't even appear until you've reached max level which means you don't need to feel like your game is over when you've maxxed yourself out.
Now some of the things I really dislike about the game.
1. Because it's Free-to-play, the micro transaction system allows people who pay for things outright to gain advantages, especially in pvp, which is why I do not recommend pvp at all. Essentially its Pay-to-win.
2. Now people will complain and sight the fact you can earn dilithium that can be converted to zen (the currency of the store) that allows you to purchase everything everyone else can get. This is true, except because the game limits the amount of dilithium you can refine per day, even if you earn more, you cannot refine it.
Thus you are prevented from equally purchasing the items using the dilithium system, and therefore someone who buys zen outright always has an advantage on you, and its a huge advantage.
Each ship cost 2500 zen to purchase. You can refine a maximum of 8000 dilithium per day. At a rate of 134 dilithium per zen (as of right now) it will take you 41 days at 59.7 zen per day earned by maxxing dilithium (NO SMALL TASK) if the dilithium to zen exchange does not flucuate much.
Earning dilithium is not much fun, all the tasks to earn it are extremely tedious and boring, like farming in wow, and after doing it a while you will get bored with it and just logoff or stop farming the dilithium altogether. You can earn it by running fleet missions against the borg, however this too is a lengthy process, and remember you will only get 59 zen from spending hours doing this.
3. Understanding that the microtransaction model allows them to keep the content free for everyone, does not excuse them from bad form. I understand the high cost of ships, and gear, and things of this nature, but charging someone for utility needs is a little underhanded.
A good example is that the game doesn't do a good job of explaining what skills you will need at max level, and so you may put points into something that you wont need later on. The problem with doing this is that when you reach max level, you cant respec, at least not for free. They charge you money to fix this flaw, and it costs 850 zen to change it. That means just to get a playable character at max level, you will need to spend 2 weeks grinding dilithium just to be able to respec and get it right.
4. They also charge you to raise the Energy Credit Cap in the game. All the best items can cost 20 million energy credits or more, except that until you pay zen to remove the limit, all you can have on your character at one time is 10 million making it virtually impossible to buy some of the things you want.
5. You cannot trade zen, or dilithium, only energy credits, and the only way to get anything from one character on your account to another without using the mail is a shared bank account they charge you zen for.
6. The game is missing customization, something that wow allowed through the LUA interface.
7. As I've said, ground combat is terrible, and with the addition of the Dyson Sphere in Season 8, it doesn't get better. Instead the developers seem to have taken a page out of quake book and tried to redesign it with powerups and such, its ugly and terrible.
8. The game is very buggy. Even 6 months after I started playing bugs remain annoying as ever, apparently never to be fixed. Some are annoying, some are game breaking. Now when I say its very buggy, let me clarify and say the game is very playable even with the bugs, as it rarely crashes. It's just some weird things happen that may make you unhappy.
For example, switching ships causes me to have to redo all of my skills on the bars, not a game ender, but it certainly makes me not want to own additional ships.
9. There are little things that make little sense that kind of drive me crazy.
For example, now 25 years after the first encounter with the borg you need to manually remodulate your weapons, something that should be automatic on all weapons, after all even the Enterprise had that during later encounters.
Even with its problems, I cant help but recommend the hell out of this game. It's lore alone makes it amazing.

This is the horror game I've been waiting for. Atmosphere is one of the most important aspects of a horror game for me, and this game hits it out of the park. Layers of Fear takes very heavy inspiration from the masterpiece that was P.T, while still putting a very heavy, very personal twist on the formula that made it so successful.
From a gameplay perspective, it is extremely familiar as a player of works such as Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
From a design perspective, the game makes fantastic use of the tension and release cycle that is so key to great horror. Though there are a few jumpscares, there is an overwhelming atmosphere of terror, one that I have not seen replicated since Silent Hills' teaser.
Personally, I recommend the use of the standard field of view; one of the things that made P.T so fantastic was its use of right angles to make it impossible to see everything at once - there was always the possibility of a threat looming just out of view. By its nature as a game that implements right angles heavily, something is lost when you widen the field of view dramatically.
At its extremely low price point, fantastic graphical fedility, and incredible atmosphere, Layers of Fear is one that any fan of horror simply cannot ignore.

I'm kind of torn on this one, I wasn't completely sure if I wanted to recommend it or not.  But I have gotten quite a bit of fun out of it, so I am going to recommend it.
It's a fun little game, but after a few hours or so it tends to get fairly repetitive.  I do like the multiple classes and the many characters to play as, but once they're all unlocked you'll have figured out which is your favorite and pretty much stick with that character, and only upgrade them.
And speaking of upgrades, I like that you can spend gold you've previously accumulated to make the character better, but upgrades do nothing except increase the attack power of said character.  Why there isn't an option to increase health or defense is beyond me, and it makes it so you have to play the game as a glass cannon every time.
And speaking of the repetitive nature of the game, sure, it's randomly generated, but you'll almost always fight the same enemies on the same floors, and the floor layouts are very similar.  On 1-2 there are a ton of traps.  On 1-3 there are holes with never ending slime monsters spawning from them, and so on.
Adding a mechanic where you could choose where to put your upgrade points would add a much needed level of depth to the game, and even better yet, a mechanic where you could put upgrade points in a stat when you level up during the game.
I have almost 7 hours on Overture so far, and I have enjoyed it, and I would recommend it, 5 bucks isn't very steep, and I've gotten my 5 dollars worth.  That being said, at this point, I'm wishing for a little more depth and customization, and a little more 'randomization' to break the monotony of trudging through the first few floors, fighting the same big slimes, and fighting the same bosses.

Overall this game will be worth your money, but it can be frustrating at times. The aesthetic is nice but it also hinders gameplay as the screen becomes so busy it's hard to see and find what you are doing. All that said I keep finding myself coming back for nice short sessions with the game - it's the perfect 15 minute distraction when trying to kill some time.

This is a fantastic game. Of all the steam games I own so far, this is one of only two that I enjoyed and admired enough to put in the time and effort required to earn 100% of the achievements. Few games entertain me to the degree that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has.
As a sequel, Hotline Miami 2 vastly exceeded my expectations. It builds on the original Hotline Miami in almost every respect. It takes the gameplay, story, and design of the first game to new heights, heights that quite frankly awed me.
The level design is very well done. Each level is cleverly layed out so as to allow the player to approach it a variety of ways while also forcing him/her into intense combat scenarios that hardly ever give him/her any time to catch their breath. The gameplay is intense, high-octane, and often exhillirating; I experience more than a few adrenaline rushes while playing this game.
The art direction is fantastic. Hotline Miami 2 has tons of beautiful visuals and vibrant colors that are both extravagant yet very tasteful. Combined with a soundtrack to match each scene, the atmosphere and tone of Hotline Miami 2 is delectable.
The story is lengthy and much deeper than that of the original Hotline Miami. The narrative is non-linear and features several different playable characters, which gives the story a level of complexity that I found engrossing.
Hotline Miami 2 also features the new Level Editor feature, in which playes can create their own levels with the same tools that the game designers had while making the game. Players can add their own custom sprites and share their levels on the Steam Workshop. Already, players have created lengthy sets of levels that are comparable to a full game, complete with their own storyline.
To summarize, Hotline Miami 2 is a phenomenal sequel and a spectacular game in general and I have no regrets in purchasing it.
Overall Score = 8.6/10 (two thumbs up, and a delighted smile)

In simple terms, here's what I would have liked to know about Quiplash before buying the game.
* Quiplash is a party game for 3-8 players where each player is tasked with responding to various questions (usually comedic in nature), with the answers then being pitted against each other and voted on for points.
* The game is divided into three rounds (lasting 5-10 minutes each), with increasing point values for each round.
* You can't play the game with any less than 3 players, all of whom will require a web enabled device (ex. smartphones, tablets, etc) to join a game. You can't play with regular controllers.
* The host is the only one who actually needs to own Quiplash, everybody else just visits
and enters the room code and their player names.
* This game is primarily designed as a local multiplayer experience where the computer running the game is broadcast to all players like an actual game show host, and each player is coming up with funny answers in secret using their phones.
* There are some Twitch integration options for people who'd like to attempt to play with people regardless where they are.
* Quiplash is an easy recommendation. It's fun and easy to play (even grannies can get in on the fun).

TL;DR:  Fast-paced, casual bullet-hell with some fun classes.  Worth the $5 entry fee for a couple afternoons of entertainment.
It's a fantasy-themed bullet hell with random loot, terrain generation and boss fights.  There isn't a great deal of depth and that's to be expected.  Most difficulty stems from the fact that enemies come from all angles and bosses take up a huge portion of the screen.  If that doesn't sound appealing, it probably won't be.
That said, what it does, it does very well.  The gameplay is addictive, fast-paced and very streamlined.
---Best parts:
*Pretty substantial class variety changes your optimal attack range/attack speed and such, making for substantial gameplay changes (for a bullethell)
*Fantastic music
*When loot drops, it shows its relevant stats in red or green---if it's green it's an upgrade, if it's red it's a downgrade.  You simply swap the gear by walking up to it and hitting the hotkey.  There is no loot hording.  This system keeps the fast-pace going.
---Worst parts:
*Boss fights are pretty much just "Here's a giant thing to take up your entire screen, shoot it and dodge the green bits"...while most game boss fights could probably be broken down to something similar, they usually do a better job of hiding it.  I'm not sure how you could do boss fights better in a fantasy bullethell, but they simply weren't fun.
*There isn't really any information on the class you'll unlock until after you unlock it.  Showing that information ahead of time would be great.  --Big caveat, unlocking a new class isn't particularly difficult, so this is a minor issue.

Multifarious avenues of approach vie for attention as potential retorts to Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's indelicate prevarications. The issue here is that I, hardheaded cynic that I am, am not up on the latest gossip. Still, I have heard people say that either Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has no real conception of the sweep of history, or it is merely intent on winning some debating pin by trying to pierce a hole in my logic with “facts” that are taken out of context. Of course, I'm generalizing a little here. But that's only because there's a time to keep silent and a time to speak. There's a time to love and a time to hate. There's a time for war and a time for peace. And, I contend, there's a time to denounce those who claim that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's prolix psychobabble is based upon a firm and vivid grasp of the concrete truths of life itself. Or, to put it less poetically, if you think about it you'll see that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's tyrannous objectives are merely a distraction. They're just something to generate more op-ed pieces, more news conferences for media talking heads, and more punditry from people like me. Meanwhile, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's shills are continuing their quiet work of advancing Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's real goal, which is to deny the obvious.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number reminds me of the thief who cries “Stop, thief!” to distract attention from his thievery. Hence and therefore, I frequently wish to tell it that its grungy insults bring to mind the maxim that despite numerous court decisions condemning metanarratives similar to its, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number continues to infiltrate and then dominate and control the mass media. But being a generally genteel person, however, I always bite my tongue. Once, just once, I'd like to see Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's famuli make Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number answer for its wrongdoings. But until they do that (if they ever do that), we must realize that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number likes to talk about free speech. Lamentably, its model of free speech is not free at all. To Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, free speech is speech that it controls and can use as an ideological weapon to dilute the nation's sense of common purpose and shared sacrifice.
Why does Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number want to violate the basic tenets of journalism and scholarship? Psychologists might suggest that even acknowledging its power-hungry projects is beneath my dignity. Counselors might maintain that thought should precede any attempt at intellectual writing. Sociologists might point out that the world is suffering from its lack of faith in a transcendental truth. I agree with the above assessments, but I am hurt, furious, and embarrassed. Why am I hurt? Because Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has called people like me rapacious, neo-tactless stumblebums, abysmal, querulous goofballs, and unforgiving, pathetic deadbeats so many times that these accusations no longer have any sting. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number honestly continues to employ such insults because it's run out of logical arguments. I suppose an alternate explanation is that by brainwashing its rank-and-file followers with voyeurism, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number makes them easy to lead, easy to program, and easy to enslave. Why am I furious? Because Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is an opportunist. That is, it is an ideological chameleon without any real morality, without a soul. And why am I embarrassed? Because I am not au fait with Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's latest subliminal psywar campaigns. I am, however, quite familiar with the manner in which it has been heating the cauldron of terror until it boils over into our daily lives. In particular, I know that some people apparently believe that if we don't bother it, it won't bother us. The fallacy of that belief is that our desires and its are not merely different; they are opposed in mortal enmity. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number wants to construct the spectre of a terrible armed threat. We, in contrast, want to alert people that if it were to get its hands on the levers of power it'd immediately deflect attention from its unwillingness to support policies that benefit the average citizen. If you don't believe me then consider that we must tell the truth no matter who doesn't like it. That may sound unbelievable, but it's the truth. Another unbelievable but true statement is that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's rodomontades are based on a denial of reality, on the substitution of a deliberately falsified picture of the world in place of reality. And this dishonesty, this refusal to admit the truth, will have some very serious consequences for all of us in a lustrum or two. As a final, parting thought, I assert that we must fight Leninism in all its sleazy forms. This is a long road and not one for the fainthearted, but if pursued with integrity and conviction it could lead to a world in which people are no longer afraid to shatter the illusion that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number knows the “right” way to read Plato, Maimonides, and Machiavelli.
But it was only tree- fiddy.

Heroes and Generals as a free to play game is surprisingly effective at trying to blend a first person shooter with vehicular combat and a strategic RTS. However the game's parts never quite come together into a cohesive package. The phrase jack of all trades master of none is an apt descriptor for this game. However there is fun to be had here. The game is free to play but you may find it difficult to progress without the temptation to spend some money in a cash shop. But bear in mind this game is constantly changing. Many of the impressions below are from my last play session and may not reflect the current state of the game.
From my time with the game I found matches to be heavily unbalanced with the US forces always being outnumbered by German players. This issue is compounded if your 'general' doesn't allocate enough resources to help you out in a given battle. Its important to note that every thing in the game hinges on something else. The general who views a map moves various units. These units determine the number of troops on the ground that are actually fighting the battles. The battles play out in a typical capture the point fashion. Secure one point to help your team advance.
The maps themselves are pretty expansive and to effectively traverse them you can hitch a ride on a bike or a jeep. Some of this can result in some comical situations with two or three guys riding on a bicycle or jeep. Of course you can always hop in a tank or plane too. The vehicles themselves are a bit of a mixed bag. Aircraft feel unwieldy especially coming from a game like WarThunder. However you can jump out of an aircraft to parachute to a new area. The tanks perform pretty well but take some getting used too.
Finally there is the gunplay. It gets the job done but doesn't feel quite as refined as what you might find in a game like RO2/Rising Storm. The weapons have some decent sound effects but everything feels a bit loose. For a free to play game though it has a lot going for it and will surely become better over time with subsequent updates.

Despite this being "Early Access", Scrap Mechanic is already wonderfully functional and remarkably fun.  The sheer joy that comes from finally switching something on and seeing what it does is worth the price of admission.  Even if a machine doesn't do what you expect it to, the results are usually entertaining.  The game also works as a Wile E. Coyote simulator.  (Once there's a Survival mode, you'd still probably want to practice in Creative, just to avoid killing yourself every five minutes until you get the hang of things.)
If you're curious about the game, but concerned about the very early version number, don't be.  Development is proceeding very quickly.  Aside from the welding tool (which I'm very much looking forward to), the build tools are nearly complete and already very robust.  I've gotten about 6-8 hours of game time in so far and have already built a few ground vehicles, a flying platform, a working crane, a transforming, drive-able building, a rocket-assisted Ferris Wheel, and an in-progress reproduction of a Transformer toy.
Scrap Mechanic will probably draw comparisons to MineCraft, but the sense of motion and the physicality of objects sets it apart.  The basic tool and part sets can be used to create most mechanical devices, and the upcoming welding tool will allow for even more.
In short, Scrap Mechanic is amazing!  If you think you want it, you do!

I gave this game an honest shot. I love the concept of this game. I love the style of this game (played a lot of Doom, Wolfenstein, and Nightmare 3D). I loved finding the questions about the Noah's Ark story and testing my knowledge (and being rewarded for getting them right). However...

I got all the way up to 5-3 before I got so sick of it that I uninstalled. The difficulty was challenging in some spots, but insanely cheap in others. Challenging is not the same as cheap.
Everything hits ridiculously hard. It is not uncommon later on to round a corner or open a door and have 30%-50% of your life instantly vanish before you can react. You can bypass this by saving a lot and hoping for the best (enemies are not always staring at you when you encounter them)...except when you run low on ammo. The no-ammo "melee" option is made completely useless by how hard everything hits.
For example, in 5-3, I had used up all the available ammo drops and did not have enough ammo to take out the next room's enemies in either of the remaining paths I had to go through. I died, thinking the reset would help. When you die, however, you are placed at the start of the level with only the most basic "gun" and 8 bullets. The two enemies right on the other side of the door take more than that collectively and hit for insane chunks of health. I could kill them, but would always be left so low on health and ammo that later enemies would easily kill me. So either way, I was sol.
This is where I finally grew so tired of situations like this that I uninstalled. The game just was not fun to me anymore.
If I'm missing something, let me know and I will remove this review. Right now, based on my personal experience, I can't recommend this game.

I finally managed to beat this game the other day. Loved it. A proper "survival horror" title if I've ever seen one (emphasis being on "survival" - walking around with half health, two bullets, and wondering what to do about the three enemies down the hallway lumbering toward you).
It's not so much scary, as it is just plain brutal. It's difficult. Everything can and will kill you. I would compare it to Dark Souls, but that game is more about recognizing and adapting to patterns, then it becomes easy. Not so much in The Evil Within. The game will sometimes punish you for stuff that isn't even your fault, just to say "screw you". There are some situations that will hurt you which there will be no way you could have predicted ahead of time. Sometime's it's outright unfair and I've yelled at my screen on several occasions because of it.
That said, it has some of the best artistic design and creative direction I've ever seen in a horror game... ever. I don't want to spoil too much, but the way the game builds tension and introduces you to enemies and bosses is brilliant sometimes. There are some scenes in the game that are burned into my memory because of how striking and memorable they are.
Also worth noting is that the game isn't very well-optimized. My OC'd i7-4790k and GTX 980 can't quite run it at a steady 60fps. But it was worth bearing through the FPS drops for everything else.

Short Version: A must have for Warhammer Fantasy fans with very satisfying combat. Skaven are much more entertaining enemies than zombies. Just prepare to become FURIOUS with everything else.
Long Version:
Pros
-Glorious graphics. Great lighting and the architecture gets the Warhammer Fantasy art style to the point. Weapon and character models are insanely detailed. Half of my enjoyment of this game is tied to how well the Skaven die. The way their foul black blood sprays on walls and seeps into their fur is an absolute joy. This game is one where you're missing something if you don't play on max settings.
-Gameplay is super fast paced. It is A CLICKFEST. In a way, think of it as a first person Diablo. And more broadly speaking, the gameplay is a copy off of Left 4 Dead's style, only you can't play as the enemy in this game.
-I'm a HUGE Warhammer fan so being able to explore this world via first person is a treat to me. It also softens how frustrated I can be with the game.
Cons
-Game is way too unforgiving when it comes to loot. Measures have been implemented since the game's release to mitigate brain dead itemization but it still isn't enough. Going back to my analogy that this game is like Diablo... in that game, you logged in, killed♥♥♥♥♥♥and got a little reward, your carrot on the stick. Here I log in, fight hard, get killed, and get a cup of♥♥♥♥♥♥as my reward (tiny xp, tokens).
This does not make me want to play again. This makes me want to kill somebody.
-Random groups are terrible. I hate saying this because we've all been the new guy at one point, and maybe it's always been there, but it seems recently the game has become peopled by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You got people lagging behind, not using bombs, dicking around in random rooms... I've had about 5 playthroughs today, I DID NOT PASS A SINGLE ONE. One of them was on EASY because I just wanted to kill something... and we failed on a difficulty you can SOLO WITH BOTS.
Now there's always the possibility I'm the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one, but I doubt it. The terrible nature of the players compounds the loot issue tremendously, which turns this game into a time sink, which is a shame because if I just wanted to kill♥♥♥♥♥♥for the sake of killing♥♥♥♥♥♥I'd just play Doom.
VERDICT: Buy it for a usually good and gory co-op experience, and after the initial glow is gone, get used to the idea of becoming murderously angry over simple things that could be easily fixed.

While being very loyal to its predecessor on a surface, this game calls for a noteiceably different playstyle - HM1 felt more frantic, intuitive, situational, and allowed for a more frequent use of melee weapons. HM2, however, feels more methodical and deliberate(at least until you git gud), favoring firearms, which is necessitated by more open level design, which brings larger levels and lots of windows through which you will be shot repeatedly. Difficulty is definitely up a notch or even two, so if the first game felt too punishing to you, maybe skip this one for the sake of your sanity.
Story is much easier to comprehend despite being more complex, and provides a worthy conclusion. Soundtrack is just beyond awesome and easily beats even HM1's already great score.
Mask system was overhauled too - sometimes player can choose one of 3-4 masks or starting weapons, sometimes he has no choice at all, but when given the choice, it impacts the gameplay in much more profound way, often completely changing tactics and playstyle.
Definitely worth a buy if you enjoyed the first game and it didn't feel too difficult for you.

Total time played on this FREE game has surpassed 90% of my games on Steam put together.  That 90% of games total roughly $700.
At first glance this game appears cheesy, but if you actually learn how to play it you will find a depthy strategic game with a well rounded fighting system and intense action.
The graphics might be getting a bit dated, but the gameplay is something i've seen yet to be matched.
Games such as For Honor, Dark Souls series, Skyrim, etc... are all good games for various reasons, but when it comes down to it the fighting, movement dynamics, and on point timing are all things that matter here.
I've played countless hours on these other games that I paid 60 bucks for and I enjoyed them until this game came along, it kind of showed me that I put my money and time into something that wasn't produced as well as a game entirely free with no option to even buy cosmetics; whoever builds this game does so out of pure joy for gaming.
It's truly sad that games sell for 60 dollars and have the majority believing that this is truly the furthest these types of games have come, I get that many will enjoy other aspects such as conversing with NPCs, finishing quests, sneaking around, pickpocketing, etc... But when it boils down to it, the games are heavily fighting influenced, and that influnce is sadly not integrated as well as a completly free game that generates no money whatsoever.
My overall conclusion is that this game has set a bar for any game of the medival influenced fighting genre for me, the glitchy combat systems of the other games is terrible considering this game was made 5 years ago.  Stop getting ripped off, those games sell for such a high price, this game is free and will provide one of the greatest in-game fighting experiences there is out there.

This is a tentative recommendation, especially given the huge amount of bad press this game got.
PLEASE NOTE: I just need to declare first that I played this after an aparrent patch that fixed a lot of the interface and control grievances people had, I got it in sale (at around 90% off the original price) and that I use a Razer Orbweaver, meaning I could customise my controls further even than that already present in the options.
Basically, this game is not as good as Human Revolution, or even the original Deus Ex. It's also a pretty poor port for the most part, there's a lot of conventions that were obviously intended for its tablet-roots, for example the store being accessible any time from the menu, and likely originally driven by microtransactions, and bodies always fading out (even when unconcious as opposed to dead).
But the story? It picks up from after the novel the Icarus Effect, and, without spoiling too much, deals with the character's reliance on the drug Neuropozene, and essentially ensuring a supply. None of the previous characters from the previous Deus Ex games have needed this, being in some way special, and it adds an interesting new angle to the Deus Ex world.
As for that world, I'd say the it mixes combat and social/story moments as well as the best moments in HR. There's defnitely an emphasis on stealth over combat, as I found fighting moments a lot more clunky than stealth. So do keep that in mind.
So if you're willing to look past its shortcomings, the few bugs and the weird tablet vestiges, The Fall's a fun way to spend a few hours and learn a bit more about the Deus Ex world.

Super MNC provides a fun, free, and interesting game to fans of shooters or ARTS games. Being a sequel to Monday Night Combat, this free to play third person ARTS game adds more influence from Dota along with evolution in style and feel. Each character, or pro, plays similarly to some others but have unique weapons and abilities to them. The art style is eclectic, ranging from the outdoors or urban environments of each arena to the differing styles of each pro. Like MNC, gameplay is a mix between TF2 and Dota, with more Dota style to the game. However, a new mode brings back the faster pace from the original MNC. In vein to games like LoL and Dota 2, weekly updates change pro rotation and add new features while a store offers cosmetics or pros for a fairly high price. SMNC is a unique kind of free to play multiplayer open to all the masses with strong developer support.

There is a stage where I just can't get past because, well, I’m genuinely scared and couldn't stop looking behind my chair to see if there's something or someone there. Not many games ever make me feel this scared, and when the jump scares come, every part of your body is stimulated and a shock is induced through your core that leaves you f**ked up.
Atmospheric, enjoyable, horrifying, tense and genuinely intelligent this game pieces together emotions and recreates classic works of art and mixes generically clever horror to craft an entirely new perspective… one we may never have thought the artists or ourselves might’ve had.
