The only game simulating captain and crew aboard a large starship. Not perfect but the best out there atm.
Reasonably immersive in star trek lore with the sights and sounds your familiar with.
A lot of depth with ship and crew options and combinations, including costume, skills, professions, devices, weapons, armor, I was surprised.
A decent story driven campaign that will take you from logging in to cap pretty much on all three factions. Altho parts are repeated for each faction.
Voiced npcs on some featured missions, its pretty good and immersive.
Nice customisable ui.
Variable difficulty levels.
Nice space battles. Can be a little over the top with effects at times in large player battles.
Boarding a borg cube. (sorry my inner trekkie appeared lol).
Cons:
Instanced, altho this has improved since the game launched and unbelievable as it is for me to say this but it fits in with parts of the game (teleporting, transwarp etc they get a partial ok on this one.
Some very annoying bugs with the ui that have been around since the launch, like losing the saved or setup quickbars every time you change ship, sometimes when you zone etc.
(Fixed Apr 2014 in season 9, now you can save loadouts)
Federation biased with some love needed for the klingon side still. Altho improvements have been made since launch.
Ground combat is... quirky. Needs some improvement. Great potential tho.
The star map is poorly done imo. I was very disappointed with it at launch considering you spend a lot of time looking at it while playing.
Limited ways of exploring your bridge and ship. Better than nothing. Not intuitive. You have to beam onto and off your bridge/ship via a menu pulldown hidden aaway under the radar.
Grindy at cap.
Ui is a little fiddly at times to find what you want initially.
PVP requires a lot of knowledge and grind to compete. Gear based.
The switch to f2p reduced the capacity to acquire the more desirable ships with an awful lottery box system with about as much chance of getting a decent ship as playing the lottery. YMMV if you have money to burn or a lot of time to grind. I dont.
Overall:
Its a game I enjoy playing for the story based pve. At launch it was the other way around PVP all the way.
I would suggest playing the campaigns to cap and then logging in periodicallly for the new content releases (seasons). Or logging in periodically to restart the reputation missions for your duty officers (a kind of long term crafting reputation grind with periodic rewards which can be very good).
Its a game that has outlasted guild wars 2, the new darkfall, star wars and more for me personally. Being free to play helps a lot in that regard.

Vermintide
Short Version: A must have for Warhammer Fantasy fans with very satisfying combat. Skaven are much more entertaining enemies than zombies. Just prepare to become FURIOUS with everything else.
Long Version:
Pros
-Glorious graphics. Great lighting and the architecture gets the Warhammer Fantasy art style to the point. Weapon and character models are insanely detailed. Half of my enjoyment of this game is tied to how well the Skaven die. The way their foul black blood sprays on walls and seeps into their fur is an absolute joy. This game is one where you're missing something if you don't play on max settings.
-Gameplay is super fast paced. It is A CLICKFEST. In a way, think of it as a first person Diablo. And more broadly speaking, the gameplay is a copy off of Left 4 Dead's style, only you can't play as the enemy in this game.
-I'm a HUGE Warhammer fan so being able to explore this world via first person is a treat to me. It also softens how frustrated I can be with the game.
Cons
-Game is way too unforgiving when it comes to loot. Measures have been implemented since the game's release to mitigate brain dead itemization but it still isn't enough. Going back to my analogy that this game is like Diablo... in that game, you logged in, killed♥♥♥♥♥♥and got a little reward, your carrot on the stick. Here I log in, fight hard, get killed, and get a cup of♥♥♥♥♥♥as my reward (tiny xp, tokens).
This does not make me want to play again. This makes me want to kill somebody.
-Random groups are terrible. I hate saying this because we've all been the new guy at one point, and maybe it's always been there, but it seems recently the game has become peopled by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You got people lagging behind, not using bombs, dicking around in random rooms... I've had about 5 playthroughs today, I DID NOT PASS A SINGLE ONE. One of them was on EASY because I just wanted to kill something... and we failed on a difficulty you can SOLO WITH BOTS.
Now there's always the possibility I'm the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one, but I doubt it. The terrible nature of the players compounds the loot issue tremendously, which turns this game into a time sink, which is a shame because if I just wanted to kill♥♥♥♥♥♥for the sake of killing♥♥♥♥♥♥I'd just play Doom.
VERDICT: Buy it for a usually good and gory co-op experience, and after the initial glow is gone, get used to the idea of becoming murderously angry over simple things that could be easily fixed.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a four player cooperative action game that takes the player to the fantasy realm of Warhammer during their version of the apocalypse, and the first stage, the Skaven rat hordes.
Pros
-Beautiful graphics
-Rich story
-True to source material
-Very fun cooperative play
-Variety of game play, offers challenging levels
-Grimoire collectable system adds difficulty and reward
-Character play/ build options
-Balanced, varied characters
-Great developer support, helpful
-DLC handled very well
Cons
-Loot system (better but still eh)
-Player forced to farm few same levels to progress their equipment (Fatshark has addressed this)
-Declining player base
Graphics = 10/10
The graphics are great and current with generation. The visuals and imagery are absolutely amazing, the developers really treat it as a passion and add vast amounts of detail into the level designs.
Music = 7/10
The music is done well and appropriate to the setting, however the tavern music can get old fast while waiting for a lobby. During suspenseful moments in a level the music really adds to the atmosphere.
Cinematics = 7/10
There are not a whole lot of cinematics found in the game, the few that are present are gorgeous graphics and add to the overall experience of the game.
Story 10/10
The story of Vermintide is really where it flourishes. While progressing through the levels as they are made available, you follow the story of your band of rag-tag heroes fighting off the Skaven hordes in the town of Ubersreik during the early days of the End Times. What really makes the story so amazing in this game is the lore from the Warhammer franchise and how well developers, Fatshark, has done in utilising the source material.
Content 8/10
There is tons of content to keep you replaying, a good variety of levels and level types, as well as loot/ equipment progression (however frustrating the loot system can be). Fatshark has also struck gold in how to handle DLC, there have been a share of free updates and content, and a couple paid DLC. The paid DLC offers a good amount of content for the price, but what really makes it unique is the fact that if you own the DLC, anyone who joins your game can benefit and play the content and vice versa.
Controls 9/10
The controls are easily learned, and complicated to master, in a good way. The controls are fluent and easy to jump into the game with, as well as the further you progress in game difficulty the more you are required to use advanced controls and tactics.
Gameplay 8/10
Character selection offers plenty of variety from character to character, as well as weapon selection offers varied play styles within each character. Each level has its own goals to meet to progress and finish, with some repeated mechanics, but enough uniqueness to set each level apart. Added in an update was the Last Stand mode which offered a round based survival game mode which brought its own large amount of gameplay.
Overall 8.5/10
Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide can be paralleled in playstyle to Left 4 Dead with its four player coop mission based survival gameplay. However Vermintide goes the distance in setting itself away from Left 4 Dead and other games in the genre with its excellent story, content, character options, and fluent melee combat. I couldn't recommend this game more to fans of either the coop action/ survival genre, fans of the Warhammer universe, or even fans of lore rich dark fantasy.
*Not all DLC has been played at time of review.

I really feel like this game was misunderstood.
It's very, very hard- not in a way that rewards patience or planning; it's just brutal and often feels unfair (especially on Nightmare and Akumu difficulty, which are designed to screw you). The collectibles are almost impossible to find without a guide. Checkpoints feel needlessly far apart. It's full of hidden traps and one-hit-kill monsters. The bosses never seem to die. Contextual actions are clunky. Everything hates you.
Despite all that (or perhaps because of it), I really enjoyed this game. I haven't played anything quite like it since RE4. It's refreshing to have a game that forces you to think fast and be intuitive, constantly adapting to different types of combat situations. And the combat is great- it's intense and gritty, giving you lots of options but never letting you feel completely in control. The detail in the environments is also worth noting- locations have a 'hand-crafted' sort of quality, and each level is genuinely a completely new setting. I do really like what Tango did with the idTech5 engine, despite the technical issues at launch. Speaking of which, it still has some performance issues (don't expect a solid 60 fps through the whole game unless you have some extremely powerful hrdware), but patches have improved things considerably since launch.
So, I recommend this game because I loved it; it gave me exactly the kind of hardcore horror experience I wanted. However, I can understand why a lot of people hate it. The game really isn't for everyone, and I think it's been unfairly treated just because it's really quite a niche sort of experience. If the above sounds appealing to you, give The Evil Within a go. It is absolutely worth your time and money.

Multifarious avenues of approach vie for attention as potential retorts to Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's indelicate prevarications. The issue here is that I, hardheaded cynic that I am, am not up on the latest gossip. Still, I have heard people say that either Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has no real conception of the sweep of history, or it is merely intent on winning some debating pin by trying to pierce a hole in my logic with “facts” that are taken out of context. Of course, I'm generalizing a little here. But that's only because there's a time to keep silent and a time to speak. There's a time to love and a time to hate. There's a time for war and a time for peace. And, I contend, there's a time to denounce those who claim that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's prolix psychobabble is based upon a firm and vivid grasp of the concrete truths of life itself. Or, to put it less poetically, if you think about it you'll see that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's tyrannous objectives are merely a distraction. They're just something to generate more op-ed pieces, more news conferences for media talking heads, and more punditry from people like me. Meanwhile, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's shills are continuing their quiet work of advancing Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's real goal, which is to deny the obvious.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number reminds me of the thief who cries “Stop, thief!” to distract attention from his thievery. Hence and therefore, I frequently wish to tell it that its grungy insults bring to mind the maxim that despite numerous court decisions condemning metanarratives similar to its, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number continues to infiltrate and then dominate and control the mass media. But being a generally genteel person, however, I always bite my tongue. Once, just once, I'd like to see Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's famuli make Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number answer for its wrongdoings. But until they do that (if they ever do that), we must realize that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number likes to talk about free speech. Lamentably, its model of free speech is not free at all. To Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number, free speech is speech that it controls and can use as an ideological weapon to dilute the nation's sense of common purpose and shared sacrifice.
Why does Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number want to violate the basic tenets of journalism and scholarship? Psychologists might suggest that even acknowledging its power-hungry projects is beneath my dignity. Counselors might maintain that thought should precede any attempt at intellectual writing. Sociologists might point out that the world is suffering from its lack of faith in a transcendental truth. I agree with the above assessments, but I am hurt, furious, and embarrassed. Why am I hurt? Because Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number has called people like me rapacious, neo-tactless stumblebums, abysmal, querulous goofballs, and unforgiving, pathetic deadbeats so many times that these accusations no longer have any sting. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number honestly continues to employ such insults because it's run out of logical arguments. I suppose an alternate explanation is that by brainwashing its rank-and-file followers with voyeurism, Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number makes them easy to lead, easy to program, and easy to enslave. Why am I furious? Because Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is an opportunist. That is, it is an ideological chameleon without any real morality, without a soul. And why am I embarrassed? Because I am not au fait with Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's latest subliminal psywar campaigns. I am, however, quite familiar with the manner in which it has been heating the cauldron of terror until it boils over into our daily lives. In particular, I know that some people apparently believe that if we don't bother it, it won't bother us. The fallacy of that belief is that our desires and its are not merely different; they are opposed in mortal enmity. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number wants to construct the spectre of a terrible armed threat. We, in contrast, want to alert people that if it were to get its hands on the levers of power it'd immediately deflect attention from its unwillingness to support policies that benefit the average citizen. If you don't believe me then consider that we must tell the truth no matter who doesn't like it. That may sound unbelievable, but it's the truth. Another unbelievable but true statement is that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number's rodomontades are based on a denial of reality, on the substitution of a deliberately falsified picture of the world in place of reality. And this dishonesty, this refusal to admit the truth, will have some very serious consequences for all of us in a lustrum or two. As a final, parting thought, I assert that we must fight Leninism in all its sleazy forms. This is a long road and not one for the fainthearted, but if pursued with integrity and conviction it could lead to a world in which people are no longer afraid to shatter the illusion that Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number knows the “right” way to read Plato, Maimonides, and Machiavelli.

While being very loyal to its predecessor on a surface, this game calls for a noteiceably different playstyle - HM1 felt more frantic, intuitive, situational, and allowed for a more frequent use of melee weapons. HM2, however, feels more methodical and deliberate(at least until you git gud), favoring firearms, which is necessitated by more open level design, which brings larger levels and lots of windows through which you will be shot repeatedly. Difficulty is definitely up a notch or even two, so if the first game felt too punishing to you, maybe skip this one for the sake of your sanity.
Story is much easier to comprehend despite being more complex, and provides a worthy conclusion. Soundtrack is just beyond awesome and easily beats even HM1's already great score.
Mask system was overhauled too - sometimes player can choose one of 3-4 masks or starting weapons, sometimes he has no choice at all, but when given the choice, it impacts the gameplay in much more profound way, often completely changing tactics and playstyle.
Definitely worth a buy if you enjoyed the first game and it didn't feel too difficult for you.

TL;DR:  Fast-paced, casual bullet-hell with some fun classes.  Worth the $5 entry fee for a couple afternoons of entertainment.
It's a fantasy-themed bullet hell with random loot, terrain generation and boss fights.  There isn't a great deal of depth and that's to be expected.  Most difficulty stems from the fact that enemies come from all angles and bosses take up a huge portion of the screen.  If that doesn't sound appealing, it probably won't be.
That said, what it does, it does very well.  The gameplay is addictive, fast-paced and very streamlined.
---Best parts:
*Pretty substantial class variety changes your optimal attack range/attack speed and such, making for substantial gameplay changes (for a bullethell)
*Fantastic music
*When loot drops, it shows its relevant stats in red or green---if it's green it's an upgrade, if it's red it's a downgrade.  You simply swap the gear by walking up to it and hitting the hotkey.  There is no loot hording.  This system keeps the fast-pace going.
---Worst parts:
*Boss fights are pretty much just "Here's a giant thing to take up your entire screen, shoot it and dodge the green bits"...while most game boss fights could probably be broken down to something similar, they usually do a better job of hiding it.  I'm not sure how you could do boss fights better in a fantasy bullethell, but they simply weren't fun.
*There isn't really any information on the class you'll unlock until after you unlock it.  Showing that information ahead of time would be great.  --Big caveat, unlocking a new class isn't particularly difficult, so this is a minor issue.

Let me start by saying that this isnt a fully fledged Deus Ex game, the design solely considered use on tablets and phones. Why bother coding advanced features (as seen in HR) when iOS devices of 2013 cant run them? This port is just to expand the audience slightly. Its not the greatest port as there are still some slight control issues and not being able to jump feels wierd but given its orignal design intentions there is nothing too obtrusive, think of it as Deus Ex: Lite.
The art style is the same as HR but the graphics quality is rather poor. The world certainly has the same feel as HR but its not nearly as detailed. Combat is a wee bit clunky too. The story is standard Deus Ex affair (meaning good), it focuses on the aug mercenaries that made up the boss fights in HR. Its not a perfect story though as I sometimes felt the characters had no motive to do what they were doing and the game is actually only the first part of an episodic series (no word on future installments though). Voice acting and music is very much up to par (minus the robot woman in the tutorial.) .
Ultimately what Im saying is that you shouldnt be expecting a game of the same standards as HR. Its Deus Ex: Lite and that is also reflected in the price. I got it on sale and I dont regret it.

First off, I have to say that I like deus ex. I bought the original deus ex in a bargain store in 2003 or 2004, I first thought to myself: dis sux. Later I enjoyed it before it got ported to steam or whatever because it is a thinking man's shooter. You get to use your augmentations and your writable notepad (really, you could press I think an f key and it would pop up a functional wordpad to write down all the codes and what they said to put together what the hell was going on). Then Hummus Revolution came out and I found that to be a good modern interpretation of the original, pretty damn good. I think the first time I played through was like 15 hours which was pretty short but that's better than what we get these days.
Then The Fall...
Oh gawd, non.
I don't know if this game's title was supposed to be foreshadowing but this is like invisible war which was mediocre at best, but now it makes you sad in the light of your computer, all alone, expecting to stay up all night long to play this mobile version.
First, let's get the engine out of the way: Hummus Revolution was a reworked Crystal Dynamics Engine that was used in Tomb Raider: Underworld. This one uses unity probably because it is better built for the mobile market, and probably this was a low budget so they didn't want to waste a lot of money. But without splitting any hairs, this looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥ I swear this looks like 2005 quality. This may seem unfair because it was a moblie game at first, but you have the name Deus Ex on the box. After coming off Human Revolution, the shock was jarring. I was playing a beautiful well lighted game to OH GAWD.
I was expecting the porting people to try to rework the UI to be more faithful to Human Revolution because it was a Unity game which is a very flexible engine, but no. There is no multiple saves like in any other good PC game, there isn't a smooth UI. Hell, not even the mouse works properly. It won't detect blatant clicks I started to click furiously and I might have cut the like of the damn thing in half. The difficulty of inventory management (which is a good thing, mind you) was cut completely, going for a teleport my rocket launcher from nowhere into my hands, kaboom. Going around people is the suggested idea in Deus Ex, not anymore. You can get a stun gun, and then stun your enemies, pick up the credits and keep buying the ammo and you won't run out of cash money. Hell, you can't even jump in this game, really. It is a port from iOS and it shows. The stealth detection is wonky, half the the time they will ignore you, the other time they are a god damn eagle. At least the level design is okay for the most part.
People are probably going to ask me why I am so focused on Human than the ones before. That's because it has the same art style, the same year as Human Revo. (instead of the 25 year difference between the first two), and the same weapon designs and praxis system.
You might say that I haven't played enough to make an objective opinion. Well that's because the game has only one section, Panama City, and it's shorter than the shortest part of Hummus Revolution: part 2 of Hengsha. Half of that time is me going idle or killing random people and resetting the save. I feel awful for those that bought this at full price, because that is barely any content. What I hate about that is when you click on "More Content" it says "MOAR TO COME!". We know that is unlikely, don't lie you French ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Even if they did, it's irrelevant because I know how this ends because I'm the Batman.

A great game if you are a fan of the TV series alone, or the books as well. Taking place years after the events of Star Trek : Voyager, players get to encounter beloved characters from their favorite Star Trek show (Niomy Wildman, Ambassador Worf, and many more).
Quests take the form of Episodes that are written in the same style as the tv shows. You can group up with other players but you can easily progress without having to group. Further more level progression happens during the course of episodes, thus eliminating the need to grind.
Yes, there is content that requires money to buy but it does not give you more of an edge than the free content does. When it comes to starships it is more about your style of combat. Do you like a speed over raw fire power or do you like the fire power of slow capital ships. As far as the ships you can buy with cash, it boils down to do you want a classic D7 Klingon Battle Cruiser or are you happy with the Vortcha Battle Cruiser (in short mostly cosmetic stuff).
Oh and who can resist the urge to play as a member of the Klingon Empire or a Romulan, thus exploring these two cultures more deeply than the shows ever did.
In short on a scale from 1 to 10, this game rates a solid 10.

A very solid MMORPG, Star Trek Online allows you to create your own Starfleet (or Klingon (or Romulan)) officer using incredibly deep customization options, but what sets this free MMO apart from the others is the use of starships; around half the game is spent in your own custom space vessel, with further vessels to unlock as the game progresses (or to buy with real money). This helps add a sense of individuality to the game, and adds incentive to roll new characters with different classes.
Surprisingly, Star Trek Online rarely puts any content behind a paywall, besides more costumes or special ships, allowing free players to reach the level cap without having their experience points restricted, and without being pestered by the game to subscribe.
However, the game can become lonely if played by yourself, so it is best to play with some friends who have a mutual interest in the Star Trek brand.
TL;DR: A good MMO with solid visuals, and a must-play for Star Trek fans. It's also free, so if you're looking for a free MMO to play with friends, Star Trek Online is definitely worth a look.

Star Trek Online is a very decent MMO that does a fair job at capturing the expansive Star Trek Universe. You will encounter a plethora of memorable personalities on your journeys throughout the game while exploring both the famous and uncharted systems across the galaxy.
At the time of this review you can currently play as a Star Fleet Officer, a Citizen of the new Romulan Republic, or a Warrior of the Klingon Empire. There are three career paths that you can chose - Tactical, Science, or Engineering - which determine what skills you have access to as well as what kind of ship you will command.
STO is one of my top 3 best MMOs and is the second best MMO for Free to Play Players as there are literally no content restrictions unlike games such as Star Wars: The Old Republic (End Game content + Expansion Pack) or The Lord of the Rings Online (all content beyond The Lone Lands (level 30ish) requires individual purchase or subscription). You can easily reach max level (50) and beyond without subscribing. That being said there are the common account restrictions for F2P players, such as a currency cap, limited character slots (3), no account bank, and limited character bank storage space.
If you do decide to play STO here are a few tips:
* Levels 1-49 are essentially a giant tutorial that helps familiarize you with the mechanics of the game.
* At level 50 the game content changes from Single Player to Group as you take part in STFs (Special Task Force) missions and their Elite counterparts where you fight extremely tough enemies such as the Borg and Tholians for reputation items.
* At End Game, Lock Box and Cryptic Store Ships are vastly superior to anything else. If you are serious about playing the game throughout the End Content you should consider purchasing one as well as a subscription.
